all-s-well-that-ends-well-pg2246: Helena's daring drives this edition: she cures the King, claims Bertram, and wins him through the bed-trick and the impossible tasks. "All's well that ends well" is tested by a heroine who refuses to lose. The problem comedy at its most provocative.
an-exposition-of-dr-cobb-s-art-of-discov: An Exposition of Dr. Cobb's Art, 1846. The Cobb art. This book preserves that work. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
arxiv-2510-00046:
Zou exposes a security hole in the commercial prompt-trading market, where creators sell carefully curated text-to-image prompts that carry trademark styles. By showing those prompt templates can be stolen from just a few public sample images. His RLStealer frames template stealing as a sequential decision problem and trains a reinforcement learning agent. Using several similarity-based feedback signals as rewards, to search the full prompt space efficiently in this study.

Solved with the PPO algorithm, the attack reaches reported state-of-the-art stealing performance while cutting total attack cost to under 13 percent of what existing baselines need. And it also generalizes across image styles to unseen templates and subjects. An ablation against random search confirms the gains come from guided policy learning, and Zou urges the community to build defenses and protective standards for prompt marketplaces in the future.
arxiv-2510-00446:
Yuling Shi and four colleagues published this 2025 paper on LongCodeZip, a tool that shrinks the code fed to language models. Repository-scale tasks force models to read enormous code contexts, which costs money and time. General text compressors ignore how code is structured, so they cut the wrong pieces. LongCodeZip compresses in two stages built around that structure.

First it ranks whole functions by how relevant they look to the instruction, using conditional perplexity. Only the top functions survive to the second stage. There, each function splits into blocks, and a budgeted subset is chosen to maximize relevance. Across completion, summarization, and question answering tasks, the tool beat baseline compressors. It reached compression ratios up to about five and a half times with no loss in task performance. The framework needs no training and works across different code models.
arxiv-2510-00946:
Andleeb, Kantorski, and Carver study what ChatGPT does to first-year programmers in this 2025 paper for the ACM SIGCITE conference. Introductory students now routinely ask chatbots for code, debugging, and explanations, which could build skill or quietly replace it. The authors ran a counterbalanced quasi-experiment in a CS1 course: students alternated between ChatGPT and no-ChatGPT conditions across two C programming assignments, one on functions and one on structures. Rubrics graded the code, and post-surveys probed concepts and perceptions.

With ChatGPT, students produced significantly higher code quality scores and finished faster than without it. Conceptual gains were uneven: lower for the functions topic, higher for structures. Students liked the tool for debugging and practice, while worrying about its accuracy and their long-term skill growth. The authors recommend structured integration and complementary teaching strategies so the efficiency gains do not crowd out independent problem solving.
arxiv-2510-01146:
Anugraha and five co-authors release mR3 in this 2025 arXiv paper, a multilingual reward model that judges language model outputs by rubric. Reward models grade candidate answers during training and evaluation, but strong judges exist almost only for English. Building one for many languages is hard, since human judgements are costly and evaluation habits differ across datasets. The team trained their model on material spanning seventy-two languages, the broadest coverage reported for reward modelling.

Their study compares data sources and curriculum choices systematically, including reasoning traces written in the target language. The resulting model beat existing reward models on multilingual benchmarks, including systems up to nine times larger such as GPT-OSS-120B. Ablations showed English still works best as the reasoning language, while targeted multilingual training made target-language inputs far more robust. Models, data, and code are open source.
arxiv-2510-01446:
Milyushkov tests whether machine learning prices options better than the classic formulas that finance has trusted for decades. Black-Scholes and Heston assume tidy markets, while real prices bend with frictions and shifting volatility. Neural networks, random forests, and a boosting method enter the contest.

Synthetic data with controlled distortions came first, then real market options. The learning models captured nonlinear price patterns the formulas missed. In several settings they beat both traditional benchmarks outright. Feedforward networks and the boosting method looked strongest in the three-stage comparison. Closed-form elegance loses to learned flexibility on messy markets. Hedging and arbitrage both depend on prices being right. Linear and nonlinear distortions stress the models in stages. Constant volatility is the assumption reality violates daily. Data-driven pricing reflects market dynamics the equations idealize away. The title's question gets a qualified yes.
arxiv-2510-01546:
Wang and co-authors give language-vision models the ability to generate images without giving up what they already understand. Unified models often trade away either meaning or fine detail, and hybrid designs break the clean next-token pattern. Their model, Bridge, grows generation onto a pre-trained understanding model through a mixture-of-transformers design.

A two-layer visual code carries compact meaning tokens alongside fine pixel tokens. Understanding scores stayed intact while generation quality climbed toward specialist tools. One prediction stream now handles reading images and producing them. The approach offers a practical upgrade path for the many strong understanding models already deployed. Pure autoregressive design keeps training and serving simple compared with bolted-on diffusion parts. Semantic tokens keep generated scenes faithful to the prompt's meaning. Pixel tokens then restore texture and small detail. Both token kinds share one vocabulary with the text stream.
arxiv-2510-01846:
Provenzano and Ferraresso study how electromagnetic vibration frequencies behave on very thin domains in this 2025 mathematics paper. Their domains are thin tubes built around surfaces inside three-dimensional space. As the tube thickness shrinks toward zero, they track Maxwell's eigenvalues for the full field problem. The question is whether those values settle into a simpler limit.

They prove the Maxwell eigenvalues converge to the Laplacian eigenvalues of the underlying surface. The proof recasts the problem through the Hodge Laplacian acting on differential forms with relative boundary conditions. That limit has sharp side effects for spectral geometry. It yields new domains where the Faber-Krahn inequality fails for Maxwell's eigenvalues. It also produces domains with any chosen number of arbitrarily small eigenvalues. The authors further construct Maxwell eigenfunctions explicitly on product domains, extending older Euclidean constructions.
arxiv-2510-01946:
Master and Moeller recast colored Petri nets as functors in this 2025 category theory paper. Petri nets model systems of processes and resources as places, transitions, and tokens. Colored nets attach extra data to those pieces, which tames repetitive structure in complex systems. Their classical definition, though, hides how the color data acts like a semantic interpretation.

The authors show each colored Petri net is exactly a monoidal double functor from a syntactic category into spans of commutative monoids. That framing yields canonical definitions for standard constructions on colored nets. Morphisms between colored nets become natural transformations between the functors. The unfolding construction, which expands colors away, is characterized through free symmetric monoidal categories. A displayed-category result equates lax double functors with ordinary functors into a reworked domain. The payoff is a compositional foundation for colored nets inside applied category theory. Open nets with boundaries are the conjectured next step.
arxiv-2510-02146:
Požar and five co-authors simulate water-amine mixtures to explain a puzzling X-ray signal in this 2025 chemistry paper. Water-rich amine mixtures show a prominent scattering pre-peak, while pure amines barely show one and water-rich alcohols show none. Atom-level simulations were needed to see what the molecules actually arrange into.

The pair correlation functions revealed micro-segregation rather than uniform mixing. Amine head groups coat the surfaces of water domains, and longer tails stabilize that coating better. The amine regions form disordered bilayers, like an inverse micelle melt or a precursor micro-emulsion. This stable micro-segregation creates the long-range oscillations behind the pre-peak, plus destructive anti-peaks. Only when water dominates and amines grow scarce does the coating fail and demixing threaten. The microscopic picture resolves the scattering paradox completely.
arxiv-2510-02246:
Hosseinabadi and co-authors build a minimal model for atoms held inside optical cavities. Their 2025 physics paper joins two kinds of interaction in one system. Cavity light links atoms across long distances. Excited Rydberg atoms, by contrast, block their near neighbors from firing. That blockade creates strong short-range rules. The team calls the combined setup the squared PXP model. They study it in one dimension under a strong blockade.

At rest, the model shows plain magnetic phases and an ordered Neel phase. Away from rest, special states called quantum scars appear. Scar states keep memory of their start far longer than normal states. Long-range links reshape those scars in new ways. The model gives experiment teams a clean test bed. It also helps theorists compare short-range and long-range forces inside one system.
arxiv-2510-02946:
Lieskovský and co-authors build the simplest possible swinging robot. Brachiation is how gibbons swing hand over hand between branches. Most robots copy it with many linked arms. This one is a single rigid rod. A gripper at each end grabs a horizontal bar. A crank-slide unit shifts the rod's center of mass. That shifting pumps the swing, much like a child on a playground swing.

Two control strategies drive the mass shifting. A bang-bang plan gives the best swing growth in theory. It demands more force than the small motor can give. A second, continuous plan respects the torque limit and the mechanism's shape. It rests on a method that flattens the nonlinear dynamics. Both plans were checked in simulation first. The continuous plan then ran on cheap STM32 hardware. Real tests confirmed both the swing and full rotation stages.
arxiv-2510-03146:
Alvarado-Gómez and co-authors chart the magnetic cycle of a young Sun-like star. The star, iota Horologii, is active and spins fast. HARPSpol watched it for nearly three years of campaigns. Zeeman-Doppler imaging rebuilt its surface field eighteen times. Those maps span about one hundred thirty-nine rotations. The team tracked poloidal and toroidal parts separately.

Toroidal strength pulsed in step with chromospheric activity. For the first time, stellar butterfly diagrams were reconstructed. They trace how magnetic features migrate across the surface. A polarity reversal takes roughly one hundred rotations there. Field-weighted latitudes gave the first drift speeds beyond the Sun. Some features drift poleward while others slide equatorward. Unlike the Sun, axisymmetry rose near activity maxima here. The toroidal-to-poloidal energy ratio followed activity most cleanly. Young dynamos may thus run on a different balance than ours.
arxiv-2510-03246:
Song, Bai, and Zhao make global structured pruning of giant language models fit on ordinary hardware. Pruning trims models, but global methods need memory for everything at once. Local pruning fits one layer yet ignores how layers interact. Structured patterns suit real GPU kernels, unlike scattered zeros. Those patterns suffer most under purely local decisions, though. Their STRUPRUNE framework splits the global problem across modules. An ADMM optimizer coordinates the pieces toward one solution.

A closed-form rule allocates sparsity layer by layer. An energy-based scheme softens that rule into a softmax form. Heterogeneous layer importance shapes the allocation automatically. Memory demand falls from linear to square-root scaling in model size. Billion-parameter pruning becomes practical on limited cards. Experiments on OPT models confirmed the savings. Perplexity stayed close to full global structured pruning. Hardware-friendly masks add real speed at inference time.
arxiv-2510-03346:
Shi, Chiesa, Maguire, and Kostic present a 2025 arXiv paper on how language models in a team can talk to each other more cheaply. Teams of models now tackle hard jobs together, but chat in plain words is slow and lossy. Sharing raw hidden states has its own flaws, including bias and bulk. The authors propose KVComm, which shares selected key and value pairs, the memory traces models keep while reading text.

A scoring rule picks the most informative layers to send, guided by attention strength. In tests across many tasks and model pairs, KVComm matched the score of a no communication upper bound. It did so while sending as few as thirty percent of the layers' pairs in some setups. Communication cost fell by up to three times in the reported runs. Leaner model teamwork could cut the price of agent systems that must reason together at scale.
arxiv-2510-03846:
Howell and Aravkin wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on estimating hidden states of a moving system from noisy measurements. This task, called smoothing, matters for tracking and navigation. Two families of methods compete: unscented Kalman smoothers, which push sample points through the system, and optimization-based smoothers. The authors compare the two families across standard settings.

They show that the classic extended Kalman smoother can be read as an optimization method, which makes fair comparison possible. In their tests, the optimized smoother matched the unscented one when noise was low. It pulled clearly ahead for strongly nonlinear systems and higher noise levels. Extra computing could also improve the optimized result, with no clear way to do the same for the unscented method. The study gives clear guidance on which smoother to pick.
arxiv-2510-04046:
Nishimura, Sakumura, and Ikeda present this 2025 arXiv paper on classifying data where one class vastly outnumbers the other. Imbalance plagues tasks like medical diagnosis and fraud detection, where the rare class is the one that matters. Classifiers trained on such data favor the majority and miss the minority, and standard remedies fail when imbalance is extreme. The authors adapt kernel density estimation so the decision boundary responds to local crowding.

Their method, KOTARO, tunes the width of each Gaussian kernel by the density around its sample. In dense majority regions the kernels shrink, stopping the majority territory from bleeding outward over minority ground. In sparse regions the boundary stays generous, recognizing minority areas that rival methods erase. Experiments on synthetic and real imbalanced datasets showed KOTARO beating conventional approaches. Its advantage was largest under severe imbalance, exactly where help is most needed.
arxiv-2510-04146:
Kim and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper comparing the raw performance of diffusion and autoregressive language models. Autoregressive models generate one token at a time, which keeps arithmetic intensity low and hardware underused. Diffusion language models generate text in parallel, better hardware efficiency. Whether that promise survives long contexts and batched serving was unclear.

Combining theory with profiling, the authors find diffusion models do achieve higher arithmetic intensity across the sequence. Plain diffusion decoding, however, scales poorly as context grows. Block-wise decoding fixes that weakness, keeping the intensity while matching autoregressive scaling to long contexts. Batching flips the verdict: autoregressive models gain more across sequences and win on throughput. Open-source diffusion models could beat autoregressive latency mainly by needing fewer steps. The study gives systems builders a grounded map of when each paradigm pays off.
arxiv-2510-04646:
Johanna Sommer and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on speeding up molecule generation with flow matching models. Such models draw high quality three dimensional molecule shapes, but each shape costs hundreds of network passes. Sampling a million drug candidates at that price is out of reach. The team caches hidden features inside the network and predicts them ahead across solver steps. No retraining of the base model is needed.

The cache works directly on the symmetry aware backbone that these models use. It also stacks with other speedups instead of competing with them. On a standard drug like molecule data set, caching halved the generation time at equal sample quality. Pushed harder, it reached a threefold speedup with only slight quality loss. Combined with other lossless tricks, the total speedup rose to about sevenfold. The method is training free, so any lab can bolt it onto a released model.
arxiv-2510-04746:
Eze, Handler, Kahraman Aliçavuş, Pawar, and Miszuda wrote this 2025 astronomy paper on measuring massive stars that orbit each other. Massive stars show a stubborn puzzle: masses from spectra disagree with masses from evolution models. The likely cause is that models understate the size of the churning core. Eclipsing pairs offer a rare check, since their geometry reveals true sizes and masses. The team adds starquake data, which probes the deep interior directly.

They observed their sample from space with the TESS telescope between 2021 and 2024. Ground spectrographs in South Africa, Chile, Europe, and Slovakia added radial velocity data. Fits yielded the orbital shapes and the absolute sizes, masses, and temperatures of the stars. Seismic analysis then exposed how their cores move and mix. The paper presents itself as groundwork for later theoretical modeling. Precise numbers for these stars will test whether bigger cores fix the mass mismatch.
arxiv-2510-04846:
Aprile and the XENON Collaboration wrote this 2025 physics paper measuring a rare nuclear decay spectrum with a dark matter detector. The XENONnT experiment hunts dark matter underground with a tank of liquid xenon. The same tank records other rare events, including decays of bismuth 214. This decay drops the nucleus to the ground state of polonium 214. Its energy spectrum shape tests nuclear theory and matters for background modeling.

The collaboration measured that spectrum and compared it with calculations. Precise spectral shapes feed the background budgets of rare event searches. A misunderstood decay tail can mimic or mask the signals these experiments seek. Bismuth 214 seeps from radioactivity in detector materials, so its behavior must be known well. The measurement also checks the nuclear models used across the field. Ground state transitions are the cleanest case for such tests. The paper adds a reference spectrum that other low background experiments can reuse.
arxiv-2510-05346:
Hui-Huang Chen solves exactly how a quantum chain evolves after a sudden quench in this 2025 arXiv paper. The starting state is a thermal pure quantum state, already encoding thermal averages. An integrable system like the spin-half XX chain should then simply sit still. Instead, its entanglement evolves in a surprisingly structured way.

Chen derives the behavior three ways: conformal field theory, exact numerics, and a quasiparticle picture. Local observables settle at their thermal values after dephasing. The entanglement entropy, however, rises through a characteristic double plateau. That non-monotonic shape traces to coherent dephasing of anomalous pairing correlations in the initial state. The result defines a third dynamical paradigm, between chaotic stillness and standard non-thermal relaxation.
arxiv-2510-05446:
Zhou and colleagues study how a learning agent can reuse lessons across many tasks. In meta-reinforcement learning, an agent faces a stream of related problems in sequence. Knowledge from early tasks should speed up learning on later ones. Their 2025 paper builds that transfer into Thompson sampling, a classic exploration strategy.

The method assumes that good action values across tasks follow one shared prior pattern. Two algorithms learn that prior from experience, with the second also learning its spread. A new prior-alignment proof links the learned prior to an all-knowing oracle version. The proof yields the first regret guarantees of this kind for finite-horizon tasks. Recipes cover warm starts and prior widening tricks. Simulations on a recommendation setting show the methods beating rivals that ignore prior knowledge. The gains appear once enough tasks have taught the prior, matching the theory.
arxiv-2510-05846:
Lasbordes and Gad specialize small language models for French. Large models remain English-centric, leaving French performance far behind. Small models suffer the gap most, yet adapt cheaply when targeted. Their 2025 Luth family post-trains compact models on curated French data.

Five models span from three hundred fifty million to under two billion parameters. A French instruction dataset of five hundred seventy thousand pairs drives the training. Luth beats every open-source counterpart of comparable size on French benchmarks. English capability survives the specialization intact. Strategic model merging then improves both languages further. The largest average gain reaches about eleven points across six benchmarks. The family sets a new state of the art for French small models. French has over two hundred eighty million speakers worldwide. The recipe transfers plausibly to other under-served languages.
arxiv-2510-05946:
Heilmann and colleagues teach sum-product networks without any party revealing its data. Sum-product networks support fast, exact probabilistic inference. Hospitals and similar parties cannot simply pool sensitive records for training. Their 2025 protocol privately learns both network structure and parameters.

Secret sharing protects privacy against honest-but-curious participants. Privacy holds even if up to half the parties collude. A forest of randomly generated networks is trained and weighted privately. Private inference on new data points follows after training. Log-likelihood matches non-private learning on homogeneous and heterogeneous partitions alike. Scales tested reach one hundred thirty-five features and twelve parties. Homomorphic encryption alternatives can take thirty hours on smaller data. End-to-end runs finish in under an hour at realistic scales. Runtime and memory scale favorably against neural network protocols. Privacy regulation like GDPR motivates the whole design.
arxiv-2510-06346:
Nelson, Rajakumar, and Gullans sharpen the known limits of noisy geometrically local quantum circuits in a 2025 quantum physics paper. Noisy circuits eventually converge to uniform and become trivially simulable. With geometric locality, structured classical algorithms succeed at shallower depths than that trivial limit suggests.

They consider arbitrary local lattice circuits from product states, with depolarizing noise of any constant strength. Once depth passes a threshold scaling like noise inverse times log size, outputs are approximately samplable in quasipolynomial time. The proof rests on new information-theoretic bounds. Local regions decorrelate and turn maximally mixed before the whole system becomes uniform. Structural results suggest a sharper transition at depth set only by the noise rate. After coarse-graining, Pauli weight on long paths truncates with exponentially small error. The percolation-like picture motivates their constant-depth simulability conjecture.
arxiv-2510-06746:
Zhiliang Zhu and four co-authors build a model that removes rain from photographs. Their 2025 paper improves image deraining, which also helps later vision tasks work in bad weather. Recent Mamba-based models handle sequences efficiently. They struggle, though, to keep fine detail and to use frequency information about rain streaks.

Their model, DeRainMamba, adds two new parts to the state space design. A frequency-aware module uses the Fourier transform to separate rain streaks from true fine detail. That balance lets the model erase rain without smearing textures. A multi-directional convolution part then rebuilds local structures from gradient cues in several directions. Tests on four public benchmarks beat leading methods on both quality scores used. The model also needed fewer parameters and less computation than rivals. The authors note that extreme rain still challenges the method. Better generalization to complex storms is their stated next step.
arxiv-2510-07346:
Nemati builds a real-time ship-spotting system for cameras at sea, trained partly on synthetic images. The 2025 paper uses RT-DETR, a fast transformer-based detector. Maritime targets are often tiny and pale against glittering water. Labeled real photos are scarce, so fake ones must help without corrupting judgment. All scoring uses real images only. Multi-scale feature blending sharpens small, low-contrast vessels. A query selection step favors the most reliable candidate detections from the start.

A domain-aware weighting scheme balances synthetic against real training samples. Augmentation also evens out the class mix in the data. On the test collection, the system reached a strong mean accuracy score and beat its baseline. A component analysis shows what each added module contributes. Harbor surveillance and autonomous shipping need detectors that stay fast in ugly conditions.
arxiv-2510-08146:
Sharma and Chopra wrote this 2025 paper using a model's own uncertainty to stop its reasoning early and save compute. The authors compute Shannon entropy from token probabilities as a confidence signal. When entropy stays low, the model likely already has its answer, and generation can stop. Across models and datasets, the framework saved between a quarter and a half of the compute while holding accuracy steady.

The catch is that the signal only exists in some models. Entropy-based confidence calibration appeared as an emergent property of advanced post-training in modern reasoning models. It was absent in standard instruction-tuned and pretrained models tested, including a large Llama model. Where the property exists, the stopping threshold calibrates from a few examples in one shot. Advanced models often know when they are right long before they finish talking. Exploiting that self-knowledge cuts cost and latency.
arxiv-2510-08646:
Eric Hanchen Jiang and co-authors steer language models away from false refusals at inference time in a 2025 arXiv paper. Safety alignment teaches models to reject harmful prompts, but over-caution makes them refuse benign ones too. Their Energy-Driven Steering framework fixes behavior without fine-tuning the model itself. A lightweight external energy-based model scores internal states as desirable or undesirable.

Undesirable states, false refusals and jailbreak successes, get high energy; helpful replies and safe rejections get low energy. During generation, the energy function's gradient nudges hidden states toward low-energy regions in real time. Model weights never change, decoupling behavior control from core knowledge. On the ORB-H benchmark, compliance rose from 57.3 percent to 82.6 percent, while baseline safety performance was maintained across their experiments.
arxiv-2510-08946:
Chen and co-authors force AI-generated molecular structures to obey basic physics, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Foundation models now draft the shapes of interacting biomolecules with impressive skill, yet their all-atom structures often place atoms impossibly close, violating simple steric rules. A shape that cannot exist is useless for drug design, no matter how plausible it looks. The team enforces physical validity as a hard constraint during both training and use.

Their module projects each draft structure onto the nearest physically valid arrangement. A Gauss-Seidel scheme, which fixes clashes one neighborhood at a time, makes that projection fast and stable at scale. Because the step is differentiable, models fine-tune through it end to end. With the module in place, just two cleaning steps produced complexes as accurate as leading diffusion systems that need two hundred. The wall-clock speedup was about tenfold, with validity guaranteed.
arxiv-2510-09046:
Yu and colleagues take a census of pulsars, the spinning remains of dead stars, at a low radio frequency, in this 2025 arXiv paper. They mined archival data from the Murchison Widefield Array in Australia, gathered as the sky drifted overhead. Forty-eight such drift scans covered some thirty thousand square degrees, reaching faint sensitivities in the deepest patches. A search pipeline built on standard pulsar software ran on a Chinese SKA computing center.

The search found all eighty known pulsars in its sights, about sixty percent more than the previous census at this frequency. Thirty of them had never been detected at this frequency before, and the paper presents their pulse shapes and brightnesses. The team also measured how the pulses spread and scatter on their way to Earth. Those properties constrain where signals fade at low frequencies and how pulse width grows with spin period.
arxiv-2510-09146:
Mikkola, Acerbi, and Klami reconstruct what an expert believes from nothing but their pairwise preferences, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Asking an expert for a full probability distribution is hopeless, but asking which of two options they prefer is easy. The team's goal is to turn many such comparisons into the underlying belief distribution. The bridge is the winner density, the distribution of whichever option tends to win each comparison.

Winners follow a tempered, meaning flattened or sharpened, version of the true belief. The authors prove the two distributions' score vectors, the arrows pointing uphill in probability, point the same way, linked by a tempering field they can write down and estimate. A diffusion model then learns the winner density from comparisons, and undoing the tempering recovers the expert's belief. In simulations, a few hundred to a few thousand comparisons sufficed to learn complex beliefs over several variables.
arxiv-2510-09246:
Daugulis and co-authors fill in missing entries in a dataset by asking which completed version stays closest to the data's main patterns, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Missing values plague real datasets, and guessing them well, called imputation, shapes everything computed afterward. Their method mixes classical mathematics with a machine learning flavor. The known data is summarized by a flat subspace, spanned by its first principal components, the directions of greatest variation.

A candidate completion is shifted and compared against that subspace, and distance decides the winner. The completion whose geometry hugs the principal subspace most closely supplies the imputed values. The authors work out the solutions explicitly for the Euclidean metric, the ordinary straight-line distance. The appeal is transparency: unlike a black-box predictor, the geometry can be inspected and the choice justified. The paper presents the method as a principled alternative for data scientists facing incomplete tables.
arxiv-2510-09546:
Julia Gehrlein, Joachim Kopp, Margot MacMahon, and George Parker propose a new use for a neutrino detector technique in a 2025 arXiv paper. Upcoming long-baseline experiments, which fire neutrino beams across hundreds of kilometres, will be limited by uncertainty in the beam's flux and in how neutrinos strike nuclei. The PRISM technique answers by measuring the spectrum at several angles to the beam and combining the measurements into a data-driven prediction for the far detector.

The authors ask how far the off-axis measurements alone can pin down the beam model. Their method, called LENS, extracts the fluxes and spectra of the different meson species in the beam separately. They show this sharpened flux model further constrains the far detector prediction. The improvement feeds directly into better oscillation measurements, the experiment's main goal, since the beam is characterised by measurement rather than by simulation alone.
arxiv-2510-09946:
Chen derives a regularity estimate for spacetimes in this 2025 arXiv paper in differential geometry. Regularity asks how smooth the metric of a spacetime must be, given bounds on its curvature. The paper works with any four-dimensional spacetime.

Chen's estimate rests on two a priori bounds, limits assumed before solving. One bounds the Ricci curvature, which measures how spacetime volume bends. The other bounds the Lie derivative of the Lorentzian metric along an arbitrary timelike vector field, which tracks how the metric changes along a flow of time. From those bounds alone, the paper extracts control on the metric's regularity. Such estimates underpin proofs that rough initial data still evolve into well-behaved spacetimes.
arxiv-2510-10246:
Shi, Zhongwen Li, and Xiaoqi Li review password security in this 2025 arXiv paper on system security. System passwords guard login to operating systems and applications, and a valid password opens the door to system resources. Frequent cracking attacks have made password defense a severe concern for information systems.

The authors survey attack and defense mechanisms for system passwords. Attacks range from guessing and brute force to theft of stored password data. Defenses include hashing choices, rate limits, and policy design. Organizing both sides in one review helps administrators see which defenses answer which attacks. The paper treats password security as an ongoing contest, not a solved problem with one best setting.
arxiv-2510-10446:
Makrehchi analyzes reverse supervision in this 2025 arXiv paper on machine learning theory. Standard supervision labels a training set and fits a model. Reverse supervision flips the search: it hunts over labelings of a large unlabeled set, scoring each by error on a small labeled set.

Makrehchi ties this strategy to the economics of annotation, where labels cost money and unlabeled data is cheap. The search space over labelings grows as two to the power of the set size, and the complexity stays exponential even under huge constant-factor speedups from quantum or parallel hardware. That hardness result sets honest limits: reverse supervision cannot be made cheap by hardware alone, so its use must be rationed wisely.
arxiv-2510-10746:
Kshitij Duraphe and eight co-authors mine twelve years of X-ray observations of the black hole Cygnus X-1, in this 2025 arXiv paper. They analyze 26 observations from NASA's NuSTAR telescope, taken between 2012 and 2024. Their timing analysis characterizes how the accretion flow, the gas spiraling into the black hole, varies across spectral states. They find that hard X-rays, from 8 to 79 keV, split into two well separated flux peaks, making them the best diagnostic of which state the system is in.

Characteristic frequencies shift from 0.050 hertz in the hard state to 0.074 hertz in the intermediate state, which the team links to the disk's inner edge moving inward. Time lags between energy bands shrink toward zero in soft states, quantifying the collapse of the hot corona. Most strikingly, one observation caught a failed state transition with anticorrelated band behavior. The authors say this challenges standard transition models.
arxiv-2510-10846:
Kaixuan Ren, Preslav Nakov, and Usman Naseem benchmark how vision language models handle requests that mix harmless text with risky images, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Safety training can backfire into over-refusal, where models decline benign requests from excess caution. The visual side of this problem lacked a systematic benchmark. Their DUAL-Bench tests over-refusal and safe completion, the ideal behavior of fulfilling the benign part of a request while flagging the harmful element.

They evaluated 18 models across 12 hazard categories, using meaning preserving visual perturbations. In dual use scenarios, models showed extremely fragile safety boundaries. They fell into a binary trap: either refusing defensively or generating dangerous content. Even the best model, GPT-5-Nano, managed only 12.9 percent safe completion, with the GPT-5 and Qwen families averaging 7.9 and 3.9 percent respectively in the reported results. The authors hope the benchmark pushes alignment strategies that balance safety with usefulness in multimodal systems.
arxiv-2510-10946:
Onil Boussim identifies treatment effects when outcomes are unordered categories, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The setup is an instrumental variables model: a binary treatment, a binary instrument, and an outcome like a chosen category with no natural ranking. Yet most tools in this area were built for ranked or numeric outcomes, not for plain labels. Boussim introduces an assumption called association similarity. For each instrument value, it requires the odds ratio link between potential treatment and outcome to be the same whether the outcome is evaluated under treatment or under no treatment.

Under this assumption plus a testable condition called categorywise dominance, the data pin down the full distributions of potential outcomes exactly, and estimation uses sample frequencies. Boussim also studies weaker limits on departures from the assumption, which lead to sharp partial answers instead. He tests the method on the effect of insurance on health.
arxiv-2510-11046:
The Tutte polynomial is a classic counting tool in graph theory that also encodes information about matroids, abstract structures that generalize the idea of linear independence. Xiaxia Guan, Xian'an Jin, and Weiling Yang study its extension to polymatroids in this 2025 arXiv paper. Earlier work defined the polymatroid Tutte polynomial through a bases expansion and through a rank generating function, and a recursive formula appeared in 2025.

For ordinary matroids, three definitions of it are known to agree, including a deletion-contraction recursion that builds it by removing or shrinking one element at a time. Guan and co-authors show that the existing recursive formula for polymatroids can stand on its own as a definition. That result completes the parallel with the classical theory. It now rests on the same three independent foundations as the original.
arxiv-2510-11146:
Methylidyne, a simple molecule known as CH, is widely used to trace molecular gas, but it is rarely observed in cold, dense clumps. Gan Luo and co-authors observed CH toward 27 Planck Galactic Cold Clumps in this 2025 arXiv astronomy paper. They used the Arecibo 305-meter telescope and combined the CH data with carbon monoxide emission, atomic hydrogen absorption, and dust-based gas column estimates.

The team found CH velocity dispersions that are almost everywhere subsonic, unlike the mostly supersonic carbon monoxide, suggesting CH traces dense, low-turbulence gas. Their upper limits on the cosmic-ray ionization rate favor an attenuation model whose low-energy cosmic-ray spectrum matches Voyager spacecraft measurements. The abundance of CH falls as column density rises and grows with the ionization rate. Fitting the abundance constrains the atomic oxygen and ionized carbon content, linking CH formation closely to ionized carbon regulated by cosmic rays.
arxiv-2510-11246:
Multi-agent systems built from language models let several AI agents collaborate through shared tools, creating attack surfaces that single-agent security work does not cover. Pengyu Zhu and co-authors present the first distributed backdoor attack designed for such systems in this 2025 arXiv security paper. The work is a red-team study: it builds the attack to expose the weakness.

The attack splits a backdoor into small primitives hidden inside the system's tools. Each primitive stays dormant on its own, and the full backdoor assembles only when agents collaborate in a specific sequence, enabling targeted actions such as data exfiltration. The authors also built a benchmark of multi-role collaborative tasks and a sandboxed evaluation framework. In their experiments the attack succeeded more than 95 percent of the time without degrading performance on benign tasks, arguing that defenses must move beyond single-agent protection.
arxiv-2510-11946:
Fabrizio Canfora and four colleagues argue that a crystalline phase of nuclear matter is nearly unavoidable. The chiral soliton lattice is a stack of evenly spaced domain walls made of hadrons. Theory predicts it becomes the ground state of quantum chromodynamics, the theory of quarks and gluons, at high baryon density in a strong magnetic field. Their 2025 arXiv paper asks how robust that prediction is when the underlying model is made more realistic.

From the gauged Skyrme model, they include the electromagnetic field's back-reaction. The lattice survives unchanged. More surprisingly, it survives the sub-leading corrections of the large-color expansion, fiercely nonlinear as they are. The Callan-Witten term lets baryon number appear even where the usual topological charge density vanishes. The magnetic field may even be generated by the hadronic layers. The formulation also opens a way to couple the lattice to quark matter.
arxiv-2510-12246:
Wang and colleagues present PromptFlow, a framework that trains prompts for language models much like neural networks are trained, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Good prompts can adapt a general model to a specialized task without retraining, but writing them by hand is slow and expert dependent. Automated methods exist, yet most use fixed update rules and rewrite the whole prompt at each step.

PromptFlow is modular, combining meta prompts, operators, optimization, and an evaluator in the style of TensorFlow. It explores prompt refinement paths through gradient based meta learning and needs little task specific training data. A reinforcement learning component recycles experience gathered during the prompt engineering process, so past attempts inform later ones. The framework also edits prompt sections at a finer grain instead of replacing everything. Across a range of datasets, the authors report that PromptFlow effectively finds strong prompts and can host the latest optimization methods.
arxiv-2510-12446:
Lu and Xi connect periods of certain automorphic forms to sums of special values of L-functions, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. Automorphic periods are integrals of automorphic forms over subgroups, and often encode deep arithmetic information. The setting is a Hamiltonian variety whose dual side has a specific form built from a general linear group and a Levi subgroup.

For some cuspidal Eisenstein series, the authors prove that the associated period equals a fixed sum of special values of L-functions. These L-values come from evaluating the zeta like functions of number theory at specific points. The sum is organized by the fixed points of its associated extended L-parameter acting on the dual variety. The result confirms a conjecture of Ben-Zvi, Sakellaridis, and Venkatesh in this case. That conjecture, part of a broad program linking periods to L-values through duality, gains concrete new evidence.
arxiv-2510-13046:
Jiang and colleagues classify heart abnormalities from electrocardiograms in this 2025 arXiv paper. A twelve-lead ECG records the heart's electrical activity from many angles. Detecting multiple simultaneous abnormalities in these long signals matters greatly for clinical decisions. Residual networks and transformers have been applied, but both struggle when sequences grow long.

Their hybrid model pairs a convolutional front end, which spots local waveform patterns, with Mamba. Mamba is a selective state space model built for efficient sequence modeling. They use a bidirectional variant adapted from Vision Mamba. The pairing strengthens how the model captures dependencies across the heartbeat. On the PhysioNet Computing in Cardiology Challenge datasets from 2020 and 2021, the model scored far higher than the best published algorithms on standard ranking metrics. The authors highlight uses in early diagnosis, telemedicine, and resource-limited care.
arxiv-2510-13246:
Sisodia and Jalan explain how reservoir computing predicts crises in this 2025 arXiv paper. Reservoir computing trains only a simple readout on top of a fixed recurrent network. Yet it forecasts chaotic time series and even discontinuous transitions called crises. In a crisis, a system's attractor suddenly changes size or vanishes. Why the black box works so well was unclear.

The authors dissect good predictions of boundary crises and attractor-merging crises, showing how the reservoir's internal dynamics come to mimic the true system's dynamics. That mirroring lets the reservoir reproduce the correct scaling exponent near a boundary crisis, the number that governs how behavior changes as the crisis approaches. They show the mechanism at work in two distinct test systems, the logistic map and the Gauss map, giving a dynamical explanation that should guide more robust forecasting methods.
arxiv-2510-13646:
Quintela and co-authors compute how strain reshapes light absorption in monolayer CrSBr, a two-dimensional magnet. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies a material prized for its high magnetic ordering temperature and stable, lopsided lattice. Its optical response is dominated by excitons, bound electron-hole pairs. Magnetism and optics intertwine here in ways still largely uncharted.

The study is theoretical, working out the material's optical response under several distinct strain layouts. Stretching a sheet that is only one atom thick is easy, so strain is a practical tuning knob. The authors track how each strain pattern shifts the excitonic absorption peaks. They also follow changes in the overall shape of the conductivity response along each direction. Because the lattice is anisotropic, the two in-plane directions respond differently. The work maps a playground for devices that couple light with magnetism.
arxiv-2510-13946:
Rei Nishiura and Tsuyoshi Inoue investigate how cosmic rays, high-energy particles from space, gain energy at shocks driven by ultrafast outflows from active galactic nuclei, in this 2025 arXiv paper. These outflows are winds of gas moving near light speed from the centers of galaxies. A process called the Bell instability can amplify magnetic fields at such shocks, which should help accelerate particles.

The authors use a one-dimensional model that follows cosmic rays, magnetic fields, and the shock together over time. They find a sharp transition set by the background field strength. With weak background fields, the instability amplifies turbulence efficiently and the maximum particle energy settles into a self-regulated state. With stronger fields, the escaping cosmic-ray current is too weak to drive the instability, turbulence decays, and acceleration likely suffers. They discuss whether these shocks could reach the extreme energies needed for PeV to EeV particles.
arxiv-2510-14146:
Arman Maesumi and co-authors introduce PoissonNet, a neural architecture for learning on 3D surfaces such as character meshes, in this 2025 arXiv paper, published in ACM Transactions on Graphics. Mesh learning architectures usually trade off against each other: they may miss high-frequency detail, see a small neighborhood, depend on how the mesh is triangulated, or cost too much to run.

PoissonNet borrows the local-global strategy from mesh processing. Each block applies learned local transformations in the gradient domain of the mesh, then solves a Poisson equation, a partial differential equation, to spread those updates across the surface. This preserves the frequency spectrum, gives a global receptive field, ignores triangulation details, and needs far less computation than other methods. Experiments reach state-of-the-art results on semantic segmentation and on parameterizing detailed animated surfaces. As a headline application, learning deformations of shapes outperforms previous surface-learning methods.
arxiv-2510-14346:
Dingding Li and Chao Zhang prove results for solutions of perturbed fractional 1-Laplace equations, a class of nonlocal equations with singular traits, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The theory asks how smooth solutions must be, which controls whether the answers can be trusted. The fractional 1-Laplacian is a rough one, tied to total variation and image processing.

Assuming weak solutions are locally bounded, the authors show the subquadratic case behaves like the superquadratic case, understood before. Guided by a threshold value of the fractional parameter, they split the analysis into two cases. They establish Sobolev regularity, membership in function spaces with integrable weak derivatives. The result strengthens once it crosses the threshold. Their analysis combines a nonlocal finite-difference quotient method with a Moser-type iteration scheme. It gives a step-by-step approach to such singular problems.
arxiv-2510-14746:
Rémond and co-authors present, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a quantum algorithm for simulating how cracks open in materials, a task that normally eats large amounts of classical computing. Their variational algorithm stores the displacements of a mesh's nodes as quantum amplitudes in a parametrized circuit. The circuit is tuned to minimize the elastic energy of the structure, computed by the finite element method, and the energy needs only a polylogarithmic number of measurements to evaluate.

Once the solution has converged, useful quantities such as the stress intensity factor, which predicts crack growth, can be extracted efficiently. Scaling up is the hard part, because optimization landscapes flatten into barren plateaus. The authors counter with a warm start: solve a coarse mesh first, then remesh finer and reuse the solution. They validated the approach on Quandela's photonic quantum processor, Ascella, and in simulations across growing system sizes.
arxiv-2510-14946:
Aalishah, Navardi, and Mohsenin build, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a navigation system for robots whose computers are too weak for deep learning. Edge devices have little memory and compute, yet navigation needs object detection in real time. The authors pair a reinforcement learning navigation policy with a detector built on Mamba, an efficient architecture. They train it on a dataset of shapes photographed in varied indoor settings.

The detector finds objects and passes their bounding boxes to the policy, which steers toward goals. The student model shrank by sixty-seven percent relative to its teacher. On two edge platforms, an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and a Raspberry Pi 5, it used up to seventy-three percent less energy per inference while matching the teacher's performance. In the MiniWorld and IsaacLab simulators, it kept high detection accuracy with thirty-one percent fewer parameters than the baseline.
arxiv-2510-15046:
Yang presents, in a 2025 arXiv paper, an analytic framework for how cosmic structure grows when dark matter comes in several species at once. Mixtures blend parts with varied masses, speeds, and abundances, from cold particles to warm species to sparse objects like primordial black holes or solitons. Two wrinkles matter: each species has speed dispersion, warmth, and discrete populations fluctuate randomly, Poisson noise seeding its own patterns.

It solves a truncated BBGKY hierarchy, the chain linking a distribution to its correlations, by way of Volterra integral equations. An algorithm delivers the total power spectrum plus the spectra within and between species. Worked examples with two-component mixtures show that isocurvature patterns, born from the Poisson noise, and ordinary adiabatic fluctuations evolve quite differently depending on the warm or sparse fraction's properties. Free-streaming and Jeans scales control the outcome, and the results match estimates and N-body simulations.
arxiv-2510-15146:
Qili Hu and seven colleagues report the first femtosecond laser built entirely on a chip, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Femtosecond lasers fire pulses lasting quadrillionths of a second and underpin work from chemistry to precision sensing, but they have stayed bulky bench instruments. Shrinking one onto a chip, within tight size and power limits, had resisted decades of effort.

The breakthrough is a new mode-locking mechanism, the process that keeps a laser's pulses regular, assisted by photorefraction, a light-induced change inside the chip material. Running from a simple low-voltage supply, the device switches on reliably and emits pulses shorter than ninety femtoseconds. Its settings can be retuned electronically, and its optical comb, the evenly spaced set of colors it emits, showed an exceptionally narrow linewidth of 53 hertz. The authors see the result clearing a key barrier for chip-scale sensing, communications, and computing hardware.
arxiv-2510-15246:
Hsuan-Lin Liao and Van Tien Nguyen construct a new kind of failing solution for a model of micro-electromechanical systems, tiny devices where a membrane can snap down and touch an electrode. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies quenching, where the solution reaches zero in finite time and the model breaks down. All earlier quenching examples were radially symmetric, looking the same in every direction from the center.

The pair build a solution on a disc that quenches only at the origin, yet its final shape is genuinely non-radial, depending on direction in a mixed pattern of the two coordinates. To their knowledge it is the first such example. The proof starts from a carefully built approximate solution in self-similar variables. Spectral analysis and an energy method then show a true solution stays close to that approximation all the way to the quench.
arxiv-2510-15346:
Heecheol Yun, Kwangmin Ki, Junghyun Lee, and Eunho Yang ask when combining several language models mid-sentence helps and when it hurts. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies ensembling, where models pool their next-token probabilities to pick each word. Pooling at every token works for short answers, but the team shows it often degrades long-form writing.

Two factors decide where pooling is safe. One is tokenization mismatch, since models chop words into different pieces. The other is consensus, meaning the models roughly agree on what comes next. Their framework, SAFE, ensembles only at points that pass both checks. A sharpening step merges probabilities spread across sub-word pieces of the same word into one representative token. On benchmarks including MATH500 and a broad reasoning suite, SAFE beat existing ensemble methods in accuracy and speed. Remarkably, it gained while ensembling fewer than one percent of tokens.
arxiv-2510-15546:
Marwa Ennaceur and Amel Jadlaoui study Hodge Laplacians, operators that generalize the familiar Laplacian to networks and higher-dimensional meshes, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their setting is weighted simplicial complexes, where edges and triangles carry weights. The key questions are how large these operators can be and when they are essentially self-adjoint, a property that makes their physics and spectra well behaved.

For regular unweighted graphs they prove a clean universal bound on the operator's norm. Weighted versions follow with a sharp comparison constant. The bounds need no assumptions about curvature or geometric completeness, which widens their reach. The approach extends to higher degrees using up and down degree data, and a unitary equivalence links the skew and symmetric versions on colorable complexes. For periodic lattices they compute exact constants, confirming the general bounds grow at the right rate.
arxiv-2511-00146:
Michael Landry and Mingda Li introduce chimeric states of matter, phases where traits of broken and unbroken symmetry coexist in a way enabled by mixed anomalies of higher-form symmetries. Ordinary sorting says solids break translation symmetry and superconductors break gauge symmetry, but anomaly-based generalization widens the options. Their headline example concerns the Meissner effect, the pushing out of magnetic fields taken as the key sign of superconductivity.

Using an effective field theory building, they show that effect can occur in media that are lossy or even insulating under electric probing. Condensed matter readers get a phase concept that scrambles textbook expectations, splitting magnetic pushing out from superconductivity itself.
arxiv-2511-00346:
Kayua Oleques Paim and four co-authors report an attack method against large language models that exploits gaps in their latent space, the internal map where meanings are encoded. Sparse training data leaves discontinuities in that map, and the authors craft inputs that steer models through them. The aim is twofold: universal jailbreaks that bypass safety rules, and extraction of data the model should not reveal.

Unlike many earlier attacks tuned to one system, theirs transferred across seven leading language models and one image generator. Even layered defenses failed to hold consistently in their tests. The authors frame the flaw as architectural, not a surface bug, which would make it a systemic risk that model makers need to address at the design level.
arxiv-2511-00446:
Xin Yao and five co-authors attack CLIP, the model that learns to match images with text from web-scale data. Because CLIP trains on uncurated internet pairs, poisoned data can plant hidden backdoors. Most studied attacks poison images, leaving the text channel oddly unexamined. Their framework, ToxicTextCLIP, crafts adversarial texts that corrupt the model during pre-training itself.

Two hurdles shape the design: poisoned texts must fit the target class's background, and such background-matched texts are scarce. A selector picks texts whose backgrounds align with the target, and an augmenter generates more coherent, varied samples in that style. In classification and retrieval tests the attack reached very high poisoning and backdoor success rates, and it slipped past three published defenses. The study exposes text as a serious entry point for supply-chain attacks on foundation models.
arxiv-2511-00546:
Loukas Kokkinos and Joo-Von Kim survey the behavior of spin-torque vortex oscillators, nanoscale devices where magnetic vortices spin and emit microwave signals. Most studies fix one layer as a polarizer that drives the other. Here both layers are free vortices, and each acts as the moving polarizer for the other, doubling the interplay and the possible dynamics.

Extensive micromagnetic simulations, run with the open-source Mumax3 code and the authors' own coupled equations, map how the relative vortex arrangement and layer asymmetry shape current-driven motion. Regimes include self-modulated gyration, where the orbit rhythmically swells and shrinks, and a distinct C-state pattern. Chaotic transitions between steady gyration and the C-state also appear. The overview helps designers predict which regime a dual-layer device will land in.
arxiv-2511-00746:
Andrew Moore links two computing worlds that rarely meet: Ising machines and neural networks. Ising model computation powers quantum annealers, adiabatic quantum computers, and thermodynamic classical devices, and tradition equates the computed answer with the machine's ground state, its lowest energy configuration. Moore generalizes the picture from ground states to spin averages, letting computation happen at high temperatures instead of only in the cold ground state.

On that basis he builds a systematic correspondence between Ising devices and neural networks, plus a simple method to run trained feed-forward networks on Ising-type hardware. A mathematical proof shows these implementations always succeed. For builders of unconventional hardware, the result means a trained network need not wait for specialized chips: it can be compiled onto the physics of spins.
arxiv-2511-00846:
Zhihao Peng and a large team introduce OmniBrainBench, a benchmark for testing how well multimodal language models read brain images. Existing question answering benchmarks cover few imaging types or only coarse descriptions of disease, so they miss much of the clinical workflow.

The benchmark spans fifteen imaging modalities from thirty verified medical sources, with more than nine thousand validated question pairs and over thirty thousand images. Its fifteen tasks follow clinical stages and were checked by a professional radiologist. Testing twenty four leading models, the team finds the best proprietary model scores far below physicians. All models struggle with complex reasoning before surgery, exposing a gap between seeing an image and clinical judgment.
arxiv-2511-00946:
Fenglong Song, Roland Schwan, Yuwen Chen, and Colin Jones speed up a core computation inside the PIQP optimization solver. Multistage problems, such as model predictive control and racing trajectory planning, repeatedly produce Karush-Kuhn-Tucker systems, the linear equations an interior point method must solve at every step.

Their contribution is a parallel Cholesky factorization and triangular solve designed for the block structured matrices these problems generate, with a banded part plus an arrow shaped border. It is implemented as a new backend for PIQP and released as open source. On chain of masses benchmarks and on a minimum curvature racing line problem, the solver shows substantial speed gains over other state of the art solvers.
arxiv-2511-01046:
Vedant Acharya and colleagues show VayuChat, a conversational tool for air quality analysis in India, where air pollution contributes to about one point six million early deaths each year. The data needed for decisions sit scattered across agencies, and existing tools demand expertise and offer only static dashboards.

VayuChat lets users ask plain language questions about air quality, weather, and policy programs. Answers come back as both executable Python code and interactive charts. The system unifies monitoring data from the Central Pollution Control Board, state level demographic data, and funding records from the National Clean Air Programme, all driven by a large language model. The platform is publicly deployed for policymakers, researchers, and citizens.
arxiv-2511-01446: Eva Horvat studies the symmetries inside a link diagram's cube of smoothings, a knot theory structure where each crossing can be resolved in two ways, generating a cube of related surfaces. A labeled barycentric subdivision adds extra combinatorial structure to that cube. She studies the symmetries preserving this structure, and from them constructs a combinatorial link invariant based on the symmetries of triangulated smoothings.
arxiv-2511-01646:
Bastian Castorene, Francisco Peña, Martin Groves, and Patricio Vargas count, exactly, the states of a classic magnet model at its critical point. The one-dimensional antiferromagnetic Ising chain, spins on a line preferring to oppose their neighbors, has a ground-state level crossing when the magnetic field reaches twice the coupling strength.

At that crossing, the number of ground states follows the Fibonacci sequence for open chains and the Lucas sequence for closed rings. The authors extend the counting to the full excitation spectrum: states are built from topological defects counted through Diophantine equations and repeated Fibonacci convolutions. Open chains step through energies in units of twice the coupling, rings in units of four times, and near full polarization some top energy levels are strictly forbidden. Closed forms and residual entropies follow.
arxiv-2511-01846:
Thang Luong and a large team of collaborators introduce IMO-Bench. It is a benchmark suite pitched at the level of the International Mathematical Olympiad. It measures real mathematical reasoning in foundation models, rather than easy short answers. Every problem was vetted by a panel of top specialists.

IMO-AnswerBench holds 400 diverse Olympiad problems with verifiable short answers. IMO-ProofBench goes further, grading full proof writing at basic and advanced levels with detailed grading guidelines for automatic scoring. The benchmarks were central to the team's gold-level Gemini Deep Think result at IMO 2025. The model scored 80 percent on AnswerBench and about 66 percent on the advanced ProofBench. It beat the best non-Gemini models by wide margins. A companion GradingBench, with a thousand human-graded proofs, supports progress in automatic evaluation.
arxiv-2511-02046:
Soham Joshi, Shwet Kamal Mishra, and Viswanath Gopalakrishnan tackle a data bottleneck for systems that answer questions about text visible in images, such as signs and labels. Building such datasets normally needs skilled human annotators, which is slow and costly. Their alternative is an automated pipeline that manufactures question and answer pairs from scene text in a given image.

The pipeline chains optical character recognition, region detection, caption generation, and question generation, then validates what it produces. The authors report a dataset of about seventy-two thousand question and answer pairs drawn from about forty-four thousand images. They present the method as the first pipeline able to synthesize and check a text-based visual question answering dataset at this scale.
arxiv-2511-02546:
M. H. Naghizadeh Ardabili, Omid Yahyayi Monem, Morteza Nattagh Najafi, and Hosein Mohammadzadeh invent a dial that slides between bosons and fermions, the two great families of quantum particles. Bosons follow Bose-Einstein statistics and fermions Fermi-Dirac statistics. Haldane's exclusion statistics long ago pointed to something in between. Their alpha scheme, built around a changed filling weight, slides between the two. For negative values of its dial setting, it pushes past bosons into a hyperbosonic regime.

Thermodynamic geometry supplies the test: the sign and singularities of its curvature reveal whether the interactions act attractive or repulsive. A crossover temperature marks where the curvature flips sign. Its ratio to the condensation temperature depends only on the dial's setting. In that regime it blows up at certain fugacities, signalling condensation unlike usual Bose condensation.
arxiv-2511-02946:
Srikumar Sastry and six colleagues introduce ProM3E, a model that embeds ecology data of many kinds into one shared space. Field ecology mixes photos, sounds, and text, and a useful model should generate any missing kind from the ones at hand. Their 2025 model learns by masked reconstruction in the embedding space, hiding one modality and inferring it from the rest.

Because the model is probabilistic, it can judge which modality mixes are feasible for a task, in effect learning what is worth fusing. It also supports flipping a query inside the embedding space. Their retrieval method blends cross-modal and same-modal similarity and topped all retrieval tests they ran. Linear probes on the hidden features further showed strong representation learning for ecology tasks.
arxiv-2511-03146:
Kaiyuan Zhang and twenty-one colleagues built MME-CC, a benchmark that probes the visual thinking of multimodal models. Existing tests lean on text reasoning or skip whole kinds of visual cognition. Their 2025 benchmark organizes eleven tasks into three groups: spatial reasoning, geometric reasoning, and knowledge-based reasoning, all grounded in images, with fine-grained scoring per group.

Sixteen leading models took the test. Closed models led overall, with the best near 43 points against about 30 for a strong open rival. Spatial and geometric reasoning stayed weak almost everywhere, at or below thirty percent. The team catalogued common errors: flipped orientations, losing track of objects across views, and ignoring counterfactual instructions. Thinking traces tended to run in three stages: extract, reason, then verify.
arxiv-2511-03446:
Anwesh Ray and Tanushree Shah study the zeros of Alexander polynomials for torus knots and links through an arithmetic lens. The knot-prime analogy has long guided such work. Their family wraps a torus with two winding numbers, and the polynomial is taken against the total linking cover.

As both windings grow, the zeros spread evenly around the unit circle. The authors give an explicit rate at which primitive roots of unity appear among them. A moment sequence for the zero pattern gets a closed-form generating function, capturing finer statistics. Iwasawa invariants for the linked branched covers are also determined, plus growth control from a logarithmic measure. Knot theory and number theory meet cleanly in the shared formulas.
arxiv-2511-20046:
Fu asks whether pulsing convection can spin up a tropical cyclone faster. His 2025 paper models vortex growth under periodic convective activity. Cyclones need a deep warm core to form. Steady convection is known to build that core. Real convection flickers with daily cycles and waves.

Simulations used a round model on an f-plane. A bulk-plume scheme modeled the convection itself. Periodic mass flux mimicked a diurnal mesoscale system. Convection produced heating plus convective momentum transfer, called CMT. CMT breaks a phase balance inside the vortex. Each cycle then leaves behind some lasting spin. A cyclonic core forms wrapped in an anticyclonic shell. Turning CMT off erased the spin anomaly entirely. Turning it on restored the core-shell structure. An analytical solution reproduced the simulated pattern. Vertical advection and stretching build the core. Radial advection and tilting build the shell. Periodic convection may genuinely speed cyclone genesis.
arxiv-2511-20146:
Collins and Feldman prove stability for a classic surface-tension experiment as containers widen. Their 2025 paper models the Wilhelmy plate setup. A thin plate dips into a liquid bath. Slow lifting measures dynamic contact angles on it. Contact angle hysteresis makes the motion history-dependent.

The model treats evolution as rate-independent and energy-driven. Vertical plate motion drives the contact line's movement. The key limit widens the container versus the plate. As that ratio grows without bound, solutions stay stable. The finite setup's volume constraint vanishes in the limit. A cleaner Dirichlet-forced evolution emerges instead. Monotonicity and uniqueness were already known for that limit. Contact line regularity also carries over from prior work. Comparison principles for mean curvature equations do the heavy lifting. Barrier arguments control the energy uniformly in the ratio. Volume-forced and boundary-forced theories are thereby connected. Capillarity modeling gains a firmer mathematical footing.
arxiv-2511-20346:
Willert, Hoyer, Grubert, and Bronold derive what plasma electrons really do at the wall. Their 2025 paper builds a detailed boundary rule for plasma kinetics. Every lab plasma touches a solid wall somewhere. Electrons hitting it scatter, lose energy, and spawn secondaries. Simple absorber assumptions erase that rich physics.

A surface scattering kernel encodes the wall cascade. It tracks how electrons rattle inside the solid. Secondary electron excitation enters the same kernel. The resulting condition depends on angle and energy. It is inelastic, unlike constant-coefficient reflections. The solver uses a Legendre expansion Boltzmann scheme. Extra computing cost stays modest in practice. A silicon wall faced argon, helium, and oxygen plasmas. Glow discharge tests showed where inelasticity bites hardest. Distribution functions near the anode change most. Constant bounce values failed to match silicon results. Perfect absorber models miss energy detail entirely. Discharge models gain physical wall honesty.
arxiv-2511-20546:
Vaidya, Bhagat, Nagar, and Nanavati model social media users as toxicity transformers. Their 2025 paper studies how hateful content mutates as it spreads. Older models sort users into just hateful or not. Real users amplify, soften, or copy what reaches them. Each user applies a shift to incoming toxicity before forwarding.

Data from Twitter, Koo, and Gab grounded the analysis. Toxicity is not conserved as it travels the network. Only a subset of users change their behavior class over time. On Twitter nearly half of users stayed in one class. Shifts depend on both the user's class and the input level. Neither epidemic nor activation models captured the pattern well. The team then simulated peace-bots as a countermeasure. Bot placement mattered more than bot count in the trials. Targeting low in-degree users won on random networks only. On real platforms random placement often did as well.
arxiv-2511-20646:
Wang, Tang, Yue, and Li inject 3D awareness into networks juggling several vision tasks at once. Their 2025 paper tackles multi-task learning for dense scene understanding. One network predicting segmentation and depth together saves compute. Most prior designs relate tasks only in flat image space. The resulting features lack a sense of real geometry.

Their Cross-view Module shares information between different camera views. Cost volumes capture how views geometrically agree with each other. The module bolts onto existing multi-task encoders unchanged. Single-view and multi-view inputs are both supported. A spatial-aware encoder with multi-view transformer does the work. Tests ran on the NYUv2 and PASCAL-Context benchmarks. Geometric consistency improved results across attached base methods. Strong backbones like SAK and DINOv3 variants all benefited. Static scenes remain the comfort zone. Moving objects and camera motion remain future work.
arxiv-2511-20746:
M. J. Yantovski-Barth and colleagues present in 2025 a neural shortcut for weighing the supermassive black holes at galaxy centres. The weighing needs a three-dimensional map of the galaxy's stellar mass, usually deprojected from telescope images. Dust or a bright active nucleus can block that route by hiding or outshining the starlight. Their neural network replaces the imaging step entirely.

The network translates Nuker profile parameters, numbers describing how starlight is concentrated, into Multi Gaussian Expansion components that deproject analytically. It was trained on 6.25 million simulated profiles spanning the usual parameter ranges. Inside SuperMAGE, a Bayesian pipeline for black hole masses, the approach was applied to ALMA radio data. Its masses matched the best existing models, and the method now reaches dust-obscured and active galaxies where optical analysis struggles. That widens the set of galaxies whose central black holes can be weighed at all.
arxiv-2511-20946:
Xiao-Xi Yao, Bo Zhang, and Yusuf Turek generalise in 2025 the heralded optical parametric amplifier, a workhorse for engineering exotic light states. Heralded amplifiers were previously fed only ordinary coherent light. The new protocol accepts any non-classical input, widening what one setup can make. Fed with squeezed vacuum, it behaves as a built-in two-photon subtractor. That operation once needed a complex bench of loose parts.

The subtraction yields, on demand, squeezed Schrödinger cat states, superpositions of opposite-phase light, with amplitude near 1.4 and high fidelity, beyond the sub-1.2 amplitudes typical of single-photon subtraction schemes. Fed instead with a small cat state, the same device amplifies the effect, distilling purer approximations of photon-number states. The authors argue the amplifier becomes a versatile platform: many non-Gaussian resources, prized for quantum computing and metrology, from a single device with practical success rates.
arxiv-2511-21246:
Kostiantyn Drach and Jonguk Yang settle a conjecture for one family of chaotic maps in a 2025 mathematics paper. The maps are complex polynomials of degree at least two that contain a Siegel disk, a region where the motion rotates calmly at an irrational rate instead of spiraling or settling. Their rotation numbers are of bounded type, and the maps cannot be simplified by renormalization, the usual zooming trick.

Drach and Yang prove three results for these atomic Siegel polynomials. Their Julia sets, the filigree boundaries between calm and chaotic behavior, are locally connected. The sets support no invariant line fields, a rigidity property meaning the shape admits no hidden wiggle room. Finally, any two maps sharing the same combinatorial description coincide up to a rescaling. That verifies the Combinatorial Rigidity Conjecture for this whole class. It also extends famous rigidity theorems beyond the setting they previously covered.
arxiv-2511-21346:
Mohamed Shahawy, Julien de Castelnau, and Paolo Ienne build a bridge from parallel software to custom chips in 2025. Their compiler, Bombyx, takes programs written in OpenCilk, a language for task-level parallelism where work spawns dynamically, and retargets them to FPGAs, chips whose circuits are rewired for each job. OpenCilk's implicit task style forces costly context switching in hardware, so Bombyx first rewrites programs into an explicit continuation-passing form inspired by the older Cilk-1.

Shahawy and his coauthors give Bombyx two outputs: an OpenCilk-compatible runtime, and a generator of synthesizable processing elements for high-level synthesis tools such as Vitis HLS. A decoupled access-execute optimization separates memory fetching from computing so the two overlap, lifting throughput. On a synthetic graph traversal benchmark, the optimization cut runtime by up to 26.5 percent, and the design leaves room for further hardware targets.
arxiv-2511-21946:
Hudson and colleagues set computer vision a new task: tracking points that have left the camera's view entirely. People effortlessly keep a mental panorama and know where things are behind them, but tracking systems today forget points once they exit the frame. Their task, TAPVid-360, asks a model to predict the 3D direction to a scene point through a whole video, even when the point sits far outside the narrow visible view.

To train systems without expensive 4D ground truth, they resampled 360-degree panoramas into narrow views while computing point directions across the full sphere. The resulting dataset, TAPVid360-10k, contains 10,000 perspective videos with ground-truth directional tracking. Their baseline, adapted from CoTracker v3 to predict rotations updating each point's direction, outperformed existing tracking and 3D methods on the new benchmark, a first step toward object permanence.
arxiv-2511-22246:
Lv and colleagues teach a neural network to measure particle hits in silicon detectors without labeled examples. Their model, the Histogram AutoEncoder, learns from data alone, a style called unsupervised learning. A custom loss, built on histograms, forces the model's inner code into a physically meaningful shape. The code is just two numbers for each hit.
