Earlier unsupervised models gave codes that physicists could not read or control.

Those two numbers turn out to be the particle's charge and its impact position along the strip. On beam-test data, simple post-processing reads the charge to within 0.25 of an electron charge. It reads the position to within 3 micrometers, matching the standard conventional approach. The model can also generate synthetic hits, which opens a path to fast detector simulation. The results show unsupervised models can make precise, interpretable measurements in particle physics.
arxiv-2511-22846:
Leonov and Shigenaga map the lives of hopfions, three-dimensional topological solitons, in chiral magnetic films. Skyrmions, their two-dimensional cousins, are well studied, but how hopfions form, stabilise, and interact under confinement was unexplored. Using three-dimensional micromagnetic simulations in a material-independent framework also applying to liquid crystals, they generate hopfions by rotating bimeron and finger-like precursors around an axis, with surface anchoring from the film.

Four types of hopfions emerge, their metastability regions tracking the modulated finger phases' boundaries, so size can be tuned continuously via anisotropy-driven inflation and collapse. Near the inflation threshold, hopfions cost about as much energy as the uniform state, letting them enclose pockets of phases or other solitons as bag-like domains. Periodic hopfion lattices proved unstable under confinement, relaxing into finger phases. The work lays out principles for stabilising three-dimensional solitons, with liquid-crystal experiments a suggested route.
arxiv-2511-23346:
Soriano and Chudnovsky show that a fast-moving defect can flip a magnet. Demonstrating numerically that edge dislocations racing through a ferromagnetic film reverse its magnetization through the Barnett effect. A moving dislocation twists the lattice, and by the Larmor theorem that rotation acts on spins like a magnetic field. Stress effects on magnetization are usually blamed on magneto-elastic coupling, which the authors argue has made researchers overlook moving dislocations.

Simulating the Landau-Lifshitz spin dynamics on a hexagonal lattice of over 100,000 sites with cobalt's hexagonal close-packed parameters. They start from a metastable state prepared by an external field and watch the passing dislocation trigger full reversal within a few picoseconds. Because shock stress can launch dense dislocation avalanches at near sound speed. The effect should grow in larger samples, suggesting a mechanical route to switching magnetic memory that experiments could test directly.
arxiv-2512-00046:
Angelina Parfenova, Andreas Marfurt, Alexander Denzler, and Juergen Pfeffer compare human experts with language models on inductive coding. Inductive coding is the qualitative method where labels emerge from the data itself. It contrasts with deductive coding, which applies a fixed label set from the start.

The study evaluates six open-source language models against human experts on this task. Automating inductive coding could speed social science analysis of interviews and open text. Knowing where models match experts, and where they drift, sets safe limits for that use. Six open-source models give the comparison breadth, spanning the tools researchers can actually download and run themselves.
arxiv-2512-00246:
CI Tau is a young, magnetically active star that hosts a planet on a short orbit, according to earlier studies. Stephen Skinner and Manuel Güdel report Chandra X-ray observations of the star in 2025. Earlier work had reported periodic variability attributed to the massive planet.

CI Tau was clearly detected in four separate Chandra observations taken in late 2023. The authors examine how its X-ray emission varies over time. X-rays from a host star can erode a young planet's atmosphere, so measuring them helps astronomers judge how harsh the planet's early environment really is. Four separate detections give the variability claim a firmer base than a single snapshot.
arxiv-2512-00646:
A pair of pants surface, a sphere with three openings, is a basic stage for hyperbolic geometry. Sergio Herrero Vila and Cheikh Lo characterize geodesic rays that diverge on average on such a surface in 2025. Their description uses coding, turning paths into symbolic sequences.

The rays studied spend less and less time in any compact region as they wander. The characterization builds on limit point sets described by Riquelme and Velozo. Symbolic coding of geodesics is a classic bridge between geometry and dynamics, letting ergodic theory answer questions about how typical paths escape. A pair of pants with one cusp is among the simplest infinite hyperbolic surfaces.
arxiv-2512-00746:
Yusef Maleki, Luis Zambrano Palma, and M Suhail Zubairy study weak measurements in quantum physics in a 2025 paper. A weak measurement probes a quantum system gently, learning a little without wrecking its state. The team asks how information is shared out among the parts of such a setup.

They focus on multilevel systems that decay while being watched continuously, with no clicks recorded. They derive exact relations, like conservation laws, that hold for each outcome in the record. Similar relations hold when the measurement is reversed, with the chance of success entering the formulas. Such bookkeeping rules help design gentler, smarter quantum sensors.
arxiv-2512-00846:
Neeraj Anand and coauthors at Adobe present AFRAgent in a 2025 paper on phone automation. Demand is growing for software that can operate mobile interfaces on its own. Visual language models have moved GUI agents from writing instructions for people toward carrying out the tasks themselves.

Screens vary in size and sharpness, which trips up agents that must tap small targets. AFRAgent uses adaptive feature renormalization, a way to rescale what the model sees, with high-resolution screens in mind. Sharper, better-scaled perception could make phone agents more reliable at real tasks like booking, ordering, and settings changes.
arxiv-2512-00946:
Alvaro Paredes Amorin, Andre Python, and Christoph Weisser fine-tune small language models for finance in a 2025 paper. Markets leave trails in text: tweets, news stories, reports, and microblogs all carry sentiment that can move prices. Large language models read such signals well, but they demand costly computing power and often proprietary data.

Lightweight models could open this work to more researchers and firms. The team adapts small models for sentiment classification across mixed financial text sources. Data from different sources vary in style and noise, which makes the task hard. Strong small models would make market text analysis cheaper and more private.
arxiv-2512-01246:
Shuai Wang and seven coauthors introduce COMET, a coaxial drone design, in a 2025 engineering paper. Coaxial bi-copter aircraft stack two rotors on one axis, promising better rotor efficiency and a compact form. Balancing efficiency, maneuverability, and compactness in such systems is a key design challenge that has limited their practical use.

COMET is an autonomous aerial vehicle built around a dual swashplate mechanism. Swashplates tilt the rotors to steer, and having two gives finer control over both rotors. The design aims for high maneuverability and long endurance together, a pairing that could suit inspection and delivery work in tight spaces.
arxiv-2512-01346:
Youngjae Kim and Kwon Park predict new states in graphene under bright light. Graphene is a sheet of carbon one atom thick. Shining round-polarized light on it can change how charge flows. Fresh tools now let teams probe such driven states.

The pair say the lit sheet can host two states with no resistance. One is a Floquet Chern insulator, a driven state with edge flow. The other forms its own patchy current pattern on its own. Both states would be new kinds of matter made by light. Tests could guide future low-loss devices.
arxiv-2512-01746: Unai De Miguel Sárraga wrote this doctoral thesis in 2025. It was sent in for a Doctor of Philosophy degree. Groups in the Basque Country and Spain that study gravity, the cosmos, and basic physics helped fund the work. The record keeps the front pages and thanks pages. It does not sum up the results. So the thesis's own claims cannot be described from the evidence at hand.
arxiv-2512-02546:
Jan Meizner and Maciej Malawski test ways for supercomputers to borrow memory from each other. Their 2025 study runs on two distinct high performance computing clusters, so results reflect real hardware variety. Remote memory access could ease jobs whose data outgrows one machine's local memory.

The pair compares options built on shared storage and on MPI messaging, over InfiniBand and Slingshot networks. Each option is measured against plain local memory access as a baseline. The study also notes medical use cases that stand to gain most, where fast access to large shared data can speed care related computing. Fast shared memory can shave hours off large scans of the brain, the chest, or the heart.
arxiv-2512-03546:
A layered crystal magnet offers a test bed for frustrated magnetism. K. U. Akshay and co-authors study a depleted-kagome compound in this 2025 work. The material is a copper tellurium sulfate hydroxide with spin one-half ions.

The team measures structure and magnetism with X-ray diffraction, magnetization, and heat capacity. They also use proton nuclear magnetic resonance. Frustrated magnets resist simple ordering and can host exotic states. Careful measurements reveal whether this compound orders, freezes, or stays liquid-like at low temperature. Several probes together guard against mistaking one signal for magnetic order.
arxiv-2512-03646:
Firms deciding whether to build new capacity face a one-way door: capacity once installed cannot easily be removed. Constantinos Kardaras, Alexandros Pavlis, and Mihail Zervos model that dilemma in a 2025 probability preprint. A large population of unlike producers sells one perishable good into a market where demand wanders randomly.

In their model, prices adjust moment by moment so supply matches demand. Each producer reacts to those prices while choosing output and investment. Because every producer both shapes and responds to the crowd, the setup reads naturally as a mean-field problem. The authors show equilibrium prices can be written as a nonlinear function of the underlying demand. Each producer faces a three-dimensional control problem, whose Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation they solve explicitly. The solution includes a closed-form boundary separating states where investing is worthwhile from states where waiting is better.
arxiv-2512-03746:
Multimodal models that think with images can call tools to inspect a picture while they reason. Zirun Guo and colleagues at Zhejiang University and ByteDance show in a 2025 preprint that even leading models stumble on rotated or corrupted images. Tool sets offered to such models also tend to be narrow.

Their framework, CodeVision, replaces a fixed tool registry with code itself: the model writes programs that can invoke any image operation. Training begins with supervised fine-tuning on curated examples of multi-step tool use and recovery from errors. Reinforcement learning follows, guided by a dense process reward that favours strategic, efficient tool calls. The authors built fresh training sets and a harder benchmark stressing orientation changes and multi-tool problems. On two Qwen model families, the method improved performance and produced flexible tool chaining and self-correction from runtime feedback.
arxiv-2512-03946:
People are exposed to chemical mixtures, not one substance at a time, and gauging the health effect of a mixture strains standard statistics. Nate Wiecha, Emily Griffith, Brian J. Reich, and Jane A. Hoppin ask a practical question in a 2025 preprint: when do the specialised new methods for them actually beat familiar general ones?

The team ran a broad head-to-head test across simulated scenarios, scoring methods on false-positive control, detection power, interpretability, and prediction accuracy. General tools such as generalised linear models won in many ordinary situations: moderate correlation among chemicals, simple exposure-response shapes, or components pushing in opposite directions. The purpose-built methods earned their keep when exposures were highly correlated or the response involved strong interactions. The authors close with a summary matching method choice to the situation, a guide against reaching for novelty by default.
arxiv-2512-04046:
Inverse problems ask us to reconstruct something hidden, like the Sun's hard X-ray sources, from few and indirect measurements. L. Bruni Bruno and colleagues argue in a 2025 numerical analysis preprint that where those measurements are taken deserves as much care as the reconstruction method itself. They propose a greedy framework that selects measurements in the data space of the problem's operator.

The selection runs in two steps built on kernel-based interpolation and extrapolation. Greedy schemes come in two flavours: residual-based choices follow the current error, while error-based choices use advance indicators. For the second flavour, the authors derive explicit error bounds tracking how errors propagate through both steps. Applied to solar hard X-ray imaging, their strategy rebuilt high-quality images from only a few measurements. Smart sampling, the authors argue, can substitute for expensive data.
arxiv-2512-04246:
Machine ethics for reinforcement learning usually means rules bolted on as constraints, or morality squeezed into a single reward number. Majid Ghasemi and Mark Crowley argue both habits fail, in a 2025 preprint on virtuous reinforcement learning. Rules struggle under ambiguity; a lone scalar hides trade-offs and invites proxy gaming.

Their alternative treats ethics as dispositions: stable habits that persist when incentives, partners, or contexts shift. Evaluation should report trait summaries, durability under interventions, and moral trade-offs, not just returns. The roadmap has four parts. Agents can learn virtue-like habits socially, from imperfect yet normatively informed exemplars, in multi-agent settings. Multi-objective and constrained formulations keep value conflicts visible and add risk-aware criteria. Affinity-based regularisation pulls policies toward updateable virtue priors, steadying them under distribution shift. Finally, diverse ethical traditions should be operationalised as practical control signals, with assumptions stated openly.
arxiv-2512-04346:
Leon Janzen and Matthias Hollick ask what happens to phone networks when a disaster or attack cuts a region off from the core network. Modern 5G service leans on that central core for nearly every task. A cut-off region becomes an island, and key help goes dark: emergency calls, alert broadcasts, messengers, and news apps all fail. Their 2025 arXiv paper argues the next network round, 6G, should be built island-ready from the start.

An island-ready design would let phones link to local servers inside the region, a thing current setups cannot do. The authors stress this takes joint work from users, operators, app builders, providers, and authorities. They grade how close current 5G systems come to island-ready status. They then lay out the open problems and design steps that remain. The goal is crisis-proof local service that holds up when the wider network falls.
arxiv-2512-04746:
Wenhua Cheng, Weiwei Zhang, Heng Guo, and co-authors present SignRoundV2, a method for shrinking large language models to a handful of bits per weight without wrecking their skill. Post-training quantization compresses a trained model cheaply, yet at two bits, and even at four, quality often craters. Their 2025 arXiv paper takes a step toward closing that gap with smarter bit budgets and steadier tuning.

The first idea allocates bits layer by layer, guided by gradient signals and the damage each layer's rounding causes. Layers that suffer most keep more bits. The second idea is a set of light stabilizers: filtering the tuning loss and searching scale settings before fine-tuning begins. Across many models, the quantized versions held up far better than prior tools at the same tiny sizes. Cheaper, smaller models mean language AI that fits on phones and laptops.
arxiv-2512-04946:
Dylan Magill, Matt Nicholl, Vysakh Anilkumar, and co-authors release MALLORN, a dataset and classifier challenge for spotting stars being torn apart by black holes in the coming flood of survey data. The Vera Rubin Observatory's decade-long LSST survey will multiply known transients a hundredfold. Spectrographs cannot chase them all, so light curves alone must rank targets. Tidal disruption events are prize catches, since they reveal sleeping black holes. Their 2025 arXiv paper simulates the hunt before the flood arrives.

MALLORN holds more than ten thousand artificial LSST light curves, modeled on real nuclear transients. A public challenge asks classifiers to pick the tidal disruptions from the crowd. Training on realistic fakes lets teams tune their filters early. When the real survey opens, proven classifiers will steer scarce follow-up time toward the rarest events.
arxiv-2512-05046:
Tassilo Scheffler and five co-authors ask whether supernova blasts create more interstellar dust than they destroy. Remnants are seen holding large amounts of dust, yet the outward shock that sweeps up gas also grinds grains down, and the balance is poorly pinned down. The team studies the shock during its most destructive phase, inside a realistically churning interstellar medium rather than a smooth one.

They first simulate turbulent gas at several densities and stirring strengths, then set off a supernova inside it and follow the blast for ten thousand years. A second stage tracks the dust itself — dragged, sputtered, and shattered — for both silicate and carbon grains. Destruction turns out to depend strongly on density and turbulence. Dense filaments shield some grains, and carbon survives better than silicate. But the shock always destroys more than remnants typically make, marking most of them net dust sinks.
arxiv-2512-05146:
Alice Kutsyy, Adeline Wihardja, Victoria Lee, and Kaushik Bhattacharya report new measurements of nematic elastomers, rubbery materials threaded with liquid-crystal order. The pairing gives these soft solids unusual heat-and-stretch behavior, including a soft mode in which they deform with little resistance. Such materials are candidates for soft robots, sticky surfaces, and impact protection, but their behavior shifts with temperature and with how fast they are pulled.

The team built a new experimental setup and gathered a comprehensive dataset of the soft response across a range of temperatures and strain rates. They then fit the data to a recently developed theory of nematic elastomers. A shared, well-characterized dataset matters because models of these materials have proliferated faster than the measurements needed to test them. This work supplies both the numbers and a check on whether current theory keeps up.
arxiv-2512-05446:
Cheng-Yuan Ho and four co-authors compress dynamic three-dimensional scenes without flattening what makes them move. Gaussian splatting represents scenes as clouds of blobs, and its dynamic extension animates them — but storage balloons. Existing approaches either spawn short-lived blobs for every moment or deform a canonical scene. They give no explicit control over when things appear and vanish. Rate-distortion-optimized compression for the dynamic case is largely unexplored.

Their scheme, TED-4DGS, builds on anchors in a canonical scene. Each anchor learns when to switch on and off, and queries a shared deformation bank through a temporal embedding to fetch its motion. For compression, a hyperprior models how anchor attributes distribute, and an autoregressive model captures correlations within anchors. The combination reaches state-of-the-art rate-distortion performance on datasets — among the frameworks to optimize splatting for the size-versus-quality tradeoff.
arxiv-2512-05746:
Shizhuo Mao, Hongtao Zou, Qihu Xie, and Song Chen, with Yi Kang, shrink diffusion models, costly generators to run. Quantization stores numbers in fewer bits, but extreme values in the activations spoil quality at low bit counts. Their 2025 method, HQ-DM, trains the model with quantization in mind. A single Hadamard transformation is applied to the activation matrices, spreading the extreme values out.

Using one transform instead of two brings practical wins. It fits naturally with integer convolution hardware, and it avoids inflating outliers in the weights. The team tested conditional image generation on ImageNet with a standard latent diffusion model. At four bit weights and activations, their scheme raised the Inception Score by roughly an eighth over the best prior method. At an even harsher setting, with three bit activations, the score rose several fold. The results point to capable image generation on modest hardware.
arxiv-2512-06046:
Ramprasath Ganesaraja and a large team of co-authors present AI4UI, a multi-agent system that promises to take enterprise software interfaces from a designer's canvas to production code largely on its own. Enterprise front ends demand security, compliance, and maintainability. The human role is deliberately narrow. At design time, developers annotate Figma prototypes in a grammar the AI can interpret precisely. At the end, domain experts refine the output for nuance and compliance. Between those bookends, specialized agents work autonomously.

The machinery includes knowledge graphs, templates, and a change oriented workflow. In benchmarks it posted over ninety seven percent platform compatibility, and ranked among the leaders in blind studies with two hundred experts. It generates thousands of screens in weeks. The authors supply unusual amounts of measurement. Bookended autonomy is the shape enterprise adoption will take.
arxiv-2512-06746:
Ruoxin Chen and eight co authors argue that detectors of AI generated images fail to generalize because of how they are taught, not how they are built. A detector trained on one generator's output often collapses on the next. Most training blends two signals in every example: what the image shows, its semantics, and the faint artifacts the generator leaves behind. The authors show by controlled tests that this blend is actively harmful.

Their fix separates the signals completely. One branch of their detector, a vision language model, is taught only semantics; a vision expert branch is taught only artifacts. Each gets the kind of model that suits its signal. Trained on images from just two generators, the detector gained a large margin across five real world benchmarks. The team also releases a diagnostic benchmark spanning eight current generators.
arxiv-2512-06846:
Xiaoqi Li and co-authors build a tool to catch a costly class of bugs in smart contracts, the self-running programs used on blockchains. Access control flaws let the wrong accounts invoke functions that should be restricted, and they sit behind many real losses. Older checkers read code through trees or flow diagrams, which can miss meaning and intent. Li's team instead turns a contract into a knowledge graph, a web of named parts and their links.

On top of that graph sits a large language model. The system, called CKG-LLM, turns plain-language descriptions of flaw patterns into precise graph queries, then runs them to locate suspect code. In tests it found access control problems better than the existing tools the authors compared against. The paper closes by sketching extensions, suggesting the graph-plus-model pairing could widen to other contract flaws.
arxiv-2512-06946:
Stanisław Marek Sergiusz Halkiewicz and Andrzej Kałuża propose a new way to judge whether a difference-in-differences estimate, a workhorse of applied economics, is truly significant. The popular method compares change over time between a treated group and a control group. Standard error formulas for it can badly overstate confidence when samples are small. The authors instead shuffle the data: both the treatment labels and the time labels are permuted at random, over and over.

That double shuffling builds an honest picture of what pure chance would produce, against which the real estimate is judged. In simulations, including messy non-standard error patterns, their test held its stated error rate at every sample size, while common rivals cried wolf far too often. A small loss of power fades as samples grow. It ships as an R package, checked on four data sets.
arxiv-2512-07046:
Ralph Sabbagh and co-authors give control engineering a new quantity to minimize: attention. Borrowed from cybernetics, the term here measures how hard a control law must work at recalibrating its actions from fresh data. A law that ignores time and position entirely needs no attention at all, if it still meets its goals. Building on Brockett's early formulations, the authors ask what minimal-attention schemes look like in the cleanest possible setting.

That setting pairs linear dynamics, the Gauss-Markov world, with Gaussian uncertainty about the state. Within it they characterize controllers that steer a system between two end states, each described by a Gaussian uncertainty profile, while spending as little attention as the task allows. The analysis reveals the structure such schemes must take.
arxiv-2512-07446:
Khurram Abbas and Jonathan Squire wrote this 2025 space physics paper on why the solar wind stays hot. As the wind streams away from the Sun, it cools far less than simple expansion predicts. One leading heat source is reflection-driven turbulence, where waves bounce and stir each other.

Older models of that process assume the Sun's magnetic field points straight outward. Far from the Sun, though, the field twists into a spiral shape called the Parker spiral. The authors extend the turbulence picture to that twisted field. They test the ideas with three-dimensional simulations in an expanding box. The basic dynamics stay much the same, but the key scales shrink. Eddies get cut across by the sideways field, so the cascade resists freezing into stiff structures. More wave energy then turns into heat. The authors also list concrete signs that spacecraft data can check.
arxiv-2512-07546:
Yuandong Jia and ten co-authors wrote this 2025 instrumentation paper for space gravitational wave missions. Detectors in space float a test mass that must stay electrically neutral. Charge builds up on the mass over time, so a management system must bleed it away.

One strategy shines weak ultraviolet light on the mass without pause. Done right, charging and discharging balance each other continuously. That removes the need for frequent charge checks. The team tests light-emitting diodes with longer wavelengths than the standard choice. Their sensor model copies the surfaces and work function of a real cubic test mass. It follows the example flown on the LISA Pathfinder mission. Four candidate wavelengths go through the bipolar discharge tests. One mid-range option performs best, holding the mass potential nearest to zero. It supports both rapid and continuous discharge. The results feed future design work on charge management systems.
arxiv-2512-07646:
Patrik Schönfeldt and Elif Turhan wrote this 2025 energy planning paper. Cities planning future heat supply must model hundreds or thousands of buildings. Every added building swells the model's variables, and computing time can explode.

Planners also need long horizons at fine time resolution, to catch morning load peaks. The usual remedy is aggregation: merging buildings into groups before modeling. Blocks or neighborhoods are the standard grouping keys. The authors test a richer key that includes energy performance indicators. Their case study uses real data from the Neu-Schwachhausen district. Buildings are grouped by location, by geometry, and by energy traits together. The indicators cover yearly heat use and the potential for solar generation. Their workflow runs from raw geodata to a set of Pareto-optimal supply options. Those options balance technical, social, and economic goals at once. Blending geography with energy traits, they find, beats either key alone.
arxiv-2512-07846:
Guoyao Li and twenty-four co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on ranking results with language models at LinkedIn. Language models judge relevance with a fine sense of meaning. Their cost, though, strains the speed and volume limits of industrial search.

Standard rankers feed the model long text covering user, query, and item. That long context makes every ranking call prefill-heavy and slow. Their framework, MixLM, shortens the input by mixing two token kinds. Item descriptions are pre-encoded into a few embedding tokens, cached near the serving path. Online, the model reads text for the query and embeddings for the items. Semantic strength survives while context length collapses dramatically. The paper shares deployment lessons from a real LinkedIn search product.  At equal latency and relevance, throughput jumps by a large multiple. Full traffic now runs on language-model ranking at the company.
arxiv-2512-07946:
Pietro Capuozzo, Brandon Robinson, and Benjamin Suzzoni wrote this 2025 physics paper. Neural networks can quietly define whole field theories through their design. Priors over network settings complete the recipe for building such theories.

Conformal field theories, prized for their symmetry, arise that way too. Defects inside them, lower-dimensional seams, probe rich physics. The authors build a method for defects that respect conformal symmetry in such theories. Two toy models of scalar network theories supply the test cases. A defect version of the operator product expansion is worked out. It sorts two-point functions by the defect's influence. A neural network reading of that expansion comes along with it. The work extends the network-theory dictionary to seam-like structures. Defects may help sort what network designs can express. Conformal symmetry and machine learning keep converging here.
arxiv-2512-08446:
Maximilian Pierer von Esch, Andreas Voelz, and Knut Graichen, control engineers in Germany, posted an overview paper on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is solving large optimization problems in distributed fashion, where many subsystems each compute locally and talk only to their neighbors. The sensitivity based approach they survey coordinates those subsystems through sensitivity information and a primal decomposition of the whole problem.

The study gives a short history of how the method developed. It then applies the method to both static optimization, done once, and dynamic optimization over time. The highlight is a distributed model predictive controller fast enough for real time use. The authors validate that controller experimentally on a coupled water tank system, a classic laboratory stand in for industrial process control. For engineers facing systems too big for one central solver, the overview offers a compact map of a mature coordination technique.
arxiv-2512-08646:
Maximilian Kreutner and coauthors introduce QSTN, an open source Python tool for running survey style studies with large language models. Researchers can use it to generate model answers to questionnaire prompts, for use in simulated surveys or in labeling tasks. The tool is built to test how question form, prompt changes, and answer methods affect the results.

In a large test with tens of millions of model responses, the team finds that question structure and answer method matter a great deal. Some presentation choices match human answers more closely, and some cut compute cost sharply. QSTN also offers a no code interface, so researchers without coding skills can set up careful tests. The goal is more reliable and repeatable work with language models in survey research.
arxiv-2512-08746:
Federica Fieramosca and coauthors study radio frequency sensing inside dense internet of things networks. Such sensing uses the radio waves of wireless networks to detect presence and movement of people and objects, without cameras. An electromagnetic model predicts how a human body blocks signals in different scenes, giving a basis for analysis.

The team trains a deep graph neural network on signal strength samples generated from that model. In the graph, nodes are antennas and edges are radio links between them. The task studied is counting how many people are present in a monitored area over time. The authors derive theoretical limits on how many subjects can be told apart, based on link count, area size, and body size. An indoor case study supports the approach and shows the model can predict performance before a network is installed.
arxiv-2512-08946:
Zacchary Sadeddine, Winston Maxwell, Gael Varoquaux, and Fabian Suchanek examine the societal challenges that could arise if large language models replace search engines as the main gateway to web information. Such a shift would change how people find, trust, and pay for content online. The analysis is organized around three roles in that ecosystem.

Those roles are model providers, content creators, and end users. Across them, the authors identify fifteen types of challenges. For each challenge, they review current mitigation strategies from both a technical angle and a legal angle. They also discuss the likely impact of each challenge if it is left unaddressed. Open research opportunities are pointed out throughout. The article offers a structured map for policymakers, builders, and researchers who must prepare for a possible change in how the web is accessed and governed.
arxiv-2512-09046:
Aqeel Ahmed and coauthors explore signals from a composite hidden sector that couples to the Standard Model through neutrinos. In their scenario, that same coupling gives rise to neutrino masses. The hidden sector is conformal at high energies, and its compositeness scale lies below the weak scale, so its bound states are light.

If the lightest composite state is a scalar, its decay back to Standard Model particles is suppressed by angular momentum. Its lifetime can therefore be naturally long, producing long lived particle signals in detectors. The authors determine current limits on this class of models from past searches. They then explore the reach of future collider and beam dump experiments. Facilities named in the study could probe a significant part of the still unexplored parameter space. The work links neutrino mass generation to a concrete experimental program for hidden sector particles.
arxiv-2512-09546:
Murat Karayaka and colleagues present DDSRNet, a lightweight neural network that sharpens hyperspectral images, pictures recording many narrow color bands beyond ordinary red, green, and blue. Raising the resolution of a single such image is valuable for remote sensing, but heavy models are costly to run. Their design works in two domains at once, ordinary space and the wavelet frequency domain.

The network has three parts. A shallow spatial module learns residual detail and handles the upscaling. A low-frequency branch, built on the discrete wavelet transform, refines the coarse structure of the image. A shared refinement branch then enhances the three high-frequency wavelet subbands, horizontal, vertical, and diagonal, with shared weights, keeping the model small. An inverse transform rebuilds the final image. On three hyperspectral datasets the network reached highly competitive quality at low computational cost, which the authors offer as evidence for the dual-domain approach.
arxiv-2512-09746:
J. M. García-Garrido and colleagues compare two laser techniques for spinning molecules up to very high rotational states. Their focus is the regime where the rigid-rotor picture fails because rotation and vibration become coupled, each distorting the other. Controlling rotation without wrecking the vibrational state is a delicate problem in molecular physics.

The first technique is the optical centrifuge, a laser pulse whose linear polarization rotates at an accelerating rate, dragging molecules around with it. The second is a Gaussian pulse narrow in spread, matched in spectral width and energy for fairness. Their analysis shows the centrifuge achieves controlled excitation of high rotational states while keeping the spread along the vibrational axis low. The plain pulse produces comparable rotation but broadens the vibrational state. The comparison identifies the centrifuge as the cleaner tool when ro-vibrational coupling cannot be ignored.
arxiv-2512-09846:
Alex Stornelli and Anish Agashe model charged balls of fluid held up against their own gravity, in a universe with a cosmological constant. The fluid follows a polytropic law, linking pressure to density by a power, and the electric charge grows as another power of the radius. With these choices, the relativistic balance equation becomes an equation for the mass profile, solved numerically across the two exponents.

Not every solution describes a believable star. The authors keep only configurations where sound stays slower than light and standard energy conditions hold. Inside those physical models they study trapped circular orbits, paths where particles or light circle forever inside the sphere. For uncharged light rays, trapping turns out to be fixed by geometry alone. In the other cases, the particle's own charge or energy also matters. Trapping of every particle type occurs across a broad parameter range.
arxiv-2512-10046:
Yan Zhuang leads a team building SimWorld-Robotics, a simulation platform for robots working in cities. Robot foundation models have mostly been developed indoors, on household tasks. Cities are harder: huge spaces, moving pedestrians, and live traffic. Their platform, built on Unreal Engine 5, procedurally generates unlimited photorealistic urban scenes with dynamic people and traffic systems. It also supports several robots that can communicate with each other.

On this platform they build two benchmarks. In one, a robot follows multimodal navigation instructions to a destination amid pedestrians and traffic. In the other, two robots must communicate and cooperate to find each other and meet. The tasks test instruction grounding, three dimensional spatial reasoning, safe long range navigation, collaboration, and grounded communication together. Leading vision language models struggled badly at all of it, lacking the perception, reasoning, and planning cities demand.
arxiv-2512-10246:
Hongyu Li and Shanpu Shen put reconfigurable pixel antennas to work for multi user wireless transmission. A pixel antenna is built from small switchable elements; by choosing which are active, a coding pattern, its radiation behavior can be reshaped on the fly. The authors deploy such antennas at the user devices in a downlink system with multiple transmit antennas. They model the full chain, including the beamspace channels the coded antennas create. The design goal is maximizing the total data rate summed over users, by jointly choosing the transmitter's precoding and each user's antenna coding.

Two cheaper codebook based designs follow: one optimizes the coder online against a precomputed codebook, and a hierarchical version searches that codebook layer by layer for a better complexity trade off. More importantly, the codebook methods keep most of the sum rate while cutting computation sharply.
arxiv-2512-10346:
Ye Cao and co-authors build one shared explanation for the weak decays of two hyperons, the lambda and the charged sigmas, into a nucleon and a pion. Working inside the non-relativistic constituent quark model, they combine several mechanisms at once: direct pion emission, a colour-suppressed internal W emission. And pole terms where an intermediate baryon appears.

Most channels match the measured branching ratios and asymmetry values well inside that single framework. One channel, the lambda decaying to a neutron and a neutral pion, refused to fit until the authors added final state interactions, where the dominant decay route rescatters into it. They also show the pole terms are indispensable, with one intermediate state doing essential work in the sigma channels. And that a dynamical selection rule silences one candidate excited nucleon entirely.
arxiv-2512-10446:
Chiara Boetti, Matthew Nunes, and Marina Knight propose new models for time series that remember their past for a long time. Many fields, from finance to environmental science, produce several linked series whose correlations fade only slowly. Standard long memory models buckle as the number of series grows, because the parameter count rises with the square of the count.

Their two models add a network that records which components are connected, and estimation is adapted to use that structure. The network keeps the parameter space small, so fitting stays fast and stable where older models fail outright on computing grounds. Simulations favoured the new estimates, and the authors demonstrate the models on environmental and financial data, arguing the same machinery suits any field with network-linked, slow-forgetting series.
arxiv-2512-10646: Nicolas Monod proves an eigenfunctional theorem for positive operators, in the spirit of the Krein-Rutman theorem. Where that older result finds an eigenvector for a well-behaved positive operator, his version finds an eigenfunctional, a positive linear map that the operator simply rescales. A more general form gives one joint eigenfunctional shared by a whole family of commuting positive operators. The paper is set to appear in the Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society.
arxiv-2512-10846:
Shounak De and Yakov Landau start a theory of light-ray operators in de Sitter space, the expanding spacetime of an accelerating universe. In flat Minkowski space, one object, the integral of the stress tensor along a light ray, wears many hats at once. It is the energy flux operator, a piece of a conserved charge, the averaged null energy operator. And the light transform of the stress tensor. Unity like that invites generalisation.

In de Sitter space the hats fall apart. The authors show the various flat-space interpretations do not coincide when carried over, but instead define distinct, observer-dependent light-ray operators. They construct four such analogues and compute their matrix elements in a free, conformally coupled scalar theory. Each shows the symmetry and positivity properties its flat-space ancestor would suggest. The forty-two page paper opens a careful programme rather than closing one.
arxiv-2512-11146:
Dror Shvadron, Hansen Zhang, Lee Fleming, and Daniel Gross track what happens to scientists trained in the United States who later leave. Using newly assembled data spanning more than four decades, they find that a quarter of scientifically active American trained STEM doctoral graduates leave the country within fifteen years of graduating. Departure rates are lowest in the life sciences and higher in artificial intelligence and quantum science, and they have stayed stable for decades.

Leaving, however, does not mean the United States stops benefiting. Patents worldwide keep citing these graduates' work, and the American share of those citations remains far larger than the destination country's share, even after migration. The results suggest training foreign scientists pays off for the United States whether they stay or go. The authors frame openness as a durable source of national advantage.
arxiv-2512-11246:
Jeffrey Streets and Xiaokang Wang study a geometric flow on a special class of complex manifolds called Oeljeklaus Toma manifolds. The pluriclosed flow deforms a geometric structure over time, somewhat like heat smoothing a surface, and mathematicians ask whether solutions exist for all time and what shapes they approach. These manifolds are important test cases because they sit outside the more familiar Kähler world.

The authors prove the flow exists globally for any starting data on these manifolds. Under natural conjectured bounds on the flow's behaviour far out, they show that rescaled limits settle down to a torus, a doughnut shaped space. For a related generalised flow they prove refined estimates that support those conjectured bounds. The results extend the understanding of how non Kähler geometries evolve and simplify under geometric flows.
arxiv-2512-11346:
Kalyan Banerjee, Ankurjyoti Chutia, and Azizul Hoque construct infinitely many sets of four real quadratic fields whose class numbers are all divisible by three. The class number measures how badly unique factorisation fails in a number field, and forcing several related fields to share a divisibility property at once is delicate. Results of this kind for tuples of real quadratic fields had not been obtained before.

Their construction produces endless quadruples rather than isolated examples. As an application, the same ideas yield elliptic curves that possess a point of order three in their torsion subgroup, a concrete arithmetic feature prized in curve studies. The work opens a direction on simultaneous divisibility of class numbers, a topic number theorists connect to deep conjectures about how often prime divisors appear in class groups.
arxiv-2512-11446:
Ahmed Mujtaba, Gleb Radchenko, Marc Masana, and Radu Prodan improve the labels used to train drowsiness detectors that watch for yawning drivers. Driver fatigue causes a large share of road crashes, and yawning is an early warning sign. Existing video datasets mark yawns only coarsely in time, and that systematic label noise teaches models the wrong frames.

The team built a semi automated pipeline with human checking to re annotate the YawDD video collection frame by frame, producing YawDD+. Training two established architectures on the refined labels raised frame level accuracy and detection scores over video level supervision. The trained models ran in real time on small in vehicle computers, including entry level edge hardware. Better labels alone, the authors argue, can deliver dependable on device fatigue monitoring without cloud support.
arxiv-2512-11546:
Federico Pennino and Maurizio Gabbrielli challenge the assumption that training a forecasting model on all available sensor data is best. Raw sensor streams are imbalanced and redundant, so many points teach the model nothing new while others dominate unfairly. Instead of tuning the model, they fix it and optimise the composition of its training data, a search for the best training diet.

A large encoder first embeds the unlabelled time series corpus, and clustering partitions it into behaviourally consistent groups, the available ingredients. An optimisation framework then proposes mixture ratios for the groups, builds the corresponding training set, and scores the model trained on it. The search consistently found diets that beat training on the entire dataset, including a marked error reduction on an electric motor dataset. The paper makes a data centric case that less, chosen well, can be more.
arxiv-2512-11746:
Hana Kopecka and Jose Such ask whether a robot face shapes what people expect the robot to say. A robot look is known to sway how users picture its mind. What had not been tested is how looks shape the explanations people expect to hear.

In the study, people saw one of three home service robots, from plainly mechanical to strongly human like. Each person wrote the explanation they would expect for the same robot actions. Most answers gave the robot human like motives in all groups. Still, the more human the robot looked, the more human like the expected explanations grew. Finer trends in plain, non human style answers are also reported.
arxiv-2512-11946:
Pramudita Satria Palar and co-authors propose a sharper way to rank which inputs drive an engineering model. Designers use Partial Dependence Plots to see an input average effect. When inputs interact strongly, that average can hide the real story.

Their metric averages feature importance over Individual Conditional Expectation curves, which trace the effect for each single case, and adds the spread across cases. Math shows the old plot based score is a lower bound of the new one. An extra correlation value flags how interactions bend input output links. Tests on a math function, wind turbine fatigue, and airfoil flow show the new score adds insight that SHAP and Sobol methods miss, while all three views complement each other.
arxiv-2512-12046:
Vittorio Giammarino and Ahmed H Qureshi reframe goal reaching in reinforcement learning through a classic physics equation. In goal conditioned learning, the best value function forms a quasimetric, a distance that need not be symmetric. Earlier quasimetric methods enforced that shape with discrete checks along trajectories.

Their Eik-QRL instead ties learning to the Eikonal equation, a continuous law for wavefront travel times. The switch frees training from full trajectories; sampled states and goals suffice, and unseen goals generalize better. Theory guarantees come with known limits under complex dynamics. A hierarchical version, Eik-HiQRL, posts top scores on offline navigation tests and steady gains on manipulation tasks.
arxiv-2512-12146:
Ayush Vaibhav Bhatti and co-authors run a unified study of deep models facing the open world. Deployed models must accept known classes yet stay wary when brand new ones appear. Two tasks test that nerve: open set recognition and few shot class incremental learning.

On CIFAR-10, three frozen backbones meet four scoring rules for open set tests. CLIP separates known from unknown best, and the Energy score is the steadiest across backbones. For incremental learning, three prototype methods train on 1, 5, and 10 shots per new class. ConCM reaches 84.7 percent at 10 shots with the cleanest confusion pattern, and all methods saturate after 5 shots. Backbone choice and scoring rule, the study shows, steer open world success.
arxiv-2512-12246:
I Putu Andika Bagas Jiwanta and Ayu Purwarianti find video moments and highlights with a language model in a 2025 paper. Users ask in words for a scene, and the model must mark which frames match. Models that print time stamps as text cannot learn directly from frame level scores, since they emit only word tokens.

The new method makes the model print one 0 or 1 per frame, for background or foreground. Training uses segmentation losses on those outputs plus normal language loss. With only 25 frames sampled, the method scored 56.74 HIT@1 on QVHighlights for highlights. It also beat the 35.28 MAP baseline for moment retrieval.
arxiv-2512-12346:
George E Andrews and Aritram Dhar extend a classic partition result in a 2025 math paper. A partition splits a whole number into a sum of parts. Glaisher's theorem says partitions where each part repeats at most m minus 1 times match in count those using no part divisible by m. The m equals 2 case is Euler's famous theorem.

Andrews, Kumar, and Yee had added two new partition functions tied to Euler's case. Lin and Zang extended one of them to Glaisher's setting. Andrews and Dhar now extend the other function, D(n), and prove a matching identity for m equals 3. They also give a new series for Glaisher's product.
arxiv-2512-12846:
Yue Pan and co-authors present the first data release of the Merian Survey, a count of bright satellite galaxies around galaxies like the Milky Way. Their sample has 393 host galaxies at redshifts 0.07 to 0.09. Each host sits at the center of its own dark matter halo.

Using color, size, and other photo based cuts, the team found 793 satellite candidates. About 80 percent of hosts have zero to three large satellites. About 13 percent, plus or minus 4 percent, have two, much like our own galaxy. The results give a firm test for ideas about how small galaxies form and fade.
arxiv-2512-13046:
You-Wei Ding, Yen Chin Ong, and Hao Xu ask how measurement changes the roughness of a quantum path. In quantum theory, paths are not smooth lines; their jaggedness is captured by the Hausdorff dimension. A famous early result set that dimension for free quantum paths.

The authors study what happens when measurements disturb those paths. Measurement is not passive in quantum mechanics, so the fractal character of a path may shift when it is watched. Their work examines those shifts and what they reveal about observation itself. The study links three themes: quantum paths, fractal geometry, and the act of measurement.
arxiv-2512-13246:
Xiaomei Yang and Zhiliang Deng build a q-analogue of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, a sampling method that uses physics-like motion to explore chance distributions. Their version replaces plain calculus with q-calculus, a deformed form where derivatives become special finite differences.

Starting from a Lagrangian, they derive the deformed dynamics and prove its shape structure is preserved. A Jackson-derivative version yields a usable algorithm with a Metropolis correction, and they prove detailed balance, so the target distribution is kept. When q equals one, the method reduces to the classic one. Tests suggest strengths for positive targets that scale by times factors, where it tracked log-scale methods closely.
arxiv-2512-13846:
Roman Krivonos and co-authors search for a wide X-ray halo around the Geminga pulsar with the SRG/ART-XC telescope. Past searches used narrow field telescopes, which can miss a halo of the expected large size. Their wide-field scan images a 3.5 by 3.5 degree region in the 4 to 12 keV band for the first time.

A physical model of particle injection, diffusion, and cooling, tuned to past multiwavelength data, predicts the halo flux. After accounting for a high particle background, they find no significant emission in the target region and set flux upper limits. The limits are up to three times weaker than narrow-field results, but they directly constrain Geminga's ambient magnetic field. Simulations show a 68% detection chance with a 20-day exposure at a 3 microgauss field.
arxiv-2512-14046:
Boyang Li and co-authors present E-Navi, an environmental-adaptive navigation system for drones on resource-constrained platforms. Fixed navigation settings ignore how settings change, wasting computation or degrading flight. Adapting workloads dynamically is hard because scene complexity is hard to quantify.

E-Navi redesigns the perception-planning pipeline to adjust mapping resolution and how often tasks run on the fly. Changes are driven by scores of scene complexity and by the compute actually available. The system deploys flexibly across hardware platforms of varied power. Hardware-in-the-loop and real-world experiments beat the baseline across platforms. Gains reached up to 53.9% reduction in navigation workload and up to 63.8% flight time savings, with more stable speed control.
arxiv-2512-14146:
K Aditya and A Mangalam ask whether tiny dwarf spheroidal galaxies around the Milky Way can host a central black hole, in a 2025 paper. These faint galaxies hold mostly old stars and dark matter, and any central black hole would be hard to see directly.

The authors build mass models with three parts: stars, a dark matter halo, and a central black hole. Star motion data only sets an upper limit, with a 95 percent credible bound below one million solar masses. They then combine their limits with published values to build a single mass versus velocity spread relation. Growth models predicting ten thousand solar mass black holes fit within those limits.
arxiv-2512-14446:
Marco Moriconi gives a geometric proof that the spacetime interval is invariant in a 2025 paper. Invariance means all inertial observers agree on the interval between two events. That agreement is a cornerstone of special relativity, the theory of space and time for moving observers.

The proof rests only on the constancy of the speed of light. It also uses the fact that spacetime is homogeneous and isotropic, meaning it looks the same in every place and direction. The key device is a light rectangle, whose area stays the same across inertial frames. From that simple construction, Moriconi also derives the Lorentz transformations. Those are the standard rules for converting space and time measures between moving frames.
arxiv-2512-14846:
Arth Bhardwaj, Sia Godika, and Yuvam Loonker build a team of AI agents to defend computer networks in real time. Single, central security tools often miss attacks that shift shape and strike on several fronts at once. Their framework, MALCDF, splits the work among four large language model agents with clear roles.

The four agents handle detection, intelligence, response, and analysis, and they talk through a secure layer with coded, shared terms. Their reports map findings to the MITRE ATT&CK catalog, which eases review. On a live stream of 50 records drawn from a known test set, the system reached 90.0 percent detection accuracy with an 85.7 percent F1 score. It beat a lightweight random forest tool and a single model setup, with each event taking 6.8 seconds on average.
arxiv-2512-14946:
Shaoting Feng and thirteen coauthors present EVICPRESS, a system that helps big language models answer faster by managing their memory. Serving models reuse a key value cache of past text, but with many users the cache outgrows fast GPU memory. Older fixes either move cache to slower storage or compress it, each on its own.

EVICPRESS makes both choices together, weighing how compression and eviction for every conversation affect speed and quality overall. A profiling module scores each option with a shared utility function, and a fast heuristic places caches across storage tiers. Risky compression is spared for conversations that suffer most from errors. On 12 datasets and 5 models, the system reached up to 2.19 times faster time to first token at the same quality. The gain matters for busy services that answer many users at once.
arxiv-2512-15146:
Weiqin Wang and three coauthors improve a way to train language models when no labeled answers exist. Test time reinforcement learning uses majority voting among a model's own answers as stand in labels. Voting breeds confirmation bias, though, and gives sparse rewards, which caps the gains.

Their framework, SCOPE, weights pseudo labels by step wise confidence, favoring strong reasoning paths over mere frequency. It also splits the pool of candidate answers into subgroups, balancing quality against diversity, and draws a local consensus from each by repeat sampling. Those varied targets push the model to explore more broadly. Across models and benchmarks, SCOPE beat recent baselines. It gained 13.1 percent in relative terms on the hard AIME 2025 contest and 8.1 percent on AMC, and the code is public.
arxiv-2512-15346:
N. J. Lopez-Alamilla and four coauthors reconstruct the hidden energy landscape of the bacterial flagellar motor, the rotary engine that swims E. coli. The motor turns ion flow across the membrane into rotation, but the friction and energy barriers shaping its torque were poorly known. The team combines single molecule rotation records with stochastic thermodynamics to measure them.

Three methods, all built on the Smoluchowski equation for diffusion in a tilted periodic potential, take steady speed and rotational diffusion data as input. None needs outside torque control or prior knowledge of drag or torque. The methods agree: the potential has about 26 fold symmetry, barriers of 2 to 4 times thermal energy, and an internal friction near 0.1 piconewton nanometer seconds per radian squared. Near the critical tilt, the torque speed relation bends away from the linear guess. The framework should transfer to other stepping molecular motors.
arxiv-2512-16046:
Shu Wan and four co-authors present a river forecasting model in a paper made public on arXiv in 2025, accepted to IEEE Big Data 2025. Predicting streamflow helps managers handle water supply and flood risk. Deep learning models forecast well but often ignore the physical processes that drive rivers, which hurts trust and performance on new conditions.

Their model, CauSTream, learns two causal maps at once: how weather inputs drive runoff, and how water routes between stations. Unlike earlier causal methods, the maps adapt to the data rather than staying fixed. Tested on three major United States river basins at three forecast horizons, CauSTream beat prior state-of-the-art methods, with bigger gains at longer horizons. The learned maps also match known hydrology, giving insight into how watersheds behave.
arxiv-2512-16346:
Shaoshuai Chu and three co-authors sharpen a plasma simulation method in a paper released on arXiv in 2025. Magnetohydrodynamics equations govern conducting fluids like the solar wind, and one rule is sacred: magnetic fields have no sources, so numerical schemes must keep the field divergence-free or errors explode.

Their scheme, LCD-PCCU, builds on a path-conservative central-upwind method that already keeps the field locally divergence-free. The new ingredient is a local characteristic decomposition, which untangles the waves inside the flow before updating it, cutting the numerical smearing that dulls sharp features. A series of standard benchmark tests confirms crisper solutions than the base scheme. Low-dissipation, divergence-free methods matter wherever simulated magnetic fields must stay physical over long runs, from fusion devices to space weather.
arxiv-2512-16446:
Enis Yalcin and four co-authors automate robot teaching in a 2025 arXiv paper, accepted at a 2025 robotics conference. Humanoid robots learn to walk from reward functions, and writing those rewards by hand takes days of expert tuning. Vision-language models can draft rewards, but they are blind to the terrain the robot must cross.

Their framework, E-SDS, pairs a vision-language model with live terrain sensor analysis and example videos to write rewards automatically. On a Unitree G1 humanoid crossing flat ground, gaps, obstacles, and stairs, E-SDS was the only method whose robot managed stair descent. Manually designed rewards and a non-perceptive automated baseline both failed there. Velocity tracking error fell by 51.9 to 82.6 percent across terrains, and reward design time dropped from days to under two hours.
arxiv-2512-17046:
Russell Zimmerman and a large team show attosecond control of squeezed light, a quantum light form with noise squeezed below the standard level in one trait. Squeezed light serves precision measurement, but its squeezing is usually fixed by the material that makes it.

The team modulates the third-order response of a dielectric with strong ultrafast laser fields. Tuning a sub-cycle phase delay between femtosecond input pulses flips the output between amplitude-squeezed and phase-squeezed states. Frequency-resolved homodyne measures then read the full coherency matrix across pulse tones. The work opens quantum light sources whose squeezing can be switched within one cycle of light.
arxiv-2512-17146:
Huixin Zhan introduces SAGE, an agentic auditing frame that probes genomic foundation models for hidden security flaws. Models such as ESM predict variant effects well, but their robustness to adversarial nudges had gone largely unchecked.

SAGE runs an automated loop: it injects soft prompt perturbations, watches model behavior across training checkpoints, computes risk scores such as AUROC and AUPR, and writes structured reports with language model narratives. No change to the audited model is needed. Even top models like ESM2 proved sensitive to targeted soft prompt attacks, with clear performance drops. The work argues that agentic risk auditing belongs in clinical variant pipelines.
arxiv-2512-17546:
Avishek Sarbajna and a team at the Technical University of Denmark couple tiny air cavities, called Mie voids, to excitons in an atomically thin sheet of tungsten disulfide. The voids are formed in tungsten diselenide, a high index semiconductor, and the pairing aims to make the thin material emit far more light.

The coupled structure boosts photoluminescence by up to 600 fold compared with plain tungsten diselenide, and it beams the emission forward with a 2.6 dB gain over off axis directions. A two step fabrication process sets the void diameter and depth on their own, which gives precise control of the resonance. Results like these point toward brighter, more directed light sources built from materials only a few atoms thick.
arxiv-2512-17846:
Carlos Vélez García, Miguel Cazorla, and Jorge Pomares present Planning as Descent, a method for teaching robots to reach goals from past data alone. Instead of learning a policy, their system learns an energy score for whole paths. Paths that are feasible and reach the goal get low energy, and planning means sliding downhill in that landscape.

Training uses hindsight relabeling, so failed tries still teach the system something. At test time, several candidate paths are refined and the best low energy one is chosen. On cube handling tasks the method reached 95 percent success, well above the 68 percent peak of earlier methods, and noisy training data helped rather than hurt.
arxiv-2512-18046:
Ami Pandat, Punna Rajasekhar, Gopika Vinod, and Rohit Shukla build a faster eye for spotting small drones. Drones are tiny, quick, and low in contrast, so standard detectors miss them. Their design tweaks a YOLO network with an attention block and a two way feature ladder to sharpen small object sense.

Training used a fresh set of 28,000 images, and tests added 2,500 local images of very small drones. Older YOLO5 based versions beat newer releases on the speed and accuracy balance here. A squeezed student model scored 0.6573 on the detection scale, 6.51 percent above its teacher, and ran 82.9 percent faster than the base model.
arxiv-2512-18246:
Shiye Lei, Zhihao Cheng, and Dacheng Tao trim the training data for robots that learn by copying. Copy based learning, called behavioral cloning, feeds on huge logs of expert moves, and training on all of them is costly. The team finds a sharp saturation: a small slice of the log already gives nearly the full skill.

The slack comes from a mismatch between test loss and real driving skill. Their Stepwise Dual Ranking method picks a compact slice that favors early moves, high value actions, and rarely seen states. On the standard D4RL test suite, policies trained on the picked slice beat those trained the usual way, with far less data to chew through.
arxiv-2512-18346:
Vishesh Bhardwaj leads a four author team reading feelings straight from brain waves. Head sensors pick up faint electric patterns that track mood as it shifts, which could aid mental health checks and kinder software. Their model reads the ZuCo 2.0 brain data, recorded with 128 channels while people read text with feeling.

A pyramid network pulls out patterns at several scales at once, from brief local flickers to broad waves, and a memory unit then tracks how those patterns unfold in time. The pairing scored 6.88 percent above past methods on the main set. It also held up on two other standard mood data sets, DEAP and SEED, a sign the design travels well.
arxiv-2512-18546:
Alexander Doudkin runs a playful experiment with a serious point: he prompts a language model to act as if it were on drugs. Persona prompts are known to sway model behavior, but psychoactive framings had never been benchmarked carefully. His paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, tests GPT-5-mini on ARC-Challenge questions under four one-sentence personas: LSD, cocaine, alcohol, and cannabis.

Against a sober control accuracy of 0.45, alcohol collapses performance to 0.10 and LSD to 0.19, with cocaine at 0.21 and cannabis at 0.30, all statistically significant. Much of the damage comes from the personas breaking the required answer format. Doudkin calls persona text a few-shot consumable: it can wreck reliability without changing a single model weight. He releases all code and raw results so others can check the work.
arxiv-2512-18746:
Guibin Zhang and seven co-authors let AI agents redesign their own memory. Language model agents already store past trajectories and lessons to improve over time, but the memory architecture itself has always been hand-built and fixed. Their framework, MemEvolve, posted to arXiv in December 2025, evolves the memory design alongside the knowledge it holds.

To experiment fairly, they built EvolveLab, a shared codebase that distills twelve existing memory systems into four modular stages: encode, store, retrieve, and manage. On four hard agent benchmarks, MemEvolve improves frameworks such as SmolAgent and Flash-Searcher by up to 17.06 percent. The memory designs it discovers also transfer across tasks and across different backbone models. The work suggests future agents will tune not just what they remember, but how remembering itself is organized.
arxiv-2512-19046:
Jihua Yang studies a family of cubic Hamiltonian systems, equations that describe motion with a conserved energy. A 1999 result by Cima and co-authors gave an exact form for systems with an isochronous center, a point where all nearby orbits take the same time.

Yang asks how many limit cycles, isolated closed orbits, such systems can produce. The question is a small piece of the weak Hilbert sixteenth problem. He proves the maximum number is set by the degree term in the analysis, and that the bound can actually be reached. That settles the weak problem for this cubic family.
arxiv-2512-19146:
I. Adachi and a very large Belle II author list describe the aerogel ring-imaging detector that identifies particles in the Belle II experiment. Belle II collides electrons and positrons at the SuperKEKB collider in Japan. In its forward region, telling pions, kaons, and protons apart is the detector's job.

The device focuses Cherenkov light rings from a layered aerogel radiator onto sensors close behind it. It separates the three particle kinds across the full energy range of the experiment. The report covers design, operation, and measured performance. By the time of writing, the detector had run through data taking for nearly six hundred inverse femtobarns of collisions.
arxiv-2512-19246:
Moncef Garouani and Ayah Barhrhouj turn hyperparameter tuning from blind search into guided reading. Tuning a model is costly, and knowing which knobs matter, and how they interact, saves most of that cost. Their method, MetaSHAP, learns from history rather than from fresh runs alone.

The history is vast: more than nine million evaluated pipelines. For a given algorithm and dataset, a surrogate model recalls past performance, and Shapley-based analysis scores each hyperparameter and its interactions. The output names which settings deserve attention and the ranges where they bite. Practitioners get directions for tuning, not just a single winning recipe.
arxiv-2512-19746:
Joonsung Kang builds a stats framework from a match between quantum physics and missing data. In quantum physics, the act of looking at a system changes it. In stats, data that are missing not at random hinge on the values no one saw. Both flaws bias what we can learn. His framework aims to infer which way cause flows. The flow may run from system to observation, from observation to system, or both ways.

The method blends several tools. A neural autoencoder holds latent limits in place. Selection models face the missing-data flaw head on. Other parts steady the regression and tune the search. Theory with the method promises a double safety net and stable results. Tests on fake data and on cancer gene and protein data showed less bias. Coverage of the true values was close to what the method claimed.
arxiv-2512-19846:
Francisco Gonçalves, Ryan Bena, and Néstor Pérez-Arancibia propose new steering laws for things that rotate. The laws fit spacecraft and robot joints alike. Most past laws rest on quaternions. Their frame extends the axis-angle view of a rotation, past those older designs. A rotation is given by its axis and its angle. Lyapunov theory certifies that the closed loop settles, for sure, at its one fixed point.

The extra freedom pays off with switching schemes. Such schemes change their rules based on how fast the body spins. In tests and in real-time trials, the new laws settled faster. The trials were high-speed tumble-recovery moves. The new laws also used less control effort than the two rival methods. The work appeared in IEEE Control Systems Letters.
arxiv-2512-20246:
Songnan Gu and co-authors propose an uplink system built from segmented waveguides fitted with pinching antennas. Users send data upward to the network, and the antennas can be positioned along the waveguides to improve reception. They study two working protocols: selecting one segment at a time, or aggregating several segments together.

For each protocol, the authors map out the total data rate on offer under time-division and non-orthogonal multiple access. They also design low-complexity rules for placing the pinching antennas. Numerical results show their design beats standard pinching-antenna systems. Joining segments adds a further gain over using a single segment, at the price of the more involved protocol.
arxiv-2512-20346:
Emilia Majerz, Witold Dzwinel, and Jacek Kitowski speed up simulations of the Zero Degree Calorimeter, a detector in the ALICE experiment at CERN. Detailed physics simulations of particle showers in this detector are slow. Their approach blends physics knowledge into a machine learning model instead of learning from data alone.

The team uses normalizing flows arranged in a teacher-student setup. A new loss function and a scaling rule based on output variability help the model capture shower shapes while ignoring rare artefacts. The resulting simulator beats classic data-driven assimilation methods on accuracy. It also runs hundreds of times faster than earlier flow-based simulators for this detector, a gain that matters for large production campaigns.
arxiv-2512-20746:
Tony Tran and Bin Hu teach tiny devices to spot litter. Trash detection on the TACO dataset must run on microcontrollers and edge hardware, so the detector family has to be both accurate and frugal. Their approach searches architectures iteratively with hardware in the loop, using a once-for-all style supernet built from residual detectors.

Evolutionary search alternates between optimizing the backbone and the neck and head, steadied by a population passthrough mechanism and an accuracy predictor that trims search cost. The resulting TrashDet family spans from about one million to thirty million parameters, trading accuracy for budget smoothly. The largest variant tops prior detectors on the five-class task with far fewer parameters. On a real microcontroller dataset, specialized variants slash energy and latency against the benchmark.
arxiv-2512-21246:
Gaia Ebli, Bianca Raimondi, and Maurizio Gabbrielli compare how younger and older students experience learning with artificial intelligence at their side. Most prior research studied university students in conventional classrooms, leaving school-age learners unexamined. In real programming classes, middle and high school students used AI tools. The researchers measured four factors: experience, clarity, comfort, and motivation. They asked whether the four hang together the same way at both ages.

Correlation analysis combined with text mining says they do not. Middle schoolers rate holistically: all four factors correlate strongly, so a good feeling about one aspect spills into the rest. High schoolers show weak or near-zero correlations, judging each dimension independently, a more differentiated stance. The practical upshot is that AI integration cannot be age-blind: tools and teacher strategies should match the developmental stage, because the very structure of students' perceptions changes with it.
arxiv-2512-21346:
Planning a week of driving in an electric car means weaving appointments, battery range, and charging stops into one schedule. Dominik Köster, Florian Porkert, and Klaus Volbert model that problem for a cross-platform navigation service aimed at individual drivers. Their mixed-integer formulation spans several days, respecting battery capacity, charger types, and the time windows of each appointment.

Exact solving does not scale to daily use, so they race three metaheuristics against it: tabu search, adaptive large neighborhood search, and ant colony optimization. Generated test ensembles estimate how each behaves under realistic conditions, benchmarked against exact results from Google's OR-Tools. The comparison tells navigation builders which heuristic earns its place when charging stops must inconvenience drivers as little as possible.
arxiv-2512-21546:
Wenyu Gao and Fan Xu work in homological algebra, on stability conditions and Harder-Narasimhan filtrations for triangulated categories. Such filtrations sort the objects of a category into layers, from most to least stable, and they feed into derived Hall algebras, which count extensions between objects.

Much of the theory was built for abelian categories. Gao and Xu extend several of its pillars to triangulated categories: Reineke inversions, wall-crossing formulas, and Joyce's special elements. The results arrange themselves into a diagram of exactly the same shape as in the abelian case. As an application, they characterize every stability condition on the derived category of the A2 quiver, one of the smallest nontrivial examples.
arxiv-2512-21646:
Yi Zhang, Apurav Tambe, and Zhao Pan ask how large a droplet can grow on a horizontal fiber before it falls off. Droplets clinging to fibers appear everywhere, from fog nets to filters, and the maximum stable volume sets the limit of what a fiber can hold. Existing models capture poorly how that limit depends on fiber size and surface wettability.

The authors combine numerical simulations with experiments to map the maximum volume across conditions. From the data they build a semi-empirical model, validated against measurements and reference simulations. The model reveals a new scaling: once the maximum volume is normalized properly, it depends only on the contact angle, the angle the droplet's edge makes with the surface. The rule holds from sub-millimeter fibers to the flat-surface limit, across all droplet shapes. It gives engineers a quick design check for fiber-based water capture and coating.
arxiv-2512-22046:
Prompt-driven video segmentation foundation models such as SAM2 are entering autonomous driving and digital pathology, but their backdoor risks were unexplored. Zongmin Zhang and colleagues show classic attacks like BadNet largely fail here, with success rates below five percent. Clean and triggered samples produce aligned encoder gradients, while attention stays on the prompted object.

Their BadVSFM framework attacks in two stages: first teaching the encoder trigger-specific features, then training the decoder to map triggered prompt representations to an attacker-chosen mask while clean behavior is preserved. Across five models and two datasets the backdoor is strong and controllable, ablations confirm both stages are needed, and five representative defenses remain largely ineffective.
arxiv-2512-22346:
Sroyon Sengupta works in analytic number theory, proving a general duality between prime ideals in number rings at arbitrary order.
