The result extends earlier work by Alladi and by Sweeting and Woo on lower-order dualities. Prime ideals are the number-field analogue of usual prime numbers, and dualities of this kind trade one hard counting sum for another, easier one.

As a first application, Sengupta uses the second-order duality to derive a new formula for the Chebotarev density, a central measure of how prime ideals split in extensions. The formula involves sums of a generalized Möbius function against the prime ideal counting function. Two estimates of such sums follow as further applications. A closing discussion treats the duality in a slightly more general setting.
arxiv-2512-23546:
Text-to-image generators can produce unsafe pictures when prompts steer them badly, and simple defenses such as keyword blacklists are easy to dodge. Zongsheng Cao and five co-authors present PurifyGen, a safety method that cleans the prompt itself before generation, without retraining or changing the model's weights.

First, each word of the prompt is scored by its semantic distance to known toxic and clean concepts, flagging risky tokens without relying on exact keyword matches. Then a dual transformation pushes flagged embeddings away from the toxic concept space and toward the clean one, preserving the prompt's intent while removing harmful meaning. Only risky tokens get replaced. Across five data sets, PurifyGen cut unsafe outputs more than current methods and rivaled approaches that need extra training.
arxiv-2512-23646:
Keda Tao and five co-authors built OmniAgent, a system that answers questions about videos by actively looking and listening rather than passively scanning frames. Models that read both audio and video often miss fine cross-modal detail and struggle to align the two streams. The arXiv record's title governs here; the catalog entry folds in the system's name differently.

OmniAgent plans its own investigation, calling specialized single-modality tools when needed and concentrating attention on task-relevant cues. Its audio-guided strategy works coarse to fine: sound first localizes interesting moments in time, then visual reasoning examines them closely. Without any training, the agent beat leading open and closed models on three audio-video benchmarks by margins reported between ten and twenty percentage points of accuracy.
arxiv-2512-23946:
Tien-Tai Nguyen proves that a still viscous fluid with slippery walls can be unstable in the strong, nonlinear sense. The setting is the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with Navier slip boundary conditions, and the equilibrium in question is the trivial state of rest. Linear analysis comes first: using an operator method from earlier work, he shows the linearized equations admit finitely many normal mode solutions, the seeds of instability.

Nonlinear instability is then proved by adapting a framework developed for viscous boundary layers, producing two solutions that separate from each other by an escaping time. The route differs deliberately from an earlier treatment of the same problem by Ding, Li, and Xin. Results like this delimit where slip-boundary fluid models can be trusted to stay near equilibrium and where perturbations must grow.
arxiv-2512-24046:
Xiaomei Yang, Jiaying Jia, and Zhiliang Deng tackle an inverse heat problem. They want to recover a Robin coefficient that changes over time. The coefficient describes how heat leaves a surface. Such recovery is ill-posed. Small measurement errors can badly distort naive answers.

Their approach is Bayesian and hierarchical. The prior comes from persistent homology. That tool tracks when topological features appear and vanish. The prior thus imposes a global structural constraint. Complex time profiles survive without staircase distortions. Total variation priors cause such steps. Gaussian priors blur the profile instead. The hierarchy also picks tuning values from the data itself. In tests, accuracy matched a standard rival method. The fine multi-scale shape of the coefficient was kept better.
arxiv-2512-24246:
Jie Luo, Wenyu Zhang, Xinming Zhang, and Yuan Fang improve sequential recommendation. Such systems predict what a user will want next. Item side information helps, like category and brand. Three weaknesses persist in current models, though. They gloss over fine timing patterns in timestamps. Noise in interaction histories hurts them. Their fusion machinery is also expensive.

The proposed framework, TASIF, answers all three. A time span partitioning step captures global timing patterns. It is simple and plugs into other models. An adaptive frequency filter denoises the feature sequences. A learnable gate controls that filter. The fusion layer follows a guide-not-mix design. Attributes steer attention without entering the item embeddings themselves. Four public datasets hosted the tests. TASIF beat strong baselines clearly. Training efficiency stayed excellent at the same time.
arxiv-2512-24346:
Svante Linusson and Alperen Özdemir study a growth process on partitions. Partitions of n with largest part at most k correspond to core partitions. A natural measure on them extends the classical Plancherel measure. It arises in the theory of k-Schur functions. The process grows cores while keeping that measure stationary.

Two limits frame the study. As k grows without bound, the measure approaches the classical Plancherel measure. That limit goes back to Vershik and Kerov. Fixed k with growing n is the open direction. The authors conjecture a limit shape near Rost's uniform-growth shape. They prove the behavior is governed by a finite Markov chain. It has k factorial states on the bounded partitions. The chain is also a TASEP on cyclic permutations. Theorems and computation-born conjectures open the topic.
arxiv-2512-24446:
Patrick Wyrod, Ashesh Chattopadhyay, and Daniele Venturi reframe forecasting of chaotic systems. Chaos limits prediction through sensitivity to starting conditions. Unresolved small-scale processes add to the difficulty. Models that generate samples offer a way out by learning distributions of futures. Most still predict one step ahead, conditioned on the last state.

The authors instead learn the joint law of lagged states. Short time windows of the system are modeled as one object. Forecasts then come from marginalizing that joint law. Multistep segments and nonlinear time links are captured natively. A model-agnostic training and inference frame supports the approach. Three metrics assess reliability without ground truth. Ensemble variance, short-horizon correlation, and Wasserstein drift do the work. On the Lorenz-63 system and the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, forecasts beat conditional models. Attractor shape and long-range statistics both improved.
arxiv-2512-24546:
Yuto Nogata compares finite groups that share the same subgroup count profile. A group's zeta function sums over subgroups by order. Two non-isomorphic groups can share that function. No general criterion says when this happens. Nogata studies one family closely: metacyclic p-groups of split type. Each group is set by parameters m, n, and an action parameter k.

With m and n fixed, the question becomes which k values collide. Nogata characterizes the parameter pairs whose zeta functions agree exactly. Presentations of the groups make the counting possible. Subgroups of each order are tallied inside the family. Equality of the resulting Dirichlet series is then decided. The result gives a complete criterion inside this family. Group theorists gain a case where the zeta function's blindness is fully understood.
arxiv-2601-06646:
Sophie Weber and Veronika Sunko show how magnetic fields can select antiferromagnet domains in 2026. Antiferromagnets hold promise for applications in digital logic, they write. Switching their domains, however, has been a stubborn practical challenge.

Magnetic fields do not couple to bulk antiferromagnetic order directly. That is why ordinary fields seem useless for domain control here. They show field-driven switching can be enabled another way. A generic reduction of magnetic exchange at surfaces does the enabling. Surface effects thus unlock what bulk physics forbids in these materials. Their result matters for future low-power logic and memory devices. Condensed matter readers get a mechanism, not just an observation.
arxiv-2601-06746:
Yazhuang Miao and five co-authors find edge modes that can be steered in a 2026 paper. Their chain has a near-repeat pattern and is of a non-Hermitian kind. A fake field runs through it, with a mean of zero and shifts from site to site.

They spot a mode in a gap, hugging one edge, that can be steered. With open ends, the chain maps in exact terms to a Hermitian twin. A gauge change that is not unitary gives that map, they show. The end-open spectrum and growth rates stay the same through the change. The states, though, gain an wrap that rests on the gauge in use. To steer where a wave clings, with no shift in its tones, has clear use. Fake fields turn from a flaw into a knob for wave control.
arxiv-2601-07746:
Purushottam Saha and Diganta Mukherjee sharpen a bound for the card game Rummy, in a 2026 preprint. MinDist is a recent metric measuring how far a Rummy hand sits from a valid declaration. It plays a central role in computer evaluation of hands and in optimal play. Earlier results bounded the MinDist of any thirteen-card hand from one deck by nine.

The authors prove the bound is actually less than seven. A tighter bound narrows the search space for algorithms that grade hands. It also tells players the worst hand is closer to completion than previously shown. Results like this mix combinatorics with practical game analysis. The paper should interest scholars in game algorithms and anyone building Rummy-playing software. It turns a loose guarantee into a sharper one.
arxiv-2601-07846:
JTM Campbell invents a playful classification of whole numbers and studies its patterns. A number is patterned if at least one of its positive divisors appears as a digit in its base-ten form. The definition mixes divisibility with decimal digits, a recreational starting point. Campbell's 2026 preprint studies the first hundred natural numbers under this rule. Frequency, density, and prime versus composite behavior all come under review.

The paper also proposes a generation rule for patterned numbers. Visual shape diagrams along the number line show transitions between patterned and unpatterned numbers. The author frames the idea with structural and quantum algebraic perspectives. Recreational definitions can still expose real structure in the integers. The work should interest readers of recreational mathematics and elementary number theory. It treats a simple digit game with systematic care.
arxiv-2601-07946:
AmirPouya Hemmasian and Amir Barati Farimani rebuild flow fields from compressed data with a coupled diffusion and encoder model. Data-driven reconstruction usually relies on autoencoders that squeeze flow states into low-dimensional codes. Classical variational autoencoders often fail to keep the higher-order statistics of fluid flows under strong compression. Those statistics carry the turbulence structure engineers care about. Their 2026 preprint proposes the coupled approach.

Diffusion models excel at generating realistic fine detail. Coupling one with an encoder may restore what compression discards. Reconstructing full flow fields from few sensors would help wind tunnels, weather models, and design loops. The latent code must still respect the physics of the flow. The paper serves scholars in computational fluid dynamics and machine learning. It targets a known weakness of the standard reconstruction pipeline.
arxiv-2601-08146:
Khumaisa Nur'aini and three co-authors ask whether learned skills move between languages inside a model. Their 2026 arXiv paper addresses low-resource language adaptation, where labeled data is scarce. Full fine-tuning there is unstable, and cross-lingual tuning can cause catastrophic forgetting.

The team proposes circuit-targeted supervised fine-tuning, called CT-SFT. It finds a sparse set of task-relevant attention heads in a proxy-language checkpoint. Scoring uses a label-balanced mean baseline and task-directional relevance, with no counterfactual step. Tuning only those circuits aims to transfer the mechanism, not just the words. The approach targets cheap adaptation that keeps prior knowledge intact.
arxiv-2601-09446:
Ramya Keerthy Thatikonda and three co-authors work on turning plain sentences into formal logic. Their 2026 arXiv paper improves symbolic translation, the step where a language model rewrites a statement in first-order logic. An external solver can then check the logic, giving reasoning that can be verified.

Smaller language models often stumble at this translation. They produce outputs with formatting slips and wrong symbols, which break the solver. The authors aim to cut those errors so small models can still feed a reliable reasoning pipeline. Better translation would bring verifiable logic within reach of cheaper systems.
arxiv-2601-09546:
Wesley Quaresma Cota and Thais Silva do Nascimento count special polynomials tied to an algebra. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with algebras that obey fixed polynomial laws, over a field of characteristic zero. Two spaces matter: multilinear polynomials modulo those laws, and central ones, whose values always land in the center.

The authors study the central cocharacter, which records how each symmetry type shows up in these spaces. The counts encode how fast the spaces grow and how the algebra is built. Knowing them helps sort algebras by the wealth of laws they obey. The paper adds worked-out cases to a theory built on exact sequences.
arxiv-2601-09646:
K. L. Helmes, R. H. Stockbridge, and C. Zhu solve a class of long-term control problems in closed form. Their 2026 arXiv paper treats impulse control and a related singular control problem, averaged over the long run. The system under control is a one-dimensional diffusion with well-behaved boundaries.

The model is driven by a growth process with two revenue sources. Problems of this shape arise in managing renewable resources and in portfolio choice. Explicit solutions are rare in control theory, so a solved class is valuable. Managers can read the best policy straight off the formulas.
arxiv-2601-09746:
Philip Xu, Isabel Wagner, and Eerke Boiten use a team of agents to teach vision-language models new concepts. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents a multi-agent cooperative learning framework. The target problem is cross-modal alignment collapse on out-of-distribution concepts, with few or zero examples.

Four agents, for image, text, name, and coordination, pass structured messages to balance the modalities. The framework adds a context exchange method for few-shot learning and an adaptive balancing mechanism. Working together, the agents anchor new concepts in both words and pictures. That could help models handle novel objects they meet in the wild.
arxiv-2601-09846:
Deepak K. Deo questions whether recently quenched elliptical galaxies are as alone as catalogs claim. His 2026 arXiv paper reassesses the environments of these galaxies across scales. Recently quenched ellipticals are a test case for separating internal quenching from environmental effects.

They are usually classed as isolated central galaxies in low-mass halos. But central-versus-satellite labels and isolation calls vary between group catalogs. Misclassification can badly bias the physics inferred. Deo checks the labels across scales to see how many truly stand alone. The answer shapes what quenching story the data can tell.
arxiv-2601-09946:
Chenxi Qiu works on privacy that scales with how far apart two values are. In this scheme, close values get strong cover. Far values need less. It can keep more use in the data than a flat rule. But fine or smooth value sets make the math hard.

Past best plans build large grids of noise. Those grids cost too much to build for fine sets. Qiu gives a plan based on blends of known plans. It aims to cut loss while it keeps the cost low. The work fits data such as place or score, where values form a fine scale.
arxiv-2601-10246:
Prottay Kumar Adhikary, Reena Rawat, and Tanmoy Chakraborty build an aid for mental health pros. Demand for care is high. The pool of pros is thin. An aid that can back a pro could ease the load. It must act with the care a pro would show.

The aid is named coTherapist. It uses a small language model at its core. The model is tuned on care tasks. It can fetch facts and plan steps like an agent. The aim is help for the pro, not a swap for the pro. The paper sets out how the aid is built and checked.
arxiv-2601-10446:
Adonai Hilário da Silva and co authors tune two qubit gates on a superconducting chip with low power. Such gates link two qubits. They are key to any quantum run. But stray links and drift can spoil them. Noise that shifts in time adds to the harm.

The team pair two tools. A steady drive shields the qubits as they work. A search then finds the least power path to the gate. The shield keeps the true link form firm. It holds the ZZ link that the gate needs. The aim is a true gate at the least drive cost.
arxiv-2601-10646:
Rupak Majumder and Shamik Gupta study synchronization when disorder is annealed and interactions reach past the first harmonic. Synchronization is the pull of many oscillators into one rhythm. Disorder can be quenched, frozen in place, or annealed, shifting over time. In higher-dimensional Kuramoto models, frozen disorder gives odd effects.

With frozen disorder, transitions to sync are smooth in even dimensions and abrupt in odd ones. The authors ask what changes when disorder is annealed instead, and when higher harmonics join the coupling. Two dimensions turn out to be special. Their results refine how physicists predict when shared rhythm starts in noisy systems.
arxiv-2601-10846:
Linjie Yan and co-authors design radar setups that use a reconfigurable intelligent surface to spot hard targets. Low observable targets, with small radar cross-section, are built to slip past radar. An RIS is a surface whose reflection can be tuned in real time. Placed well, it can bounce extra signal toward a hidden target and back.

The paper sets out detection architectures that include the surface as an active partner. The extra path can lift a faint echo above the noise. Design choices cover where the surface sits and how it is tuned during a scan. The work speaks to radar engineers who must find targets that were designed not to be found.
arxiv-2601-10946:
Hiroo Azuma studies Leggett-Garg inequalities for a superconducting qubit in a cavity. Leggett-Garg inequalities test macrorealism, the idea that a system has definite states at all times. Quantum systems can break them. Azuma uses a two-time version, which compares measurements at just two moments. The qubit is a Josephson-junction device coupled to thermal photons.

The model extends an exactly solvable one. In it, the qubit talks to single-mode photons through a coupling built from the Pauli z operator and photon creation and annihilation terms. A magnetic flux threads the junction as well. Exact models let violations be computed cleanly, showing how heat and coupling tune the quantum character of the device.
arxiv-2601-11046:
Shahbaz Alvi and co-authors present OpFML, a pipeline for operational forecasting with machine learning. Machine learning now serves many areas of science, and climate and Earth sciences are no exception. Operational systems must issue forecasts on a schedule, again and again, without manual care. Data-driven models are being deployed for exactly that duty.

A pipeline wraps the model in the plumbing operations need: data intake, checks, runs, and delivery. Without it, a good model stays a demo. OpFML aims to make ML forecasts routine and repeatable for weather and climate services. The work speaks to forecast centers that must trust a model's output every day, not just on paper.
arxiv-2601-11146:
Kewen Bu, Youjun Deng, Yan Jiang, and Kai Zhang study an inverse problem in math. Their 2026 preprint asks what can be learned from spectral data. The unknown is a radial refractive index, a map of how waves bend. The index here may be rough, with low regularity in math terms.

The team asks if the index is fixed by the data alone. Their first result is a warning for a clean case. For smooth pieces joined in steps, the index is not fixed. The special transmission eigenvalues do not pin it down. That holds for modes with radial symmetry. The result marks a clear limit on what such data can prove.
arxiv-2601-11446:
Elias Pescoller and five coauthors couple free electrons to a trapped-ion computer. Their 2026 preprint sets out the proposal in detail. Free electrons can act as quantum probes of other systems. They can grow coherently linked to the systems they probe.

Such links could give access to advanced metrology tools. The team's setup joins an electron microscope to a processor. The processor is a trapped-ion quantum computer in the design. Detection stays non-destructive and quantum-coherent throughout. Data can pile up across many electrons that pass by. Few setups join flying probes to ion qubits at all. The proposal opens a new interface for quantum sensing.
arxiv-2601-11746:
George Mihaila, Suleyman Olcay Polat, Poli Nemkova, Himanshu Sharma, Namratha V. Urs, and Mark V. Albert seek better ways to explain model choices in text tasks. A well known tool, LIME, tests a model by hiding words at random. Those tests can make broken text that no one would write.

Broken text can mislead the small stand-in model that LIME fits. New tools that write fresh text try to fix this flaw. The team's method, named in the title, tests models with smooth, fluent counter cases in place of broken text. Fluent tests should give a more true view of why a model chose its output.
arxiv-2601-11846:
Natalia Tomashenko, Xiaoxiao Miao, Pierre Champion, and a large team report the third VoicePrivacy Challenge, held in 2024. The task is to hide who is speaking in a voice clip. At the same time, the words and the felt mood must stay clear.

Voice anonymization guards privacy in shared speech data. The challenge lets teams match their tools on the same tests. Keeping mood is a fresh stress, since mood helps health and speech tools. The report sums what teams built and how well each tool did on the shared tests.
arxiv-2601-11946:
Kwame Agyei-Baah, Muhammad Rizwanur Rahman, and E. R. Smith frame a neural network route to linear fluid dynamics. Fluid flow rules acts at scales from a breakfast table to cosmic and quantum systems. That vast range is why the field is called a core science.

Their frame rests on convolutional neural networks. Such nets learn traits from grid data, which suits flow fields. A learned tool could solve some flow tasks much faster than step-by-step maths. The work sets out the design and its use for linear flow cases.  The frame tests a fast route to explain text model calls.
arxiv-2601-12146:
Viktor Kjellberg, Miroslaw Staron, and Farnaz Fotrousi study what changes when a language model agent gets a compiler. Models write code well, but the code may fail to build or miss quality bars. Many agent tools add steps to plan before they write code.

A compiler gives hard, fast feedback on each draft. The team weigh how that feedback shifts agent acts and results. A tight build loop could cut broken code in auto tools. The work tests that gain in program tasks.  Build checks give a clear pass or fail at each step.
arxiv-2601-12446:
Angelo Russomanno studies how operators spread in disordered spin chains. A spin chain is a line of quantum spins, and disorder means the links vary at random. As time passes, an operator that starts small can grow and spread. How fast and how far it spreads tells us about the phase of the system.

Russomanno adds a new measure of operator complexity to the known one. The old measure is operator mass. The new one is operator length. Both come from writing the time evolved operator in the Pauli basis. He computes exact marginals with a matrix product operator method. That exact route keeps the new measure on firm ground.
arxiv-2601-12646:
Ha-Chi Tran writes on liability law in the age of artificial intelligence that crosses borders. AI systems can cause harm in many countries at once, while law stays bounded by place. The rapid growth of AI has exposed deep flaws in risk governance. Much work has gone into spotting and preventing harm before it happens.

Far less work treats what should happen after harm occurs. That ex post side covers liability, compensation, and blame. Tran argues this side of responsible AI scholarship is underdeveloped. Courts and lawmakers need rules for harms that no single state contains. The paper maps that gap and presses for stronger legal responses.
arxiv-2601-12746:
Eli Berger, Daniel Carter, and Paul Seymour characterize digraphs where every directed cycle can share one weight. A digraph is weightable if real weights on its edges make each directed cycle total one. That is a strong global condition linking all cycles at once. The team give several equivalent conditions for this property.

One version uses only zero and one weights with the same property. Another forbids a subdivided double cycle as a subdigraph. A third concerns triples of vertices and the cyclic order of cycles through them. Equivalent characterizations let researchers test weightability in many ways. The work sits in structural graph theory, a field Seymour helped shape.
arxiv-2601-12846:
Hyungkee Yoo takes a diagrammatic approach to the three page index of a link. A link is a tangle of closed loops in space, a core object in knot theory. The three page index measures how complex a link representation must be in a three page book. A book embedding spreads a link across pages meeting at a spine.

The index admits a linear upper bound in terms of the crossing number. Equality in that bound is realized by the Hopf link, the simplest true link. Diagrammatic tools can make such invariants easier to compute. Sharp bounds tie a new invariant to a classic one. The work helps knot theorists judge what the three page index really measures.
arxiv-2601-13046:
Lin Ma, Xiaodong Yang, Xinjia Zhou, Gang Sun, and Zhen Wei Wu study odd flow traits in metal glass forming liquids. Plain fluids such as water show many strange traits. Past work ties some of those traits to sharp swings near a point where two liquid forms would meet.

The open point is if metal glass liquids hide a like point. These liquids pack atoms in tight groups, which sets them apart from water. The authors argue that a Griffiths like zone can explain the odd change seen in how these liquids move. In such a zone, rare local spots act far from the bulk norm. Their claim gives a fresh frame for tests on how metal glasses form and flow.
arxiv-2601-14146:
Federico Binda, Tommy Lundemo, Alberto Merici, and Doosung Park study a lifting problem in algebraic K-theory in 2026. The setting is semistable schemes, a class of spaces with mild singularities. They establish a semistable generalization of the Beilinson-Bloch-Esnault-Kerz fiber square. That square relates algebraic K-theory to logarithmic topological cyclic homology.

They prove the obstruction to lifting K-theory classes is governed by one map. That map is the Hyodo-Kato Chern character. K-theory tracks vector bundles and their twists over a space. Clear obstructions tell algebraists exactly where a lift can fail.
arxiv-2601-14446:
Ye Yuan, Can Chen, Zipeng Sun, and their co-authors use diffusion language models for design search in this 2026 paper. Offline black-box optimization aims to find optimal designs from a fixed dataset of designs and labels. No new tests can be run during the search. Such cases arise in DNA sequence design and robotics, where labeled data are scarce.

The team's tool is a diffusion large language model, a model that builds text by gradual denoising. They adapt it to propose strong designs from the offline set alone. Readers get a new way to squeeze value from small, costly datasets where each label was hard to earn.
arxiv-2601-14546:
Fangzheng Tian, Debasis Ganguly, and Craig Macdonald study retrieval-augmented generation in this 2026 paper. In RAG, a language model answers with help from retrieved documents. Answer quality depends largely on the context those documents carry. A key challenge is predicting that quality before the answer is graded.

The authors define two prediction tasks within RAG. One predicts retrieval utility: the performance gain from using context, versus generation without context. The other predicts final answer quality, in terms of correctness and relevance. Readers get tools to forecast when retrieval will help a model, and when it may be dead weight.
arxiv-2601-14646:
James Tian studies a tree construction in operator theory in this 2026 paper. He works with iterated weighted residual splittings. They are generated by a positive operator on a Hilbert space, together with a finite family of contractions. Each splitting step splits off a weighted residual piece. Repeated steps form a tree of such pieces.

The paper's title names its focus: boundary disintegration for weighted residual energy trees. Disintegration here means breaking a whole into its boundary parts in a controlled way. The abstract in the evidence pack gives the formal setup only. Readers get a technical study of how the energy in these trees sits at their edges.
arxiv-2601-14946:
Honglin Zhou, Xinman Ye, and a team of co-authors study spin waves in a family of nickel-based crystals. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with bilayer nickelates doped with rare-earth elements. These materials can carry current with no loss at high temperatures.

Spin fluctuations are widely thought to be the glue that pairs electrons in such materials. That pairing is what lets the current flow freely. The team probes those fluctuations in the doped bilayer crystals. Their work adds fresh data to the long search for what drives this kind of high-temperature superconductivity.
arxiv-2601-15046:
Nils Klement, Veronika Eyring, and Mierk Schwabe ask why adding quantum parts to a physics-based network helps. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with physics-informed neural networks. Such networks aim to solve partial differential equations, the math behind climate models, material science, and much more.

These networks are promising but still lag behind classic numeric solvers. Quantum-enhanced versions claim an edge. The authors probe where that edge comes from. Knowing the source of the gain matters most for fields that lean on fast, trusted equation solving, from weather and climate work to finance.
arxiv-2601-15146:
Björn R. Severitt, Yannick Sauer, Nora Castner, and Siegfried Wahl guard against wrong clicks made by the eyes alone. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with gaze-based interaction in virtual reality. Gaze control is hands-free and feels natural, but stray looks can trigger inputs no one meant.

The team builds a real-time error prevention system. A temporal convolutional network autoencoder watches the gaze signal as it unfolds. It flags odd patterns in gaze dynamics during selection tasks. Flagged selections can then be stopped in time before they cause an error in the scene.
arxiv-2601-15346:
Edwige Tolla states conjectures about what happens when consecutive primes are added up. Her 2026 arXiv paper deals with the additive properties of the prime numbers. Start at any prime and add the next ones in a row, for an odd count of terms.

Those block sums have their own patterns. Tolla studies when the sums are themselves prime. She also studies the broader additive behavior of such blocks. The paper sets out conjectures, claims that fit the computed cases but await proof. Number theorists can test and attack them in turn.
arxiv-2601-15446:
Lily Wang and four co-authors study limits on quantum error-correcting codes in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their focus is quantum low-density parity-check codes, known as qLDPC codes. These codes can be run by measuring only low-weight checks. That trait suits noisy quantum hardware well. It also makes the codes central to the push for machines that resist noise.

One basic question stays open in this field. How do limits on check weight cap what a code can achieve? The paper takes up that question directly. Its title promises both bounds and examples. Bounds mark what no code of this kind can beat. Examples show what can in fact be built. Together they map the room left for better code design.
arxiv-2601-15546:
Charles B. Delahunt and three co-authors question a standard habit in machine learning in a 2026 arXiv paper. Builders must make many choices while training a model. They pick hyperparameters and decide when to stop. The usual guide is validation loss. That means scoring the model with the training loss on held-out data. The authors argue this guide fits clinical work poorly.

Their title states the fix: use metrics tailored to the clinic. A model's loss can improve while its clinical value stalls, or the reverse. Choosing checkpoints by clinical performance changes which model ships. The paper shows such tailored metrics improve a model's clinical performance. For medical AI, the lesson is broad. Measure what care teams need, not just what training optimizes by default.
arxiv-2601-15746:
Einav Berin and Hillel Aharoni design woven fabrics that change shape in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their fabrics are smart: the threads shrink unevenly by design. Weaving them tightly imposes strong local rules on how the material deforms. Those rules reduce the local geometry to one scalar degree of freedom. That simplification is the heart of their framework. Inverse design works backward from a target shape to the thread pattern that yields it.

Smart fabrics could serve wearables, soft robotics, and adaptive structures. A sheet that morphs on cue needs exactly this kind of planning tool. Geometry, rather than trial and error, drives their approach. For materials designers, a single scalar control per point is a gift. It turns a complex weave problem into something tractable.
arxiv-2601-16046:
Junha Lee, Eunha Park and Minsu Cho teach robots to grasp with the hand from words. Their 2026 preprint, named DextER, starts from a hard task. A robot hand must grasp in ways that fit the task, the shape in 3D, and fine hand touch. Past vision and language tools map views straight to grasp values. They skip clear thought about how the hand will touch the thing.

DextER adds that thought step in the chain. The model first works through the touch and force at play. It then picks grasp values that fit the words and the shape. Step by step thought should give grasps that are safer and more true to the task. The work targets hands with many joints.
arxiv-2601-16246:
Jaume de Haro and Emilio Elizalde rebuild the late view of Einstein on gravity. Their 2026 preprint goes back to the base of General Relativity. Key points are the true sense of the line term ds squared. The same weight rests on the Equivalence Principle, the rule that gravity and speed up act as one. The pair trace how Einstein read space form in his late work.

They argue his first reads of these points later shifted. A clean rebuild aims to set the late view in plain terms. That view shapes how gravity maths is taught and used. The work is a close read of past texts and proofs.
arxiv-2601-16546:
Michael Strunk studies rim smooth of weak solves to growth systems with odd growth. His 2026 preprint deals with systems where growth rests on slope size. Growth terms have a two grade form, named p q growth. Such terms break the plain rules used for one grade growth. The zone has smooth, bent rims in his study.

Local weak solves may act wild at such rims by past tales. Strunk asks which solves stay smooth up to the rim. Smooth to the rim lets teams trust solves for real flows. It also sets which rim shapes are safe for use. The work is a pure growth maths study.
arxiv-2601-16746:
Long chats with code agents grow slow and dear in cost. Each step adds text to the agent's view. Fees and lag rise as that view bloats. Past trims used fixed scores to cut text. Those cuts miss what the task at hand needs. A 2026 preprint builds a trim tool that adapts on its own.

The tool learns which parts of code text count for the task. It keeps those parts and drops the rest. The agent then works with a lean view. Lean views cut fees and speed each step. They may also cut slips caused by stale or stray text.
arxiv-2601-18246:
Giorgio Guercio and co-authors shape light with a patterned surface made of a nonlinear crystal alloy. Their 2026 preprint studies AlGaAs metasurfaces. Dielectric metasurfaces are strong platforms for making new harmonics and for steering wavefronts at the nanoscale. One shaping route uses geometric phase, where the pattern's orientation sets the phase of the light. The authors bring a tensor-driven view to that geometric phase in a nonlinear setting.

A tensor view captures how the response changes with direction and polarization. That gives designers more knobs for harmonic wavefronts. Such control serves imaging, holography, and optical computing. The work refines a key design rule for nonlinear flat optics.
arxiv-2601-18646:
Hongliang Jiang draws facts about a quantum field world from a famed string maths of waves in curved space. The field world sits on one bank of a deep pair: on the next bank, strings move in a space that curves like a bowl with a twin sphere. A wave score from the string bank is said to hold all the facts of the field bank. Jiang works out that score for the case at hand.

From the score he pulls the core facts of the field world: how its fields weigh and how they meet. Those facts are hard to get from the field bank by a straight path. A new path by the string bank thus opens a fresh road to them. The work is a brick in the proof that the pair is true. It also gives field staff new counts to test in their own frame.
arxiv-2601-18746:
Alessia Stefano and three colleagues join two ways to make pairs of light bits in one chip, and they show the two ways can clash as waves. Each way bends light in a crystal, but one uses a two-step rule and the next a three-step rule. In most work the two ways are used one at a time. Here they run at once on the same chip.

When they run as one, their waves can add or wipe each other out. That clash is a true quantum one, not a mere clash of beams. It gives a dial: by a shift of phase, staff can steer the pairs that come out. Such a dial could serve chips that route light bits for quantum nets. It is a new kind of hand on a key part of those nets.
arxiv-2601-18846:
Urban Skvorc and six colleagues ask if language models can design fresh test tasks for search tools that hunt best plans. A good test set needs tasks of many forms, so a tool can't ace it by one trick. The main set in use has a thin range of forms. That thin range can hide a tool's weak spots. The team put models in a loop that breeds new tasks gen by gen.

Each new task must hold set traits of its form: how rough its land runs, how many peaks it has, and where they sit. The loop grades each task on those traits and keeps the ones that fit. A bred set could be both wide in form and strict in traits. Such a set would make tool grades far more hard to game. It would also let teams build tests for the land forms they care about.
arxiv-2601-18946:
Toon Van de Maele and three co-authors model how the brain reuses old frames for new events. A schema is a broad pattern drawn from past events that share a shape. Such frames may let people and animals learn fast, slot new facts into old frames, and bend their acts to new settings.

Yet how schemas form and get used, in code and in the brain, stays unclear. The team ties schema based active inference to fast learning gains. They also link it to how the front of the cortex codes broad structure, giving the old idea a testable form.
arxiv-2601-19346:
Junhao Wei and a large team upgrade a sparrow inspired search method with geometry for drone path planning. Metaheuristic methods, modeled on nature's tricks, are widely used for hard optimization because they need no gradients. The sparrow search algorithm mimics how sparrows forage and flee danger.

Their geometric variant, GeoSSA, sharpens that search for drone routes and for engineering design problems. A drone path must dodge obstacles, save energy, and stay smooth all at once. The same holds for many design tasks with a clash of goals. Better general optimizers earn their keep wherever many goals and hard limits meet.
arxiv-2601-19446:
Yalin Luo and three co-authors segment two key shapes in birth ultrasound to track how labor is going. The pubic symphysis and the fetal head must both be outlined to judge labor's progress and spot delivery risks early. The task is hard: classes are imbalanced, borders are fuzzy, and the images are noisy, with too few labeled examples.

Their framework pairs two student models with a teacher and help from the Segment Anything Model. Semi supervised learning lets unlabeled scans teach as well. Reliable outlines during birth could back clinicians where expert sonographers are scarce.
arxiv-2601-19746:
Nahid Sultana, M. M. Rizvi, and I. B. Wadhawan build a model for sharing irrigation water wisely. Water managers must balance farm output against groundwater sustainability and the flow rivers need to stay alive. Rainfall varies and the climate is uncertain, which makes the balance harder. The authors present a multiobjective optimization model for this allocation problem.

The model jointly decides which crops to plant, how much groundwater to pump, and how much flow to release for the environment. It keeps the plan economically and hydrologically feasible. A case study grounds the model in a real setting. Tools like this help regions farm productively without draining their aquifers. The approach suits water-stressed areas worldwide.
arxiv-2601-19846:
Qian Huang, Christian Rohde, and Ruixi Zhang prove that a simpler system can stand in for the equations of incompressible flow. The incompressible Navier-Stokes equations govern slow, dense fluids. The authors study a two-parameter hyperbolic relaxation system that approximates them. It blends first-order relaxation with the artificial compressibility method.

Starting from tiny perturbations of the initial velocity, they prove convergence. Both velocity and pressure approach the Navier-Stokes limit as the parameters vanish. The proof builds an intermediate affine system to control the error. The result is stated for the three-dimensional case, the hardest and most relevant. Rigorous limits justify using relaxed systems in computation, where they are often easier to solve.
arxiv-2601-19946:
Nikhil Raghav, Avisek Gupta, Swagatam Das, and Md Sahidullah work on speaker diarization, the task of marking who spoke when in a recording. Unsupervised diarization gets no labelled examples and no pretraining to lean on. That makes it hard, but the payoff is a system that works on any new recording collection.

Their method builds a sparse graph from speaker embeddings. Multiple kernels measure similarity between voices in complementary ways. The graph then feeds spectral clustering to carve the recording into speaker regions. A key observation concerns how those kernel similarities should be combined. Accurate diarization underpins meeting transcripts and media archives. The work pushes the label-free end of the field.
arxiv-2601-20146:
Claudio Hernández-Vera and a large team map where complex organic molecules sit. They work in the Horsehead nebula, a cloud of gas and dust shaped like its name. Such molecules are seen as steps toward the chemistry that precedes life. How they form is still unclear, above all where ultraviolet light is strong.

Ultraviolet light was once expected to destroy these molecules quickly. Yet they are found in regions bathed in that light, called photodissociation regions. The team reads the spatial pattern of the organics as signposts of chemistry driven by atomic carbon. The map helps test how hardy carbon chemistry can be near bright stars.
arxiv-2601-20446:
Yusei Fujimaru and nine colleagues simulate the remnants of Type Ia supernovae in three dimensions and predict their X-ray spectra. These explosions of white dwarfs serve as standard candles for measuring cosmic distances. Yet recent work shows a diversity of progenitor systems and explosion mechanisms behind them.

The authors run hydrodynamic simulations of the expanding remnants and synthesize the X-ray light they should emit. Comparing those spectra with telescope data can reveal which explosion path a given remnant took. That in turn tests whether all Type Ia events are alike enough to trust as distance markers.
arxiv-2601-20546:
Kumiko Nakajima, Jan Zuiderveld, and Sandro Pezzelle evaluate creativity in large language models using human-based methods grounded in creativity theory. Models are increasingly used for verbal creative tasks. Yet earlier assessments rest weakly on human creativity research and are hard to interpret.

The widely used Divergent Association Task measures only novelty. It ignores appropriateness, a core part of what makes an idea creative rather than merely odd. The authors move beyond divergent creativity alone. Better grounded measures would help buyers and researchers judge what models can truly contribute to creative work.
arxiv-2601-20646:
Zhejian Yang, Songwei Zhao, Zilin Zhao, and Hechang Chen present TGSBM, a transformer-guided stochastic block model for link prediction. Link prediction powers recommendation, search, knowledge graph completion, and collaboration forecasting. Large networks are hard: they hold hundreds of thousands of nodes and edges, with overlapping communities that change over time.

Stochastic block models capture community structure; transformers capture rich patterns in data. Guiding one with the other aims at both structure and flexibility. Better link prediction improves friend and content suggestions, and helps forecast which scientific teams will form. It is built for the web as it is, not as we might wish it to be.
arxiv-2601-20746:
Eduardo Souza, Rafael Leite, and Andre Souza study the food web of Chesapeake Bay. Their 2026 paper treats the bay as a complex network. Chesapeake Bay is one of the largest estuaries in the United States. Its web of who eats whom has thirty-six trophic components. All of them are linked to each other in some way.

The team analyzes these links with network methods. Their focus is robustness: how the web holds up when energy flow is cut past a set level. Such a cut mimics stress, like the loss of a food source. The study maps which parts of the web bear the most strain. It gives ecologists a view of where the bay's food web is strong and where it is thin.
arxiv-2601-20846:
Jamie Hathaway, Alireza Rastegarpanah, and Rustam Stolkin teach a robot skill in simulation and move it to the real world. Their 2026 paper concerns sim-to-real transfer for reinforcement learning policies. The test task is robotic cutting. Learning in simulation is cheap and safe. But the gap between simulated and physical systems blocks deployment. Real-world samples are also scarce.

Their approach is end-to-end and example-based. It uses neural stylisation to make simulated experience look more real. The policy then transfers with less shock. Cutting is a hard test: contact forces shift fast and materials vary. Success here suggests the method can handle other contact-rich tasks. The work speaks to factories that want trained robots without costly real-world trials.
arxiv-2601-21146:
Francesco Paladino, Shulu Li, and Edward Lee present a simple rule that unifies many classic timing methods. Their 2026 paper introduces maxwait, a coordination rule for distributed time-sensitive systems. Such systems must balance timing needs against consistency. Delays and sync errors make that balance hard. Maxwait makes the trade-offs explicit. Each node waits a set time before it acts on stamped events.

The authors show the rule subsumes classic methods. It covers PTIDES and Chandy-and-Misra protocols, with or without null messages. It also covers Jefferson's Time-Warp and Lamport's fault detection by time. One rule that covers so many is a real economy. The rule enables real-time behavior in cyber-physical systems. It gives builders a single knob for safety and speed.
arxiv-2601-21846:
Konstantinos Varsos, Adamantia Stamou, George Stamoulis, and Vasillios Siris look for ways to save energy across information and communication networks. Energy demand from these systems keeps surging. Providers need users to accept greener choices, such as adaptive bitrate streaming, without feeling that quality has dropped.

Their 2026 preprint introduces an approach built on gamified incentives, rewards and game-like prompts that nudge users toward energy-efficient behavior. It also models how users decide whether to accept such incentives. Managing services with energy in mind could cut a real share of global electricity use. Since networks and data centers run around the clock whether anyone is watching or not.
arxiv-2601-22246:
Ya Jiang, Massieh Kordi Boroujeny, Surender Suresh Kumar, and Kai Zeng tackle proof of who wrote a text in the age of chatbots. Their 2026 preprint, MirrorMark, hides a mark in model output that can carry more than a yes-or-no sign. Past marks could warp the text or prove too weak to find.

Their mark leaves the word choice odds just as they were, so the text reads the same. Yet the mark can still hold a short code with more than one bit. Strong, clean marks help firms trace text back to a model. They also help fight false claims of authorship.
arxiv-2601-22346:
Chris Mascioli, Satyam Goyal, and Mithun Chakraborty built a transformer that splits goods that cannot be cut. Their 2026 preprint, FairFormer, tackles fair division: who gets what when each person values the items in their own way. No money changes hands, so the split itself must feel fair.

FairFormer reads items and people as loose sets, not fixed lists. It then gives each item a set of odds for who should get it, all in one pass. The design trades pure gain against envy, the sense that a peer got more. It offers a fast, learned path to fair splits.
arxiv-2601-22746:
Pingping Liu and a large team built UrbanMoE, a sparse mixture-of-experts frame that profiles city zones across many tasks at once. Region profiling guides planning and resource use. Their 2026 preprint notes that most tools do one task at a time, missing how a zone's traits interlock.

Their frame mixes data of many kinds and routes each zone to expert sub-models. Joint profiling should catch links a single-task tool would miss. Cities could then plan housing, transit, and services as one problem. The work fits the multi-faceted truth of urban life. It is built for breadth.
arxiv-2601-22846:
Guy Shtotland extends a famous bridge between algebra and geometry to a new symmetric setting. The Kazhdan–Lusztig picture links the Hecke algebra of a p-adic group with the geometry of its dual group. That link was a key step in proving the Deligne–Langlands conjectures on smooth representations.

Here the setting is a quotient involving general linear and symplectic groups, a classic symmetric pair. A relative version of the isomorphism would organize representations in this paired world. Such results deepen the Langlands program, which unifies large parts of modern mathematics.
arxiv-2601-23046:
Keitarou Matsumoto and eight co-authors explain the X-ray sources seen in a giant solar flare. The flare, classed X7.1, erupted on October 1, 2024, in active region 13842. Two space telescopes viewed its hard X-rays from different angles, giving a stereoscopic picture.

They match those views with a data-constrained simulation of the Sun's magnetic field in three dimensions. The aim is to find the structures that accelerate particles during the flare. Understanding big flares helps forecast space weather that can harm satellites and power grids. Stereoscopic views from two observatories give depth, letting the team place X-ray sources in the flare's three-dimensional structure.
arxiv-2601-23146:
Ahmed Farag Ali counts quantum states in de Sitter space from an observer's point of view. De Sitter space models a universe with steady accelerated expansion. Following Maldacena's observer-centered approach, the count depends on where the observer sits.

The observer is modeled as a heavy worldline at the equator carrying an SU(3) clock, an internal quantum marker. State counting here is relational: it depends on the clock and path chosen. Such frameworks probe how gravity and quantum theory fit together in an expanding universe. An observer-dependent count reframes entropy in de Sitter space as something measured relative to a worldline, not absolutely.
arxiv-2603-01646:
Lizhe Wan and Jiaqi Yang prove that two-dimensional hydroelastic waves can be steered exactly in this 2026 work. Such waves run on a fluid topped by a thin elastic sheet that bends with the flow. Control comes from outside pressure applied on a chosen patch of the surface.

Working in a periodic setting, they show exact controllability for small start and end states. Exact means the system can be driven from one state to the other, not merely close to it. The pressure patch may be any non-empty open set, however small or placed. The drive can also finish in an arbitrarily short time, a strong form of the claim. Results like this anchor control theory for coupled fluid and elastic systems, where free surfaces move with the flow itself.
arxiv-2603-01746:
Alexandru Manole and Laura-Silvia Diosan test whether learning two linked car tasks at once beats learning each alone. Their 2026 work uses car make and model, a natural hierarchy where each model sits under one make. Most deep learning ignores such structure and trains a lone specialist per task.

The pair compare parallel and cascaded multi-task designs across image networks and transformers. They vary dropout rates and loss weights to see when shared learning helps or hurts. Tests run on two known car photo benchmarks with many makes and models. Multi-task learning helps the image network in almost all settings tried. On the larger, messier benchmark, both model types gain a lot, which supports hierarchy-aware training for fine-grained sorting tasks.
arxiv-2603-01846:
Mengchu Cai, Hai-Yang Du, Xiangyu Jiang, and colleagues from the CLQCD Collaboration pin down bottom quark traits with lattice simulations. Their 2026 work computes the bottom quark mass plus masses and decay constants of bottom mesons. Precision here sharpens probes of matter-antimatter asymmetry, a deep open question in physics.

The team uses an anisotropic clover fermion scheme for the heavy quark on many lattice ensembles. Sixteen ensembles span six lattice spacings and a range of light quark masses. A non-perturbative renormalization method is built and checked through its own predictions. That framework handles the physical bottom mass even on coarse lattices, with errors that shrink in the continuum limit. Using a known bottomonium mass as input, they extract the bottom mass with tight uncertainty. They also give the full S-wave meson spectrum and decay constants for all such mesons.
arxiv-2603-02146:
Guanzheng Chen, Michael Qizhe Shieh, and Lidong Bing improve long-document reasoning in this 2026 paper. Reward-based training helps models reason, but it often fails on long inputs. The usual reward grades only the final answer, which gives weak guidance. Models get no credit for finding the right passage inside a long text.

The team proves that answer-only rewards make the finding step nearly impossible to learn. Their fix, LongRLVR, adds a second reward for picking the correct passage. That reward can be checked directly, so learning gets a strong signal. On tough long-text tests, the method beat standard training for every model tried. One mid-size model gained large jumps on two benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-02246:
Marcin Pietroń, Szymon Piórkowski, Kamil Faber, and colleagues compare speech recognition for Polish in this 2026 study. Their focus is medical talks, where clear transcripts matter for care. New systems use deep networks or transformers to turn speech into text end to end. One setup pairs the Whisper model with a language model that fixes its output.

The team tested that pair against a commercial tool and five open models. Tests used two public Polish speech sets plus medical talks, in clean and degraded sound. Errors were counted at word and letter level. Whisper led all open models by far, the results show. The commercial Scribe tool scored best overall on Polish, for both general and medical speech.
arxiv-2603-02346:
Timothy Zaklama, Max Geier, and Liang Fu present one network that predicts electron ground states in this 2026 paper. Electrons repel and correlate strongly, which makes their lowest-energy wave hard to find. Their Large Electron Model outputs a trial wave for any setting of the system. One trained model covers all coupling strengths and particle counts at once.

The design rests on a universal form for many-electron waves, tuned by system settings. Tests use electrons trapped in a two-dimensional bowl potential. The model predicts charge patterns and ground energies with high accuracy. It handles up to fifty particles and settings never seen in training. The authors frame it as a foundation model for material discovery, grounded in the variational principle.
arxiv-2603-02646:
Yixin Zhang, Yunhao Luo, Utkarsh Mishra, and colleagues present a way to plan long robot tasks with video diffusion models. Diffusion models plan short moves well, but long tasks strain computing power and training data. Older fixes stitch short clips by averaging overlaps, which often yields shaky, mismatched plans.

Their 2026 method links overlapping video chunks in a chain and forces the chunk ends to agree on the cleaned-up picture, not the noisy draft. Message passing, run in sync and out of sync, spreads that agreement across the whole plan with no new training. Tests beat earlier baselines and reached start-goal pairs never seen in training. Long plans stay coherent because every seam is checked.
arxiv-2603-03546:
Radu-Andrei Cioacă and five colleagues fuse satellite and inertial navigation in real time, loosely. Autonomous systems need precise positioning, and satellite signals falter exactly where streets get interesting. Factor graph optimization, which blends satellite fixes with motion-sensor data on one graph, is accurate but usually too heavy for live use. Their 2026 paper builds a loosely coupled version and tests whether it can run in real time.

Loose coupling merges finished position solutions rather than raw signals, which keeps the graph light. On a Hong Kong urban dataset known for canyon-like streets, the method ran in real time and stayed available more often than batch processing versions. The gain costs some positioning accuracy. The authors map the three-way trade-off between accuracy, availability, and computing effort in detail, giving designers honest numbers for live systems.
arxiv-2603-03646:
Mohamed Elmoghany and twenty-nine colleagues, from Adobe Research and partner institutions, generate story videos that can run for an hour without losing the plot. Long-form synthesis usually breaks three ways: backgrounds morph between shots, characters pop in and out, and quality collapses as length grows. Their 2026 framework, InfinityStory, attacks all three, with character-aware transitions as its signature.

A background-consistent pipeline holds scenery, character identity, and spatial relations steady across scenes. A transition module then choreographs smooth shot changes for several subjects entering or leaving the frame at once, beyond the single-subject limits of earlier work. A synthetic dataset of ten thousand multi-subject transition sequences trains the skill. Anne Askew holds her faith gainst her foes in The Examinations, the record of 1546 and 1547, set here in the Parker Society text of 1849. Askew was a gentlewoman of Lincolnshire whose views broke the king's law on the mass. Chiefs of church and court quizzed her in the Tower. bonus-margarita-pretiosa-novella-1546:
Petrus Bonus of Ferrara wrote his Margarita Pretiosa Novella, The New Pearl of Great Price, in the 1330s, and printers issued it in 1546. Bonus was a scholastic thinker, trained in the logic of the universities. His book is the great scholastic defense of alchemy's possibility.

He argues that the philosophers' stone is real, that nature ripens metals toward gold, and that the adept's art only speeds her work. His method weighs authorities, answers objections, and builds the case like a disputation in the schools. Later alchemists quoted Bonus as proof that their art had reason on its side.
braid-power-of-mind-over-body-1846:
Braid tested Baron Reichenbach's claimed new force in The Power of the Mind over the Body, from 1846. Reichenbach said certain people could see flames from magnets and crystals in the dark. He called the force odic, a new imponderable in nature. Braid's experiments cut the claim down piece by piece.

The sights, he shows, arise from the subject's own mind and body. Expectation and suggestion, not any fluid, produce the marvels. The inquiry marks Braid's turn toward suggestion as the key to trance. It also models how to test a wonder claim fairly. The small book is a classic of skeptical method.
bronte-poems-1846:
Charlotte, Emily, and Anne Brontë published Poems in 1846 as Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell. The slim book was their first publication, paid for with their aunt's legacy money in full. It sold two copies, yet it set three major writers on their road to print.

Charlotte's verses muse on faith, loss, and the life of feeling in a minor key. Emily's poems, the strongest here, sing of the moors, freedom, and a stern inner God. Anne's gentler pieces weigh duty, grief, and hope of heaven with quiet, steady grace in verse. The male pen names hid their sex from a market quick to scorn women's verse then. Critics now prize Emily's lyrics here among the finest short poems of her century.
browne-pseudodoxia-epidemica-english-164:
Thomas Browne, a Norwich doctor, published Pseudodoxia Epidemica in 1646. Its subject is vulgar errors, the false beliefs held by the common run of people. Browne examines each belief with learning, courtesy, and a doctor's questioning mind, asking how error takes root and spreads.

He tests tales about animals, plants, magnets, and pictures, and finds many wanting. His discussion of witchcraft is famous for its care and its hedges. Browne writes prose of great beauty even while doubting. The book wages learning's patient war on easy belief. It remains the classic English anatomy of error, and a model of how to question without scorn.
