cia-0000012246:
Crisis was gathering over Indonesia in June 1964, and a CIA paper that month weighs the archipelago's prospects. The communist party, the PKI, was growing fast under Sukarno's protection. The army watched and waited, its patience thinning, while the economy slid and the Confrontation with Malaysia drained the state.

The paper judges how the balance among Sukarno, the army, and the communists might break. It weighs the chances of a showdown and what might follow one. Written the year before a bloodbath killed hundreds of thousands, it shows the storm's shape forming, unnamed, on the horizon.
cia-0000012346:
Support is the quoted word that survives in a Helms memo to the CIA director from March 1962. Its full subject, a Military Thought matter, is cut short in the file's title. Another veiled page thus joins the summit file: the substance hides behind truncation, while the significance shows in the letterhead and the names it joins.

Guarded memoranda like this one carried the important things that could not be said openly. The file keeps them in sequence with the plainer papers. For readers, the memo marks how much of the era's greatest case still moves behind black bars.
cia-0000013246:
A change in food ration policy toward prisoners of war is noted in a CIA item from November 1967. Even the prisoners' rice bowls were policy instruments in the camps. Rations rose or fell with orders from above, with the harvest, and with the captors' wish to reward, punish, or display their charges. A note on rations is, in truth, a note on life and death at the slowest scale.

The item tracks the change and its meaning for the men held. Small entries like this fed the great accounting's picture of conditions. For readers, it is logistical detail with a human weight: the bowls, measured.
cia-0000013846: A CIA note dated April 2, 1967, carries only a short title: Captured US POW. No place or unit is named in the title itself. The note still mattered, since each capture report fed the wider count of Americans held in Vietnam. Even the bare records helped officials track who was missing and where prisoners were last seen.
cia-0000014746: Gerard Piel, also written as Jerry Piel, is the subject of a CIA file dated November 4, 1967. Piel was a noted science publisher in those years. Why a publisher drew a file, the title does not say. Name files of this kind mark the wide net the agency cast over public life.
cia-0000015346: FCC monitoring and flying saucers meet in a CIA file dated November 2, 1952. The FCC watched the airwaves, where saucer tales spread by radio. Broadcast claims could stir crowds faster than print. A file joining the two shows officials tracking the story's spread, not just the sightings in the sky. The FCC file now sits in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015446: Flying saucers seen over Sweden are the subject of a CIA record dated February 5, 1959. Sweden produced steady sighting reports through the nineteen fifties, and this entry adds one more. The title names no town, witness, or shape, so the description stays at that level. What it shows is reach: a report from Scandinavia was read and filed in Washington.
cia-0000022246: Identity cards of captured American pilots were shown on television, a CIA record dated November 4, 1967, reports. The same title notes an appeal by AALAPSO for thirty seven of something the catalog cuts off. Showing ID cards proved captures to the world. It also handed watchers names and faces that could be matched against the lists of missing airmen.
cia-0000027646: Probable consequences of the forthcoming West German elections are weighed in a CIA paper dated in 1949. The vote that year founded the Federal Republic and made Adenauer its first chancellor. Judging consequences before a first election meant guessing a whole country's direction. The paper stands at the birth of the West German state that anchored Europe for forty years.
cia-0000036846:
A Pravda dispatch titled Missiles in the Air, by Shoephov, is noted in a CIA record dated November 5, 1967. Pravda was the Soviet Communist Party's main newspaper. The item reached the file through a review of what the Soviet press was saying.

The dispatch deals with missiles and air power, themes at the heart of the Cold War arms race. American readers of Pravda looked for signals about Soviet aims and claims. The file shows how even a single newspaper piece was clipped, translated, and kept on record. Soviet papers were read in Washington almost as closely as they were read in Moscow itself.
cia-0000038946: The United States Vietnam Mission and its domestic service in Vietnamese are the subject of a CIA record dated March 1, 1970. The title notes the service as of April 16, in a year the catalog entry leaves unstated. The record concerns broadcasting or information work aimed at a Vietnamese audience at home. Little else can be grounded from the title alone. The file is best read as a small piece of the mission's daily information work in wartime Saigon.
cia-0000042346:
Soviet media reported a multitude of UFO sightings, in a CIA record dated October 3, 1989. The late Soviet press was newly open under glasnost. Stories once kept out of print now reached Soviet readers in large numbers.

Inside, the record gathers the wave of sighting reports from Soviet outlets. American readers tracked Soviet media for far more than flying saucers. An open press was itself the bigger story of 1989. Soviet readers were suddenly free to read about almost anything their editors chose to print. The saucer reports showed, in a curious form, how much the old controls on Soviet news had loosened by that autumn.
cia-0000045246:
The armed forces backed Duarte on the kidnapping, in a CIA record dated August 4, 1985. An army's public backing steadied a president under personal attack. It also reminded everyone where the guns in the argument lived.

Inside, the military's support for its commander in chief is recorded. Such backing was not automatic in El Salvador's strained politics. The army and the president had quarreled before over how the war should be fought. Generals had their own view of talks with the guerrillas. The file preserves the moment they closed ranks behind Duarte anyway, a show of unity that held the state together while the crisis ran its course.
cia-0000046646: General John Vessey's planned trip to Vietnam hung in doubt in the spring of 1987, and a CIA item dated March 1, 1987, records the uncertainty. A second envoy's visit, by Richard Childress, was reported as not considered at all. Vessey was Washington's senior envoy on the missing-men issue, so his travel plans carried real diplomatic weight.
cia-0000049046: An alleged massacre of civilians in Sonsonate Department by members of the armed forces fills a CIA item from 1983. Sonsonate lies in western El Salvador, coffee country that saw steady war. Allegations of this kind reached the files by the hundred; the Truth Commission's work was to sort the provable from the rest.
cia-0000049246:
A CIA study from 1988 examines the FMLN, the guerrilla front fighting El Salvador's government. Its subject is double: the front's strategy in negotiations, and its human rights abuses. By 1988 the war was a stalemate, and both sides were testing whether talks could do what battles had not. The study belongs to the war's analytic record.

Inside, the front's bargaining is weighed beside its conduct: how it talked, what it demanded, and how its forces treated the people under their guns. Pairing the two subjects was the analysts' point, since a movement's record at the table and in the field shaped each other. The study shows Washington reading the rebels as a government in waiting, flaws counted.
cia-0000095146: Comment on certain questions relating to the situation in Laos is the title of declassified CIA document 0000095146, dated May 6, 1964. The heading is cautious and general, naming Laos and questions rather than answers. Readers find a short declassified comment item whose vagueness is worth noting, since the record promises questions about a situation, not findings.
cia-0000096946: Opening statement regarding CIA involvement with ITT Chile is declassified CIA document 0000096946, dated January 3, 1973. The heading frames the text as an opening statement on that involvement. The brief file begins a small cluster of Chile and ITT records, preserved as formal testimony material rather than field reporting from the agency's files.
cia-0000102946: Use of Forced Labor in Mining, Railroad and Construction Enterprises, plus locations in cut-short form, is declassified CIA document 0000102946, dated September 3, 1983. Three industries share the heading. Readers find a short multi-industry labor record, broader than the single-project items, filed as the cluster's coverage of forced labor reaches its widest spread.
cia-0000108046: Classifications of Types of Labor and Uses of Forced Labor in the Soviet Union is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000108046, dated September 2, 1982. The heading promises sorting: types of labor, and uses of forced labor, set side by side. That sorting task is stated in the title itself. The brief record is a classification study item from the autumn of 1982.
cia-0000112346: China Ufo Society Meets; to Continue Scientific Study is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000112346, dated April 4, 1992. The title reports a meeting of the China UFO Society and a resolve to keep studying. A semicolon joins the meeting and the resolve in one heading. The brief record shares its date with a companion legal official item.
cia-0000117846: Letter to the Inspector General re: Interview and Questions and Answers Provid is the heading, cut off mid-word, on declassified CIA document 0000117846, dated June 5, 1995. The title describes a letter to an inspector general about an interview. Questions and answers are named before the heading breaks off at Provid. The brief record preserves the break exactly as released in the files.
cia-0000119746: As of 1 a.m. on November 3, 1956, this CIA report gives the Hungarian situation on the last quiet night before the Soviet assault. Within a day the tanks returned to Budapest. The paper preserves the calm recorded just before that storm. Reports from that night carry a special charge for readers now, since everyone in the story was hours from learning how Moscow would answer defiance.
cia-0000124246: An August 1959 CIA scientific intelligence report, Monograph Two of its series, sets out the objectives of the Soviet space research program. Two years after Sputnik, the agency was taking Moscow's space effort apart piece by piece. This volume lays out what the Soviets were trying to achieve. Monograph series broke a large subject into numbered parts so that specialists could update one section without rewriting the agency's whole account of the program.
cia-0000126946: A June 1989 CIA Terrorism Review assesses the growing threat in Bolivia from the Zarate Willka group, with a passage deleted and the heading breaking off. The guerrilla force was stepping up its campaign that year. The review weighs the danger the group posed. The group took its name from an earlier Bolivian rebel leader, a choice that told analysts much about the history its members wanted voters to remember.
cia-0000132546: Daily brief work on Cuba from the Office of Current Intelligence fills a CIA paper dated September 3, 1960. That office wrote the brief the White House read each day. Its Cuba work kept the picture fresh through 1960. The short paper gathers its reports on communist work inside the revolution. It keeps the daily record in the form it was made.
cia-0000132646:
The Situation in Cuba promises a full overview, and this CIA paper of May 2, 1960 delivers a snapshot of the island at one date. Castro's government was sixteen months old. Tensions with the United States climbed steadily that spring.

Overview briefings stepped back from daily events to judge the whole picture: the regime's strength, its direction, and the state of U.S. interests. This one catches Cuba between revolution and open break, before exile training and invasion plans took over. Released decades later, it preserves the agency's spring 1960 baseline for everything that followed.
cia-0000132746: Events in Cuba and Central America, with the stress on Central America, fill a CIA paper dated November 4, 1960. It stands beside a broader roundup on the same pairing from that month. Here the lens narrows to the isthmus and its small states. The short paper surveys events there, with Cuba's shadow falling across each one in turn.
cia-0000135746: This Spanish text, dated 1 March 1961, belongs to the 2506 Brigade papers released by the CIA. Several brigade documents share this date, a sign of heavy paperwork as training wound toward its end. The brigade was the exile force landed at the Bay of Pigs that April. The catalog names no subject for this item. It is kept in Spanish, dated and placed, with its contents for the reader to find.
cia-0000135946: Routing sheet in the declassified files, dated 3 January 1954, covers a routing sheet with a cable reporting that the minister of defense had acted, the rest cut off. Lincoln was where PBSUCCESS staff worked the Guatemala operation day to day, under code names, in 1953 and 1954. The file rewards slow reading, since its short heading is often the only summary the agency ever gave it.
cia-0000136146: 3 April 1954 is the date on a declassified CIA cable about rumors about Fernando Romeo, the heading misspelling his first name, passed to two readers. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. For readers of the coup, the value lies in the plain wording, written before anyone knew how the story would end.
cia-0000136246: A cable in the declassified CIA files, dated 5 May 1954, covers an answer on the coordination of operations, noting a lack of it inside the mission. Traffic like this ran the field side of PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala. Small as it is, the sheet documents one task, one report, or one order inside a much larger secret effort.
cia-0000136346: Detailed arrangements for a San Salvador meeting were cancelled too late to change, LINCOLN tells CALLIGERIS in this 30 June 1954 cable. The ambassador in Guatemala, acting as invited intermediary, had laid the arrangements on; the junta had agreed to the meeting and was being flown from Guatemala City in his plane. CALLIGERIS is suggested to come and contact a man who knows of the meeting and will arrange his flight to El Salvador.
cia-0000136646: Filed among the Spanish papers of Brigade 2506, this document is dated 2 February 1961. The exile force was drilling daily in its final training period. The catalog gives the item no individual subject. Preserved in Spanish through the CIA Reading Room, it is a dated record of the brigade in the weeks before it sailed for Cuba, presented as the agency released it.
cia-0000136746: A document in Spanish dated 4 March 1961, held in the declassified 2506 Brigade files. March 1961 was the brigade's closing month of training and planning under CIA direction. The catalog record carries no subject for this item. It is kept in the original Spanish through the CIA Reading Room, one of the early-March records of the exile force.
cia-0000136946: Only one of two flights is approved, headquarters tells LINCOLN in May 1954. The station may pick whichever it deems best. The reasoning is stated plainly. Headquarters does not want to shoot its bolt in this phase. Spreading the effort over time is better. A maximum wallop too soon would waste it. A double flight would also send a signal. Inside Guatemala and worldwide, it would suggest big official backing. Indigenous planes and pilots should be found for simple leaflet drops.
cia-0000137346: An estimated 1961 Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade papers; the catalog gives only the year and flags it as estimated. The brigade was the CIA-trained exile force that landed in Cuba in April 1961. The record names no subject for this item. It is preserved in the original Spanish in the declassified release, and its place in the brigade's crowded final year cannot be narrowed from the catalog alone.
cia-0000139446: Next steps on the American hostages is the title of this June 1986 document. It moved through NSC intelligence channels. The sample kept here holds only its routing header. Channel, document number, and classification markings survive. No body text survives in this excerpt. The proposed steps cannot be recovered from this copy. No fuller summary would be honest. The entry belongs to the Lebanon hostage crisis files. American hostages in Beirut dominated covert attention that year.
cia-03191546: June 11, 1959: another daily bulletin for the intelligence leadership. The analysts' summary of world affairs, typed and filed. The Cold War's paper trail. The archive keeps the paper open to all. This file preserves that declassified bulletin.
cia-06232646: CENTRAL INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1958/11/22, a CIA publication. The November briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it. Its pages add to the record of the past.
cia-06828146: OHB MAIN CAFE, a CIA document. The cafe file. This file preserves that declassified paper. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Later readers can locate it. Its pages add to the record of the past.
cia-06835146: Liberia's sanctions weren't biting, this assessment found. The measures had limited impact. The West African file. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. This declassified CIA assessment is preserved, it is archived, it is stored, it is filed.
constitution-japan-1946: Japan's 1946 Constitution, written under US rule, renounced war forever. Article 9 is famous. The Tower library holds the full text. It pacified an empire. Bombs fell. Swords sheathed. Peace reigned. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
currus-triumphalis-antimonii-fratris-bas: Currus triumphalis antimonii, 1646. The triumphal chariot, in Latin. This book preserves that work. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
darwin-geological-observations-1846:
Charles Darwin's Geological Observations on the Voyage of the Beagle, complete in the 1846 form, gathers his three geology books from the Beagle voyage. Darwin sailed as a young naturalist from 1831 to 1836. His rock work, more than his animal studies, first made his scientific name.

Three parts treat coral reefs, volcanic islands, and the geology of South America. Darwin argued that coral atolls form as volcanic islands slowly sink beneath the sea. He also traced raised beaches and fossils that showed land moving over long ages. Readers see the young Darwin building the deep-time habits of thought that later supported his theory of evolution.
doe-osti-3409104-toyota-highlander-fchv-: Highlander FCHV got CRADA-finalled, and this DOE final covers the Toyota vehicle. The pages detail the report findings. The transport folks get their closeout. The report was final. The closeout was transport. The FCHV were Highlander. The Toyota were vehicle.
dumas-chicot-the-jester-1846:
Alexandre Dumas published Chicot the Jester in 1846, as La Dame de Monsoreau in French. The classic abridged English version gives the Valois trilogy's middle volume in one book for readers. Its scene is the court of Henri III, last of the Valois kings of France.

Chicot, the king's jester, is in truth a Gascon noble with a sharp sword and wit. He guards his feckless king against the Guise faction and the League's rising plots in Paris. Bussy d'Amboise loves Diane de Monsoreau, whose husband traps him for a fatal ambush at night. Duels, disguises, and monkish conspiracies crowd the pages at Dumas's swiftest clip of storytelling here. Many readers rank the jester among Dumas's finest and most human creations in fiction.
edwards-religious-affections-1746:
Jonathan Edwards preached through the Great Awakening, the revival that swept New England in the 1740s, and saw both its power and its excesses. His Treatise Concerning Religious Affections, published in 1746, asks how to tell true religious experience from false. It is the Awakening's deepest piece of self-examination.

Edwards lists signs that prove nothing: loud emotion, fluent talk, even love of praise disguised as zeal. True grace, he argues, shows in changed practice, humility, and a new taste for the beauty of holy things. Pastors and psychologists of religion still argue with his tests today.
esdaile-mesmerism-in-india-1846:
James Esdaile cut flesh with no pain in Mesmerism in India, his report of 1846. Esdaile was a Scot healer at a jail ward in India. He found that deep trance, wrought by passes and breath, could dull all pain. Scores of great cuts, some dire, were done while the sick slept calm and woke with no tale of hurt.

He prints each case with care and zeal. Word of his work shook the wards of Britain. Ere sleep drugs came, his proof stood as the best hope of pain free craft. The book is that proof.
etheridge-syrian-churches-gospels-1846:
John Wesley Etheridge, a Methodist scholar of the Syriac tongue, wrote this 1846 study of the churches of Syria and the east. He paired it with his own literal English version of the four gospels, translated straight from the Peshitta, the Syriac Bible. Longman published the volume in London.

Etheridge traces the Syrian churches, their rites, their writers, and their missions as far as India and China. Then the gospels follow, in wording that often differs in small, telling ways from the Greek-based versions. His aim was to let English readers hear the gospel in a language close to the one Jesus spoke. The book serves both church history and Bible study.
europmc-pmc10066346:
Kim reviews how short-chain fatty acids made by gut microbes shape immune tolerance and autoimmunity, in a 2023 paper. These fatty acids form when gut bacteria ferment fiber from food. Immune tolerance is the system that stops the body from attacking itself, and it is built and tuned across a lifetime.

The review explains how the fatty acids calm some immune cells and guide others. It links weak production of these acids to higher risk of autoimmune disease. The paper connects diet, gut microbes, and immune balance in a clear chain.
europmc-pmc10324146:
Ye and co-authors reviewed breast cancer care in 2023, with a focus on two newer forms of treatment. Breast cancer is the second top cause of cancer death in women. Its many forms make it hard to treat with one plan. Targeted drugs aim at one molecule that helps a tumour grow.

Ye lists targets now in use, such as CDK proteins and PARP, an enzyme that fixes DNA. Some drugs have won FDA approval, alone or with other drugs. One hard form, called triple-negative, still resists targeted drugs. For that form, Ye points to immune therapy, such as drugs that lift brakes on immune cells.
europmc-pmc10434946:
Chari and Pachter argued in 2023 that a standard chart in single-cell gene studies misleads users. The chart squeezes data with hundreds or thousands of measures into a flat 2D plot. Such plots open most papers in this field and guide first looks at the data. The authors test how much truth survives that squeeze.

Their checks show the squeeze warps the data in deep ways. Cells that look close on the plot may sit far apart in the full data. Chari found that habits in making these plots vary and can flip the tale a plot seems to tell. They urge targeted plots built for one clear question instead. Broad all-in-one plots, they say, block real finds more than they help.
europmc-pmc1069646:
Foster and a large team read the full genome in 2005 of a bacterium that lives inside a parasitic worm. The worm, Brugia malayi, infects humans and causes filarial disease of skin and lymph. Its tenant, Wolbachia, is a bacterium the worm needs to breed and live. Killing the tenant may thus kill the worm.

The tenant genome is small and worn, with many genes lost. Foster found it kept key paths to make riboflavin, heme, and DNA building blocks. Those gifts may be its main pay to the host worm. The worm in turn feeds it amino acids. Next to its kin in fruit flies, this tenant lacks virus bits and repeat DNA. The map gives fresh targets to end the disease.
europmc-pmc10763046:
Iqbal and co-authors reviewed in 2024 how oxidative stress feeds cancer through cell signals and gene switches. Stress from reactive oxygen can break DNA and warp the signals that steer cell growth. High levels push cells to drop normal jobs and gain cancer traits. The team traced which paths carry that push.

Named paths include the guard gene p53, the Keap1-NRF2 stress reply, and RB1 and p21, two brakes on cell division. Iqbal shows how faults in each can free growth, blunt DNA repair, and dodge cell death. Care ideas aim to reset the redox balance, the cell's stress ledger. Antioxidant drugs and redox-tuned agents lead that work. Proof in patients is the next test.
europmc-pmc10781646:
Cui and colleagues built a reference map of how immune cells react to signal proteins in this 2024 paper. Cytokines are small proteins that cells use to send messages to each other. They guide immune responses and are targets for many drugs. No one had charted how each cell type answers each cytokine in one place.

Working in mouse lymph nodes, the team tested 86 cytokines on more than 17 cell types. Most cytokines sparked a distinct response in each cell type, they found. The data revealed over 66 driven cell states, some never described before. The team also made free software that reads gene activity data and infers which cytokines are at work. They used it to map signals in tumours after a common cancer therapy.
europmc-pmc11075546:
Sternberg and a large team report the state of the main worm genetics database in this 2024 paper. WormBase has held genome and genetics data on the nematode worm Caenorhabditis elegans for over two decades. The worm is a staple lab animal for studying development and disease. The team states three goals: stay current, link better with other resources, and stay sustainable.

The paper describes WormBase as it stands and the plan to move its core systems into the Alliance of Genome Resources. The Alliance is a shared infrastructure for model organism databases. As a member, WormBase will keep curating key findings from papers and large projects. It will also keep building features the worm community needs. The move is framed as a way to cut duplicated effort across databases.
europmc-pmc11299546:
Gaser and colleagues introduce a toolbox for measuring brain structure from MRI scans in this 2024 paper. Brain morphometry quantifies features such as cortical thickness and folding from magnetic resonance images. Many sophisticated tools exist, but they often demand expert handling. The Computational Anatomy Toolbox, called CAT, aims to serve beginners and experts alike through a graphical interface or scripts.

CAT covers the full workflow: preprocessing, statistical analysis, and display of results, the authors report. It supports voxel-based, surface-based, and region-based analyses, shown on an example dataset. Voxel means a 3D pixel, the smallest cube in a scan. Multiple quality control options are built in. Both one-time and repeated scans over time are handled. The paper offers the toolbox as a citable standard for the brain mapping community.
europmc-pmc11701646:
Szklarczyk and colleagues update the STRING database of protein networks in this 2025 paper. Proteins work by binding, regulating, and cooperating with each other. STRING compiles, scores, and merges evidence on protein-protein links from experiments, predictions, and prior knowledge. Its goal is a full, objective global network of physical and functional links.

Version 12.5 adds a new regulatory network. For it, the team gathers evidence on the type and direction of each regulatory link, using curated pathway databases, plus a language model fine-tuned to parse the literature. Users can now view three network types on their own: functional, physical, and regulatory. The pathway enrichment tool, which flags processes over-represented in a protein set, was also updated. Network clustering remains part of the package.
europmc-pmc11760946:
Chandimali and colleagues review free radicals and the body's antioxidant defences in this 2025 paper. Free radicals are molecules with unpaired electrons, which makes them highly reactive. They form inside the body during processes such as mitochondrial respiration, where cells burn fuel with oxygen, and immune cell activation. Outside sources include radiation, pollution, and smoking.

In balance, radicals serve cell signalling and immune defence. Overproduction breaks the balance between oxidants and antioxidants and causes oxidative stress. That stress damages DNA, proteins, and lipids. It is linked to cancer, heart disease, brain-wasting diseases, and inflammatory diseases. The review covers radical types, how they form, and their biological impacts. It also details the defence systems and ways to restore balance.
europmc-pmc1308846:
Ginaldi, Di Benedetto, and De Martinis reviewed osteoporosis through inflammation and aging in 2005. Osteoporosis thins bones and raises fracture risk in older people. Hormones, metabolism, and mechanics were the classic explanations. New evidence adds chronic inflammation as a driver.

Inflammatory signaling molecules regulate both bone-building and bone-eating cells. Aging remodels the immune system toward a more activated profile. That shift may tip bone turnover toward loss. Conditions linked to osteoporosis often share chronic inflammation too. Ginaldi reads osteoporosis partly as an inflamed aging disease. Bone loss in old age is the core concern. Old age is when the risk is at its peak for most men and women. Falls and breaks are the main harm that comes from thin bones.
europmc-pmc1363346:
Link, Shevchenko, and Heisenberg set up protein analysis for early zebrafish embryos in 2006. Zebrafish are a leading model for vertebrate development. Genetic tools were strong, but protein gel methods lagged. Yolk in embryos blocked clean protein separation.

A new method removes yolk efficiently from large embryo batches. That step enabled high-resolution 2D gel separation. Western blotting improved considerably with the same prep. Protocols run from sample prep through mass spectrometry identification. Database choices for matching zebrafish proteins were compared. Link opens protein-level study of early development. Gel steps and blot steps are spelled out in full.
europmc-pmc1821046:
Yooseph, Venter and colleagues mined the Global Ocean Sampling data in 2007 for new protein families. The expedition sequenced microbes from ocean water around the world. The team clustered proteins by similarity, merging public databases with millions of proteins predicted from the new sea samples.

Their combined set held 6.12 million predicted proteins from 7.7 million sampling sequences, and it covered nearly all known bacterial protein families. They found 3,995 medium and large clusters made only of ocean sequences. Of those, 1,700 had no detectable match to any known family, marking genuinely new families. Ocean-only clusters held an excess of viral sequences, showing how poorly viruses had been sampled. Some protein domains once thought limited to one kingdom appeared in others.
europmc-pmc1914346:
Gaugler and co-authors pooled in 2007 the evidence on what predicts an older American's move into a nursing home. Many single studies had named risk factors, but no fuller pooled picture existed. Knowing the strongest predictors helps families plan and helps programs target support that delays admission.

The search swept four databases plus theses and reference lists, turning up 736 candidate reports. Seventy-seven reports from 12 data sources met the bar: long-term designs with community samples that mirrored a region or the nation. The team pulled admission counts, follow-up length, and candidate predictors under a standard protocol. Random-effects models then pooled each predictor family one by one. The families covered social traits, physical function, thinking, service use, and family or friend support.
europmc-pmc1940246:
Bhattacharya and colleagues charted in 2007 how a first-time mother's body mass index relates to pregnancy outcomes. Obesity in young women is rising fast, with consequences for both mother and baby. The study used routine records for all first-time mothers who delivered single babies in Aberdeen over the three decades ending in 2005.

Women were split into five bands from underweight to morbidly obese. Compared with the normal band, morbidly obese women faced the highest pre-eclampsia risk, a dangerous blood pressure disorder, with odds over seven times higher. Underweight women had the lowest risk, at about six tenths of the normal odds. Induced labor was most common in the morbidly obese group and least in the underweight group. Emergency cesarean rates also peaked in the morbidly obese, at nearly triple the normal-band odds.
europmc-pmc1955446:
Wolozin and colleagues mined a veterans health database in 2007 to test whether cholesterol drugs differ in their links to dementia and Parkinson disease. Statins lower cholesterol by blocking a liver enzyme. Past studies of statins and dementia clashed, and the authors guessed the drugs are not all alike.

The database held records on 4.5 million people, with case, drug, and background records. Models compared users of lovastatin, simvastatin, or atorvastatin with users of other heart drugs, with traits tied to dementia and Parkinson risk held constant. Simvastatin stood out: in people aged 65 and over it was tied to a clear drop in new dementia cases under all three models. The title reports a matching reduced incidence for Parkinson disease. The authors stress these are links from records, not proof of a real effect.
europmc-pmc2124946: A medical paper on the production of foreign body giant cells in vitro. The giant cells, grown. This article preserves that cell biology. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.

europmc-pmc2206446:
Mehta and co-authors, for the Acute Kidney Injury Network, reported an initiative in 2007 to standardise acute kidney injury care. The disorder ranges from tiny rises in blood creatinine to complete kidney failure, yet it had no accepted definition. Experts from critical care and kidney societies met in Amsterdam in September 2005. Three workgroups drafted recommendations, refined them with the full group, and gained endorsement from participating societies.

The group proposes the term acute kidney injury to cover the whole spectrum of acute renal failure. Diagnosis rests on sudden changes in urine output or in serum creatinine. Severity is then graded by a staging system using the size of those changes. The network itself offers a standing forum for collaboration across disciplines. Its standards now need validation in future studies.
europmc-pmc2211546:
Thomas and co-workers identified in 2008 a family of proteins that sit in plasmodesmata, the channels linking plant cells. Those channels carry signals and materials between cells and shape growth and defence, yet how proteins are targeted to them was unknown. The new family, called PDLP1, resembles cell-surface receptor proteins. The team studied the first member, PDLP1a, tracing its route through the cell and testing altered versions.

PDLP1a reaches plasmodesmata through the secretory pathway, in a route blocked by the drug Brefeldin A. Changing its expression altered how much traffic passed between cells. Its single membrane-spanning segment holds all the targeting information. That segment alone could drag unrelated proteins to plasmodesmata. The finding gives plant biologists a delivery tag for probing these channels.
europmc-pmc2233646:
Bui, Sidney, Li, Fusseder and Sette built a software tool in 2007 for measuring how conserved immune epitopes are. Epitopes are the protein fragments that trigger antibody or T-cell responses. Vaccine designers prefer conserved epitopes, shared across many strains, for broad protection. Diagnostic designers may want strain-specific ones instead. Either way, the degree of conservation must be measured concretely before choosing.

Their tool analyses epitope variability across any given set of protein sequences. It was implemented as part of the Immune Epitope Database (IEDB) and its linked Analysis Resources, a public resource for immunology. Users can check how widely an epitope is preserved before committing to it. The authors expect the user-friendly tool to aid design of epitope-based vaccines and diagnostics alike.
europmc-pmc2289846:
Fedorova and a very large team compared genomes in 2008 of the pathogenic fungus Aspergillus fumigatus and two close relatives. This fungus is a major allergen and a dangerous invader in immunocompromised patients. The team sequenced a new clinical isolate plus Neosartorya fischeri and Aspergillus clavatus, rarely pathogenic species. Comparing all three against the first sequenced isolate revealed which genes are core, variable or unique to each genome.

Core genes were 99.8 percent identical between the two Aspergillus fumigatus isolates. Variable genes dropped as low as 40 percent identity. Species-specific genes made up 8.5 to 12.6 percent of each genome. They clustered in thirteen chromosomal islands rich in pseudogenes and jumping elements. At least twenty percent of the pathogen's unique genes appear functional. Their origin likely involves duplication and differential loss, not horizontal transfer.
europmc-pmc2374446:
Zeng and co-authors summarised twenty years of rheumatic disease surveys in China in 2008. Rheumatic diseases cover joint, bone, and connective tissue disorders that cause pain and disability. The team pooled 38 population surveys with 241,169 adults from 25 provinces and cities, covering 1980 to 2006.

Joint and muscle complaints ranged from 11.6% to 46.4% of adults depending on place and method. Symptomatic osteoarthritis, worn-joint disease, hit the spine and knees most. Beijing's older women had more knee osteoarthritis than US women, while hip and hand rates stayed far below Western rates. Rheumatoid arthritis ran lower than in rich countries. Gout rose over time, and Taiwan's aboriginal people showed the highest rate, at 11.7% in the records.
europmc-pmc2375446:
da Fonseca and co-authors traced how mammal mitochondria adapted over evolution in 2008. Mitochondria are the cell's power stations, making up to 95% of its energy through a process called oxidative phosphorylation. Their small genome holds 12 protein-coding genes that the team compared across 41 placental mammal species.

Change clustered at working hotspots. One energy protein, cytochrome b, varied at key regions in animals with special needs. These included low-energy diets in sloths and pangolins, diving in whales, flight in bats, and thin air in alpacas. The ATP8 piece, which helps assemble the energy turbine, showed the strongest adaptive signal of all. Another part, ATP6, varied in its loop regions, which affect how the turbine spins. The authors mapped these shifts onto protein shapes to guide future lab tests.
europmc-pmc2440546:
Wu and colleagues reported a first human trial of malaria vaccines meant to block transmission in this paper. Most malaria vaccines protect the vaccinated person. These two, Pfs25 and Pvs25, target proteins the malaria parasite shows while in the mosquito, so antibodies would stop it passing to the next person.

The dose-rising trial at Johns Hopkins planned 72 healthy volunteers but was halted early for unexpected reactions, enrolling 36. Groups got 5 or 20 micrograms of either vaccine in an oil-based booster called Montanide ISA 51, or the booster alone. Local reactions were frequent. Two volunteers developed erythema nodosum, a painful skin inflammation, judged probably linked to the vaccine mix. Still, those finishing the lowest Pfs25 dose made real antibody responses. Their antibody levels matched the strength of transmission blocking measured in lab tests. The authors said the concept works, but this formula is too reactogenic to develop further.
europmc-pmc2631046:
Ware and colleagues conducted an ethnographic study in 2009 to explain a puzzle: HIV patients in sub-Saharan Africa take their antiretroviral therapy more faithfully than patients in wealthy countries. Adherence above 90 percent of doses was routine, defying early fears that extreme poverty would make treatment fail. The team interviewed 252 patients, their treatment partners, and health workers at clinics in Nigeria, Tanzania, and Uganda, with 136 observation sessions.

Patients overcame money obstacles deliberately: borrowing or begging transport funds, making impossible choices to fund treatment first, and doing without other needs. Help flowed from treatment partners, family, friends, and providers, who expected adherence in return. Patients stuck to their regimens partly to preserve goodwill, keeping help available for future needs. The authors frame adherence as fulfilling social responsibilities that protect social capital.
europmc-pmc2673046:
Ribeyre and colleagues found in 2009 that a yeast enzyme guards the genome against a knot-like DNA structure. Certain DNA stretches rich in the letter G can fold into four-stranded knots called G-quadruplexes. The team planted a human repeat prone to such folding into baker's yeast and watched what happened with and without the unwinding enzyme Pif1.

Without Pif1, the planted repeat kept changing length, a sign of genomic instability, while other repeats stayed calm. Knocking out a different unwinding enzyme did nothing. In test tubes, the repeat did fold into the knots, and Pif1 unwound them faster than ordinary DNA. When the team edited the repeat so it could no longer fold, the instability vanished even without the enzyme. Pif1, they conclude, patrols the genome for these knots and undoes them before they cause damage.
europmc-pmc2736946:
Stewart and co-authors described in 2009 a new case register. It was built from electronic records at South London and Maudsley. That trust is Europe's largest secondary mental health provider. Older registers used manual data entry, which limited depth. Full electronic records plus search software that strips identity offer a richer, safer research resource.

Their CRIS tool lets researchers search anonymized numerical and free-text clinical data under strict security rules. By October 2008 the register held over one hundred twenty-two thousand cases, reasonably matching the local population by sex and ethnicity. Mood disorders were the commonest primary diagnosis, followed by schizophrenia-related disorders, substance misuse, neuroses, and organic disorders. About thirty-five thousand patients were under active case management.
europmc-pmc2763246:
Bouayed, Rammal, and Soulimani reviewed in 2009 the relationship between oxidative stress and anxiety, in both normal and pathological forms. The brain uses much oxygen and holds rich fat stores. Its antioxidant defenses are modest. That mix leaves it prone to redox imbalance and damage. Oxidative stress had already been tied to depression and anxiety disorders, raising the question of whether it helps cause anxiety itself.

They weigh findings linking oxidative status to normal anxiety levels in people and animals. They also examine claims that cellular oxidative stress could generate emotional stress, and they set out the methods used to test a causal link. The evidence, they conclude, supports an association, while the direction of cause and effect remains disputed and needs direct tests.
europmc-pmc2795146:
Rutherford and co-authors used brain scans to check whether cooling newborns after oxygen loss at birth truly protects brain tissue. Babies in the TOBY trial had hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, brain harm from low oxygen and blood flow, and were cared for with or without moderate cooling. The 2010 substudy read scans from one hundred thirty-one of the infants.

Cooled babies showed fewer injuries in deep brain areas that steer movement, and fewer damaged tracts in the white matter, the brain's wiring. They were also more likely to have normal scans and less likely to show patterns that predict later movement problems. Scans predicted death or disability equally well in both groups.
europmc-pmc2827546:
Zijnge and colleagues mapped the layout of bacterial films on natural teeth in 2010, using glowing probes that light up set species in place. Dental plaque causes gum disease and cavities, yet its mature structure below the gumline had barely been studied since the nineteen seventies. The team examined seven pulled teeth from four people.

Below the gum, five groups dominated, including Actinomyces and the gum disease germ Tannerella forsythia. One little-known group sat right against the gum tissue, close to immune cells. Lactobacillus formed the core of clumps below the gum, while above it, Streptococcus and the yeast Candida albicans built corncob-shaped clusters. Gum pathogens arrived late and colonized films already built.
europmc-pmc2833246:
Heddleston, Li, Lathia, Bao, Hjelmeland, and Rich reviewed in 2010 how low oxygen inside tumors protects cancer stem cells, the rare tumor cells that can regrow a whole cancer. Solid tumors are riddled with oxygen-poor zones because their blood vessels grow in chaos. Oxygen-sensing proteins called HIFs switch on survival programs in those zones.

Brain tumor stem cells cluster in two homes, near blood vessels and beside dead tissue, the review reports. Low oxygen grows their numbers and pushes ordinary tumor cells toward a stem-like state. These cells depend on HIFs for survival, self-renewal, and tumor growth. That dependence raises a hard problem: killing stem cells may fail while oxygen-poor zones keep minting replacements, so therapy may need to strike the zones themselves.
europmc-pmc2841246:
Sobolewski, Cerella, Dicato, Ghibelli, and Diederich reviewed in 2010 the role of COX-2, an enzyme switched on in inflammation and cancer, in tumor cell growth and death. COX enzymes drive the making of prostaglandins, hormone-like signals. The always-on family member COX-1 handles housekeeping, while COX-2 rises sharply in many solid tumors, colorectal, breast, and prostate among them, and lately in blood cancers too.

Evidence ties COX-2 to faster tumor cell division and slower programmed death. Pairing COX-2 blockers with standard treatments may sharpen those treatments, the authors argue. They survey the combination studies run so far and judge COX-2 control a promising field for improving future cancer care.
europmc-pmc2859946:
Low oxygen inside tumors triggers a survival program, and Favaro and colleagues traced in 2010 how one tiny RNA drives much of it. The RNA, called miR-210, rises when oxygen falls and marks tumors with a poor outlook. It works by silencing a helper protein named ISCU, which builds iron-sulfur clusters that many cell enzymes need to function.

In cancer cell lines and real tumors, Favaro found that silencing ISCU was the main cause of harmful free radicals building up under low oxygen. Blocking ISCU also weakened energy-making parts of the cell, pushed cells toward sugar burning, and helped them survive. Tumors with low ISCU levels belonged to patients who fared worse, tying the pathway to real disease course.
europmc-pmc2893946:
Gold and colleagues gave in 2010 the first clear job description for MAIT cells, an unusual T cell subset that patrols mucosal tissues like the gut and lung lining. Unlike ordinary T cells, which each target one specific germ, MAIT cells respond broadly across bacterial infections. The team tested what switches them on using infected human cells.

MAIT cells detected airway lining cells infected with the tuberculosis bacterium and with other bacteria as well. They read the infection through MR1, a display molecule that is nearly identical across all mammals, the most conserved of its family. That unusual conservation now makes sense: the molecule flags bacterial chemistry rather than variable germ proteins, letting one cell type watch for many invaders at body surfaces.
europmc-pmc2941746:
Parri and Chiarugi reviewed two families of molecular switches, Rac and Rho, that govern how cancer cells move, in a 2010 article. Both families reorganise the cell's actin skeleton, the inner scaffolding that sets shape and motion.

Tumour cells invade in three broad styles: moving as a linked cohort, crawling singly with a stretched shape, or squeezing along in a rounded amoeba-like mode. Rac drives the stretched crawling style, while high Rho activity powers the rounded style through strong contraction. Cells can switch styles as conditions change, a flexibility that helps them spread.
europmc-pmc3081346:
Liu and coauthors traced in 2011 how one small RNA pushes tumors to grow their own blood vessels. The RNA, called miR-21 in short, is abundant in many cancers and tied to growth and spread, but its role in vessel growth was unclear. Forcing prostate cancer cells to make extra copies raised two vessel promoting factors and sparked new vessel growth in a standard membrane test.

The chain ran through a brake protein the RNA normally suppresses. With the brake down, two signaling routes switched on, which in turn raised a low oxygen master switch and the vessel growth factor it controls. Blocking the RNA, restoring the brake, or drugging either route each cut the effect. Removing the oxygen switch alone erased it completely. The pathway gives drug makers several linked points to attack tumor blood supply.
europmc-pmc3134446:
Michael Clark and a large group of colleagues defended a bold claim about the human genome in a 2011 paper in PLoS Biology. Only a tiny share of DNA codes for proteins, yet many studies reported that most of the genome still gets copied into RNA. A rival paper had blamed that signal on lab artefacts and background noise.

The authors rechecked the rival data and found its arrays unusual and its sequencing too shallow to catch faint copies. Several independent methods, from copy catalogues to genome-wide chips, agree that copying is widespread across cell types. They conclude the copying is real, while granting that the purpose of many of these RNA copies remains unknown and needs study.
europmc-pmc3169446:
Benjamin Solomon reviewed a rare pattern of birth defects in a 2011 paper in the Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases. The pattern, known by an acronym of its parts, is diagnosed when at least three of six defect types appear together. The six are spine, blocked anus, heart, a windpipe-food pipe link, kidneys, and limbs. It occurs in roughly one in tens of thousands of newborns.

Diagnosis is clinical and requires ruling out a long list of look-alike syndromes, several of them genetic. The cause remains unknown in most patients, likely because many different causes converge on the same pattern. Surgery soon after birth fixes the most urgent defects, followed by lifelong management of lasting effects. Thinking ability is typically unaffected, and with good surgical repair the outlook can be fairly positive, Solomon reports.
europmc-pmc3234246:
Torsten Schaller and colleagues mapped how HIV's capsid uses helper proteins to enter the nucleus, in this 2011 paper in PLoS Pathogens. HIV infects non-dividing cells, so its core must cross the nuclear pore. The team showed the capsid binds directly to a cyclophilin domain on Nup358, a protein of the nuclear pore itself.

Grafting that domain onto a viral restriction factor created a new HIV blocker, confirming the interaction matters in living cells. Blocking the other capsid partner, cyclophilin A, changed which import machinery the virus depended on, suggesting it steers the choice of route. Capsid mutations shifted where the virus inserted its DNA in the genome, toward or away from gene-rich regions, and weakened replication in test cells and macrophages. The work links capsid helpers to import route, insertion targeting, and fitness.
europmc-pmc3276346:
Ernestina Schipani, Christa Maes, Geert Carmeliet, and Gregg Semenza reviewed how blood vessel growth and bone growth are coupled, in this perspective in the Journal of Bone and Mineral Research. Bone is richly supplied with vessels, yet what angiogenesis does in shaping and maintaining the skeleton was poorly defined. Work in altered mice had recently thrown the coupling into relief.

The mouse experiments highlight a pathway in which the oxygen sensor HIF drives production of VEGF, a vessel-growth signal, linking low-oxygen sensing to both vessel ingrowth and bone formation. The authors review the current understanding of the mechanisms that keep the two processes in step during development and throughout adult remodeling. They argue that clarifying this coupling will deepen knowledge of bone biology and may yield therapies that speed bone regeneration and repair. The signals that summon vessels also instruct bone-forming cells.
europmc-pmc3291446:
Chomel and colleagues reviewed germs of the Bartonella group carried by pets in a 2006 article. These bacteria live in blood, spread through insects such as fleas, and can pass from animals to people. Cats are the main source of the species behind cat scratch disease, a common infection after a scratch or bite.

The review counts eleven species or subspecies thought to harm people, six of them found in pet cats and dogs. Dogs can carry several kinds for long periods and sometimes develop heart valve infection. Infection rates in cats range from almost none in cold Norway to very high in the warm Philippines. The authors update the germs, symptoms, and spread patterns known at the time.
europmc-pmc3313946:
Collins and Koechlin explored how the brain's frontal lobes juggle competing strategies while making decisions, in a 2012 article. Everyday choices unfold in changing settings where no single approach always works. A person must track several possible strategies, judge which is paying off, switch when one fails, and sometimes invent a fresh one altogether.

Drawing on computer models and behavior experiments, the authors argue the frontal system can keep watch over about three or four strategies at once. One part of the system adjusts the strategy in use by its recent rewards, while monitoring functions estimate how trustworthy each option is. The open puzzle is how the brain decides to create new strategies instead of recycling old ones, a problem the authors connect to statistical models that grow their own categories.
europmc-pmc3328746:
Pester and colleagues built a master family tree of microbes that turn ammonia into nitrite in soil, reporting in 2012. These archaea, single celled organisms distinct from bacteria, drive a key step of the nitrogen cycle that fertilizers depend on. Researchers use one of their genes, called amoA, as an identity marker, and the team assembled every public sequence of that gene into one agreed tree.

The tree sorts the organisms into five major clusters, one of them newly recognized, holding eighty three species level groups. Deep sequencing of soils from Austria, Costa Rica, Greenland, and Namibia found each soil home to anywhere from a handful to dozens of species. One cluster dominated almost everywhere, and the mix in each place tracked geography, hinting that travel limits and history shape these communities as much as soil conditions do.
europmc-pmc3352246:
Hunter and Hölscher asked whether two diabetes drugs modelled on the gut hormone GLP-1 can reach the brain and act there. Liraglutide and lixisenatide strengthen insulin signalling, and because type 2 diabetes raises the risk of Alzheimer's disease, a brain effect could matter beyond blood sugar control.

Injecting the drugs into mice, the researchers tracked them across the blood–brain barrier and measured receptor activation through cyclic AMP levels. Both compounds entered the brain; lixisenatide did so at every dose tested and proved the stronger activator. Both also increased the formation of new neurons. The authors suggest these agents merit study as treatments for neurodegenerative disease.
europmc-pmc3374546:
Neter and Brainin surveyed Israeli adults in 2012 to test whether the digital divide follows people into online health searching. eHealth literacy means the skill to find, judge, and use health information from electronic sources. Their telephone survey reached a representative sample of more than four thousand adults.

Adults with high eHealth literacy tended to be younger and better educated than those with low scores. The skilled group searched more, used more strategies, and checked information more carefully. They also gained more, from understanding to managing their own care and talking with doctors. The authors warn that online health tools may widen social gaps unless weaker groups get training and simpler designs.
europmc-pmc3419346:
Boeing led a panel that critically reviewed in 2012 whether eating more vegetables and fruit prevents chronic disease. These foods supply nutrients, fiber, and plant chemicals, but the strength of the protective evidence was unsettled. The panel weighed study quality, size, and design across a long list of conditions, from heart disease to dementia.

For high blood pressure, coronary heart disease, and stroke, the evidence that higher intake lowers risk was judged convincing. A general cancer benefit looked probable, and possible benefits covered weight control, some eye diseases, dementia, and bone loss. For a few conditions the data were too thin to call. National campaigns urging more vegetables and fruit, the panel concludes, stand on justified scientific ground.
