In a letter dated 26 July 1861, William H. Seward gave James Shepherd Pike his latest word from Washington. It was printed as Document 246 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. By then, in the first summer of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d46:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams on 21 May 1861. The letter is document 46 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The letter of 21 May became famous for its harsh tone toward Britain. Lincoln and Seward softened its sharpest lines before it went out. Even so, it warned London plainly against any step that aided the South. Few single letters in the volume carry such weight in the history of the war. Lincoln's edit of the letter is one of the great acts of his early war leadership.
frus-1862-d146:
On 17 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent a dispatch from Washington to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The letter is printed as Document 146 in the Foreign Relations volume that the State Department laid before Congress with the President's yearly message.

That same day, Union and Confederate armies fought at Antietam in Maryland, the bloodiest single day of the Civil War. News crossed the Atlantic by ship, so London learned of battles days after Washington did. Dispatches from this week show the lag built into wartime statecraft, and the care both men took with news that could sway British policy.
frus-1862-d246:
On 26 December 1861 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris, in a dispatch printed as Document 246 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It was Seward's first Paris letter in this file.

Boxing Day 1861 was also the day Washington decided to free the envoys seized from the Trent, ending the crisis with Britain. Seward wrote to Paris as that settlement took shape. His letters to Dayton through the next year pressed one point. France should leave the American war alone and expect no Union blessing for adventures elsewhere. Edouard Thouvenel ran the French foreign ministry for most of 1862 and set Dayton's agenda there.
frus-1862-d346:
Filed out of order as Document 346, a Dayton report dated 6 November 1862 went from Paris to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. William L. Dayton was the American minister to France.

Dayton wrote two days after the Northern elections and in the week of the British cabinet's decision on the truce plan. His report thus sits at the crossing of the war's political and diplomatic threads. In the printed file it arrives late, among mid-November papers, a placement the reader must correct by its date. A steamer's sailing day set the legation's week, and Dayton wrote against that clock.
frus-1862-d446:
On 17 February 1862 Norman B. Judd reported from Berlin to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is Document 446 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record laid before Congress.

Judd's February report came as Union forces took Fort Donelson and opened the Tennessee River, victories that strengthened the Union's name in Europe. In Berlin he watched a Prussia busy with its own army reforms and its rivalry with Austria. His letters told Washington how the German world weighed the American war. For readers, the Berlin file is a useful contrast to London and Paris. At this court the Union's task was to keep goodwill warm. It did not have to head off harm.
frus-1862-d46:
News and judgment from Charles Francis Adams reached Seward's desk in a letter dated 11 April 1862. It was printed as Document 46 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. It was written in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d546:
Roest van Limburg received this reply from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 13 September 1862. The note is Document 546 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

Seward's mid-September notes to resident ministers were written in the shadow of the Maryland campaign, four days before Antietam. His Dutch reply handled the standing business between the governments with the Department's usual exactness. For Van Limburg, a written American answer was the useful thing: it could be sent home to The Hague as the Union's stated position. The exchange illustrates why both sides valued this formal traffic. It fixed positions, prevented surprise, and kept a useful friendship in repair during the war's most anxious fortnight.
frus-1862-d646:
On 30 April 1862, Robert H. Pruyn wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Pruyn was the new American minister to Japan, picked to take over the legation from Townsend Harris. His dispatch appears as document 646 in the Foreign Relations volume that covers 1862.

A new envoy's early letters told Washington what he found on taking up his post. Pruyn's report belongs to the hand-over between the first American mission to Japan and the men who would run it through the Civil War years. It is a plain, working piece of the record that tied a far-off legation to the State Department.
frus-1863p1-d146:
On 7 April 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. A dispatch from Adams bears the same date in the volume. The letter is document 146 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Seward wrote in the same week Adams reported on the seized raider, though neither man yet had the other's sheet. The cross of dates is the sea mail at work. His letter fed the brief at a bright point: Britain had at last held a Southern ship. This one is Washington's half of the day's exchange, set beside London's in the printed file.
frus-1863p1-d246:
Reporting on 23 July 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, wrote home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The report is document 246 in the 1863 diplomatic papers. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

For historians, this run is a prime source on Britain's choices. It shows how close London came to stepping into the war, and why it never did. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d346:
Writing in Washington on 31 December 1862, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, addressed Secretary of State William H. Seward on British business. The paper is document 346 in the 1863 volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Lyons knew that harsh words could push the two nations toward a fight neither wanted. His notes are firm on British rights but measured in tone. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war. Each side kept copies of the whole exchange, which is why the printed volume can show the argument from both desks.
frus-1863p1-d446:
The date 4 April 1863 heads a letter from William H. Seward, the Secretary of State to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d46:
On 28 October 1862, Judah P. Benjamin wrote again to James M. Mason, the South's envoy in London. Benjamin headed the Confederate state office in Richmond. The letter is document 46 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

A month had passed since Benjamin's last letter to Mason in this file, and the ground had shifted. Antietam was fought, and the freedom edict was on its way. Letters from Richmond had to keep envoys' hopes up as the facts grew hard. This one is part of that strain. Kept in the Union's printed record, it shows the South's London brief run from Richmond, sheet by sheet.
frus-1863p1-d546:
Writing on 1 June 1863, Assistant Secretary of State F. W. Seward addressed Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington in an official letter. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the early summer of 1863. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d646:
Dated 23 October 1863, document 646 is a letter from Charles Francis Adams to William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

That autumn the sharpest issue was the pair of ironclad rams built for the Confederacy at Birkenhead. Britain held them back, and this mail ran while that fight played out. The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d146: Secretary Hull wrote to Ambassador Steinhardt in Ankara on November 20, 1943, the same day the president also wrote to him. The letter is Document 146 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. A president's letter and a secretary's letter landing together marked a coordinated push on the Turkish question. The record gives the parties and the date and no topic. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d246:
The President's Log continues with the Cairo days, 22 to 25 November 1943, kept hour by hour. It opens with Roosevelt's flight from Tunis on 22 November, which ran late and worried the welcoming party at Cairo West airport.

Two fighter groups missed their rendezvous with the President's plane, which had swung south to the Nile and flown up the river over the Sphinx and the Pyramids. Roosevelt settled at Ambassador Kirk's villa near Gizeh, while the Sextant Conference met at the Mena House Hotel by the Pyramids. Churchill and the Chiangs, who had arrived the day before, called that afternoon, and a first meeting with staffs ran from nine until after eleven that night.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d346:
Alexander Kirk sent Harry Hopkins a second urgent, secret telegram from Cairo on 29 November 1943 about the held Cairo communiqué. It follows his alarmed message of the day before on the release arrangements.

The Chinese chargé has just called on Kirk to say he has cabled the text to Chungking, with orders to hold release until his own flash. Kirk reminded him that he, Kirk, was charged with giving the notice once word came from Tehran. The position now, Kirk points out, is that the text sits in the foreign offices of London and Chungking, while Washington, unless Hopkins has sent it direct, has no copy at all. He asks whether to cable the text to the State Department in advance, to be held there, or whether Tehran is handling it.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d446:
American and British officials produced an agreed record on December 5, 1943. The meeting took place at the Second Cairo Conference. Both delegations checked agreed minutes before they stood. So the text states what London and Washington jointly said happened. The State Department included it in the published Cairo-Tehran papers.

A reader finds the two allies' common account of one day's work. The conference was crowded and near its end. The Tehran decisions still had to become firm plans. Records of this type anchor the history of the summit. Memoirs can blur or boast over time. An agreed record fixes what both sides signed at the time.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d46: Stalin wrote to Roosevelt on October 17, 1943, two days before the Moscow Conference of foreign ministers opened in his capital. The message is Document 46 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Hull, Eden, and Molotov would do the talking in Moscow, but the leaders kept their own channel open above them. The record names no subject for this letter. Its text is printed in the Foreign Relations volume.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d546:
Marked secret in the printed volume, this message from President Roosevelt to Prime Minister Churchill is dated January 14, 1944. The two leaders corresponded constantly that month as invasion planning advanced. The State Department printed it in the Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

A secret marking on a leaders' message signals matter not meant for wider eyes, even inside their own governments. Roosevelt and Churchill kept several grades of candor in their letters, and the classified ones carried the alliance's real sensitivities. For readers, the document is part of the private layer of the partnership, preserved because the State Department's historians later judged it part of the conferences' story.
frus-1944-quebec-d146:
General Wilson, Supreme Allied Commander in the Mediterranean, sent the British and American chiefs a broad review of his theater on September 2, 1944. The first half covers Operation Dragoon, the landing in southern France. Wilson calls it an outstanding success, with some 50,000 prisoners taken and the ports of Toulon and Marseilles captured ahead of schedule.

The review then works through supply, railways up the Rhone, and the Seventh Army's advance toward Lyons. Wilson proposed transferring command in France to Eisenhower and forming the 6th Army Group. Turning to Italy, he counted some 26 German divisions facing his armies, though worn down to perhaps 17 in real strength. Air support for both fronts closes the survey.
frus-1944-quebec-d246:
Acting Treasury Secretary Daniel Bell briefed Morgenthau on September 14, 1944, on the French lend-lease negotiations, and his tone is alarm. A sixth draft agreement, agreed by State and the Foreign Economic Administration, would let long-life reconstruction goods go to France on long-term credits. Requisitions could be accepted until at least the end of the war with Japan, enabling reconstruction on a large scale.

Monnet, Bell reported, had a two-billion-dollar program ready for immediate requisitions. The July design had limited lend-lease to the end of European hostilities. War Department officials McCloy and Hilldring had stated flatly that French industrial production would be no help against Germany. Its help against Japan could be, in their phrase, put in your right eye.
frus-1944-quebec-d46:
A further Churchill message went to Roosevelt on September 1, 1944. The State Department printed it in the Quebec 1944 volume. It sits next to the day's other exchange.

Two messages from Churchill came in a single day. The Atlantic crossing lay ahead of him. The pattern suggests business finished in layers. One point was settled, and another was opened. The Quebec Conference had to divide hard work. It concerned the war's last phase between the allies. For readers, this companion message shows his preparation at full stretch. It came in the last week before the leaders met.
frus-1945-50-intel-d146:
On 8 April 1946 the Third Meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Board sat, and the minutes of the session survive here. The State Department prints it as document 146 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. No CIA yet existed: a board called the National Intelligence Authority ran the work, with the Central Intelligence Group as its staff.

The text is the meeting as the secretaries kept it, topic by topic, with the results marked as they were reached. Such pages are often the only proof of when a choice was made, and by whom. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d246:
Dated 3 November 1947, this memorandum runs from the Assistant Executive Secretary (Lay) to the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers). The Office of the Historian kept it as document 246 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The old board and its group were gone, replaced that fall by the CIA under the new National Security Council.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d346:
A memorandum dated 4 June 1948 links two senior offices. The sender was the Executive Secretary of the Intelligence Survey Group (Blum). The reader was Allen W. Dulles, Mathias F. Correa, and William H. Jackson. The State Department prints it as document 346 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. With the Soviet threat in mind, the Council was deciding what secret work the United States should do abroad.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. That plainness lets a reader see how an issue moved from a working office up to the men who decided it. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d46:
A paper prepared for the Secretary of State's Staff Committee is dated 15 November 1945. The staff committee was where the department's senior men settled questions for the secretary. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Papers written for a committee are drafted to be argued over, so they often state the options with unusual clarity. This one fed the State Department's top table as the intelligence contest moved toward decision. Readers can use it to see how the department framed the choice for itself, apart from what it told rivals. The distinction matters: what an agency says in its own room is the truest map of what it wants and what it fears.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d146:
President Roosevelt wrote to Premier Mikolajczyk on 17 November 1944, and Harriman carried the letter to London. It is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Roosevelt says he would rather have waited for the general postwar settlement, but he understands the premier's need for an answer now.

The position comes in numbered points. The United States stands without qualification for a strong, free, and independent Polish state. The Polish people must have the untrammeled right to order their own internal life. On frontiers, if the Polish, Soviet, and British governments reach mutual agreement, with Germany compensating Poland, Washington would raise no objection. One point is held back for the bearer: Harriman is to discuss the city of Lwów in person.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d246:
A strong China as the anchor of Asia is the long view in this briefing book paper of 13 January 1945. Its title promises an outline of long-range objectives and policies toward China. The paper is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

Peace and security in the Far East, it argues, rest on China becoming the principal stabilizing factor there. American policy therefore aims at three things. In politics, a strong, stable, and united China, governed as its people wish. In economics, a well-knit and balanced Chinese economy, with a fuller flow of trade to the world. In culture, joint work in learning and science, as a ground for common understanding. The paper then opens out the first of these aims in detail.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d346:
Foreign ministers at Yalta turned to publicity and to Germany's future at noon on February 6, 1945, in Edward Page's minutes. Stettinius said a first press release on the Crimean Conference seemed wise. Press aide Stephen Early spoke to the plan, and a draft was attached. Molotov suggested adding the word "common" before "enemy."

Stettinius offered small cuts of his own, which Molotov accepted, though the release still needed Stalin's approval. The ministers then took up how to study the dismemberment of Germany. They agreed to refer that question to the European Advisory Commission in London. Page catches the wording games behind a famous phrase.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d446:
Freedom to move and to report home is Britain's demand for its officers in Bulgaria, in this proposal of February 10, 1945. London held two things essential. Its representatives must enjoy reasonable freedom of movement and communication. And decisions must not be taken in Britain's name without British consultation.

For Hungary, agreed statutes for the control commission had already met the first point. London proposed that identical statutes be adopted for Bulgaria. It also wanted prior consultation with British and American officers during the first period. The paper repeats, almost word for word, the British memorandum of February 1 — a sign the point had not moved.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d46: Harriman reported to Roosevelt on 8 January 1945, answering from Moscow in the summit's final preparatory month. His message is document 46 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on Malta and Yalta. Reports sent this close to departure shaped the president's expectations directly, since there would be little time to correct a wrong reading of Soviet intentions later.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d146:
Harry Hopkins reported Stalin's Far East aims from Moscow in extracts of a telegram dated May 30, 1945. The extracts form document 146 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Hopkins, the President's adviser, was in Moscow on a special mission to smooth relations with Stalin before the summit.

Stalin is very anxious to discuss Japan at the coming conference, Hopkins writes. Some elements in Japan are putting out peace feelers, so the Allies should settle a joint line on Japan's surrender. Stalin expects Russia to share in the actual occupation of Japan, with agreed zones, and wants an understanding on areas of operation in Manchuria and China. The report warned Truman that Soviet entry into the Pacific war would come with a price in territory and influence.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d246:
A briefing book paper set out the American fallback positions on Libya, dated June 30, 1945. The paper is document 246 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Libya, Italy's North African colony, was one of the territorial questions the peace settlement would have to decide.

The United States proposes no program of its own, the paper says, but would support any of three solutions in order of preference. Best is returning all Libya to Italian rule, with general demilitarization. Next is partition: Tripolitania stays Italian, while Cyrenaica becomes an autonomous Senussi state under Egyptian or British trusteeship. Last is partition with Tripolitania under an international trusteeship run by Italy. Background data follow: a vast, poor desert land of 680,000 square miles, with some 100,000 Italian settlers counted in 1939.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d346:
German interim financing is the subject of a memorandum the Secretary of State sent President Truman on July 5, 1945. Four agencies, it reports, now agreed: State, Treasury, War, and the Foreign Economic Administration. Together they had settled proposals to put to the British, the French, and the Soviets on buying and paying for essential German imports.

Under the plan, the cost of imports would be a first charge on all German exports, whether from current production or stocks on hand. The memo also records a War Department caveat. The Army's duty to pay for supplies, it said, had not yet covered every import the government's broader aims in Germany required.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d446:
A British protest to Moscow is reported in Harriman's cable from Moscow, sent at midnight on July 7, 1945. The British ambassador, Sir Archibald Clark Kerr, had written Molotov on July 6 in sharp terms. His complaint concerned recent criticism in the Soviet press and radio of the Greek government, of British policy in Greece, and of General Scobie and the British troops there.

One article is named: a piece by Shalitov in New Times of June 15, on Greece. Clark Kerr described it as misleading and hostile. Harriman's brief report, repeated to Athens and London, shows Greece already serving as a Cold War battleground in print, weeks before Potsdam's Greek election plan was complete.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d46:
On June 1, 1945, President Truman sent Marshal Stalin a personal and top secret telegram, number 278, from Washington. It is document 46 in the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The message thanks Stalin for his note of May 30 about the date of the planned three-power meeting near Berlin.

Truman confirms that he has told Prime Minister Churchill that both he and Stalin agree to meet near Berlin around July 15. With this short cable, all three leaders had accepted the same date. The exchange shows how the Potsdam Conference was arranged: not by staffs or foreign offices, but in direct, brief messages between the heads of government themselves.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d546:
Fred Vinson, who ran war mobilization and reconversion, sent a top secret wire to the Secretary of State on July 13, 1945. It is document 546 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Vinson wrote from Washington while the President was at sea.

Vinson traces the muddle over lend-lease back to March, when Stimson asked President Roosevelt for a plan. He cites a Quebec pledge to let Britain reconvert its economy in a fair way. He also cites Churchill's anxious cable of May 28 and Admiral Leahy's fears. Truman's July 5 order, he says, has left all the top aides confused. He asks Byrnes for advice before the order harms the shift of U.S. forces to the Pacific.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d646:
A top secret briefing paper on Palestine was written for the Potsdam Conference, dated June 22, 1945. It is document 646 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers. It suggests the President raise Palestine in general terms with Churchill and ask what plans Britain has.

The paper stresses one deadline above all. The quota for Jewish immigration under the 1939 White Paper would run out by summer or early fall. Britain would then have to decide the key issue in the Palestine dispute. Any choice, the paper warns, risks serious disorder and even bloodshed. Zionist Jews were growing restless at the delays in a settlement. If Britain held to the White Paper and barred further immigration, moderate leaders might not restrain well-armed extremists in Palestine.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1046:
President Truman sent this memorandum to Stalin on July 27, 1945, with his coal directive to General Eisenhower attached. An acute coal famine threatens Europe this winter, he warns, unless German coal flows out in large amounts. America is already shipping coal across the Atlantic as an emergency step, despite shortages at home. The war against Japan caps what more it can send.

Truman has ordered his commander in Germany to raise output and exports, and London and Paris have done the same. He asks Stalin to join a common four-power policy. The Control Council should frame a coal production and export program for Germany as a whole. The attached directive sets a floor of 25 million tons for export by April 1946.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1146:
Poland's President Bierut and Prime Minister Osobka-Morawski signed this joint letter to President Truman on 20 July 1945. The two men headed the new government in Warsaw, the one the Soviet Union backed and the Western powers had just agreed to accept. Writing together, they spoke with the full weight of that government.

A joint letter from a head of state and a head of government is a formal reach for goodwill. Warsaw wanted American acceptance, trade, and a friendly hearing at Potsdam, where Poland's border was being set. The letter shows the new rulers courting Washington in public form. It sits oddly, and tellingly, beside the private doubts the Western envoys voiced elsewhere.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1246:
The President wrote to Ambassador Hurley in China on 24 July 1945. Truman's word reached the China post from the middle of the German talks. A presidential message steadied an envoy's hand like nothing else in the service.

Hurley's task in China was delicate: back the Nationalist government, press it toward unity with its communist rivals, and keep China in the war. Orders from the top set the line for that work. This note is the commander in chief tending the far end of his alliance. It shows the summit's leader ruling by cable across two oceans at once.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1346:
Clement Attlee wrote to President Truman on 31 July 1945, days after becoming prime minister of Britain. Attlee had beaten Churchill at the polls and taken his seat at the Potsdam table mid-conference. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Few letters in the volume carry a change of government inside them. Attlee's note opens the working tie between the new Labour government in London and Truman's White House. It also marks the strange shape of Potsdam, where one of the three delegations changed its leader halfway through. Readers can see the new prime minister step into the talks in his own words.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-146: Printed among the unnumbered items after document 710, this editorial note belongs to the second Potsdam volume. The historians who built the volume used such notes to explain the record's seams. They give provenance, flag missing pieces, and link kindred papers. A reader can lean on this note while crossing a dense field of staff writing.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-46:
A brief undated memorandum by President Truman records a question he put to Stalin on July 20, 1945. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Like the note before it, the text is Truman's manuscript jotting on a memo from Admiral Leahy.

Question asked of Stalin after meeting on 20th, Truman writes. Had already asked him when he called. Agreed to it in a few days. The editors identify the question from the file around it. It concerned when the Soviet chiefs of staff would meet with the United States chiefs of staff. Stalin's answer, as Truman records it, promised the military meeting within a few days. The scrap is characteristic of the President's own paper trail at Potsdam: three short sentences carrying a real piece of conference business.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d746:
Arthur Schoenfeld, the American representative in Hungary, reported to the Acting Secretary of State on July 17, 1945. Document 746 opens the volume's Hungary thread. Hungary was a former enemy state under an armistice and an Allied control body. Schoenfeld watched its politics from Budapest as Potsdam began.

Reports from the former enemy capitals grounded the summit's choices. Leaders argued over lands most had never seen. Men like Schoenfeld supplied the facts. Readers get a ground-level view of a country under foreign watch. The document shows how the conference's fate was prepared in embassies as much as in palaces.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d846:
Secretary of State Byrnes wrote directly to Soviet Foreign Commissar Molotov on July 19, 1945. Document 846 is a minister-to-minister letter inside the Potsdam record. Byrnes and Molotov faced each other daily at the conference. A formal letter between them fixed words that talk left loose. It joined the second Potsdam volume.

Letters between rivals carry a special charge. Each phrase is chosen knowing the other side will parse it. Readers see diplomacy at its most deliberate. The document also shows Byrnes working every channel: plenary, committee, and now direct paper. At Potsdam, the written word between principals was itself a move in the game.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d946:
Edwin Pauley explained a puzzle in the reparations figures to the Secretary of State on July 29, 1945. American and British totals looked far apart, he writes, but the gap was only method. Britain used 1938 replacement value plus 15 percent. America used depreciated value plus the same markup, to guard against later fights over removed machinery.

Pauley offers to accept the British new cost basis, if it also governs at removal time. He reports the Ruhr holds about 45 percent of reparations due from the western zones. Still, he advises drawing from all three western zones, not the Ruhr alone. War targets lie outside it, and the Ruhr itself is hard to define.
frus-1977-80v11p1-d46: Another 1977-1980 FRUS document from the hostage crisis volume. The 444 days. This document holds that record. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Coming generations can find it. Its pages add to the record of the past.
gao-gaoreports-b-295946: Sayres & Associates doubled its April 2005 protest — two dockets, one services fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Paired filings get one careful answer.

gao-gaoreports-gao-06-846: Military recruiters' misconduct needed tracking in 2006, and GAO's report says the Pentagon and services needed better data on irregularities. The findings demand the numbers. The report warns that the enlistment pitch should be honest. The recruiters had to be watched.

gao-gaoreports-gao-07-346: Screening flyers before they boarded was half-built in 2007 — GAO's report says the international passenger vetting push was moving, but planning and execution lagged. The findings grade the rollout. The report warns that the sky's front door needed a finished lock.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-46: Paying hospitals for brand-new treatments is one of Medicare's trickiest math problems, and GAO dissected it in 2007. gao-gaoreports-gao-08-346: The Government Accountability Office dug into residential Facilities: Improved Data and Enhanced Oversight Would Help Safeguard the Well-Being of Youth with Behavioral and Emotional Challenges in this 2008 report. gaule-select-cases-conscience-1646:
John Gaule weighs a priest's doubts in Select Cases of Conscience Touching Witches, his book of 1646. Gaule was a church man in the east, in the midst of the great hunt. Folk brought him hard asks: is my sick bairn bewitched, is my dream a sign, should I shun my next door dame? He replies from the Good Book with care, and with more doubt than the hunt's chiefs liked at that hot hour.

He warns gainst rash claims and cruel tests in plain words. That nerve, in that year, took grit. The book is a rare cool voice from the hunt's own turf.
gaule-select-cases-of-conscience-1646:
John Gaule was a Puritan minister who wrote Select Cases of Conscience Touching Witches and Witchcrafts in 1646. He wrote against Matthew Hopkins, the self-styled Witchfinder General whose hunt was then filling English gaols. Gaule's manual is pastoral: it sorts hard cases for troubled consciences.

He distinguishes true witchcraft, as he believed scripture taught it, from melancholy, fraud, and the lies of frightened witnesses. His tests would have acquitted most of the people Hopkins sent to the gallows in those years. The book shows a churchman using his own tradition's tools to slow a witch-hunt.
gaule-select-cases-of-conscience-english:
John Gaule, a minister in Huntingdonshire, published his Select Cases of Conscience in 1646. Those were the years of Matthew Hopkins, the self-styled Witchfinder General, whose hunt swept eastern England. Gaule's cases examine the scruples that witch-hunting raised in a pastor's mind, and they argue against the hunt's methods.

Gaule questions the tests, the confessions, and the haste of the finders. His protest is the first English clerical voice raised from inside the persecution itself. He wrote at real personal risk, since Hopkins's party answered critics sharply. Conscience set down in print gives the book its force. It shows resistance beginning within the church that blessed the trials.
greaves-pyramidographia-1646:
Oxford scholar John Greaves traveled to Egypt and measured the pyramids with care. His Pyramidographia appeared in 1646, among the first English studies of the sites. He brought tools, patience, and a love of exact fact.

Greaves records sizes, passages, and chambers in sober detail. He tests old tales against his own tape and eye. His numbers corrected centuries of loose guessing by travelers. The prose is plain for its age. The book marks a turn: Egypt studied by measure, not just marvel. It remains vital for the history of Egyptology.
guizot-civilization-europe-hazlitt-1846:
Francois Guizot's History of Civilization in Europe appears in William Hazlitt's translation of 1846. The book prints Guizot's famous Sorbonne lectures of 1828. Guizot traces European civilization from Rome's fall to the French Revolution. Europe, he argues, grew by the clash and balance of many forces: church, kings, towns, and free thought.

No single power ruled all, and so liberty survived and grew. The lectures made Guizot famous and shaped liberal history across Europe. Hazlitt, son of the essayist, gave the work its English form. The book is the classic liberal account of Europe's rise. Its breadth still impresses students of civilization.
howards-end-pg2946: E. M. Forster's 1910 Howards End: the Schlegels, the Wilcoxes, and the house. "Only connect" — his greatest novel. The Edwardian masterpiece. The house that holds England's soul, forster's supreme novel, Forster's supreme novel, the house that holds England's soul.
huntingdon-witches-examinations-1646:
Huntingdon's accused witches were questioned in 1646, at the crest of the East Anglian hunt led by Matthew Hopkins. The Witches of Huntingdon prints their examinations and confessions in full. The county town saw the panic at its most intense that year.

Confession follows confession in these pages, as the hunt's methods pressed the accused to name themselves and others. Hopkins and his helpers filled gaols across the east with just such work. The pamphlet lets readers judge the words the courts took as proof. It stands as a key record of England's worst witch year.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowengard-max-1:
Max Löwengard, a German rabbi who changed sides in his era's religious fight, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born in Württemberg, he was a friend of the novelist Berthold Auerbach. He was also a keen student of Schelling's philosophy. He died at Basel on May 25, 1876.

The entry stresses his unusual turn of mind. A fervent supporter of Reform in his youth, he became a zealous defender of Orthodoxy later in life. He held rabbinates at Gebenhausen and other Württemberg communities. His books attack Reform efforts in the synagogue and comment on Hamburg's new temple prayer book. Another work argued that Jehovah, not Moloch, was the God of the Hebrews. His first book appeared under the pen name Juda Leon.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-machlup-adolf-1:
Adolf Machlup, a Hungarian merchant and philanthropist, receives an entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Eisenstadt in 1833, he studied at Budapest and at Vienna's Polytechnic School. He took part in the revolutionary movement of 1848. He died at Budapest on January 1, 1895.

The article credits him with two industrial firsts. In 1867 he and his brother Eduard built Hungary's first leather factory at Budapest. The next year they opened the country's first factory for stearin candles and soap. Both ventures advanced Hungarian industry and trade. Machlup also gave widely to Jewish and non-Jewish societies alike. His largest gift was 200,000 gulden to found a nonsectarian home for convalescents in Budapest. The short entry joins business success to open-handed giving.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-manasseh-jacob-:
Jacob Manasseh, a Turkish rabbinical writer, gets a brief entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He served as chief rabbi of Salonica, where he died in 1832. His books were printed at Salonica and elsewhere in Turkey. They appear in the article as a short list of three.

The first work, Ohel Ya'akob, is an alphabetical collection of the laws of religion. It appeared at Salonica in 1832, the year of his death. Be'er ha-Mayim, a volume of responsa, followed there in 1836. The third, En ha-Mayim, comments on the Yoreh De'ah section of the Shulhan Aruk. It was printed in Turkey in 1858, long after his death. The entry rests on Hazan's survey of Jerusalem scholars and on Franco's history of Ottoman Jewry. Short as it is, it preserves the output of Salonica's chief rabbi for later bibliographers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-martyrology-104:
Martyrology is the written record of martyrs and how communities remember them. Joseph Jacobs and Siegmund Salfeld treat it in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. The article opens on the Christian side of the subject. Churches kept court records of their martyrs there. They shaped them into calendars, saint lists, and books of lives meant for reading aloud and in private.

Judaism, the article explains, kept no cult of saints in that sense. Its martyrs, the Kedoshim, were honored as people who had done their duty under torture and death. Their names survived in liturgical poems. They also survived in the lists of the German Memor-Books. Those lists were read aloud in synagogue on set Sabbaths and on the Ninth of Ab, when the congregation prayed for the martyrs' souls.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-medina-10546:
Medina is also a family name, and the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 gives the family its own entry, by Gotthard Deutsch and Henry Malter. These Medinas lived chiefly in Turkey and Egypt through the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, and the name most likely comes from one of the two Spanish cities called Medina. The article lays out a numbered genealogical tree of the members whose kinship could be proved.

The first names on the tree set its tone. David ben Moses di Medina wrote cabalistic commentaries on the Pentateuch, the Five Scrolls, and the Zohar, printed at Constantinople and Salonica. Isaac Hayyim edited a prayer-book for the congregation of Sienna, and his son Jacob published liturgical poems. A darker entry follows: Judah di Medina, a rich scholar of Salonica, was murdered at his own door, and the Jews of the city hanged the killer on the spot.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-of-tikt:
Menahem of Tiktin, known as Maharam Tiktin, was a Polish rabbi of the sixteenth century. He was a pupil of Moses Isserles. The Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 enters him through the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M. Seligsohn. His work was the emending and annotating of texts. His notes on the halakic codes of Isaac Alfasi and Mordecai ben Hillel were published after his death as the "Haggahot Maharam Tiktin."

His son Asher brought the glosses out at Cracow in 1597 and 1598. They have been reprinted in editions of Alfasi ever since. In his preface Asher testifies that his father wrote much more. The list covers notes on the Targum and on Rashi and Nahmanides. It covers the prayers, the liturgical poems, the Zohar, and other cabalistic works. That remainder is unpublished. The entry records it without being able to describe it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-min-pl-minim-10:
Min, plural minim, is the Talmud's word for a Jewish heretic or sectarian, unpacked in a Jewish Encyclopedia article by Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé, published in 1906. The term never means a Gentile, Rabbi Naḥman insists: it marks insiders who broke away. Depending on the century, the same word points at Samaritans, Sadducees, Gnostics, or Jewish Christians.

Early rabbis still talked and even studied with minim, but warmth curdled into hatred as the groups split for good. Rabbi Ṭarfon said their books deserved burning even with God's name inside them. The article details the famous prayer against the minim added to the Eighteen Benedictions and the legal walls built around them, ending with Maimonides' five classes of heretics.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mosenthal-solom:
Solomon Hermann von Mosenthal was an Austrian dramatist and poet born at Cassel on January 14, 1821. Isidore Singer and Max Cohen wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He came to Vienna in 1841 as a private teacher in the Goldschmidt house. His early plays brought him little lasting success.

His turn came in 1849 with the poetic drama Cäcilia von Albano, which opened the Burgtheater to him. His Deborah, from the same year, was translated into the main modern languages and became famous in English as Leah, the Forsaken. Mosenthal worked as a librarian in the Ministry of Education while writing many more plays. He also wrote librettos, among them The Merry Wives of Windsor for Nicolai and The Queen of Sheba for Goldmark.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-b-shemaia:
Moses ben Shemaiah was a scholar and preacher of the later seventeenth century. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his short Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Nothing is recorded of his birthplace or his teachers. His name survives through two printed works on the Bible.

The first, Wa-Yiktab Mosheh, is a commentary on the Pentateuch printed at Frankfort on the Oder in 1694. It also carries notes on Rashi's commentary on the same text. The second, Kodesh la-Adonai, explains one verse of Exodus and appeared in 1700. Notices like this one keep minor preachers of the age from vanishing from the record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathan-of-avign:
Nathan of Avignon was a French Talmud scholar. Wilhelm Bacher and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the second half of the fourteenth century. His one known work deals with food law. It concerns how animals are killed and checked. Such rules decide whether meat is fit to eat.

His book is called Hilkot Shehitah u-Bedikah. It sets out laws on slaughter and on examining carcasses. Nathan quotes rules from rabbis of eastern France. Among them he cites Jacob ben Yakar by name. The work still survives in a Cambridge manuscript. It sits in the margin of Isaac of Corbeil's Sefer Mizwot. The entry preserves a small, practical corner of medieval learning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nervous-disease:
Nervous diseases among Jews drew sharp study around 1900. Joseph Jacobs and Maurice Fishberg wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Specialists claimed Jews suffered such ills more than neighbors. Hysteria and neurasthenia were named most often. Male hysteria, rare elsewhere, seemed common among Jews.

One New York count put Jews over forty per cent. That was among 333 neurasthenia cases Collins saw. Writers blamed city life and trade callings first. Others blamed cousin marriage, a claim modern views dispute. Long persecution across the Diaspora was also cited. Kishinef's 1903 massacre showed the old terror still lived. The heder's early, long study days were blamed too. Death figures, though, pointed in mixed directions by city.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nile-11546:
The Nile is the great river of Egypt. The entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee and W. Max Muller for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Bible calls it ye'or throughout its pages. That word is borrowed from late Egyptian speech. It has no Semitic root of its own.

Egypt's very life hung on the Nile's yearly flood. Summer rains in Abyssinia's mountains sent it down. The river gave even all the drinking water. Prophets threatened Egypt with rivers made dry. That threat meant utter annihilation for the land. Egyptians knew only half the river's long course. They made its god a fat, fruitful figure, Hopi. Egypt itself was rightly called the Nile's gift.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-optimism-and-pe:
Optimism and pessimism are two views of life and the world. Joseph Jacobs and Emil G. Hirsch wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. One view holds that life is at root good. The other holds that life is at root evil. Great minds of the past stand on both sides.

Plato, Aquinas, and Leibnitz speak for the first view here. Buddhism and Schopenhauer speak for the second view, it says. Judaism, the piece holds, is at root of the first kind. Genesis says that all God made was very good. Man alone is free to choose good or ill. So the ills of life flow from man's own deeds. They are the wage of sin, not a flaw in things. Yet hard facts of life shook that plain faith at times.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pikes-abraham-b: Abraham Pikes was a German rabbi known from two letters. The Executive Committee and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His name appears in the Likkute Maharil on Sabbath law. His two letters went to the community of Halberstadt. They treat the commandments and the prohibitions in detail. He asked that the letters be copied and read aloud. Both letters were printed at Basel in 1599.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pollak-jacob-12:
Jacob Pollak founded the Polish method of Talmud study known as Pilpul. Isidore Singer and Eduard Neumann wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born about 1460, he learned under Jacob Margolioth of Nuremberg. He served as rabbi at Prague about 1490 with his teacher's son Isaac.

Pollak first won fame through a hard divorce case in his own family. He held that a young wife could refuse her husband and end the match. Most German rabbis ruled against him and shut him out. One rabbi alone stood with him. Judah Minz of Padua also ruled against his view. Later Pollak became rabbi of Cracow under King Sigismund the First. His sharp method shaped Talmud study in Poland for years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-prerau-benjamin: Benjamin Wolf Prerau was a Moravian scholar of Hebrew who lived at Prerau. The Editorial Board and Peter Wiernik wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. He printed a work of Bedersi with a German rendering. He added his own notes and a first part to it. Each word of that first part starts with one letter. He also wrote notes on the notes of Ibn Ezra. That book came out at Vienna in 1823.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-purgatory-12446:
Purgatory is a state through which souls are said to pass. Kaufmann Kohler wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. There souls are cleansed of sin, the teaching holds. Only then are they let into the bliss of heaven. The belief is a base stone of the Roman Catholic Church.

Church teachers rest the belief on one text above all. It stands in the twelfth chapter of Second Maccabees. There Judas is praised for a gift for the dead. Had he not hoped they would rise again, the text says, it had been vain to pray for them. So he made an atonement to free them from sin. Kohler weighs that text and the Jewish views near it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rehfuss-carl-12:
Carl Rehfuss was a German teacher born at Altdorf in 1792. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He died at Heidelberg in 1842. From 1809 to 1816 he taught in several towns.

The article says Baden's Grand Duke named him chief teacher and preacher in 1819. His formal title was Israelitischer Oberlehrer und Prediger. In 1834 Heidelberg University gave him a doctorate. His works include Imre Emet, on confirmation among Israelites. Another book is a handbook of Judaeo-German. A third offers devotions for the afflicted. A long source list ends the entry. Readers see a state backed Jewish educator with several practical books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ridbaz-willowsk:
Jacob David Ridbaz was a Russian rabbi born on February 7, 1845. Cyrus Adler and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in Kobrin, in Grodno province. He is also known as the Slutsker Rav.

The article lists his rabbinates across Russia in order. Izballin, Bobruisk, Wilna, and Polotsk came first. At Slutsk from 1890 he founded a yeshivah in 1896. His fame rests on commentaries to the Jerusalem Talmud. He studied that Talmud for thirty years. He worked on his notes for seventeen years steadily. His edition used a copy annotated by the Wilna Gaon. When funds ran out, he raised subscriptions in America. The entry honors a lifetime given to one hard text.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosendale-simon:
Simon W. Rosendale was an American lawyer born at Albany, New York, on June 23, 1842. Cyrus Adler and G. Herbert Cone wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Admitted to the bar in 1863, he soon became a city judge.

Rosendale served as recorder of Albany, then as the city's corporation counsel. In 1892 he was elected attorney-general of New York state. Governor Theodore Roosevelt later named him a state commissioner of charities. In Jewish affairs he led B'nai B'rith's court of appeals for ten years. He also chaired the 1888 meeting that organized the Jewish Publication Society.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-sime:
Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Samuel ben Simeon. He was a French scholar who lived in Provence in the fourteenth century. He is also called Samuel Astruc d'Escola. His Hebrew surname, Kenesi, came from a loose rendering of d'Escola. That name was common in southern France.

Samuel wrote a preface to Shesh Kenafayim, a work on astronomy by Immanuel ben Jacob. The preface still survives only in manuscript. He was probably the same man as Nasi Samuel d'Escola. That Samuel explained the star tables of Bonet Don Giorno. The entry links one scholar to the study of astronomy in medieval Provence.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schaffer-scheps:
Cyrus Adler and I. George Dobsevage wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Schepsel Schaffer. He was an American rabbi. Schaffer was born on May 4, 1862, at Bausk, in Courland, Russia. He descended from Mordecai Jaffe, author of the Lebush. He studied at the gymnasium of Libau and at the University of Berlin. He also trained at the Rabbinical Seminary in Berlin.

Since January 1, 1893, Schaffer has led Shearith Israel congregation in Baltimore. He earned his doctorate in Berlin. He has presided over the Baltimore Zion Association since 1895. He is an honorary vice-president of the American Federation of Zionists. Twice he served as a delegate to the Zionist Congress at Basel. His one book treats law and morality in Talmudic teaching. It appeared at Frankfort-on-the-Main in 1889.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schweinfurt-heb:
Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Schweinfurt. The town lies in Lower Franconia. Its Jews first appear in 1243. That year Henry of Bamberg ordered fifty marks in silver paid to them. In 1263 a murdered Christian girl was blamed on the Jews. The mayor's firm action stopped a riot by the mob.

The girl, it turned out, died in a town faction fight. Schweinfurt's Jews still suffered in the persecutions of 1298 and 1349. In 1390 Wenceslaus the Fourth annulled all debts owed to them. In 1544 their schools were closed despite their advocate's pleas. Today the town seats the district chief rabbi, Dr. S. Stein. Some 415 Jews live there in 1905. The wider district holds about 1,500 Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-servi-flaminio-:
Flaminio Ephraim Servi was an Italian rabbi born at Pitigliano, Tuscany, in 1841. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He studied in his home town, at Padua, and at Florence. In 1864 he took his first rabbinate at Monticelli.

Servi later led the community at Casale-Monferrato as chief rabbi. There he edited a Jewish journal and yearly almanacs for Jewish families. He wrote on Italian Jewish numbers, on Dante and the Jews, and on women's roles. He died in 1904, still known as a busy writer. The entry presents a rabbi who served Italian Jews in print as much as in the pulpit.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sifra-13646:
Sifra is the legal midrash, or commentary, on the book of Leviticus. Wilhelm Bacher and S. Horovitz wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. The Talmud quotes Sifra frequently in its discussions. Study of it followed study of the Mishnah in schools.

Like Leviticus itself, the work is called Torat Kohanim. That name means the law of the priests. Two Talmud passages call it Sifra debe Rab as well. One old explanation ties that title to school practice. Leviticus was the first book studied by young children. So its midrash took the school name with it. The entry disputes parts of that explanation carefully. It compares similar debe Rab titles for other works. Readers learn how scholars argue over a book's very name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simon-maccabeus:
Simon Maccabeus was a Hasmonean prince and high priest who died in 135 BCE. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was the second son of Mattathias. His dying father praised him as a man of counsel. His brothers were urged to heed his advice in all things.

Simon fought beside Judah and Jonathan in the war against Syria. He saved hard-pressed Jews in Galilee. Antiochus VI made him military commander of the coast. He took Beth-zur and Joppa and garrisoned both towns. After Jonathan was captured, the people chose Simon as their leader. He then stood alone at the head of the nation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-south-and-centr:
South and Central America were first colonized by Spain and Portugal. Cyrus Adler, Joseph Jacobs, and Elkan N Adler wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Those lands still remain Spanish and Portuguese speaking today. Under Spanish rule, Jewish history there turns on the Maranos. They were secret Jews who professed Catholicism in name only.

Open Jewish settlement was barred in Spanish colonies by law. The same exclusion held in Portuguese Brazil after 1508. The Inquisition was never formally set up in Brazil, though. Its agents there spied on secret Jews and seized them. Convicted Jews were also shipped to Brazil as a punishment. Jews helped plant sugar-cane in Brazil as early as 1548.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spector-mordeca:
Mordecai Spector was a Russian Judæo-German writer born at Uman in 1859. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born there on May 5 of that year. His early schooling was in the Hasidic spirit. That training let him write for Hasidim and Mitnaggedim alike.

From 1874 he studied secular sciences under Colonel Winde. Eliezer Zweifel urged him to write novels in Judæo-German. His first novel appeared in the Volksblatt in 1883. In 1884 he became associate editor of that paper. Later at Warsaw he founded the Hausfreund and Familienfreund. He also gathered 2,056 Jewish proverbs in print there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stiassny-wilhel:
Wilhelm Stiassny was an Austrian architect born in Vienna on October 15, 1842. Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He graduated from the Vienna Polytechnic in 1861. He then studied five years at the Academy of Fine Arts. In 1862 he helped found a builders' association in Vienna.

Stiassny settled as an architect in Vienna in 1868. By 1905 he had directed about 180 building projects. They include palaces, schools, factories, hospitals, and synagogues. His works include the Rothschild Hospital at Währing. He designed synagogues in Hungary, Gablonz, and Czaslau. He served on Vienna's city board for over twenty years. In 1895 he founded a society to preserve Jewish monuments. The entry honors a builder of Jewish Vienna.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-swaying-the-bod:
Swaying the body during prayer and study is an old Jewish habit. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Jews in the Orient and eastern Europe still practice it. Other nations do not share the custom. Teachers across centuries asked why Jews alone sway.

The Zohar links swaying to the soul as God's candle. Its light flickers with the light of the Torah. Judah ha-Levi gave two plainer reasons in the Cuzari. Motion stirs energy and focus during study. Also, scarce books once forced scholars to share one volume. Leaning in by turns built a lasting habit. Yemenite Jews still study that shared way today. The entry weighs mystical and practical accounts of one gesture.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tarascon-hebrew:
Tarascon is a city in the south of France. Isidore Singer and S. Kahn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about it in 1906. It sits in the department of Bouches-du-Rhône. In 1276 King Charles the First shielded its Jews. Inquisitors had forced them to enlarge their badge. They had also squeezed large fines from the community.

Jews expelled from Languedoc in 1306 found welcome there. Two years later Jews lost the right to public office. Queen Jeanne protected the community in 1348 and 1378. Her daughter Marie treated Jews and Christians alike in 1390. Louis the Second freed them from new taxes in 1400. He gave them a letter of special protection. It charged townsfolk with guarding Jewish lives and goods. The entry shows protection and pressure alternating by reign.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tetragrammaton-:
The Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God, is studied in depth here. Crawford Howell Toy and Ludwig Blau wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Other Hebrew names for it include Ha-Shem and Shem ha-Meforash. Josephus and the Church Fathers both mention the name.

The article counts the name 5,410 times in the Bible. Genesis alone holds 153 of those cases. Psalms holds 645, the largest share of any book. Joined forms bring the total near six thousand. The name never appears in Canticles, Ecclesiastes, or Esther. That absence hints at those books' late date. Counts and patterns give readers hard data on a sacred word.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-torah-hebrew-ar:
Torah, the name for the five books of Moses, anchors this long article. Joseph Jacobs and Ludwig Blau wrote it for the Jewish Encyclopedia, published in 1906. Genesis through Deuteronomy make up the Torah. This article covers the Torah's place in later Judaism. Its contents as a whole are treated under Pentateuch.

The word Torah itself means doctrine or teaching. Greek-speaking Jews rendered it nomos, meaning law. That choice fed a false picture of Judaism as mere law. In truth the Torah holds teaching as well as law. Its laws come wrapped in ethical stories. The article lists the Torah's many Bible names. Book of the Law of Moses is one form. Tradition even speaks of the Torah as a living creature.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-troki-13846:
Troki, a district city in the Wilna government of Russia, was a Karaite center. Herman Rosenthal, J. G. Lipman, and Peter Wiernik wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Grand Duke Witold brought Karaite families from the Crimea. Tradition says 330 of 483 families settled at Troki. The city was built expressly for them.

Casimir IV granted the Karaites Magdeburg rights in 1441. Their own elder judged them, answerable to the king. Mixed lawsuits went before a joint tribunal. Alexander confirmed those privileges in 1492. Troki Jews farmed customs duties across many towns in the 1480s. By 1507 their prosperity had declined sharply. They petitioned King Sigismund for relief that year.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-turkey-14546:
Turkey, the Ottoman empire of Europe and western Asia, sheltered Jews from early times. Joseph Jacobs and Mary W. Montgomery wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Tradition places a Jewish colony in Thessaly under Alexander. The first colony in Turkey proper stood at Brusa. Sultan Urkhan repopulated Brusa with Jews in 1326.

Those Jews received a firman to build a synagogue. That building still stood as Turkey's oldest synagogue. Jews lived in a separate quarter called Yahudi Mahalessi. A head tax let them own land elsewhere too. Under Murad I the Turks crossed into Europe. Jews there welcomed the change of rulers. Muslim rule proved more tolerant than Byzantine rule. Adrianople's yeshiva drew pupils from Poland and Russia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-usury-10946:
Usury in Jewish law means any interest at all between Israelites, this article explains. Lewis N. Dembitz and Joseph Jacobs wrote it with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Modern speech limits usury to excessive rates. Biblical law instead bans all increase on a brother's debt. No limit applies toward Gentile borrowers, though.

Three passages in Torah state the ban plainly. Exodus, Leviticus, and Deuteronomy all forbid interest from brothers. The Hebrew word neshek means a bite, from its pain. Ezekiel ranks lending on interest among the worst sins. Psalm 15 counts avoiding usury a mark of righteousness. The Talmud compares the interest-taker to a shedder of blood. Sages still knew that delay on a debt costs real money.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weiss-joseph-hi:
Joseph Hirsch Weiss was a Hungarian rabbi. He was born at Podola in 1800. Isidore Singer and Stephen S. Wise wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He died at Erlau in 1881. He descended from a long line of Moravian rabbis. The family name was once Weissfeld.

In 1840 Weiss became chief rabbi of Erlau. He led Hungary's ultra Orthodox party there. He fought the founders of Reform at Pesth. In 1848 he joined the Kossuth movement. He hid from arrest in Erlau's monastery. Vienna later tried him for sedition and acquitted him. His grandson gave his library of responsa to Columbia University.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-winternitz-wilh:
Wilhelm Winternitz was an Austrian doctor and water cure expert. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Josefstadt, Bohemia, on March 1, 1835. He studied at Vienna and at Prague. He took his medical degree in 1857. Navy service followed, then a Vienna practice.

Water treatment soon became Winternitz's specialty. Experts counted him a leading authority on hydropathy. In 1865 he joined Vienna's medical faculty as lecturer. He helped found the General Vienna Dispensary. He opened a private water cure hospital near Vienna. In 1899 he became a full professor. He founded a journal of clinical hydrotherapy in 1890.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ya-aleh-15046:
Yaaleh is a hymn that opens the night prayers of the Day of Atonement. Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It stands before the added prayers of that night in the north rites. No one knows for sure who wrote the hymn.

The hymn has eight parts in a rare word scheme. Each part has three lines of set form. The last letter of the Hebrew set comes three times. That count brings the lines to twenty-four in all. Its verbs come from a feast day prayer of the rite. That prayer asks that prayer rise and be seen by God. A new English hymn drew its thought from this old one. An old tune for it from the 1700s still lives.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zera-im-seeds-1: Zeraim, which means Seeds, is the first order of the Mishnah. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. That order holds eleven tracts in its full set. Their names run from Berakot at the head to Bikkurim. All but the first treat the laws of farm and field. That scope is what the name of the order tells.
journals-of-expeditions-of-discovery-int:
The complete Journals of Expeditions of Discovery into Central Australia unite Edward John Eyre's two volumes in one file. They record his journeys of 1840 and 1841, ending in July of the second year. His route ran overland from Adelaide to King George's Sound. The colonial government of South Australia sanctioned and supported the work.

Eyre dedicates the journals to Governor George Gawler, under whose rule the expeditions went out. A long preface defends the delay in publishing them. From 1841 to 1844 Eyre worked to restore peace with the Murray River tribes instead. The complete text joins the travel record to his account of Aboriginal manners and customs. It remains a primary source for early South Australian exploration.
junius-grand-proces-rothschild-satan-184:
A Paris pamphlet of 1846, signed with the pen name Junius Grand, stages a mock trial in verse and prose. The crowned foe in its title is 'Satan,' named the last king of impostors. The man in the dock is 'Rothschild the First, king of the Jews,' in the pamphlet's own bold words.

The fake trial is a sly hit back at the pamphlet war then raging in Paris. That war made the false tale that the house grew rich on first news of Waterloo. The short piece is a sharp bit of the press fight of its day, kept as a record.
kennan-long-telegram-1946:
George Kennan, an American diplomat in Moscow, sent the Long Telegram to Washington in February 1946. The cable ran to some 8,000 words, far longer than normal diplomatic traffic. Officials had asked why the Soviet Union opposed a Western-led world bank, and Kennan answered with a full account of Soviet thinking.

He described a regime that felt insecure, pushed outward by ideology and habit, yet moved with patience rather than fixed plans. Against such a rival, he argued, the United States needed firm and patient resistance at every point. The telegram spread through the government at once and gave shape to the policy soon named containment, which guided American strategy for the Cold War.
narrative-of-a-survey-of-the-intertropic:
Captain Phillip P. King's second volume continues his Australian survey. The voyages ran from 1818 to 1822 in the ship Mermaid. John Murray issued the book in London's Albemarle Street. Chapter one opens with survey work and a hard choice.

King had to buy another vessel and plant a new post. The fourth voyage then sailed with a merchant ship through Torres Strait. A stowaway was found added to the crew, the contents tease. The party rounded Breaksea Spit and worked up the east coast. King's charts and notes mapped shores key for trade between Australia and Asia.
oliver-historical-landmarks-of-freemason:
George Oliver, an English clergyman and Masonic writer, published Historical Landmarks of Freemasonry in 1846. Oliver studied old lodge records and customs, and he wrote to defend the craft against its critics. His book treats certain rules and customs as fixed landmarks that no Mason may change.

Oliver traced those landmarks through Bible stories, old charges, and lodge tradition, linking modern Masonry to a much older past. He also answered attacks on the order and explained its symbols in moral terms. Readers get both a history and a defense, written by one of the most learned Masonic authors of his century.
openalex-w2034948246:
Abelardo Moncayo, Zoraida Fernandez, Diana Ortiz and colleagues tested how dengue virus adapted to household mosquitoes. Their paper appeared in Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2004. Epidemic dengue spreads between people by two mosquito species. Ancestral dengue circulated among forest primates. Gene evidence suggested the virus adapted to new vectors.

The team fed mosquitoes blood meals with different virus strains. They used mosquitoes from the Americas and Southeast Asia. Both mosquito species caught epidemic strains very easily. They were far less open to forest strains. Infection rates ranged from none to total. The results support the adaptation idea. Dengue likely emerged when forest viruses adapted to town mosquitoes. That shift let the virus spread among people.
openalex-w2049891146:
Mikhail Rabinovich, Ramon Huerta, Pablo Varona and Valentin Afraimovich offered a theory of how thinking unfolds over time. Their paper appeared in PLoS Computational Biology in 2008. Brain activity often passes through brief, shifting states. Such states may underlie decision making. A good theory must explain both steadiness and flexibility.

The authors describe thought as switching between metastable states. Metastable states hold briefly, then give way. Their model links such states in a stable channel. Noise helps the brain move along the channel. The path is reliable, yet open to change. That balance solves a key puzzle in the theory. The paper gives decision research a fresh mathematical picture.
openalex-w2124227746:
José Tomás Matus, Felipe Aquea, and Patricio Arce-Johnson published this study in BMC Plant Biology in 2008. They mapped one large family of grape genes, the R2R3 MYB genes, which act as switches for many plant traits. No one had yet charted this family across the whole genome of a woody plant like grapevine.

The authors found and classified more than a hundred members of the subfamily in grape. They compared gene shapes and matches with the model plant Arabidopsis. Groups tied to grape skin fate were larger in grape than in Arabidopsis or rice. Clusters linked to color and tannins, both key to wine quality, also stood out as expanded.
openalex-w2161115346:
Christoph Neumann, Sven Reichardt, Pedro Venezuela, and colleagues published this study in Nature Communications in 2015. They show that Raman light scattering can probe tiny strain variations in graphene that no microscope map can see directly. Graphene quality checks rely on this gentle laser method, but the widening of its strongest signal line was unexplained.

Raman maps average strain over the laser spot, about five hundred nanometres wide. Strain that varies on far smaller scales hides inside that average. The authors prove the width of the Raman 2D line measures exactly those nanometre-scale variations. The width thus reports local flatness, lattice warping, and crystal quality. It also ties to the electron mobility limits seen in top-grade graphene.
openalex-w2163068346:
Peter Katzmarzyk, Tiago Barreira, Stephanie Broyles, and colleagues published this protocol paper in BMC Public Health in 2013. They describe the design of ISCOLE, an international study of childhood obesity, lifestyle, and environment. The study asks how daily habits relate to body fat in children, and how homes, schools, and policies shape those links.

The plan targeted six thousand ten-year-olds across twelve countries in five world regions. Data span the child, family, neighborhood, and school levels, from motion sensors to school audits. One standard protocol was built for every site. Staff training and certification ran through web modules and regional meetings, keeping methods aligned across very different settings.
openalex-w3087284646:
Mario Valdés Tresanco, Mario Valdés-Tresanco, Pedro Valiente, and Ernesto Moreno published this application note in Biology Direct in 2020. It introduces AMDock, a friendly graphical program that helps run molecular docking studies. Docking simulates how a small molecule fits into a protein, a core step in drug hunting.

AMDock wraps two standard docking engines and several helper tools into one interface. It prepares the input files, helps set the search box on screen, and displays results in a molecular viewer. A special off-target mode makes it easy to test whether a drug candidate also fits unintended proteins. The authors aim the free program at Windows and Linux users, with beginners in mind above all.
openalex-w3210895846: Lea Berrang-Ford, A. R. Siders, Alexandra Lesnikowski, and colleagues took stock of global evidence. Their subject was how people are adapting to climate change around the world. Their systematic stocktake appeared in Nature Climate Change in 2021. The preserved sample holds only the title page and author list. It has no readable abstract or findings, so the team's conclusions cannot be described here.
openalex-w7204112546:
Gabriele Oliveira da Silva led a Portuguese-language study, in Brazil in 2026, on environmental, social, and control principles in the cement industry, one of the world's most carbon-heavy sectors. Cement making releases large amounts of carbon dioxide, and producers face rising regulatory and market pressure. The study reviewed research papers, books, tech records, and reports, sorting findings by the three ESG pillars.

Cutting emissions, the authors find, requires joined plans: better energy efficiency, burning waste as fuel, using less clinker, adding supplementary cement supplies, and capturing carbon. Success also depends on control, transparency, risk running, and relations with workers and communities. ESG integration, they conclude, can drive innovation and support the industry's shift to lower-carbon production.
openalex-w7204266446:
Bárbara Junqueira Carvalho Coutinho led a Portuguese-language umbrella review, in Brazil in 2026. It asks how quickly doctors should drain the bile duct in severe acute cholangitis, a dangerous infection of the blocked biliary tree. Treatment combines antibiotics, organ support, and decompression, but the ideal timing is disputed. The review searched four sources and official guidelines up to August 2026, weighing the forty-eight, twenty-four, and twelve hour thresholds.

Meta-analyses and large office datasets favor drainage within twenty-four to forty-eight hours, while the largest medical cohort found no mortality gain across all severe cases. Evidence for under twelve hours is inconsistent, plausible mainly in septic shock and worsening organ failure. The authors propose forty-eight hours as an outer limit, twenty-four as the working target, and twelve or less as a conditional priority.
openalex-w7208767446:
Yoshifumi Kondo and five colleagues at Osaka-area universities report a water-cleaning material made from steel waste. Blast furnace slag is an abundant industrial by-product, and the team converted it into a composite of hydroxyapatite and zeolite, two minerals known for trapping metal ions.
