Their target was cobalt ions, a toxic contaminant in water. The study tests how fast and how fully the new material pulls cobalt from solution.

The composite removed cobalt within an hour of contact, reaching nearly complete removal at lower concentrations. Its uptake pattern matched a standard model of surface absorption, and its maximum capacity rivaled a simple mixture of high-purity zeolite and hydroxyapatite. As cobalt was taken up, sodium and calcium ions were released in exchange. Turning slag into a sorbent this effective points to a double gain: less industrial waste and cleaner water.
openalex-w7212060846:
Cleverton Ricelli Santos Moura leads a team on a hard call type in Santarem, Para: people in psychotic crisis. Such calls have grown more common in Brazil. They put the person, the crews, and the public at risk at once. The study tracks one police unit, the 2nd Special Missions Battalion of the Para military police. It reads unit records from 2022 to 2026 and talks with staff from both police and the SAMU urgent care teams.

Thirty-six staff gave their views: fourteen police and twenty-two from SAMU. Calls of this kind, they report, are complex on the ground. Safe care takes health and police crews acting as one team. The authors sort the blocks the crews face and the moves that work. They also map ways the two services can train and plan as one. The Amazon setting gives the case its own weight.
openalex-w7213545246:
Deise Aparecida de Oliveira leads a team asking whether disability fits inside a symbol. Their 2026 qualitative, documentary study examines Brazilian inclusion policy from 1985 to 2026. Rules on the accessibility symbol guide the investigation, with law treated as a product of its historical moment.

Movement from the older access symbol to the United Nations accessibility symbol was not a straight line, they find. A 2026 law kept the wheelchair symbol after a presidential veto, changed its name, and demanded proof of real accessibility for its use. Medical, individual views of disability still compete with social and human rights views. The symbol dispute, the authors show, mirrors that deeper contest.
openalex-w7213562446:
Ana Nerry Miotto Cecilio and Andréa Carla Moraes Pereira Lago study women in prison and restorative justice in Brazil. Their 2026 qualitative article uses critical criminology, national and international law, court precedent, and official 2024 prison data. Female imprisonment is framed as a sharp edge of the wider prison crisis.

Many imprisoned women serve sentences for drug offences amid deep social vulnerability, the authors show. A purely retributive model cannot handle the relational and social sides of their cases. Belgian experience with penal mediation and peace-building circles are examined as alternatives. Restorative justice, they argue, could protect dignity, mental integrity, maternal identity, and social reintegration for women behind bars.
openalex-w7214118846:
Danielle Benchimol Gomes and co-authors challenge the new calculation rule for permanent incapacity retirement in Brazil. A 2019 constitutional amendment cut the benefit for insured people whose incapacity does not come from work accident or occupational disease. Their 2026 article analyses the Supreme Court case that upheld the rule by a narrow six-to-five majority.

Equality and the ban on social regression are the principles brought against the decision. Deductive method, with library, doctrinal, legislative, and case law research, supports the critique. The same incapacity now pays differently depending on its cause, they argue. Whether that split respects equal treatment of equally disabled workers is the question the article presses on the court's reasoning.
openalex-w7214176946:
Thiago Rodrigues Gonçalves and co-authors argue for a plural science in bodily schooling. Their 2026 theoretical essay is and reflective, built from library research and debate. Classic epistemology and philosophy of science are set against recent bodily schooling production and its object of study.

Many theoretical matrices cross the field, and that plurality expresses its identity rather than weakening its science, they argue. Research training challenges remain and demand permanent qualification of debate. Reading bodily schooling as praxis adds an ethical, transformative dimension. Recent turns, from physical reading to artificial intelligence, reshape the field without dissolving it. Physical schooling stands as a legitimate, autonomous research field, they conclude.
openalex-w7214784946:
Elesandra da Costa Neves led a 2026 integrative review on how media shapes the construction of female beauty. Beauty standards change over time, and social media has made comparing, sharing, and judging appearance part of daily life. The team reviewed studies from 2016 to 2026 in psychology and academic databases, keeping seventeen works and sorting them into three themes.

The themes trace how the beauty standard is socially built, how media interferes in that construction, and how thinness became the reigning ideal of female beauty. The studies connect media with body dissatisfaction, self-esteem, acceptance, digital influencers, and appearance filters. Old beauty references persist, the authors note, even as new ways of representing women's bodies gain space online. The review gives readers a map of how representation, body image, and self-worth interact in the social media era.
openalex-w7220368746:
Océlia Maria de Morais Cavalcante led a 2026 article on gaslighting, the manipulation that makes a woman doubt her own perception and memory, read through psychoanalysis. Their review joins national and international studies, classic psychoanalytic works, and the Brazilian laws that frame psychological violence against women, read through thematic content analysis.

Four themes emerged. The first was legal recognition of psychological violence. The others were the aggressor's psychic dynamics, marked by projection, denial, and a place of dominance. Then came effects on the victim, including self-doubt, guilt, isolation, and repetition of abusive bonds. The last theme was mental health impacts with paths of response. Gaslighting is not mere conscious manipulation, they conclude, since unconscious processes work on both sides and gender inequality sustains it. Psychoanalysis helps clinical grasp and listening that rebuild women's autonomy, joined with the wider protection network.
openalex-w7221053746:
Matheus Brondani Prevedello led a nine-author mapping, published in 2026. It compares Brazilian research with world research in one narrow field. The field is Building Information Modeling used to run finished buildings. Despite the broad title, upkeep and daily operation are the focus.

Thirty peer-reviewed studies from 2022 to 2026 were scored. The scores weighed new ideas, research value, and closeness to the field's frontier. World journals matched new directions more strongly. Digital twins, AI, linked sensors, and planned upkeep were those directions. The mapping shows Brazilian work present but trailing. It also shows where journals reward frontier topics most.
openalex-w7221167846:
Marianna Nunes de Alcântara Araújo Barreto led a large team reporting an unusual guest in group prenatal care: a veterinary doctor. The 2026 report comes from a family health unit in João Pessoa, Paraíba. Residents in animal medicine, nursing, psychology, and physical therapy ran shared sessions for pregnant women.

The guiding idea was One Health. Human, animal, and environmental health interlock, it holds. The animal doctor taught food safety and toxoplasmosis. Mosquito-borne diseases came up too. Attendance was low, yet the format widened dialogue. It corrected wrong ideas about how diseases spread. It also strengthened the women's share in their own care. The team concludes the guest qualified and broadened prenatal teaching.
phrenology-examined-1846: The sample hosted for this entry shows only the Google Books notice pages and a single title line of Phrenology Examined, with no argument text visible. The title line names P. Flourens, the French physiologist whose experiments on the brain made him phrenology's most scientific critic. The catalogue record dates the work 1846 and pairs Flourens's name with that of Charles Delucena Meigs, the American physician associated with its English presentation.
phrenology-its-nature-and-uses-1846:
Andrew Combe's Phrenology: Its Nature and Uses is an address, not a treatise. He wrote it for the students of Anderson's University at the opening of Dr. Weir's first course of lectures on phrenology there, on January 7, 1846. A note explains that Combe's health kept him away, so his brother George Combe read the address aloud for him.

Andrew Combe was a fellow of the Royal College of Physicians of Edinburgh and a physician in ordinary to the Queen in Scotland. The trustees of the university asked for publication. The pamphlet is a respectable doctor's public blessing on the new lectures, printed at Edinburgh in 1846.
plos-pbio-0020246:
Christopher K. Patil, Hao Li, and Peter Walter studied stress gene control in yeast for PLOS Biology in 2004. When proteins misfold in the cell's folding compartment, the unfolded protein response switches on rescue genes. A protein called Gcn4p is one of the switches, and the team found new DNA sites that help it work.

Those sites sit upstream of the rescue genes, where switches bind. Finding them explains how Gcn4p picks its targets. The study adds detail to one of the best-known stress circuits in biology. The same circuit is active in human diseases from diabetes to cancer. Each new control point is a chance to understand the response, and perhaps tune it.
plos-pone-0000046:
Alon Goren, Giora Simchen, Eitan Fibach, and co-authors studied the fine control of the genes that make hemoglobin in a 2006 paper. Globin genes produce the protein chains that carry oxygen in red blood cells. Their output must be tuned with care: too little causes anemia, and the wrong type at the wrong age causes disease.

DNA methylation, chemical tags placed on DNA, provides part of that tuning. The team showed methylation fine-tunes globin gene expression rather than simply switching it off. Fine control, not just on and off, is how the body shifts globin types from fetus to adult. The finding adds detail to a classic model of gene regulation with direct links to blood disorders.
plos-pone-0000146:
Sanja Glisic-Milosavljevic, Jill Waukau, Parthav Jailwala, and colleagues published this diabetes study in PLOS ONE in 2007. It looks at people at risk for type 1 diabetes and people who had just developed it. The team focused on a group of immune cells, the CD4+CD25+ high T-cell fraction, which helps keep the immune system in balance.

The authors report more apoptosis, programmed cell death, in that cell group among the at-risk and recent-onset subjects. Losing these peacekeeper cells could help explain how the immune attack on the pancreas gets started. The finding adds a clue to the early events of type 1 diabetes, before symptoms appear.
plos-pone-0000246:
Eva Schönenberger, Dirk Schnapauff, Florian Teige, and colleagues published this patient study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Coronary angiography pictures the heart's arteries, either noninvasively by scan or invasively by catheter. The authors measure patient acceptance of both forms, asking which patients prefer and why.

A test only helps if patients agree to take it. The study compares comfort, worry, and willingness between the scan and the catheter procedure. Its findings guide cardiology services choosing which test to offer first, balancing picture quality against the patient experience. Those answers give clinics firm ground for planning their services.
plos-pone-0000346:
Silvia Landi, Maria Cristina Cenni, Lamberto Maffei, and colleagues published this visual development study in PLOS ONE in 2007. An enriched environment, full of stimulation, speeds the development of the visual system. The authors study retinal ganglion cells, whose branching patterns, dendritic stratification, develop under that enrichment. They show the effect requires retinal BDNF, a growth factor in the eye itself.

The brain's response to a rich environment was known; this paper locates part of the mechanism in the retina. BDNF in the eye proves necessary for the enrichment effect on cell branching. The work connects upbringing conditions to molecular events at the very first stage of vision.
plos-pone-0000446:
Alex Kentsis and colleagues calculated the energetics of a protein folding, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. A protein's chain must fold into one precise shape to work, and the free energy of folding measures how stable that shape is. The team also calculated cooperativity, the tendency of folding to happen all at once rather than in pieces.

Accurate energy calculations test whether physical theory truly explains folding, biology's classic puzzle. Cooperativity matters because an all-or-nothing fold is less likely to get stuck in harmful half-folded states, which are linked to diseases like Alzheimer's. Computational studies of this kind benchmark the methods that drug designers also rely on.
plos-pone-0000546:
Marcus A. Gray and colleagues tricked volunteers' brains with false body signals and watched emotion change, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Participants in an fMRI scanner received false physiological feedback, misleading information about their own heart rate, while judging emotional material. The team measured the modulation of emotional appraisal by that feedback.

How people feel depends partly on what they believe their body is doing. Fake feedback that shifts appraisal shows emotion is partly an interpretation, not just a reaction. Brain imaging reveals where that interpretation happens, informing theories of anxiety, where body signals are often misread.
plos-pone-0000646:
Tatyana Sharpee and William Bialek wrote a theory study on how neurons sort signals, published in PLOS ONE in 2007. A neuron faces signals with many dimensions, yet its output is often binary: fire or not. The authors ask how to draw the boundary between two signal categories so the yes-or-no answer carries the most possible information.

Their motivation comes straight from the nervous system, which must squeeze rich inputs through single spikes. The math of maximal information transmission sets what the best boundary looks like. Work like this guides experiments on real neurons, and it also informs the design of artificial systems that must classify signals with limited output.
plos-pone-0000746:
Jia-Ching Shieh, Yu-Che Cheng, Mao-Chang Su and colleagues built designer gene switches and put them to work in yeast. Zinc fingers are DNA-binding motifs that can distinguish different DNA sequences, making them suitable for engineering artificial transcription factors. Their test bed was the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, genetics' favorite test kitchen, and their target gene was FLO11.

The tailor-made factors switched FLO11 on, with visible phenotypic consequences for the yeast. A gene like FLO11 changes how yeast cells stick and spread, so flipping it shows the switches truly govern traits. Success in yeast is a step toward programmable gene control in medicine and industry.
plos-pone-0000846:
Simon L. Zeller, Helmut Brandl and Bernhard Schmid studied whether soil bacteria pick their plant partners, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Belowground microorganisms influence plant performance by altering the soil environment. Plant pathogens such as cyanide-producing strains of the rhizobacterium Pseudomonas may show strong host-plant selectivity, harming some species while sparing others. The team analyzed interactions between different host plants and these bacteria.

Their model system pairs a crop with a weed, the pairing that decides farm yields. If rhizobacteria suppress the weed more than the crop, microbes become allies in weed control. If they hit the crop, they are hidden pests. Selectivity data tell farmers which story their soils are telling.
plos-pone-0000946:
Ying Sheng, Par Engstrom and Boris Lenhard built a computer model to predict microRNA genes in mammals, published in PLOS ONE in 2007. MicroRNAs are tiny RNA pieces, about twenty-two letters long, that tune gene activity. They can order a message destroyed or block its use, so finding them matters.

Hundreds were already known in mouse and human, but more were surely missed. The authors train a support vector machine, a pattern learning program, on both sequence and folded shape. Shape matters because microRNAs form a distinct hairpin. A better predictor hands biologists a fuller parts list for gene control.
plos-pone-0001046:
Teresa Treweek, Heath Ecroyd, Danielle Williams and colleagues tuned a chaperone protein and watched its protection change, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Amyloid fibrils, ordered protein clumps, mark Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and prion diseases. Chaperones such as alphaB-crystallin help stop proteins from depositing that way.

The team made site directed changes in the protein's tail extension. Those changes affected both chaperone function and the ability to block fibril formation. A tail that looks like a minor appendage turns out to carry real weight. Understanding it could guide designs for protective proteins, and it sharpens the basic picture of how chaperones grip their targets.
plos-pone-0001146:
Young malaria mosquitoes die in large numbers, but the causes are poorly understood. Krijn Paaijmans and colleagues tested one everyday hazard, rainfall, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Their subject was Anopheles gambiae, the main malaria mosquito of Africa, whose larvae live in small pools.

The team studied how rain affects larval mortality under conditions the insects actually face. Their title reports an unexpected result: losses of larvae due to rainfall were high. That matters for malaria control, because models of mosquito populations often overlook weather as a direct killer of the young stages.
plos-pone-0001246:
Genes can be cut and spliced in alternative ways, and one control point is a signal hidden inside an intron. Necat Havlioglu and colleagues characterized such a signal in the human caspase-2 gene, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Alternative splicing is an important level at which genes for programmed cell death are regulated.

The element, called In100, is a 100-nucleotide intronic sequence with upstream and downstream parts. The authors present it as an intronic signal for alternative splicing in the human genome. Since caspase-2 helps decide whether cells die, control of its splicing touches cancer and degeneration alike.
plos-pone-0001346:
Bartonella henselae is a bacterial pathogen spread from cats to people, causing cat scratch disease and other illnesses. Mardjan Arvand and colleagues typed isolates of the bacterium from three continents, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Previous investigations suggested that a limited subset of isolates may be associated with human disease.

Using multi-locus sequence typing, the authors reveal hypervirulent and feline-associated clones among the isolates. In plain terms, some family lines of the bacterium are much likelier to cause human disease than others. Such typing helps trace infections and understand what makes a clone dangerous.
plos-pone-0001446:
Qingjun Zhu and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a gene that keeps cells young. The gene makes telomerase, an enzyme that can extend cell life. A protein called LSD1 trims chemical tags from DNA wrapping proteins. The team asked whether LSD1 helps switch the telomerase gene off as cells mature.

They show that LSD1 is needed to keep that gene hushed in normal cells. When LSD1 is lost, the gene wakes up. That wake up is a step many cancers take to grow without end. The finding names a guard whose loss may help tumors start, and a target worth study.
plos-pone-0001546:
Michael Cook and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE methods paper on cheap barcode chips. Barcode arrays let labs track many cell strains at once via short DNA tags. Building such chips by the standard route is costly. The team built chips where tags bind without a fixed bond, at lower cost.

They checked the cheap chips with care, down to force scans of the surface. The chips read the tags as well as the costly kind. A cheaper chip opens pooled strain tests to more labs. It also scales to the huge libraries that gene screens now use.
plos-pone-0001646:
Kenichi Horisawa, Nobuhide Doi, and Hiroshi Yanagawa combined two lab tools to find protein partners faster, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. In vitro display methods, such as mRNA display, can fish huge numbers of protein variants for ones that bind a target. The slow step came after: cloning and sequencing each hit, which let many true hits slip through as false negatives.

The authors instead read the selected pool with cDNA tiling arrays, chips that can detect many gene pieces at once. The full text explains the combined method, the test proteins they used, and how many more hits the array step recovered. A faster readout makes display screens more complete, which helps labs map how proteins interact inside cells.
plos-pone-0001746:
Struan F. A. Grant, Mingyao Li, Jonathan P. Bradfield, and their co-authors tested an obesity gene in children in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. A genome-wide study of type 2 diabetes in adults had linked a variant in the FTO gene, rs9939609, to obesity. Whether the same gene region matters in childhood was the next question.

The team examined two stand-in variants for rs9939609 in children of Caucasian and African ancestry. They report finding a common tagging SNP associated with obesity in the children. The full text gives the child cohorts and the variant comparisons. Showing that an adult obesity locus acts already in childhood strengthens the case that FTO's effect is lifelong and starts early.
plos-pone-0001846:
Karin Anestål and co-authors studied how an antioxidant enzyme can be turned into a cell killer in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. SecTRAPs are selenium-compromised thioredoxin reductase-derived apoptotic proteins. They form from the selenoprotein thioredoxin reductase when its selenocysteine residue is targeted by electrophiles, or when the protein's tail is cut off.

Once converted, these proteins act as prooxidants that kill cells rather than protect them. The full text gives the conversion conditions and the cell death assays. A protective enzyme flipped into a killer is a possible cancer drug principle: tumor cells, rich in this enzyme, would arm the weapon themselves.
plos-pone-0001946:
Sebastien Guyader and Christina Burch tested a feeding theory on viruses that infect sea bacteria, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Optimal foraging theory predicts how a hunter should pick prey to gain the most food for its effort. In the sea, virus types that attack few host kinds tend to live where hosts are scarce, and broad attackers where hosts are many.

The pair adapted a classic diet model to these viruses, called bacteriophages. As the title states, the theory predicts the ecology of host range well, but not how that range evolved. A feeding rule can thus explain where viruses live, even if their history took another path.
plos-pone-0002046:
Jennifer Dan and co-authors tested a two-part vaccine trick against a fungal foe, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Dendritic cells are the immune system's scouts, and coating an antigen in mannose sugars targets it to their mannose receptors. Yet the response that follows is suboptimal, too weak to protect well.

The team used mannoproteins from the fungus Cryptococcus neoformans, a cause of lung and brain infection, plus CpG strands that trip a Toll-like alarm. As the title states, the two together stimulated dendritic cells cooperatively. A partner signal that lifts a weak vaccine response is a design worth reusing.
plos-pone-0002146:
Dinu Albeanu, Edward Soucy, Tomokazu Sato, and co-authors described a cheap light source for microscopes, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Fluorescence imaging, which makes tagged parts of cells glow, has grown fast thanks to new dyes and detectors. Standard widefield microscopes use arc lamps plus filters and shutters to control the light, and those parts cost money and wear out.

The team built arrays of LEDs, the small solid-state lights used in lamps and screens, to do the same job. Their setup offers a lower-cost and more efficient way to light samples. Cheaper imaging gear puts good microscopy within reach of more labs and classrooms.
plos-pone-0002246:
Douglas Axe, Brendan Dixon, and Philip Lu built a simplified world for testing ideas about protein evolution, described in PLOS ONE in 2008. Studying how proteins evolve is hard: the number of possible sequences is huge, folds are many. The links from sequence to shape to function are complex. Simple models may let researchers test broad claims that real proteins make hard to check.

Their system, called Stylus, models a protein and its proteome with functional rules that are not arbitrary. It lets users run evolution experiments in silico and see which claims hold. A clean test bed helps sort sound theory about protein evolution from mere storytelling.
plos-pone-0002346:
Jung Yoon Park, Mi-Ook Cho, Shanique Leonard, and co-authors examined the liver of mice that age too fast, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Unrepaired DNA damage is blamed as a cause of both cancer and aging. The Xpd TTD mice carry a mutation in the Xpd gene. It cripples DNA repair and transcription, giving them severe premature aging but, oddly, a reduced cancer rate.

The team looked at the balance between apoptosis, orderly cell death, and cell renewal in the liver. They found that balance tilted out of its normal homeostatic range. A liver that cannot match cell loss with cell replacement shows one concrete way DNA damage can age an organ.
plos-pone-0002446:
A research team led by Hensler reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Mary E. Hensler, Shigeki Miyamoto, Victor Nizet, and others. Its subject is group B Streptococcal β-Hemolysin/Cytolysin Directly Impairs Cardiomyocyte Viability and Function. Group B Streptococcus (GBS) is a leading cause of neonatal sepsis where myocardial dysfunction is an important contributor to poor outcome.

Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002546:
Work from Lindholm and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Eero Lindholm, Ekaterina Bakhtadze, Corrado Cilio, and others. Its subject is association between LTA , TNF and AGER Polymorphisms and Late Diabetic Complications. Several candidate genes on the short arm of chromosome 6 including the HLA locus, TNF.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002646:
Unknown led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was use of Evidence-Based practices in pregnancy and childbirth: s outh e ast a sia o ptimising r eproductive and c hild h ealth i n d eveloping countries project. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Unknown, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. The burden of mortality and morbidity related to pregnancy and childbirth remains concentrated in developing countries. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002746:
Published in PLOS ONE in 2008, research by Gilbert Q. Martinez and colleagues addresses a cytoplasmic domain mutation in ClC-Kb affects Long-Distance communication across the membrane. The catalog record names Gilbert Q. Martinez first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. ClC-Kb and ClC-Ka are homologous chloride channels that facilitate chloride homeostasis in the kidney and inner ear. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002846:
Roy A. Wise led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was cocaine serves as a peripheral interoceptive conditioned stimulus for central glutamate and dopamine release. Authorship is credited in the record to Roy A. Wise and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Intravenous injections of cocaine HCl are habit-forming because, among their many actions. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002946:
Helena Deus, Romesh Stanislaus, Diogo Veiga and co-authors proposed a semantic web model for biomedical data in 2008. Life science data are vast and varied, which defies easy linking between research groups. Rules for access and ownership add a further layer of difficulty to sharing.

Their model aims at integrative biomedical informatics, joining data while managing property and access permissions. Semantic web tools label data so machines can connect it across sources. Published in PLOS ONE, the paper is a design contribution: a management plan for data that must be both open to science and controlled.
plos-pone-0003046:
Lotfi Merabet, Roy Hamilton, Gottfried Schlaug and co-authors showed early visual cortex can be recruited for touch, fast and reversibly, in 2008. Loss of vision is tied to better touch and sound performance. Evidence suggests those gains link to the occipital visual cortex taking on non-visual processing.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team demonstrates rapid and reversible recruitment of early visual cortex for touch. The speed and reversibility are the news: the cortex can be borrowed without permanent rewiring. That informs rehabilitation training after vision loss and brain plasticity research generally. Anyone can read the full text free of charge through the journal's open access site.
plos-pone-0003146:
Wendong Yu, Rajesh Ramakrishnan, Yan Wang and colleagues look for HIV helper genes in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. HIV-1 depends on the host cell's own factors to complete its copying cycle in CD4 T cells and macrophages, the two main cell types it infects. One key factor is Cyclin T1, part of a general system that extends RNA messages.

The authors examine genes that depend on Cyclin T1 in activated T cell and macrophage lines. They report those genes appear enriched for HIV-1 co-factors. Readers see a route to finding host proteins the virus needs. Such proteins can become targets for drugs that block the virus indirectly.
plos-pone-0003246:
Aki Ejima and Leslie C. Griffith test the role of sound in fruit fly courtship in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Finding a mating partner is a critical task for many organisms. It is in the interest of males to employ multiple sensory modalities to search for females. In Drosophila melanogaster, vision is thought to be the most important courtship stimulating cue at long distance, while chemical cues act up close.

The title reports that courtship initiation is stimulated by acoustic signals in this species. Readers learn that song matters from the very start, not only later in courtship. Fly song is a model for how nervous systems produce patterned behaviour.
plos-pone-0003346:
Mei Ding, Ryan S. King, Emily C. Berry and colleagues study embryo elongation in a worm in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The epidermal cells of the C. elegans embryo undergo coordinated cell shape changes that result in the morphogenetic process of elongation. The cytoskeletal ankyrin repeat protein VAB-19 is required for cell shape changes and localizes to cell-matrix attachment structures.

The title reports the cell signaling adaptor protein EPS-8 is essential for C. elegans epidermal elongation and interacts with the ankyrin repeat protein VAB-19. Readers follow two proteins working together at attachment points. Worm embryo shaping is a clear model for how tissues change form in development.
plos-pone-0003446:
Yuuki Watanabe and Katsufumi Sato studied how the ocean sunfish swims in this 2008 paper. The sunfish, Mola mola, can weigh up to two tons. It lacks a tail fin and looks like a drifting head. Many people treated it as a slow, plankton-like drifter.

Closer study showed a lift-based swimming style instead. Its tall dorsal and anal fins beat in a symmetric way, like wings. That motion makes the body shape far less odd than it looks. The world's heaviest bony fish turns out to be an active swimmer. Divers had long reported sunfish moving with clear purpose through open water.
plos-pone-0003546:
Stephen Blake and co-authors tracked forest elephants in the Congo Basin for this 2008 study. Road building is expanding fast across that region. The basin holds rich biodiversity, including highly mobile large animals. Forest elephants range widely through dense forest.

Tracking showed roadless wilderness areas determine how elephants move. Roads acted as barriers or channels for their travel. Keeping roadless blocks intact protects elephant corridors. The finding gives planners a direct rule for new road routes. Congo forest elephants are smaller and far more shy than their savanna kin. Their numbers have fallen hard under poaching in recent years of road growth.
plos-pone-0003646:
Sylvie Remaud, Agnès Audibert, and Michel Gho published this developmental study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Working with the fruit fly Drosophila, they studied the bristle lineage, a set of cells where the Notch signal decides cell fates. They asked when, during the cell cycle, cells answer Notch best.

Using live imaging, the team followed the lineage and switched the Notch pathway on at set times. Cells responded most strongly during S-phase, the stage when a cell copies its DNA. The result shows a cell's readiness to hear a fate signal depends on its own cycle stage.
plos-pone-0003746:
Karl Schmid and Ziheng Yang published this methods critique in PLOS ONE in 2008. Sliding-window analysis is a popular way to scan a protein for signs of natural selection. It compares silent and replacement changes along the sequence, window by window. The authors argue the method has a hidden flaw.

Using the cancer gene BRCA1 as a case, they show how the sliding window can mislead. The trouble lies in how the window treats variation along the protein. The paper urges care with a shortcut many researchers had used on trust when hunting selected regions.
plos-pone-0003846:
David Sevillano, Lorenzo Aguilar, Luis Alou, and colleagues published this microbiology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The nasopharynx, the space behind the nose, hosts a normal community of bacteria. Three common species there can also cause respiratory disease. Antibiotics disturb that community's balance.

Using a computerized pharmacodynamic model, the team exposed mixed cultures of the bacteria to beta-lactam antibiotics. They watched how the population dynamics of the whole community shifted. The community view predicts treatment effects on the nasal ecosystem better than testing each germ alone. Germs that share one space do not act as they do alone.
plos-pone-0003946:
Christina T. L. Chen, David I. Gottlieb, and Barak A. Cohen examined DNA near a nerve gene promoter in 2008. Oligodendrocytes are the cells that wrap nerve fibers in myelin. That wrapping speeds nerve signals along the fibers. Loss of myelin plays a part in diseases such as multiple sclerosis.

Their PLOS ONE article focuses on the promoter that controls the Olig2 gene. That promoter holds stretches of DNA kept nearly unchanged across species. Such ultraconserved parts often mark key control switches. Mapping them helps explain how myelin-making cells switch their genes on. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004046:
Shunfu Piao, Sun-Hye Lee, Hyunjoon Kim, and co-authors studied a growth signal switch in 2008. Wnt and beta-catenin signaling guides development across animals. It also plays roles in many diseases when misregulated. Binding of Wnt proteins to the LRP6 coreceptor starts the signal.

Their PLOS ONE article reports how LRP6 shuts down the enzyme GSK3beta. A phosphorylated part of LRP6's inner tail inhibits the enzyme directly. Blocking GSK3beta lets beta-catenin build up and switch genes on. The direct mechanism fills a gap in a widely studied pathway. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004146:
Bronwen Martin and colleagues published this study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Reproductive capacity and food supply are tightly linked in animals. How an animal adjusts to changes in its surroundings and diet helps decide whether its species endures.

The team measured how changes in dietary energy intake alter gene activity in the gonads, the organs that make eggs and sperm. They tracked which genes switch on or off as food energy rises or falls. The work shows, at the level of genes, how the body senses the reproductive environment and answers with changes in fertility machinery.
plos-pone-0004246:
Zheng Wang and colleagues published this fungal evolution study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Fungi that live inside plant leaves, called endophytes, have had a major influence on how reproductive structures evolved in the Leotiomycetes. That group is one of the most problematic in fungal classification, full of disputed relationships.

The team mapped fungal body shapes onto the group's family tree, split into two major lines. They traced how the endophytic lifestyle reshaped the structures fungi use to reproduce. The study uses living arrangements to explain why these fungi look the way they do.
plos-pone-0004346:
Yong Li and Pankaj Agarwal published this disease networks study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Human diseases are increasingly seen as not isolated from each other. Understanding how diseases relate through underlying biology could give new insights into their causes, classification, and shared mechanisms. Pathways are the chains of molecular events that carry out a cell's work.

The authors construct a pathway-based view of human diseases and disease relationships. Diseases that share biological pathways are linked, forming a map of illness. Such a map can reveal why some diseases travel together and suggest drugs that might treat several at once.
plos-pone-0004446:
Prion protein sits on cell surfaces doing a job no one fully understands, and Dorothea Rutishauser, Kirsten Mertz, Rita Moos, and co-authors listed its partners in PLOS ONE in 2009. Listing everything a protein touches can reveal what it is for. The team tagged the normal prion protein with a small marker, called a myc tag, near one end.

Mice bred to carry the tagged protein placed it correctly, anchored to the cell surface in the right spots. With the tag as a handle, the team could pull the protein out and name the molecules bound to it. The result is a full native map of its contacts. That map is a starting point for explaining both its normal work and what goes wrong in prion disease.
plos-pone-0004546:
A heat shock protein helps a small insect repair the damage of winter cold, show Vladimir Kostal and Michaela Tollarova-Borovanska in PLOS ONE in 2009. The insect is Pyrrhocoris apterus, a red firebug. Adults that pass winter in a dormant state, called diapause, tolerate cold very well. Adults that keep reproducing lack the full set of cold-tolerance adaptations and survive cold poorly.

The protein is the 70 kilodalton heat shock protein, a general cell repair helper despite its name. The authors show it assists during repair of chilling injury in this insect. Studying how insects fix cold damage helps explain who survives winter and where species can live. It also informs the storage of insects used in research and farming.
plos-pone-0004646:
People, not wind or water, carry a tree-killing nematode across China, show Christelle Robinet, Alain Roques, Hongyang Pan, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The pinewood nematode is a microscopic worm that kills pine trees. Intensification of world trade is responsible for an increase in alien species introductions. Human-mediated dispersal promotes not only introductions but also expansion of a species' range through long-distance jumps.

The team modeled the nematode's spread in China, separating natural dispersal from human-carried movement. Their conclusion, in the title, is that human-mediated dispersal plays the key role. That finding directs control efforts at timber transport and trade routes. Stopping the trucks and shipments matters more than fencing forests against a worm that barely travels on its own.
plos-pone-0004746:
Eileen Kennedy and colleagues found distant spots in an enzyme that tune its activity without touching the active site, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Far apart parts of an enzyme must talk to each other for control to work. Finding the parts in those talks has been hard, since the contacts are weak and subtle.

Protein kinases, which add phosphate tags to other proteins, are a prime case. The team hunted for non cutting residues that still shift kinase action. Such spots could be new drug targets that tune, rather than block, the enzyme. That may mean fewer side effects.
plos-pone-0004846:
Cherie Bond, Martina Zimmermann, and Susan Greenfield studied upregulation of alpha7 nicotinic receptors by acetylcholinesterase C-terminal peptides, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The alpha7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor is a potent calcium ionophore implicated in excitotoxicity and neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer disease. Previous research implicated fragments of the enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine in modulating receptor levels in brain cells.

Peptide exposure increased receptor numbers. More receptors may amplify calcium damage. Or compensation may protect neurons under stress. The pathway links two classic Alzheimer players. The work also raises clear questions that targeted studies can now address. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is.
plos-pone-0004946:
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or COPD, involves long-lasting airway inflammation. Cigarette smoke is a major driver of it. Esmaeil Mortaz and co-authors studied smoke's effect on immune cells. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They exposed dendritic cells to cigarette smoke extract. Then they measured how those cells affected T cell growth.

Dendritic cells rally T cells against threats. Smoke-driven changes in them can ripple through lung immunity. The study follows that chain step by step. It links smoke exposure to altered T cell proliferation. The work shows one more way smoking distorts the lung's defenses. It also feeds the inflammation that defines COPD.
plos-pone-0005046:
Heart repair research needs large numbers of heart muscle cells. Those cells must be easy to spot and purify. Hiroko Kita-Matsuo and colleagues shared a toolkit in PLOS ONE in 2009. They built lentiviral vectors for human embryonic stem cells. Stable cell lines made with them glow for tracking. They also carry drug resistance for selection.

The protocols create lines tuned for cardiomyocyte production. Fluorescent tracking lets researchers watch heart cells develop. Drug resistance lets them select pure batches. Myocardial regeneration therapies depend on such cells. The toolkit serves development, physiology and tissue engineering studies. It removes a practical bottleneck for the whole field.
plos-pone-0005146:
The kidney filters blood and makes urine. It decides which proteins to keep and which to dump. Lulu Jia and colleagues read that decision in PLOS ONE in 2009. They compared the plasma proteome with the urine proteome. Plasma represents the kidney's input. Urine represents its output. Proteomics technology had just profiled both in detail.

Comparing the two catalogs reveals the kidney's handling rules. Some proteins pass, others are held back or reclaimed. The comparison turns two lists into insight about organ function. Many datasets had accumulated without integration. This study integrates them. The kidney's filtering logic matters for disease. Protein in urine is an early warning of kidney damage.
plos-pone-0005246:
When a soft sound comes just before a loud one, the startle response shrinks, an effect called prepulse inhibition. That gating is weak in schizophrenia and can be measured in mice. Webb and colleagues ran a genome-wide scan for it in PLOS ONE in 2009, entirely in the computer.

Large public databases hold genotypes and trait data for many inbred mouse strains. Mining them together can locate chromosome regions tied to the trait without new lab work. The in silico scan points gene hunters toward the roots of sensory gating.
plos-pone-0005346:
Trait anxiety is bred into mouse lines that run high, normal, or low in anxious behavior. Emotional information is processed differently in pathological anxiety, in people and in models. Muigg and colleagues mapped stress-induced brain activation across those lines in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Earlier rat work had already shown challenge-related activation differences in fear and anxiety circuits. The mouse maps add a second species and a three-way comparison. Consistent brain signatures of trait anxiety help researchers test calming drugs in the right circuits. Brain maps from bred lines can be checked gene by gene, since the high and low lines are known stock. And that makes them a strong test bed for new drugs for fear and stress.
plos-pone-0005446:
Monica Ardura and colleagues studied children with severe staph infections in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Staphylococcus aureus can cause deep and dangerous illness in children who were healthy before. Much is known about the germ itself, but less about how a child's immune system answers it.

The team compared blood immune cells from sick children with those from healthy children. One group of defender cells reacted more strongly than usual in the sick children. At the same time, memory T cells in the blood were lower. Those shifts may help explain why the infection hits some children so hard.
plos-pone-0005546:
Changhai Tian, L Charles Murrin, and Jialin Zheng studied methamphetamine harm in young rat brain cells, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. The drug methamphetamine can damage the ends of dopamine nerve cells and kill cells in movement areas of the brain. Harm was thought to run through stress pathways linking cell compartments.

The team looked at early nerve cells in the hippocampus, the brain's memory centre. They linked breaking apart of the cells' energy centres to the death of those young cells. That widens the known reach of the drug's harm in the brain.
plos-pone-0005646:
Emelyn Shroff and co-authors studied peptides that trigger cell death in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. A family of proteins governs whether a cell lives or dies by suicide. Small members of the family, the BH3-only proteins, start the death process by binding the family's survival members.

The team used short peptides copied from those death domains. The peptides made mitochondria split apart and cells die, even without two proteins long thought essential for death. That surprise opens a new angle on how death can be triggered in cancer cells. Mitochondrial splitting is a normal event as well, so the death route the peptides open needs more mapping.
plos-pone-0005746:
S. Ivan Perez and co-authors compared skull shapes and DNA in early Americans in 2009, and found the two records at odds. How many founding groups peopled the Americas is a long-running debate. Skulls from the Holocene vary in ways some read as signs of two distinct source groups.

Gene data, the team notes, point more toward a single shared origin. They weigh why bones and genes might tell different tales, from diet-driven skull change to drift. The clash warns against reading ancestry from one kind of evidence alone. Both records must be explained by any sound history of the first Americans.
plos-pone-0005846:
Wolfgang Wagner and co-authors compared aging in the body with aging in a dish in 2009. Stem and progenitor cells lose power with age, limiting repair. Cells grown in culture also age, enlarging and stopping division after many rounds, a state called replicative senescence.

The team found the two kinds of aging leave related marks on human stem cells. Shared marks suggest culture aging is a fair, faster model of real aging for some questions. That matters because body aging takes decades to study. The shared signature also names candidate drivers of stem cell decline that drugs might target.
plos-pone-0005946:
Cocaine changes how mammals move and behave, but the steps inside the brain are hard to trace. Alex Ward, Vyvyca Walker, Zhaoyang Feng and colleagues turned to a tiny worm for a cleaner view in 2009. Their PLOS ONE study tests how cocaine alters movement in C. elegans, a roundworm used widely in biology labs.

Cocaine blocks the pumps that clear dopamine and related signals, and the worm shares much of that machinery. If the drug shifts worm movement in clear ways, the worm can serve as a fast screen for drug action. The study brings addiction biology down to a simple animal whose genes and nerves are fully mapped.
plos-pone-0006046:
Killer cells of the immune system must learn not to attack the body's own healthy cells. Sofia Johansson, Mali Salmon-Divon, Maria Johansson and colleagues studied that schooling in mice in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper examines natural killer cells, whose Ly49 receptors read MHC class I, the identity badges on cells, and it adds computer modeling in mice with a single badge type.

A killer cell that finds no badge may strike, a rule called missing-self recognition. During development, the host's badges educate the killers and set their restraint. Combining receptor counts with modeling shows how that education is graded, a detail that matters for using killer cells against cancer and infection.
plos-pone-0006146:
A breast cancer cell line is only as useful as the tumor it truly resembles. Jessica Kao, Keyan Salari, Melanie Bocanegra and colleagues profiled the standard lines in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper uses molecular profiling, including microarray data, to define which breast cancer cell lines model which forms of this varied disease, and to resource the hunt for cancer genes.

Breast cancer is many diseases in one name, and a mismatched model misleads drug tests. A profiled catalog lets labs pick the line that matches their question. The resource shapes thousands of later experiments, since almost every breast cancer drug claim begins in one of these lines.
plos-pone-0006246:
Wind turbines kill large numbers of bats, and no accepted fix existed when Barry Nicholls and Paul Racey ran their 2009 PLOS ONE study. Earlier, the team had seen bat activity drop near large air traffic and weather radars. That hint suggested radar-like signals might keep bats away.

Bats avoided foraging where electromagnetic radiation was present, the tests showed. A signal bats dislike could guard turbines without harming birds or power output. The idea needs field trials at real turbines before use. Still, it offers a rare, testable lead for a stubborn conservation problem.
plos-pone-0006346:
Narcolepsy struck when the brain lost hypocretin, a wake-promoting chemical, about a decade before Satvinder Kaur and colleagues ran their 2009 PLOS ONE study. The disorder brings excessive daytime sleepiness, sudden muscle weakness, and dreaming sleep arriving at wrong times. The team lesioned hypocretin-sensing cells in one brain region of knockout mice.

Destroying those cells in the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray increased REM sleep in the mice. A relay station for sleep control thus came into view. Mapping the circuit explains pieces of narcolepsy's odd symptoms. It may also guide treatments that stabilise sleep states.
plos-pone-0006446:
Geoffry De Iuliis and colleagues tested mobile phone radiation on human sperm in the lab, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Whether such radiation harms human health has been much debated. Male reproduction is a key part of that debate, since some studies link phone use with poorer sperm. The team exposed sperm samples outside the body to phone-type radiation.

Their title states the outcome: the radiation raised reactive oxygen species and caused DNA damage in the sperm. Results in a dish cannot settle what happens in daily life. Still, the study adds hard lab data to a heated public question. It also suggests paths for follow-up work.
plos-pone-0006546:
Jenny Gunnersen and colleagues studied a seizure-related gene in the eye for PLOS ONE in 2009. Seizure-related gene 6, or Sez-6, is expressed in neurons of the mouse brain, retina, and spinal cord. In the cortex it helps specify dendritic branching patterns. The team examined Sez-6 in amacrine cells of the rodent retina.

They also studied the consequence of deleting the gene. Retinal amacrine cells shape how visual signals are processed before leaving the eye. A gene that patterns their branches could affect vision itself. The study links a brain gene to the wiring of the retina.
plos-pone-0006646:
Marijana Radonjic and co-authors read liver gene activity under high-fat diets in PLOS ONE in 2009. Excessive exposure to dietary fats is an important factor in initiation of obesity and metabolic syndrome pathologies. The cellular processes associated with adaptation were their focus. They ran genome-wide mRNA expression analysis of hepatic adaptation to high-fat diets.

Their title reports a switch from an inflammatory to a metabolic program over time. The liver's response evolves rather than staying fixed. Timing therefore matters when interpreting diet studies. A staged response suggests different interventions for early versus late disease.
plos-pone-0006746:
Kirsten M. Bohn and co-authors analyzed the songs of free-tailed bats in PLOS ONE in 2009. Complex songs are rare among mammals. Few studies had examined how bat song parts are ordered. The authors studied the syntax of the songs. Syntax means how syllables and phrases combine and follow each other.

They compared songs across individuals and regions. The songs showed both versatility and stereotypy. Some elements flexed freely, while others kept fixed patterns. That mix is informative about how bat communication is organized. It also invites comparison with birdsong and other animal vocal systems.
plos-pone-0006846:
Devorah Gur-Wahnon and her team made antigen-showing cells that teach calm, not attack, in PLOS ONE in 2009. These cells show bits of protein to T cells. A switch in them, called STAT3, shapes how they grow and work. Odd STAT3 use is tied to showing cells that do their job badly. The team had found that cell-to-cell touch can flip that switch.

With that touch-based flip, they made cells with a calm-teaching style. Such cells tell the immune force to stand down. Labs that work on self-attack diseases and grafts want cells like these. A sound way to make them could back new cell cures.
plos-pone-0006946:
Hiromasa Tanaka and Tau-Mu Yi reported a synthetic biology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Designing the shape and size of a cell is a standing challenge in that field. Yeast cells offer a striking test case. Prolonged exposure to a mating signal called alpha-factor makes yeast grow several mating projections at once.

The pair set out to reproduce that multi-projection shape with different inputs. They swapped the natural mating signal for alternative triggers. Getting the same form from new inputs shows a cell shape program can be rewired. Such control is a step toward engineering cells with shapes built to order.
plos-pone-0007046:
Mattias Gustafsson, Deborah Knight, and Colin Palmer examined rival hormone receptors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The PPAR receptors form a family of nuclear switches in cells. Their jobs overlap, and they sometimes oppose each other. Many tools, from drugs to gene knockouts, have been used to separate their roles.

The team showed that PPAR delta can blunt PPAR gamma's action. It does so through both gene-based and faster, non-genomic routes. The blocker effect also depended on which ligand was present. Crosstalk like this complicates drugs aimed at one family member, since the others answer back.
plos-pone-0007146:
Chantal Raherison, Christer Janson, Deborah Jarvis, and colleagues followed asthma over time in PLOS ONE in 2009. Little was known about how asthma severity is spread between men and women in the general population. Their cohort drew young adults with asthma from a random population sample. They described severity at the start and tracked how it changed.

They compared the course of disease by gender. Severity that shifts with age changes how clinics should plan care. A cohort drawn from the public, not from hospitals, avoids the bias of only seeing the worst cases. Their findings ground asthma policy in ordinary lives.
plos-pone-0007246:
Marla K. Johnson, Tamara D. Clark, Denise Njama-Meya, and colleagues examined how malaria studies measure a red blood cell condition in 2009. The condition is G6PD deficiency, a shortage of an enzyme that protects red blood cells. Studies disagreed on whether the deficiency changes susceptibility to malaria.

The authors argue that varied diagnostic methods helped cause the mixed results. They compare associations found under different ways of assessing G6PD deficiency. Their PLOS ONE paper shows that method choice can shift genetic association findings. That warning applies to many field studies of infection and inherited traits.
plos-pone-0007346:
Fang Zong, Eleni Fthenou, Nina Wolmer, and colleagues traced two proteins traveling into tumor cell nuclei in 2009. Syndecan-1 forms complexes with growth factors and their receptors at the cell membrane. The authors had earlier reported that syndecan-1 moves to the nucleus along tubulin tracks inside the cell.

The transport route and purpose of nuclear syndecan-1 stayed incompletely understood. The authors study syndecan-1 and the growth factor FGF-2 in mesenchymal tumor cells. They report both share a common transport route and co-localize with heparanase in the nucleus. The FGF receptor itself does not share that route.
plos-pone-0007446:
Robin Craven and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their subject was a toxin made by drug-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Community strains of this germ cause severe infections that destroy skin, soft tissue, and lung. Its alpha-hemolysin toxin is a key weapon in those infections. The team asked how the toxin stirs such strong inflammation.

They showed that alpha-hemolysin switches on the NLRP3 inflammasome, an alarm complex inside immune cells. The effect appeared in both human and mouse immune cells. Once triggered, the inflammasome drives the response that damages tissue. Explaining this trigger clarifies part of the germ's harmfulness. It also suggests that calming the inflammasome could limit the destruction these infections cause.
plos-pone-0007546:
Brenton Louie, Roger Higdon, and Eugene Kolker published a statistical study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on predicting what proteins do. Thousands of proteins have unknown functions. Computers guess their jobs by comparing sequences to proteins already understood. One problem is that the guesses tend to be overly specific. The authors built a model relating sequence similarity to function similarity, to see where the overconfidence creeps in.

The model shows how much functional precision a given sequence match can honestly support. Beyond a point, close spelling does not justify close functional claims. Correcting that bias should make automated annotation more honest. Honest annotations matter because databases propagate guesses into thousands of later studies. The paper is a calibration tool for a workhorse method of modern biology. It tells predictors when to say less.
plos-pone-0007646:
Qiyao Wang and colleagues published a genome study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on Edwardsiella tarda, a versatile fish pathogen. The bacterium causes edwardsiellosis, a devastating disease in aquaculture worldwide. It infects many fish species and can live inside host cells. The team sequenced the complete genome of strain EIB202, a highly virulent and multi-drug resistant isolate from China. With the full sequence in hand, they searched for the basis of its adaptability.

The genome reveals the toolkit behind the bacterium's broad host range and intracellular life. Genes for invading cells, surviving inside them, and resisting drugs all leave readable traces. Knowing the toolkit guides vaccine and treatment work in fish farming. It also helps track how such strains spread through the industry. A complete genome is a reference every later study will use. The pathogen's versatility is now written down to be studied.
plos-pone-0007746:
Vassiliki Kotoula and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tackles a practical problem in cancer diagnosis. Doctors test tumor tissue for mutations in a gene called KRAS. The result can predict whether a treatment will work.

Routine tumor samples are fixed in formalin and embedded in paraffin, which damages DNA. The team assessed KRAS mutations on such real-world material. They used a sensitive real-time PCR method in a live diagnostic setting. Showing the test works on standard hospital samples is a key step. It brings mutation-guided treatment closer to everyday oncology practice.
plos-pone-0007846:
Alok Chakrabarti and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It characterizes the H5N1 flu viruses behind India's 2008 to 2009 outbreaks. Highly pathogenic bird flu hit poultry in West Bengal in early 2008. It then spread to three northeastern states, with dozens of outbreaks reported.

Sequencing the viruses revealed their family ties. The analysis points to a third separate introduction into India. It also raises the possibility that H5N1 had become endemic there. Knowing whether a virus is newly imported or locally rooted changes control strategy. The study sharpens that judgment for Indian authorities.
plos-pone-0007946:
Haijing Hu and Stephen Leppla measured how anthrax toxin enters immune cells, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Anthrax germs must beat the body's first defenses to start an infection, and their toxin dulls those defenses. The team used a lab-built marker protein to track entry cell by cell.

Watching the marker in fresh immune cells showed which cells take the toxin in and how fast. Cells that guard the body first are among those hit, which fits how the germ gains its early hold. A clear view of entry helps the search for drugs that block the toxin at the door.
plos-pone-0008046:
Andres Arenas and colleagues showed that lessons learned young stick with bees, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Honeybees learn which scents promise food, a skill their work depends on. The team trained bees at different ages and tested how long the lesson lasted.

Bees trained in early adulthood held the lesson far longer than bees trained later. Early experience thus shapes the older bee in a lasting way, much as it does in mammals. For bee keepers and farmers, the finding says the first days of a worker's life set the quality of the forager she becomes.
plos-pone-0008146:
Alexander Link and colleagues gave a common virus a role in colon cancer spread in PLOS ONE in 2009. JC virus infects most people quietly and harms few. Its DNA and its main protein, called T antigen, show up in about half of colorectal cancers, which raised a pointed question.

Cancer cells carrying the viral protein pushed into new tissue and migrated more strongly than those without it. A quiet passenger thus looks like an active accomplice in metastasis, the spread that makes this cancer deadly. The link may suggest new ways to flag or slow the worst cases.
plos-pone-0008246:
Guadalupe Andreani and colleagues studied two infections sharing the same cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Macrophages are a major target of HIV-1 and a reservoir where the virus persists. The same cells are targeted by Trypanosoma cruzi. That protozoan parasite causes Chagas disease, a major illness in the Americas. The team used human macrophages grown from monocytes for their tests.

They found the parasite inhibited HIV-1 replication in those cells. One infection thus interfered with the other inside shared host cells. The result may matter in regions where both diseases occur. It also reveals how pathogens interact within the immune system.
plos-pone-0008346:
Michael R. May and colleagues studied an ancient oak in southern California in PLOS ONE in 2009. Palmer's oak survives in scattered, isolated populations. These are presumably relicts of a wider range that shrank as the climate dried. That drying followed the end of the Pleistocene ice age. A recently discovered stand offered a test of that history.

The team investigated whether the stand is a single ancient clone. A clone persisting since the Pleistocene would be among the oldest living organisms. Genetic evidence can date and define such a stand. The study connects botany with deep climate history.
plos-pone-0008446:
Abigail Lamikanra and co-authors study severe malaria and blood loss in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Severe anemia is the most common grave form of malaria in areas where the disease is common. In long cases, the marrow makes red cell precursors in a flawed way. The body fails to replace red cells fast enough. The team look at hemozoin, a pigment left by the malaria parasite.

They find that hemozoin drives those precursor cells to die. That death helps explain why red cells are not replaced. The work names a direct cause of the anemia. It may point to ways to protect the marrow in malaria.
plos-pone-0008546:
Filippo Caschera and co-authors use robots to find new drug mixes in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Their test case is a liposomal drug, a drug wrapped in tiny fat bubbles. Such a mix has many parts that act on each other. The parts can help or hinder each other in ways no one can predict. Trial and error by hand would be very slow. The team use a loop of fast tests guided by a computer model.

Each round of tests teaches the model which mixes work best. The model then picks the next round of mixes to try. The loop finds good mixes far faster than blind search. The same method could help tune other complex mixes.
plos-pone-0008646:
Matteo Bellone and co-authors study immune cells in mouse cancer in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Invariant NKT cells are a subset of T lymphocytes with innate effector functions. They aid establishment of adaptive T and B cell responses. iNKT cells play a spontaneous protective role against experimental tumors. The team ask if that protection needs tumor-specific cytotoxic T cells. They use mice that develop spontaneous carcinoma. CD1d presents lipid antigens to iNKT cells in this system.

They find iNKT cells control spontaneous carcinoma independently of cytotoxic T cells. Protection does not route through the classic killer cell arm. That independence suggests iNKT activation could help patients lacking strong cytotoxic responses. It broadens the rationale for iNKT-based cancer immunotherapy.
plos-pone-0008746:
Annie Frelet-Barrand, Sylvain Boutigny, Lucas Moyet, and colleagues offered a milk germ as a protein factory. Their methods paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Membrane proteins are vital but hard to study. They shun water and occur in tiny natural amounts. Standard host cells often make them poorly or not at all. Plant membrane proteins were especially underserved by existing systems.

The food germ Lactococcus lactis took up Arabidopsis membrane protein genes. It produced both surface and internal membrane proteins in working form. A safe, food-grade host lowers the barrier to such work. Biochemists gain a friendlier route to hard proteins.
plos-pone-0008846:
Mónica López Fanarraga, Javier Bellido, Cristina Jaén, and colleagues tied one helper protein to three steps of cell division. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Microtubules form the rails and spindle that organize dividing cells. Building them needs tubulin parts assembled by five cofactor proteins. One cofactor, TBCD, was known to help fold tubulin. Its wider duties in human cells were unclear.

TBCD proved to link centriole formation, spindle dynamics, and the final snip separating daughter cells. Losing it disrupted all three jobs. One helper thus coordinates the microtubule system end to end. The finding matters for cancers where division machinery runs wild.
plos-pone-0008946:
Jessica Dyszel and co-authors listed the genes that a bacterial signal-reader controls in E. coli, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The reader, SdiA, listens for chemical signals made by other kinds of bacteria. When those signals arrive, SdiA switches a set of genes on or off. One target strain was EHEC, an E. coli type that causes severe food poisoning.

The team compared gene activity with and without extra SdiA in the cell. Genes for movement, surface structures, and stress handling shifted under its control. The list shows how E. coli eavesdrops on its neighbours and adjusts. Understanding that chatter may suggest new ways to disarm harmful strains.
plos-pone-0009046:
Mariano Larzábal and co-authors designed molecular plugs for the needle E. coli uses to attack gut cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Enteropathogenic E. coli causes severe diarrhoea, especially in children. It grips gut cells using a type three secretion system, a tiny injection needle. The needle also delivers proteins that let the germ hold on and cause disease.

The team built coiled-coil peptides shaped to jam that machinery. The peptides interfered with the secretion system in their tests. Blocking the needle disarms the germ without killing it outright. Such anti-virulence drugs might sidestep the resistance that antibiotics provoke.
plos-pone-0009146:
Ardina Grüber and co-authors solved pieces of a malaria protein that grabs red blood cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Malaria parasites invade red blood cells to multiply. That invasion leans on many handshakes between parasite and cell proteins. Py235, from the mouse malaria Plasmodium yoelii, helps pick reticulocytes, the youngest red cells.

The team determined the structure of functional units in its binding domain. NBD94 is the part that grips nucleotides, the cell's energy packets. Structure at this detail exposes pockets a drug could block. Blocking the grip could keep the parasite out of blood cells.
plos-pone-0009246:
Eliyahu Khankin and co-authors published this kidney study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Erythropoietin is a hormone used to treat anemia in kidney patients. Many patients with end-stage renal disease respond poorly to it. Doctors then raise the dose again and again, often without reaching target blood counts.

The team investigated one suspect: a soluble form of the erythropoietin receptor floating in the blood. Such loose receptors could soak up the hormone before it reaches bone marrow. They report that this soluble receptor contributes to the resistance seen in these patients. The finding suggests a new way to predict, and perhaps reduce, poor responses.
plos-pone-0009346:
Michel Laurent, Jean Deschatrette, and Claire Wolfrom published this cell growth study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Populations of mammal cells often grow in long, slow waves. Their division rate rises and falls over long ranges, in dishes and in bodies alike. Such patterns mix random events with deterministic control.

The authors asked whether part of that control is chaotic, in the mathematical sense. Chaos means orderly rules producing hard-to-predict swings. They unmasked chaotic attributes hidden in time series from living cell populations. Finding chaos in growth data would change how biologists model cell populations, since chaotic systems defy long-range forecasts even when fully lawful.
plos-pone-0009446:
Claudia Miranda and colleagues examined a cancer linked protein pair in PLOS ONE in 2010. TRK proteins are changed forms of a growth receptor. When stuck in the on state, they can turn normal cells cancer like. A relay protein named STAT3 is switched on when TRK is active. The team tested what STAT3 does in that change.

Working with cells in the lab, they probed whether STAT3 is needed for TRK driven change. Their results place STAT3 inside the chain of signals that TRK uses. Knowing that chain in detail points to steps that drugs might block. It adds to the map of how these rare growth receptors cause cancer.
plos-pone-0009546:
Thierry Lefevre and colleagues tested a link between beer and mosquito bites in PLOS ONE in 2010. Malaria spreads when mosquitoes bite people. Drinking alcohol is rising in many lands where malaria is common. The team asked whether drinking beer changes how many mosquitoes seek a person. Volunteers drank beer or water, and the air around them was offered to mosquitoes.

Mosquitoes chose the air of beer drinkers more often. Something in breath or skin odor after drinking draws them in. The result joins two public health problems in an unexpected way. Advice on malaria prevention may need to reckon with drinking as a risk factor.
plos-pone-0009646:
Kiran Mahajan and co-authors pinpointed a switch on a growth protein in PLOS ONE in 2010. AKT is a central driver of cell growth and survival. It is switched on by chemical tags at specific spots. The team showed that an enzyme called Ack1 tags AKT at one spot, tyrosine 176. That tag had not been recognized as a key control before.

Tagging at that spot proved to regulate how AKT is activated. A precise switch in a cancer relevant pathway is valuable knowledge. Drugs could aim at the tagging step rather than at AKT itself. The study gives drug designers an exact molecular address to consider.
plos-pone-0009746:
Koji Isodono and co-authors published a heart study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The study found a protein called PARM-1 in rat heart muscle cells, using a screen for new membrane and secreted proteins. Tests showed the protein sits in the endoplasmic reticulum, the cell's folding workshop.

Salt-fed rats with heart failure showed more PARM-1, along with signs of stress in that workshop. Stress drugs also raised PARM-1 in cultured heart cells. When the team silenced the gene, more cells died under stress. The authors conclude that PARM-1 helps shield heart cells from such stress.
plos-pone-0009846:
Chromosomes carry the genes that run a cell. Genetic engineers sometimes need to move or mark whole stretches of a chromosome. Munehiro Uemura and colleagues presented tools for doing exactly that. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The tools pair two kinds of molecular machinery.

Site-specific recombinases are enzymes that cut and rejoin DNA at set addresses. Fluorescent protein-based vectors carry glowing markers that show where changes landed. Together they allow planned chromosomal manipulation in living cells. Such control helps researchers test what large chromosome changes do. Each tool on its own was known; the pairing is the advance.
plos-pone-0009946:
Heart failure patients often take one blood pressure drug; combining two classes might help more. Andrea Kuenzli and colleagues pooled past trials to test that idea. Their meta-analysis appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

A meta-analysis merges results from many studies into one verdict. The comparison set angiotensin receptor antagonists plus ACE inhibitors against ACE inhibitors alone. Both drug classes tame the same hormone system in different ways. Combined therapy was weighed on outcomes that matter to patients with heart failure. Pooled evidence settles questions single trials leave open. Heart failure means the heart pumps too weakly.
plos-pone-0010046:
The authors were Damien Robert, Thi-Hanh Nguyen, François Gallet, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study measured forces inside living cells. Cells move cargo in small sacs called endosomes, and control of that traffic is central to cell life. The forces pushing those sacs around are hard to measure directly.

The team combined active and passive microrheology, two methods that probe tiny motions. Magnetic labeling of endosomes let them track forces as traffic moved. The approach gives cell biology a way to put numbers on forces once only guessed at.
plos-pone-0010146:
The authors were Blaise Boles, Matthew Thoendel, Aleeza Roth, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study hunted genes behind Staphylococcus aureus biofilms. This bacterium forms sticky biofilm layers on tissue and medical implants. Biofilm growth drives chronic infections that resist drugs and immune attack, making it a key virulence trait.

Many clinical strains build biofilms without the usual sugar-based matrix, called polysaccharide. The team systematically identified genes involved in that independent route. Each such gene is a possible weak point for treatments aimed at breaking biofilms on implants. The study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.
plos-pone-0010246:
The authors were Kristiina Rajala, Bettina Lindroos, Samer Hussein, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study built a cleaner way to grow stem cells. Clinical use demands defined conditions with no animal-derived materials at all. Stem cell growth needs a fine balance of signals for survival, growth, and self-renewal, which older recipes met with animal products.

Their defined, xeno-free method let labs establish clinical-grade stem cell lines. It covered embryonic, induced pluripotent, and adipose stem cells. Removing animal materials cuts contamination risk and makes future patient treatments easier to approve.
plos-pone-0010346:
Lucy King, Joseph Soltis, Iain Douglas-Hamilton and colleagues reported in PLOS ONE in 2010 that bees can set off elephant alarms. African elephants face few predators, given their size. Yet the sound of angry honeybees sends them retreating at once. Stings around the eyes and trunk are a real threat. Earlier work had shown the retreat; this study looked for the calls that go with it.

When bee sounds played, elephants not only moved away but also made warning sounds to others. Those alarm calls could alert elephants that had not heard the bees. The result matters for farmers, who lose crops to hungry elephants. Beehive fences are one idea drawn from this fear of bees. Sound, here, works as both warning and weapon.
plos-pone-0010446:
Geneviève Mailhot and colleagues linked a cystic fibrosis protein to fat handling in gut cells for PLOS ONE in 2010. People with cystic fibrosis often show abnormal fat patterns in blood and tissues. Even carriers of one faulty gene copy can show them. The faulty protein, CFTR, is best known as a channel in airways and gut. Why its loss distorts fats was poorly understood.

Using a human gut cell line, the team lowered CFTR and watched fats change. Fat composition shifted, and fat-making activity rose. A channel protein thus influences fat chemistry more broadly than expected. That link may explain digestive troubles that burden patients daily.
