It could also suggest dietary or drug corrections worth testing.
plos-pone-0010546:
Michael Widmann, Peter Trodler and Jürgen Pleiss carried out a systematic study of the near-neutral zone of proteins in PLOS ONE in 2010. Proteins carry electric charge that changes with acidity. Near a certain acidity, their net charge falls almost to zero; that band is the isoelectric region. It predicts how proteins bind in ion exchange columns, a workhorse purification method. Labs tune acidity and salt to exploit that binding.

A systematic map of the region helps chemists plan purifications instead of guessing. Predicting binding saves costly trial and error on valuable samples. The study treats a routine lab step with unusual rigor. Protein purification underlies most drug and enzyme research. Better prediction there quietly speeds many other projects.
plos-pone-0010646:
Jeshmi Jeyabalan and colleagues studied a small protein tied to a rare bone disease, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein, SEDLIN, helps move cargo inside cells. Changes in its gene cause a childhood disorder that distorts growing joints and spine.

The team showed SEDLIN pairs with an identical copy of itself. They also mapped how disease-causing changes affect its contacts with three gene-control proteins. Some mutants kept the pairing but lost other contacts. Separating those effects helps explain why similar mutations can cause quite different severity in different patients.
plos-pone-0010746:
Chirag Patel, Jayanta Bhattacharya, and Atul Butte scanned many environmental factors for links to type 2 diabetes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Diabetes arises from genes mixed with surroundings and habits. Genome scans test thousands of gene variants at once; no matching scan existed for exposures.

Their pilot scan tested hundreds of measurable exposures against diabetes in survey data. A few strong links stood out, including some pollutants. Many weaker links were likely noise, and the authors say so plainly. The study's value is the method: a wide, even-handed screen that other diseases can now borrow.
plos-pone-0010846:
Ashkan Emadi, Ashley Ross, Kathleen Cowan and co-authors published this drug study in PLOS ONE in 2010. They worked with dimeric naphthoquinones, twin-ring compounds first made to block an HIV enzyme but later found to kill leukemia cells by an unknown route. To learn how these compounds act, the team turned to yeast.

They screened a library of yeast strains, each missing a single gene, for strains that grew better or worse when exposed to the compounds. Strains lacking genes for mitochondria, the cell's power plants, and for respiration were extra sensitive. Follow-up tests pointed the same way, toward energy production inside the cell. Emadi and colleagues use a simple organism to map a drug's weak spots, a strategy that can guide the design of new cancer compounds.
plos-pone-0010946:
Akihide Takeuchi, Motoyasu Hosokawa, Takayuki Nojima and co-authors published this splicing study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells build different proteins in different tissues by alternative splicing, cutting and rejoining a gene's message in varied ways. The hardest case is mutually exclusive exons, where exactly one of several segments must be picked, and how the cell guarantees a clean either-or choice was unclear.

The authors built reporter mice whose tissues glow one color or another depending on which exon gets chosen, making the switch visible across the body. Tracking that signal revealed a conserved switching mechanism rather than a loose balance of competing factors. Takeuchi and colleagues supply a living readout for the splice code. Such tools help explain how tissues get their distinct protein sets, and how splicing errors cause disease.
plos-pone-0011046:
Tristan Hedrick and Jack Waters published this brain cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The nucleus basalis, at the back of the basal forebrain, supplies the cortex with acetylcholine, a chemical central to arousal and attention, and it degenerates in Alzheimer's disease. Its large neurons had never been characterized electrically, unlike their counterparts in neighboring regions, so the authors recorded from them in mouse brain slices.

They patched onto magnocellular neurons from young adult mice, then stained each recorded cell afterward to learn whether it was cholinergic or not. Comparing the two classes revealed how their firing patterns, inputs, and resting behavior differ. Hedrick and Waters supply the basic electrical profile of a nucleus that attention research and dementia studies both depend on, a reference that future work on its decline will need.
plos-pone-0011146:
Krankel, Armstrong, McArdle and colleagues examined young diabetic patients in PLOS ONE in 2010. Even before heart disease appears, type 1 diabetes may harm the blood's repair cells. The team tested how blood cells that support vessels respond to kinin, a signal that normally aids repair.

Responses to kinin were altered in cells from young patients, showing early wear on the repair system. Catching vessel harm this early argues for action long before symptoms start. If repair can be restored, later heart disease might be delayed or prevented. The study gives a cell level reason to treat young patients proactively.
plos-pone-0011246:
Priest, Bereknyei, Hooper and colleagues observed hospital rounds in PLOS ONE in 2010. On rounds, medical teams visit patients, discuss cases and teach students. The team recorded where rounds happened and what was discussed, then related both to specialty, hospital, patient load and team size.

Setting and content varied in clear patterns with those factors. Bedside rounds differ from hallway or conference room rounds in what gets covered. That matters for training, since students learn medicine largely on rounds. Hospitals can use such evidence to plan rounds that teach better and include patients more fully.
plos-pone-0011346:
Kathleen Schwerdtner Máñez and Sebastian Ferse traced the history of trepang fishing in their 2010 paper. Trepang is sea cucumber, dried and sold as a prized food and trade good in Asian markets. For centuries, sailors from Makassar, on the island of Sulawesi, sailed north to fish trepang along distant coasts, including northern Australia.

Their account follows how the fishery grew, how trade routes linked Makassar with buyers in China, and how contact with Aboriginal Australians shaped the voyages. The fishery is one of the oldest sustained links between Australia and Asia, long before European settlement. Reading that history restores credit to Indigenous and Makassan seafarers. It also shows how one marine product could bind together economies and cultures across a wide sea.
plos-pone-0011446:
Kaori Tsurui, Atsushi Honma, and Takayoshi Nishida tested camouflage in a small grasshopper in 2010. Tetrix japonica comes in several color patterns within one species, and each pattern is a bet on blending into a particular ground surface. The team placed the different forms against different microhabitat backgrounds and measured how well each hid.

Some patterns hid superbly on one background and poorly on another, so no single form won everywhere. That patchwork result explains how several patterns can persist in one population: each microhabitat favors its own best disguise. The experiments are a neat field test of natural selection's oldest trick. For ecology, the study shows why variation itself can be the adaptation, when the world an animal must match is a mosaic rather than one flat color.
plos-pone-0011546:
Fei Chen and co-authors built a gene catalog in 2010 for America's two great farmed catfish. Channel catfish and blue catfish anchor a large aquaculture industry, and their hybrids are prized, yet their genetic toolkits lagged far behind those of other farmed animals. The team identified and characterized full-length cDNAs, complete copies of active genes, from both species.

Full-length copies matter because partial fragments leave a gene's true start, end, and protein uncertain. With complete sequences, breeders can track traits, design accurate tests, and compare the two species gene by gene. The catalog equips biologists to improve growth, disease resistance, and feed efficiency in fish that supply a large share of farmed freshwater protein. It also enables the hybrid's genetics to be managed deliberately rather than by habit.
plos-pone-0011646:
Anna Metaxas and Noreen Kelly compared how deep-sea communities renew themselves, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Vent and seep habitats run on chemicals rather than sunlight and occur as small, scattered patches on the dark seafloor. Their animal communities include many species found nowhere else, and they must recover from disturbance using drifting larvae.

The authors asked whether larval supply and settlement differ among these chemosynthetic settings. Their comparison shows how uneven the connection between patches can be. That unevenness matters for protecting deep-sea sites, because a damaged community can only recover if larvae arrive from elsewhere.
plos-pone-0011746:
Dashdemberel Narantuya and co-authors transplanted human immune cells into stroke-damaged rat brains, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Microglia are the brain's resident immune and clean-up cells, releasing signals and growth factors after injury that shape how damage unfolds. Their net effect after stroke can help or harm, depending on context.

The team grafted human microglia into rats with focal ischaemia, a local loss of blood flow. The transplanted cells induced protection of brain tissue and improved behaviour. A cross-species rescue like this suggests donor microglia could one day aid stroke recovery.
plos-pone-0011846:
Stephen Hughes and colleagues ran a small pilot study in 2010 on what a surgical tourniquet does to the body beyond stopping blood flow. Tourniquets are routine in upper limb bone surgery, keeping the field clear while surgeons work. Ten patients having planned operations agreed to give blood samples from the arm at set points.

Comparing those samples showed that surgery with a tourniquet raised signs of inflammation and shifted markers tied to white blood cells, clotting, and the lining of blood vessels. The changes suggest the squeeze and release leaves a wider imprint on the blood than surgeons usually track. Knowing that imprint matters when weighing how long a tourniquet should stay on.
plos-pone-0011946:
Taryn Roberts, Paul McGreevy, and Michael Valenzuela reported in 2010 that life with humans has turned and reshaped the brain of the pet dog. Dog breeds vary a great deal in skull shape, from long-nosed to flat-faced. What no one had checked was whether the brain inside is laid out in new ways to match.

By looking at the brain's midline shape across breeds, the team found signs that the brain has been rotated and its parts re-laid as the skull changed. Breeding for short faces and other traits has thus quietly re-posed the brain itself. That fact may help explain why breeds act so unlike each other, and it adds a hidden cost to breeding for looks alone.
plos-pone-0012046:
Jeffrey Chow, Eili Klein, and Ramanan Laxminarayan weighed in 2010 whether a biofortified mustard could fight vitamin A deficiency in India at a fair cost. Deficiency there raises the risk of severe illness and death, especially in children. The standing World Health Organization remedy is periodic high-dose supplements, which work but must be delivered again and again.

Golden Mustard, bred to carry extra vitamin A precursor in a food people already eat, offers a different delivery route. A cost-effectiveness analysis compares that route against supplements on equal terms. For policy, the useful question is not whether the crop works in principle but whether each case prevented costs less than the alternatives.
plos-pone-0012146:
Clelia Gasparini, Leigh Simmons, and Maxine Beveridge studied sperm competition in a small tropical fish for PLOS ONE in 2010. When several males mate with one female, their sperm race to fertilize her eggs, and traits that win that race should spread. Numbers clearly matter, since more sperm means more tickets in the draw, but whether swimming quality matters was far less sure.

In the green swordtail, faster-swimming sperm predicted which males won fertilizations. That ties a simple lab measurement, swimming speed, to real reproductive success. It helps explain how male traits evolve under this hidden contest, and it may guide breeding work in fish farms and conservation programs.
plos-pone-0012246:
Maria Vittoria Barone, Merlin Nanayakkara, Giovanni Paolella, and co-authors tracked a wheat peptide inside gut cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Celiac disease, an immune reaction to wheat gluten affecting about one person in a hundred, begins in a particular genetic setting, yet the trigger steps are still being pieced together. One gluten fragment is known to disturb gut cells directly, apart from the immune attack.

They found the fragment settles into the cell's recycling vesicles and jams their maturation. A jam in that housekeeping traffic could help explain how the fragment stresses the gut lining before immunity joins in. Each early step clarified is a possible point for a drug to protect people who cannot fully avoid gluten.
plos-pone-0012346:
John Reganold, Preston Andrews, Jennifer Reeve and fellow researchers compared organic and standard strawberry farms in a 2010 PLOS ONE study from California fields. Shoppers often pay more for organic fruit because they expect better taste, more nutrition, and healthier soil. The team set out to test those beliefs side by side on real working farms.

They measured fruit quality, taste, nutrition, and soil health across matched farm pairs. Organic berries and soils scored higher on many of the tests, though not on every single one. Because the study used commercial farms rather than lab plots, its results speak directly to shoppers, growers, and anyone weighing the true value of organic food.
plos-pone-0012446:
Nuno Araújo, José Andrade and Hans Herrmann modeled tactical voting in simple winner-take-all elections, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The authors ask how often elections end in landslides and how often in close races. Ballot results from several large countries showed odd but universal patterns that simple models had not matched.

Adding tactical voters — people who back a viable candidate rather than a hopeless favorite — made the model reproduce those patterns. Strategic behavior, in other words, shapes election statistics at national scale. The work gives election watchers a baseline for spotting results that look truly abnormal rather than merely surprising.
plos-pone-0012546:
Dawn Loh, Juliana Navarro, Arkady Hagopian and colleagues scrambled the light cycle of mice and tested their memory, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Body clocks govern learning and memory circuits, including the amygdala, which stores fear associations. Frequent flyers and shift workers know the fog of jet lag, but its direct effect on stored memories was untested in a controlled model.

Rapid shifts of the light-dark cycle disrupted the mice's memory of conditioned fear. The memories did not merely form poorly; recall itself suffered after schedule chaos. The work gives biological weight to complaints from night-shift workers and suggests sleep timing belongs in memory research.
plos-pone-0012646:
Downes, Pekalski, Angus and co-authors reported that a weaker version of an immune gene can guard against type 1 diabetes. The gene, IFIH1, helps cells sense viral RNA and launch a defence. Earlier work had already tied it to diabetes, in which the immune system attacks the pancreas.

Their 2010 study shows that having less of this gene's activity lowers diabetes risk. That flips the usual story of a gene defect causing harm, since here reduced action protects. It hints that calming this virus sensor might one day help prevent the disease.
plos-pone-0012746:
Jogi, Rono, Lund and co-authors slowed skin healing in mice by blocking one clot-dissolving activator. Wound repair needs plasmin and related enzymes to clear paths for new skin. Mice lacking plasminogen already heal very slowly, setting the baseline for their 2010 study.

They used an antibody to neutralise uPA in mice that also lacked tPA, the other main activator. Healing slowed further and plasmin formation dropped, proving uPA's own share in repair. Knowing each activator's share helps design wound treatments that speed safe healing.  Their antibody tool let them switch one activator off at will.
plos-pone-0318046:
Nunik Maharani and colleagues turned oil palm plantation workers into wildlife scientists. They piloted a monitoring system across seven Indonesian estates over five years. Their 2026 report describes how 3,950 employees logged wildlife sightings through a structured scheme. Management support and rewards backed the scheme. The team shows how the resulting flood of records can estimate where species actually live.

The haul was large: nearly 150,000 observations. They covered almost seven hundred animal species and close to two hundred plants. The cost per hectare ran far below conventional surveys. Plantations replace forest yet retain habitat fragments. Nobody knew precisely what survives in them. Employee monitoring supplies that missing map cheaply, giving companies and conservationists shared numbers to manage by.
plos-pone-0326546:
Amanda Tristao Santini and co-workers chart the gut bacteria of Brazilian stingless bees and where each kind lives along the gut. Stingless bees matter as pollinators, and their microbes aid food use and defense. Their 2026 study sequences gut bacteria from several species in one large genus and dissects one species region by region to map its inner tenants.

Five bacterial groups ruled the gut, arranged in a striking pattern. The crop and stomach-like parts favored some groups, while the rear gut held others plus a likely new partner species. Two famous honeybee symbionts were missing entirely. These bees run a different inner ecosystem from their better-known cousins, which hive care and conservation should respect.
plos-pone-0330146:
Time Fukuda and five co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One study building a survey scale that measures how anxious Japanese adults feel about COVID-19 vaccination. Such anxiety is a feeling, distinct from general vaccine doubt. No tested Japanese tool captured it. Five hundred adults filled in the new twenty-five-item scale twice, four weeks apart. They also answered measures of fear, readiness to vaccinate, and belief in conspiracies.

The scale settled into three parts. One part covers anxiety tied to trust in vaccines. One covers emotional symptoms. One covers worry about catching the virus even after a shot. Scores stayed steady over time. They also lined up well with the other measures, rising with fear and conspiracy belief, and falling as readiness rose. The authors argue that health messages should speak to feelings, not just give risk facts.
plos-pone-0337146:
Ali Eslamizadeh and colleagues searched for a mushroom growing recipe that balances profit, nutrition, and reuse of waste soil. White button mushrooms grow on a casing layer, which growers usually discard after use. Their 2026 study tested seven casing mixes and five feed supplements in a field experiment, then optimised the results mathematically.

The winning mix reused two-fifths recycled soil alongside peat, sugarcane residue, and minerals. Corn grit as a supplement beat the other feeds, lifting both yield and profit. The chosen pairing scored well across all three goals at once. Eslamizadeh and colleagues present the result as a circular-economy option for growers who must weigh money, food value, and waste together.
plos-pone-0337646:
Saima Sultana and colleagues built a computer model that recognises medical actions from depth sensor data, even when the room is poorly lit. Ordinary cameras struggle in dim light, and a robot that misreads a medical action could cause real harm. Their model, called I2I, works from depth readings rather than colour images, pulling out the most telling features before classifying what a person is doing.

Tested on a large public dataset of recorded actions, the model reached just over ninety-one percent accuracy and beat earlier methods the authors compared it against. The work matters for hospital and care robots that must keep working through the night or in dark wards. The authors frame depth sensing as a way to keep recognition reliable when lighting cannot be trusted.
plos-pone-0339746:
Amanda Santos and colleagues develop in 2026 a new lab stain to diagnose a skin disease caused by Leishmania parasites in Brazil. They built an antibody that targets a parasite protein, first checking it on infected hamster tissue and parasite extracts. Then they tested the stain on skin samples from about a hundred patients with suspected disease, against a DNA test as the standard.

The new stain found a bit over half of true cases, slightly more than direct viewing or standard tissue checks, and it was almost always right when it said negative. Combining methods raised accuracy further. The authors say wider testing could earn it a routine place.
plos-pone-0341246:
Disposable dishes and tubes used in fertility treatment can carry fever-causing contamination that standard checks may miss. Hiroyuki Tomari and colleagues measured such contamination, called pyrogens, across twenty products used in assisted reproduction, in this 2026 PLOS One study using a test based on human cells.

Seven products carried clear amounts of contamination, in some cases above levels once reported as safe for embryo work. A low-temperature gas treatment mixing ozone and hydrogen peroxide wiped the contamination out. Leftover peroxide on one dish type vanished after a day of drying, and treated items did not harm sperm or embryos in checks.
plos-pone-0341946:
Ahmet Süerdem, Svetlomir Zdravkov, and Martin J Ivanov model how knowledge, conspiracy thinking, and mistrust of science connect across Europe, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Two camps dominate debate: one says more knowledge cures mistrust, the other says worldviews coexist. Using cross national survey data gathered during the COVID-19 pandemic, the team fitted a multilevel model. It lets the pathway run at personal and regional levels simultaneously. They tested what strengthens or weakens it.

Conspiratorial reasoning turned out to be the bridge. It significantly carried the effect of scientific knowledge toward mistrust at both levels of the model. The strength of the pathway shifted with information engagement, regional value climates, and religiosity. Knowledge, the authors conclude, is a conditional resource: in some minds and regions it buffers mistrust, in others it barely dents it. Science communication that ignores the conspiratorial step will misread its audience.
plos-pone-0342546:
Zhaoying Qi and colleagues evaluate gel patches made from a partly neutralized plastic polymer in this 2026 PLOS ONE materials paper. Such gels back medicated skin patches, and their feel, stiffness, and stability depend on how the polymer chains are cross-linked. The team prepared four variants using two common acid-to-salt ratios.

Over thirty days, quality checks and flow tests showed no meaningful drift in any variant. Odor-sensing instruments, frozen microscopy, and heat-based chemical analysis found that patches with equal neutralization behaved alike, separating which recipe choices matter and which do not. For manufacturers, stable, predictable gel behavior is the difference between a patch that sticks and performs and one that fails on the shelf.
plos-pone-0345346:
Daniel Snape and co-authors tested whether five days of heat training protects athletes' kidneys as well as their circulation. Heat acclimation is known to steady heart and temperature control, but kidney stress during hot exercise was a worry. Their 2026 trial randomised fourteen trained men to hot training or mild-condition exercise, with heat tests before and after.

Heat training lowered resting heart rate, expanded blood plasma volume, and raised sweat losses, the classic adaptation pattern. A fluid-balance hormone that spiked during the first heat test no longer rose after training. One kidney stress marker rose only in the control group during the first test, and another stayed flat throughout. Snape and colleagues conclude short acclimation helps without obvious kidney cost.
plos-pone-0347046:
Elena Capelli and co-workers follow how babies learn to blend what they see and hear when someone talks. Babies at higher likelihood of autism were compared with babies at typical likelihood at six, nine, and twelve months old. Their 2026 study uses eye tracking and a classic effect where mismatched lip movements change the sound a viewer thinks they hear.

Across both groups, babies shifted their gaze from the eyes toward the mouth over the first year. Babies in the higher-likelihood group made that shift more slowly. At age two, babies showing signs linked to autism had shown the flattest shift as infants. Watching this early gaze path could help spot babies who may need extra support sooner.
plos-pone-0347146:
Abdoul Kader Ilboudo and colleagues measured exposure to Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever, a dangerous tick-borne virus, in farming households of rural Burkina Faso. They tested more than seven hundred people and nearly twenty-three hundred cattle, sheep, and goats across sixteen villages, following a One Health approach that treats human and animal health as one system.

About three percent of people carried antibodies, against over half of cattle, showing the virus circulates widely in livestock. Older animals, longer grazing, and tick infestation raised exposure, and results clustered strongly within households. Sloppy livestock biosecurity raised farmers' own risk. The authors call for tick control and safer animal handling.
plos-pone-0347346:
Xue Zhang and co-authors studied doctor photos on a large Chinese online medical platform in 2026. Patients choosing a doctor online lean on first impressions from profile pictures and reviews, and the team asked whether faces sway real bookings.

Data on more than seven thousand doctors were gathered, and software scored facial traits such as attractiveness and smiling. Attractive, smiling doctors drew higher rates of patients moving to offline visits, and doctor gender mattered too. Satisfaction reviews changed some of these links. The results raise fair minded questions for platforms, since a face is not a measure of medical skill.
plos-pone-0347646:
Anastasia N. L. Newman and three co-workers set out a plan to map a gap in care. Folk who leave the ICU often bear weak limbs, fogged minds, and low mood for years. Tricks that help folk steer their own care work well in other long ills. But they are rare here, and no one has charted the work. This paper is a plan for that chart.

The team will search six stores of past work. They will keep work on grown ICU stays of a day or more that used self-steer tricks. Two staff will screen each find, with a third to break ties. The chart should show what is known and where the holes are.
plos-pone-0347846:
SiWei Wei, Yang Yang, and ChunZhi Wang propose a new traffic forecasting network in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Road sensors form groups, not just pairs: one jam can involve a whole interchange at once. Standard graph models, which link only pairs of points, miss those group relationships, so the authors use hypergraphs that connect many nodes in a single link.

A transformer component, fitted with a time-distilling step, reads the global rhythm of flow across the network, and attention channels fuse the spatial and temporal views. Tested on two California highway datasets with repeated runs and strict statistics, the model aimed for accuracy that survives scrutiny, the standard city traffic systems need before trusting predictions.
plos-pone-0348146:
Radfan Saleh Abdullah, Naif Taleb Ali, and Mansour Abdelnabi H. Mehdi report a medical puzzle from war-torn Yemen: non-smokers looked far more likely to have abnormal blood haemoglobin than smokers, the reverse of normal biology. Smoking usually raises haemoglobin. They studied six hundred university students, collecting blood tests, smoking histories, and social background measures.

The reversal was real in the data and strongest among poorer students and women. Much of it ran through nutrition: in a famine-shadowed economy, being able to smoke marked relative wealth and better food. Sensitivity checks said hidden bias would have to be huge to erase the finding. The authors frame wealth as a fundamental cause that can flip biology.
plos-pone-0348346:
Carlos Salvador-Huerta and colleagues in Spain published a trial plan in 2026 for fibromyalgia, a long-term condition of widespread pain and tiredness. Exercise helps, but pain, fear of movement, and poor body sense keep many patients from sticking with it. No results are reported yet.

Patients will follow a full virtual reality exercise program that tricks the eyes about how the body moves. The plan is to test whether that altered feedback eases pain and improves daily function better than usual care. If it works, clinics could offer a form of exercise that feels safer to people who expect movement to hurt.
plos-pone-0348446:
Abdiweli Mohamed Abdi and colleagues interviewed four hundred twenty-seven women at Banadir Hospital in Mogadishu, Somalia about what happens to leftover and expired medicines at home. Such stockpiles invite accidental poisoning, misuse, and pollution when binned. The 2026 survey found the habits widespread and risky.

Nearly everyone kept unused medicines at home, mostly for emergencies, and a third also kept expired ones. Almost nobody read storage instructions, and most never checked expiry dates before buying or swallowing a drug. More than ninety percent threw old medicines in household trash. The authors call for public education and a national take-back scheme for unwanted drugs.
plos-pone-0348946:
Mohammed H Alshamrani and colleagues surveyed four hundred and sixty-five parents of toddlers in Saudi Arabia's Riyadh region about tooth decay in young children and how they bottle-feed. Early childhood caries is rampant in the kingdom, and parents control the sugar, brushing, and dental visits that decide it. A structured questionnaire scored knowledge and habits across family types.

Knowledge landed in the middle range, with one glaring hole: barely one parent in eight knew when the first dental visit should happen, though most valued brushing and repairing baby teeth. Night-time bottles were the norm, and most children stayed on bottles past their first birthday. Better knowledge tracked with brushing after feeds and earlier weaning, and with mothers' education and income. The authors call for parent education that starts with that first-visit message.
plos-pone-0349146:
Mateusz Gruzewski and Marek Palkowski wrote a fast computer program for predicting how an RNA molecule folds, a classic problem in computational biology. Their code implements the Nussinov algorithm, which finds the fold with the most paired bases, a task whose cost explodes as sequences grow. The trick is reorganizing the calculation so modern processors can use their memory caches and many cores well.

By splitting easy and hard cases and arranging the work like matrix multiplication, the code vectorizes cleanly and scales across very large thread counts on both major processor brands. It beat compiler-generated versions in tests. Folding speed is a bottleneck in RNA research, so a reusable, well-tuned template helps every related algorithm.
plos-pone-0349246:
Michiko Hirata and colleagues measured how Venus flytrap leaves snap shut, one of the fastest moves in the plant world. A trap closes in under a second, yet how leaf size relates to leaf bending was unclear. The team filmed closing traps and scanned leaves with micro CT imaging to rebuild their shapes in three dimensions.

Faster closing came with a higher shape index. The scans also showed that bigger leaves bend by a different amount than smaller ones, a link the authors call a size and curvature constraint. They then built a two-layer model that reproduces the bending. The design rules could help engineers shape soft robots and other bending surfaces.
plos-pone-0349646:
Leonardo F Reginato and Simon J Brandl built a computer vision tool in 2026 for tiny reef fish that hide near the bottom. These fish are hugely varied and important, yet only a handful of experts can name them from photos, so most go uncounted.

Their system, CryptoVision, learns from high quality images and answers at three levels at once: family, genus, and species, respecting how those levels nest. A design that lifts weak image features helps it separate look-alike species. If the tool proves accurate in wider use, divers and camera surveys could track these hidden fish at a scale expert time alone could never reach.
plos-pone-0349946:
Christian Raphael and colleagues ran a trial across several centres in 2026 on a soft airway tube for gut endoscopy under sedation. Patients breathe on their own while sedated, and dips in oxygen that force staff to act are common.

More than three hundred patients were split at random between care with a nasal airway tube and usual care. The main count was any airway rescue or oxygen dip. Satisfaction of patients and staff, side effects, and the role of sleep apnoea risk were also tracked. A cheap tube that cuts rescue moves would make a routine procedure safer and calmer.
plos-pone-0350046:
Fereshteh Shafiei led a lab test of ways to shield tooth enamel after radiation care. Radiation for head and neck cancers softens enamel. Acid then eats into teeth fast. The team used sixty enamel pieces cut from pulled molars. Most pieces got six weeks of radiation, in daily doses like those patients get. Four treatments were then tried on the weakened enamel.

All four treatments left enamel harder than no treatment did. A mineral paste worked best, alone or with a resin coat. It even raised hardness past the post-radiation level. A curcumin-based treatment also did well. The team says such coats may guard the teeth of cancer patients.
plos-pone-0350146:
Miena Meek Hall, Katherine R Standish, and co-authors convened focus groups of physician leaders to ask what large American health systems get right and wrong about breastfeeding care. Lactation medicine has grown as a specialty, yet families still meet patchy support because standards for organizing the care barely exist. Their 2026 study ran three focus groups with thirteen leaders working inside big health systems.

Leaders said systems should model good practice, and noted that executives' and staff members' own breastfeeding experiences sway policy more than expected. They recommended dedicated lactation divisions, better staff training, coordinated services, and support for employees who pump at work. Barriers included care split across departments, weak billing for lactation services, and low priority in training programs. Teamwork across professions and sensible record workflows were named as helpers.
plos-pone-0350446:
Correction notice: Shintaro Imamura and his team issued this 2026 fix to their past study of zebrafish and blood growth. Two figure panels had been copied by error when the figures were built. The team has now replaced them. The notice says the counts behind the figures do not change. It also adds ethics approvals and drug details that were left out the first time. The raw images and data for the fixed figures are posted with the notice.

The first study found that blocking a gene called telomerase left zebrafish embryos short of blood cells. The cells also failed to mature as they should. That result pointed to a side job for the gene, past guarding chromosome ends. The fix leaves those claims as they were.
plos-pone-0350646:
Daniele Capitanio and co-authors profiled proteins across metamorphosis in the sea squirt Ciona in 2026. The animal starts as a swimming larva with a simple spinal cord, then settles and dissolves most of its nervous system, a natural model of nerve loss.

Protein samples from swimming, settled, and mid change larvae were compared by mass measurement. Four hundred five proteins shifted across the stages, and network analysis grouped them by job. The catalogue shows which systems are dismantled and which built as the adult forms. Chordate cousins of vertebrates, sea squirts let researchers watch a nervous system taken apart by design.
plos-pone-0350746:
The surface layer of joint cartilage meets joint fluid first and takes the first wear. Fengrui Liu and colleagues grew these surface cells in dishes, then stressed them with inflammatory signals and repeated stretching to mimic early osteoarthritis, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Inflammation dimmed the cells' stem-like markers and switched on several inflammatory pathways plus a cartilage-chewing enzyme. Adding stretch raised a force-sensing channel on the cells, sharpened their calcium responses, and broke down their inner skeleton. Under combined stress the cells destroyed more matrix and died more readily. The authors say protecting this front-line layer may be key to slowing joint disease early.
plos-pone-0350846:
Simone Luongo and three colleagues explore why luxury fashion houses are opening hotels and restaurants. Their 2026 study is qualitative, built on interviews with industry stakeholders. Fashion brands from catwalk names now serve meals and rent rooms. The authors ask what drives that leap, and where sustainability fits in.

Interviewees said the ventures deepen the brand experience beyond clothing. A stay or dinner lets customers live inside the brand's world. That strengthens engagement and loyalty. Sustainability showed up in both backstage operations and customer-facing touches. Its depth varied widely between companies, though. Aligning a fashion identity with hospitality service proved genuinely hard. The study gives managers a map of the rewards and the friction in crossing industries.
plos-pone-0350946:
Jelto Branding and four colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One study on microphones for listening to insects, a tool hoped to help with pest control and wildlife surveying. Systems that recognize insects by sound work in the lab but struggle outdoors, and the authors suspected cheap microphones are part of the problem. They compared a high-end, low-noise measurement array against an inexpensive array of the kind built into home voice assistants.

Experiments and simulations showed the sensitive array could record and identify far smaller, quieter insects. The cheap array still recognized some species, even with background noise added. The authors conclude that progress in acoustic insect monitoring needs microphones built for the job, since general-purpose hardware quietly caps what the software can achieve.
plos-pone-0351146:
Zaixin Wu, Xinyi Liu, and Xiaobo Han grew tiny brain like organoids from autism related cells and bathed them for a week in two gut made fatty acids, acetate and butyrate. Gut chemistry has been tied to brain development, yet direct tests are scarce. Gene activity across the whole organoid was read and grouped by function and pathway.

Acetate mainly shifted genes for gene control, catalysis, and membrane flow. Butyrate switched on immune linked processes and a key immune signalling pathway. Two similar gut chemicals thus push developing brain tissue in very different directions. Dose and timing in early life may matter for how gut health shapes the brain.
plos-pone-0351546:
Ahmed Abuzaid and five colleagues map where irrigation farming could work on Egypt's desert fringe. Their 2026 study covers about thirty thousand hectares west of the Nile Delta. Newly reclaimed land is a gamble without good maps. The framework blends expert weighting, fuzzy logic, and geographic software. Terrain, soil, and groundwater layers were built from maps, field surveys, and laboratory tests. Each criterion earned a weight through structured pairwise comparisons.

The weighting proved internally consistent throughout. Salt emerged as the soil's master variable, joined by sodicity and soil depth. Groundwater feasibility hinged on potential salinity and how fast water sinks in. The final maps sort the land into potential zones for planners. Egypt is pushing farming into the desert as Nile land crowds. A transparent, repeatable suitability method keeps that expansion from wasting water and money on ground that cannot repay them.
plos-pone-0351646:
Emily Sirotich and four colleagues lay out a plan, published in 2026, for reviewing biologics and depression in skin and joint disease. Psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis are long-term immune conditions. Depression often travels with them, eroding quality of life and treatment adherence. Biologic drugs, antibodies that block specific immune signals, might ease depression by calming inflammation. The existing evidence is scattered and mixed. This plan fixes the review's methods in advance.

Searches will cover five major databases and trial lists. Randomised trials, cohort studies, and case-control studies all qualify. Depression may be counted by diagnosis or by tested questionnaires. Two reviewers will screen, extract, and grade bias independently. Where data allow, pooled risk estimates will follow. As a plan, the paper reports no results. Its discipline is the point: pre-set methods make the eventual answer about biologics and mood harder to dismiss.
plos-pone-0351746:
Isidro Montelongo-Alfaro and six colleagues study baby oysters settling along a Mexican river estuary. Their 2026 field study follows the eastern oyster in the Soto la Marina River, on the Gulf of Mexico. Recruitment of spat, the drifting young that must attach somewhere, decides whether populations persist. Six sites stretched from near the mouth to over twenty kilometres upstream. Collectors were checked monthly for a full year. Water temperature, salinity, oxygen, acidity, and clarity were measured beside each collection.

Only salinity separated the sites significantly. It fell steadily from the salty mouth toward fresh upstream reaches. Statistical models tied spat numbers to space, season, and conditions. Gulf estuaries on the Mexican coast are understudied compared with American ones. Local oyster fisheries and restoration projects need this baseline: where the young settle, when they arrive, and which water property sorts them. Salinity's lone starring role simplifies the monitoring managers must sustain.
plos-pone-0351846:
Ming Liu and colleagues found a protein that helps stomach cancer cells survive a common chemotherapy drug. The drug is known as 5-FU. The protein is called PTPRE, and it runs high in gastric tumors. The team studied it in cancer cells and in mouse tumor grafts. They traced how it protects the cells from a form of iron-driven cell death.

The protein switches on a chain of signals inside the cell. That chain ends at a second protein, TRIB3. With the chain active, the iron-driven death route stays shut. The drug then loses one of its ways to kill, and resistance sets in. Blocking the chain could hand the drug its power back. The work names each link, which is what drug developers need first.
plos-pone-0351946:
Lei Hua, Yongshou Tao, and Liangru Shen studied three mineral-linked blood markers across the stages of a modern syndrome. The syndrome ties heart, kidney, and metabolic disease into one tangle. Data came from over fifteen thousand adults in a United States health survey. A genetic method added a second strand. It uses inherited variants to test whether a marker may help cause disease, not just follow it.

One marker stood out: alkaline phosphatase. It climbed step by step with the syndrome's stage, from early risk to advanced disease with kidney harm. Calcium and phosphorus followed their own patterns. The genetic strand singles the enzyme out still further. A cheap, common blood test may deserve a second look as this syndrome's gauge. Stage-aware markers help doctors read a condition that otherwise blurs into its parts.
plos-pone-0352146:
Jia Wang and Xiaoyang Dong publish a protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026 for a trial of ear-based nerve stimulation to help stroke survivors move again. Stimulating the vagus nerve through the skin of both ears may beat the usual one-ear approach, judging by earlier small studies. Their planned multicentre trial will enrol one hundred and fourteen patients whose stroke left one side of the body weak.

Patients will be assigned at random to stimulation of both ears, one ear, or a control treatment, with patients and assessors kept unaware of who got what. The trial aims for the full limb picture, not just the arm. Results should show whether the bilateral method deserves a place in stroke rehabilitation.
plos-pone-0352246:
David Sjöström and seven colleagues set out a trial protocol, published in 2026, for psilocybin therapy in anorexia nervosa. Anorexia is a severe eating disorder that often begins in adolescence. It carries high death and relapse rates. Standard psychological and nutritional care helps many patients, yet outcomes stay disappointing. Psilocybin has shown early promise in other rigid, treatment-resistant conditions.

The planned trial enrols people aged sixteen to thirty-five whose anorexia has already relapsed. Half receive two psilocybin sessions with structured psychological support, plus usual care. The other half receive usual care alone. Safety and tolerability come first among the outcomes. Symptom change, mood, and brain-related measures are also tracked. As a protocol, the paper reports no results. It lays out a careful test of whether psychedelic-assisted therapy can be run safely in this fragile group.
plos-pone-0352346:
Jay Kirkham led a team of seven authors studying how North Atlantic right whales feed, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. These whales are critically endangered, so knowing how they find and take food helps protect them. The team combined motion tags on free-swimming whales with camera checks and machine learning.

Kirkham's method lets researchers read feeding events straight from tag data, without watching each whale. That means feeding can be tracked at scale, in places and seasons observers rarely reach. Knowing where and how right whales feed guides shipping and fishing rules meant to keep them alive. With so few whales left, each gain in understanding carries unusual weight.
plos-pone-0352446:
Anna-Chiara Barta and seven colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One DNA barcoding study updating Austria's inventory of woodlice, the land-dwelling crustaceans that recycle dead plant matter in soils. Austria's species list had not been reviewed in nearly fifty years. The team generated more than five hundred genetic barcodes from fresh specimens and even managed to sequence DNA from historic museum specimens.

The barcodes covered about three-quarters of the known Austrian species and added two species never before recorded in the country. Genetic splits inside several named species were deep enough to suggest hidden, unrecognized species, and in one case the team found matching subtle body differences to back the split. Older museum material worked best with a repaired short-barcode method. The dataset now anchors Austria's national barcode library for soil wildlife monitoring.
plos-pone-0352646:
Guangming Shi and four colleagues test a microbe-based method for strengthening weak loess soil. Their 2026 study uses soil from China's Ili River Valley. That loess is loose, salty, and prone to collapse and erosion. The technique coaxes bacteria to precipitate calcium carbonate, a natural cement. Three orders of applying bacteria and cementing solution were compared in the laboratory.

Applying both solutions at once worked best. Treated samples gained roughly three-fifths more compressive strength than untreated soil. Cohesion rose by over half as well. Under the microscope, the winning method built a continuous, dense cement network. It filled voids and bridged soil particles evenly. Stepwise treatments left patchy cement instead. The authors call the work preliminary, but it points to a greener way to stabilise hazard-prone loess ground.
plos-pone-0353746:
Omar Saadani and six colleagues pair faba beans with helpful root bacteria. Their goal is to clean soil poisoned by lead and cadmium. The study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The beans grew in soil spiked at three levels. Some plants got a three-strain bacterial mix. The mix promotes plant growth and tolerates metals. The bacteria colonise the roots. They help the plant thrive in hostile ground.

The partnership worked best in the middle soil. Shoots grew heavier there. Root nodules flourished. The shoots pulled up far more lead and cadmium than plain plants. Cadmium uptake rose several times over. Protective chemistry in the roots rose too. In heavier soil the gains faded. That marks the practical limit of this gentle cleanup method.
plos-pone-0353846:
Chunhui Luo and six colleagues treat grey cast iron with laser-driven cavitation and test whether the treated surface resists corrosion better, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The process fires laser pulses into liquid so collapsing bubbles hammer the metal surface, hardening it without contact. The team varied laser energy and focus, and tried the treatment with and without a thin aluminium shield layer laid over the iron.

The shield clearly helped, shielding the surface from laser burn and bubble erosion, and corrosion resistance improved as laser energy rose — up to a point, after which it fell away again. Focus distance mattered less. For foundries, the recipe suggests a cheap surface upgrade for iron parts that must survive wet, corrosive work.
plos-pone-0353946:
Isabel Cervantes-Camacho and five colleagues reconstruct the life history of lane snapper in the Gulf waters off southern Mexico, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The fish supports busy commercial and recreational catches off Yucatan, yet basic facts like lifespan and natural death rates were missing. From more than a thousand landed fish, the team aged several hundred by counting yearly rings in their ear stones.

Ages ran from youngsters under a year to sixteen years in females. Comparing several growth curves with Bayesian methods, the classic von Bertalanffy model fit both sexes best. Solid age and growth numbers let managers set catch rules that a fishery can sustain instead of guessing.
plos-pone-0354146:
Kerle-Malcharek and colleagues, in a 2026 study, show how animal tracking tags can save battery by thinking before they transmit. Tags that ride on wild animals collect rich movement data, and newer tags send it by WiFi, which drains power fast. Sending everything shortens the tag's working life.

Their fix puts a tiny decision tree, a simple machine learning model, on the tag itself. The tree reads sensor data and recognizes a chosen behavior, such as feeding or resting. The tag then sends only data tied to moments that matter and holds back the rest. On a current commercial tag, this filtering cut energy use for transmission by a clear margin in realistic tests. Gyroscope data, usually processed later on a computer, proved especially useful on the tag. The team shares a full pipeline, from training data to tag-ready software, so other animal researchers can copy the trick.
plos-pone-0354246:
Wei Zhang and Liangli Chen published this 2026 mathematics paper on solving two-dimensional equations that mix integrals and derivatives, a class arising in physics and engineering. Their method builds solutions from barycentric rational interpolation, a scheme prized for being steady and exact, paired with a precise counting rule.

They derived the full solution procedure, proved error bounds and that it settles, and tested the method on worked examples. Results matched the theory, confirming it was highly exact for both straight-line and nonlinear versions of these equations. Zhang and Chen aim the method at problems where older solvers lose precision.
plos-pone-0354346:
Adelle Holder, Henry DeBruin, and Jesse Sestito tackle a bottleneck in computer-aided design in this 2026 PLOS ONE methods paper. Bayesian optimisation searches for good designs by testing one candidate at a time, which wastes time when many tests could run in parallel. Existing parallel versions are usually built from scratch, ignoring a large library of proven one-at-a-time methods.

Their fix wraps any compatible sequential method in a penalty scheme that steers each batch of tests apart, so the batch covers fresh ground instead of repeating itself. Two converted methods matched established parallel tools on solution quality and beat them on real time. Designers gain a shortcut: upgrade familiar methods rather than rebuild them.
plos-pone-0355046:
Anh Dang Thuc Phan and five colleagues published this 2026 study of herbal medicine use among patients with long-term diseases in Vietnam. More than six hundred patients at two large hospitals described which herbal products they took and whether they told their doctors. The team then checked flagged herb and drug combinations against several interaction databases.

Many patients never disclosed their herbal use, and the databases often disagreed about the same combinations, leaving regional plants poorly covered. Phan calls for routine questions about herbs during care, better clinician training, and safety tools that include local botanical knowledge.
plos-pone-0355546:
Rebecca Gordon and co-authors use an adoption study to separate how parental stress reaches children through birth ties, womb environment, and daily rearing. Stress in parents can echo in children's self-control, but the pathway matters for any remedy. Their 2026 study follows families in a long-running adoption cohort where children were placed near birth.

The design links birth mothers' life stress to teenagers' effortful control through the children's daily cortisol rhythm, a stress-hormone pattern. It then asks whether adoptive mothers' or fathers' own stressful events strengthen or soften that chain. Because birth and rearing parents differ, genetic and prenatal routes can be told apart from household ones. The authors frame the work as a map for targeted family support.
plos-pone-0355646:
Yaxiang Gong, Jiafu Wen, and Wenqi Liu test in 2026 a new way to make a plant compound called puerarin dissolve better in water. Poor dissolving limits how well the compound can be taken by mouth. Their method melts the material while blasting it with sound, then checks the result with light tests and several tools that probe crystal shape and heat behaviour.

Treated puerarin dissolved more and faster, with smaller grains that tended to clump. Its crystal form changed to a water holding form, and part of it lost ordered structure altogether. The authors link the gain to those two changes and suggest the method could improve oral products.
plos-pone-0355846:
Debrup Ghosh and colleagues collected soils from twenty sites across the Indo-Gangetic Plain in India and watched how iron escapes from them over time under different moisture levels. Iron matters because crops there often go short of it even in iron-rich ground, since it locks into minerals that roots cannot use. Their 2026 incubation study paired release measurements with chemical models of iron's forms.

Wetter soil and longer incubation both changed how much iron came free. Acidic conditions and salt content held iron back, while clay-rich soil that holds more water released more. The findings help explain why iron fertilizer often disappoints in these soils and suggest moisture management as part of the fix for iron-hungry crops.
plos-pone-0355946:
Saadi M Saleh and a multinational team survey more than six thousand doctors across twelve Middle East and North African countries about chest pain. Doctors carry heavy stress and heart risk themselves, yet no large regional study had measured their own symptoms. A standard angina questionnaire sorted pain into definite and possible categories, and validated scales screened for anxiety and panic alongside work and health habits.

About one in eight doctors met the bar for definite angina-type pain, and nearly half reported possible angina-type pain, strikingly high for a working population. Panic disorder was the single strongest predictor, ahead of physical illness, lost sleep, anxiety, obesity, and female sex, and every kind of nicotine use added risk. Saleh and colleagues call physician chest pain a workforce warning, not just a personal one.
plos-pone-0356046:
The PLOS One Editors issued a retraction notice in 2026 for an article on AptaFluorescence, a fluorescent imaging protocol using aptamers, short DNA strands that bind targets, to visualize biomolecules. After publication, concerns were raised about figures two through four and the reliability of the reported fluorescence results.

Listed problems include partly overlapping figure panels, signal strengths that clash with raw image files, and missing exposure times, which makes signal comparisons hard to judge. The counts also rested on technical rather than biological repeats, with few images and cell counts varying widely. The first author admitted errors in preparing two figures and supplied a corrected one, while the editors record the concerns that led to retraction.
plos-pone-0356146:
Qin Yu and Tao Mai build a translation system aimed at the hardest words in English news. The targets are culturally loaded terms, metaphors, and institutional names. Such items lack support in training data. Such long-tail items drift in meaning or lose their cultural charge in standard machine translation. Their design first squeezes text into a sparse code. The code spotlights cultural elements. Then it rebuilds the translation step by step. A diffusion process does the rebuilding, guided by gates and a cultural knowledge base.

On long news sentences, the system beat three mainstream rivals on two standard quality scores. On unseen vocabulary, it kept accuracy and recall well above the baselines. So the authors report. Yu and Mai present the hybrid as a route to translations that carry culture, not just words.
plos-pone-0356246:
Ahmad Adawy and seven colleagues trace how a marker on white blood cells changes after liver surgery in mice, in this 2026 study. Neutrophils, the first-responder immune cells, can either injure the liver or help it regrow after part is removed. The team combined gene-activity data with direct cell measurement in mouse livers after seventy percent of the organ was removed. They focused on a surface protein called Cd14, which earlier screens had flagged in activated liver neutrophils.

Both the gene and the protein surged in liver neutrophils, peaking a day after surgery. The protein was linked to two signaling pathways known to drive liver cell division, which led the authors to identify it as a badge of a pro-regeneration neutrophil type. They propose Cd14 as a possible therapeutic target for boosting liver regrowth after surgery, while noting the finding comes from mouse work.
plos-pone-0356546:
Dominic Dankwah Agyei and colleagues surveyed 237 researchers in Ghana about diamond open access, the publishing model where neither readers nor authors pay. Their 2026 cross-sectional study asked what researchers know about the model, where they learned it, and how they judge its benefits, then looked for patterns by age, rank, institution, and qualifications.

Awareness was thin. Two thirds had never heard of diamond open access, over half had never published open access at all, and few could identify the standard open license. Most who knew the model heard of it from colleagues, not institutions. Knowledge rose with seniority and qualifications. The authors call on Ghanaian universities to teach open publishing properly and fund it, rather than leaving equity in publishing to chance.
plos-pone-0356646:
Rabina Baraili and co-authors brew silver nanoparticles using leaf and root extracts of a spiny shrub, aiming for a greener route to a useful material. Chemical recipes for such particles often leave harsh residues, while plant extracts can both form and coat them. The team confirmed particle formation by color change and light readings, then sized and mapped the particles with several instruments.

Leaf-made and root-made particles were both tiny and round, coated by plant compounds that kept them stable. Leaf particles fought oxidation best in a standard test, and both kinds blocked harmful bacteria strongly. A shrimp test showed the leaf version was also the more toxic of the two. Baraili and colleagues say the green recipe works, while dosing care will decide safe uses.
plos-pone-0356746:
Valia Pernidaki and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on fathers' mental health when a preterm birth threatens or happens. Mothers' distress in that situation is well documented; fathers are an afterthought. Just over one hundred men completed depression and anxiety scales during pregnancy and six weeks after the birth. They were sorted into a term-birth group and two risk groups: threatened preterm birth ending at term, and threatened ending early.

During pregnancy, fathers whose babies did arrive early carried clearly higher depression and anxiety than controls, while the threatened-but-term group showed weak signs of depression. Both risk groups had more men crossing the elevated-depression threshold than controls did. After birth, depression gaps closed, but anxiety stayed higher in the actual preterm group, and the threatened-but-term fathers sat in between. A threatened preterm birth alone, they conclude, marks a father for support.
plos-pone-0357046:
Qian Wen and co-authors design fast-settling equation systems for solving a broad class of balance problems in math, called mixed equilibrium problems. Such problems model fair points where competing effects cancel, from traffic to markets. Their systems are built to reach solutions fast. One reaches the answer within a finite time. The other reaches it within a time the user fixes in advance. Both hold no matter where the system starts, under stated conditions on the problem's shape.

The authors prove existence and uniqueness of the answer, show the underlying system is stable, and turn it into a step-by-step algorithm with steady convergence. Computer tests found the preset-time version fastest of the variants. An application to recovering sparse signals showed the method working outside pure theory. The paper is fully mathematical, aimed at optimization specialists.
plos-pone-0357146:
Senad Kolar and coauthors published a 2026 pilot study in PLOS ONE on whether autism evaluations by video still work when the connection is bad. Telehealth widens access to diagnosis, but a freezing screen could hide the fleeting behaviors assessors must catch. Using a fiber-optic test setup, the team created four freeze patterns by throttling the signal, then had blinded psychologists score children's videos under each degraded condition.

Scoring eroded gradually rather than collapsing. Past clear technical thresholds, freezes grew frequent. The items most at risk were the time-sensitive ones. Spontaneous joint attention, blending gaze with behavior, and echoed or unusual language were several times more likely to be marked unscorable. Yet overall scores stayed stable, no single item failed significance after correction, and raters agreed strongly under mild conditions. Video assessment is supported as a first-line option while connections stay above the identified thresholds, preferring wired links.
plos-pone-0357346:
Titilayo T Tajudeen led a team of four authors mapping retreating coastal forests, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Coastal forests are shrinking under pressure from storms, sea level rise, and land clearing. Satellites can track that retreat, but reading their images by hand is slow. The team applied convolutional neural networks to different kinds of satellite imagery.

Tajudeen's AI-generated maps give conservationists the retreat's true extent, free from guesswork. Comparing imagery types shows which source gives the most reliable map for the least cost. Coastal forests protect shorelines and store carbon, so their loss is a double blow. Timely maps let agencies target planting and protection where retreat is fastest, and prove losses that ground surveys would miss.
plos-pone-0357446:
Patrick Addo-Fordjour leads a national study of forest loss in Ghana covering the years from the mid twenty tens to the mid twenty twenties. Published in 2026, the work uses satellite images to map land cover across the whole country rather than a few reserves. That wider view matters because past estimates for Ghana varied a lot and left policy makers unsure of the scale of loss.

Ghana lost a large stretch of forest over the decade, and yearly loss sped up in the second half of the period. Farm growth caused most of the clearing, while mining caused a smaller share but grew fastest of all land uses. Addo-Fordjour and colleagues say the pattern threatens carbon storage and needs direct land-use action.
plos-pone-0358046:
Cleofé Peña-Gómez, Bernat Sunyer-Grau, and Marc Argilés studied how light color affects the brain, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Light does more than let us see; different wavelengths reach brain systems that control eye movement and attention. The team measured how exposure to different wavelengths changes activity in those cortical areas.

Peña-Gómez and her colleagues found wavelength-specific effects on the systems that aim the eyes and focus attention. That matters for lighting design in schools and offices, and for screen habits that fill evenings with blue-rich light. It also informs therapies that use light to shift alertness. The study adds brain-level evidence to a field often guided by comfort alone.
plos-pone-0358246:
Alejandro Leyva and M Khalid Khan Niazi subtyped pancreatic cancer patient by patient, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. Pancreatic cancer needs finer subtypes if treatment is to be matched to each tumor. The pair integrated three data layers for each patient: RNA expression, methylation-based clues to replication timing, and the tumor's appearance under the microscope.

Leyva's multi-layer integration sorts tumors more precisely than any single data type could. Patient-specific subtyping matters because two tumors with the same name can behave very differently. Better sorting can guide trials, pairing each subtype with drugs aimed at its biology. Pancreatic cancer's poor outcomes make every gain in precision count, and integration methods like this are a plausible route.
plos-pone-0358546:
Margaret Wingerd and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about a gut parasite in pet cats. Giardia duodenalis infects domestic cats across the United States and Canada. The authors measure its prevalence and judge its zoonotic potential, the chance of it passing to people.

A parasite shared between cats and humans matters for households, especially where children or people with weak immunity live with pets. Prevalence figures tell veterinarians how often to expect this infection and test for it. Public health readers also gain from knowing how much of the human risk from Giardia plausibly comes through cats.
plos-pone-0358646:
Jingcong Li and three colleagues improve the neural networks that solve physics equations by teaching them where to concentrate, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Physics informed networks learn a solution while respecting the governing equation at sampled points, but they spread effort evenly and under learn the hard regions. Their system closes a feedback loop. The equation's own error at each point estimates how difficult that point is. That estimate stretches the physical constraint around hard points. It also shifts training weight toward them.

Tested across five network designs on three one dimensional problems, the method took the lowest error on every benchmark. It cut the runner up method's aggregate error by roughly a fifth to three fifths, depending on the problem. Higher dimensional and fluid test cases followed. The principle is portable: a solver that notices its own confusion can spend its budget where confusion lives.
plos-pone-0358746: Monfort Sanchez and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a low-cost way to check cell barriers. Labs often grow cells in a flat sheet to mimic the linings of the gut or lungs. The team tested cheap, clinic-approved glowing dyes as a way to judge whether those sheets stay sealed. A cheap, safe check could widen barrier testing in labs with small budgets.
plos-pone-0359346:
Maxime Colomb and Julien Perret published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It describes systematic modelling of building land use at large scale, enriched with historical detail. The work fuses massive and heterogeneous datasets, records from many sources that were never designed to fit together.

Land use histories tell planners how neighborhoods grew and which uses persisted or vanished. Building that record by hand for a whole city is impossible, so an automated, systematic model is the only route. Urban historians and planning offices are the readers who gain a past-aware map of building use from this fusion work.
plos-pone-0359546: Arteaga-Jordá and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE plan for a review on nurses and workplace change. The planned review will map how planned communication can strengthen nurses' sense of professional identity. That identity, in turn, is meant to drive cultural change inside health organizations. The protocol follows the JBI approach for scoping reviews. Clear plans help later readers trust the review's map.
plos-pone-0359646:
Jolinda Pollock and co-authors characterized in 2026 a strain of Escherichia coli bacteria taken from dairy bred calves that had fallen ill. The strain belongs to the O78 group and resembles types known for causing disease in poultry. The calves showed an atypical form of colisepticaemia, a blood infection by E. coli that usually follows a more familiar pattern.

The team describes the strain's traits in detail, including the fact that it resists multiple antibiotics. A poultry-like strain turning up in calves raises questions about how such bacteria move between animal species and through farm environments. Multidrug resistance in farm animals also matters beyond the farm, since resistance can travel through food chains and waste into wider circulation.
plos-pone-0359846: Sangsiwarit and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE lab study on blood disease and infection risk. They took neutrophils, a front-line white blood cell, from people with beta-thalassemia. Outside the body, they exposed those cells to Pythium insidiosum, a water mold that can cause severe illness. They then checked how the cells' working behavior changed. The results bear on why these patients may fight this infection poorly.
plos-pone-0359946:
Gideon Nwankwo and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on maternal healthcare in Nigeria. It studies what decides whether women keep using maternal care steadily, from pregnancy through delivery and beyond. The evidence comes from Nigeria's 2024 Demographic and Health Survey.

Many women start antenatal care but drop out before skilled delivery, breaking the continuum where risk peaks. National survey evidence shows which social and economic factors hold women in care or push them out. Nigerian health planners designing maternal programs are the readers who can act on those determinants.
pmc-13196946:
Francesco Pichi and colleagues published a 2026 eye imaging study in multiple sclerosis. Multiple sclerosis is a long-term disease where the immune system harms nerves in the brain and cord. The retina, at the back of the eye, can be scanned without surgery and may mirror brain change.

The team scanned patients and healthy controls with two light-based eye methods. They counted immune-like cells at the retina surface and measured nerve layer thickness. Patients with greater disability had more of those cells. Cell size tracked the load of brain lesions on scans. A nerve layer in the eye was thinner in patients than in controls. Eye scans may help track disease burden.
pmc-13198546:
Mahmoud E Alsobky and colleagues built a 2026 test for smell-linked markers in nasal fluid after COVID-19. Loss of smell can linger after infection. Two messenger chemicals drive smell signaling, and their levels may track the damage, so a fast joint test for both could help clinics.

Their method uses a sugar-ring additive to boost glow signals from both chemicals at once. Scanning tricks then split the overlapping signals for clean reads. The test proved sensitive across a wide range, with very low detection limits. Nasal levels of both markers ran far lower in patients with smell loss than in healthy people. Accuracy scores for spotting patients were near perfect in this sample.
pmc-13198746: Junmei Fan and colleagues are authors of a study corrected in a 2026 note in BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth. The study tested whether uterine artery Doppler measures, an ultrasound check of womb blood flow, predict pregnancy success from a first frozen embryo transfer. After publication, the authors found an error in Figure 3. The notice supplies the correct figure, describing two prediction models, and states that the original article has been corrected.
pmc-13198946:
Sabrina G Clemens and colleagues report a 2026 brain scan study that may forecast dementia years ahead. Older brains often work harder on hard tasks, read as compensation for fading systems. Whether that extra effort predicts future decline was untested over time, so the team followed healthy adults for years.

One hundred nine cognitively normal adults did a word-color conflict task during brain scans. They also got amyloid scans and gene tests at the start. Average follow-up ran near seven years, and fifteen people reached clinical impairment. Those who later declined had shown greater brain activity at the start, despite equal task scores and test results. Extra effort may mark early disease, not strength.
pmc-13201346:
Plastic waste breaks down into tiny particles whose effects on living tissue are still unclear, and a 2026 virtual study by Emiliano Perez-Sanchez tests one possible harm. The research article models oligomers of polyhydroxyalkanoates, a biodegradable polymer family, as stand-ins for nanoplastics and studies their ability to transfer electrons.

Using density functional theory calculations, the authors mapped the electron donor and acceptor behavior of 21 oligomers. Every one ranked as a poor electron donor and acceptor, regardless of size, which suggests these particles cannot drive the electron transfer behind oxidative stress. Adding the compound phloretin, used in wrapping, did raise that transfer capacity.
pmc-13201946:
A young man's immune system spiraled into uncontrolled inflammation for no found reason, and a 2026 case report authored by Zofia Serafinowicz tells the forty-day intensive care fight that followed. The article presents a rare hyperinflammatory syndrome of unknown cause, complicated by shock, severe clotting failure, brain bleeding, and a burst spleen.

The 24-year-old arrived with an enlarged spleen, low blood counts, and very high inflammatory markers, and extensive testing found no trigger. Doctors suspected an overlap of sepsis and hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis and treated both aggressively, yet surgery was still needed for the spleen and brain. A year later he still needed neurological rehabilitation and orthopedic care.
pmc-13202446:
A plant compound from turmeric relatives protects heart muscle in a 2026 study by Jiaxiang Liao, focused on a form of cell death called ferroptosis. The research article tests germacrone in mice with drug-induced heart attacks and in injured heart cells grown in the laboratory.

Germacrone given daily for a week reduced heart injury, improved cardiac function, and limited tissue damage in the mouse model. It also blocked ferroptosis by raising protective proteins along the Nrf2 and GPX4 pathway in treated tissue. When the team added an Nrf2 blocker, the protection disappeared, confirming the pathway's central role and nominating it as a treatment target.
pmc-13202746:
Life a year after heart surgery varies widely, and a 2026 prospective study headed by Max Briefs identifies what predicts a poorer recovery. The research article follows 812 patients at a high-volume German heart center through an anesthesiology quality registry, measuring health-related quality of life with a standard questionnaire.

A subgroup of 190 patients also received an intensive frailty and delirium management pathway with extended screening and supervision. Physical outcome scores were independently lower for women, older and heavier patients, and those with anemia, smoking history, or physical frailty before surgery. Kidney injury after surgery and slow removal from ventilation also predicted worse scores, while cognitive scores followed a different pattern.
pmc-13237346:
Naeem builds a heart-reading model designed to be fair between patient groups from the start. Computer reading of the twelve-lead ECG now matches strong diagnostic accuracy. Yet most systems perform unevenly between men and women, a gap that can quietly steer care in clinics that trust the output.

Most fairness fixes are applied after training and tend to cost accuracy. This model instead builds demographic awareness into a temporal graph attention network, which follows both the heartbeat's timing and links between leads. The aim is a reader that keeps its accuracy while treating groups evenly, showing that equity in medical AI is a design choice, not an afterthought.
pmc-13241446:
González-Cabrero's team at Aveiro borrowed a crystal-growth law to chart tau spread after head injury. Repeated blows seed the tau tangles of chronic traumatic encephalopathy by unknown means. Their Avrami-style model treats clumps as seeding, then growing over time. Mouse tau-disease data set the timing.

Strain maps from mock impacts pinpointed where change should run fastest. High-strain regions indeed seeded tau damage sooner in the model. The output flags strain-prone brain areas for closer study. The authors present a numbers bridge from impact physics to disease course. It links hit strength to later harm.
pmc-13242346:
Wegner and colleagues in Lübeck CT-scanned vascular introducer sheaths to check whether labels match reality. Eighteen sheath types from four major makers were measured non-destructively. Nominal sizes spanned five to seven French and three standard lengths. Effective diameters were fitted at the hub, middle, and tip.

Non-braided shafts ran wider than specified, by up to about eight percent. Every aperture, though, measured noticeably narrower than the manufacturer's figure. Braided tips shrank furthest, roughly eleven percent below catalog specification. Wegner warns that tight apertures may force operators to choose larger sheaths.
pmc-13245546:
Tadeo and colleagues propose a new kind of reward for clinical trial volunteers in this 2026 Journal of Medical Internet Research article.
