Trials often fail to recruit or keep enough participants, and cash payments alone do not always sustain engagement. The authors suggest giving each volunteer a unique digital image, created for them and recorded as a nonfungible token.

In their example, volunteers train with a personalized digital therapy program, and their individual learning path is turned into digital artwork given at the trial's end. The authors argue that ownership, personalization, and visible recognition could motivate people more deeply than money alone. They call for real studies testing whether such meaningful incentives improve retention.
pmc-13245646:
Day and co-authors report a missed-diagnosis case in this 2026 gastrointestinal case report. Their patient, a sixty-seven-year-old man receiving intermittent hemodialysis, suffered long-running abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and loss of appetite that standard treatment could not fix. Tests showed raised lactate and a low level of thiamine, also called vitamin B1.

Dialysis can wash thiamine out of the body, and its deficiency, beriberi, is usually linked to malnutrition or alcohol use and known for heart and nerve damage. This patient's gut form of the disease improved rapidly once doctors gave intravenous thiamine, and his lactate settled. The authors urge dialysis teams to consider the vitamin in stubborn gut cases.
pmc-13245746:
Nogales Crespo and co-authors mapped the policy landscape for HIV across Europe in this 2026 PLOS One study. Laws and rules can help or hinder prevention, testing, treatment, and care for the key populations most at risk. The team searched for relevant policies in fifteen countries and six subregions, judging them against fifty-seven policy areas drawn from international frameworks, and reviewed studies on how the policies work in practice.

They catalogued over four hundred policies and dozens of studies. Most countries covered forty or more policy areas, but coverage varied widely and, in many places, some at-risk groups were served far less equitably than others. The authors recommend cross-country learning and removing structural barriers to reach the UNAIDS targets.
pmc-13246546:
Lanman and co-authors surveyed brain-tumor specialists on how they treat IDH-mutant glioma, in this 2026 Journal of Neuro-Oncology study. Care for these tumors shifted quickly after United States regulators approved vorasidenib, a drug targeting the mutant IDH enzyme, in 2024, and many treatment choices still lack firm evidence. The team sent case-based scenarios to oncologists and neurosurgeons who manage these patients.

One hundred fifty-three clinicians answered. They agreed strongly on half the scenarios but split on the rest. Specialty predicted choices: radiation oncologists favored radiation-based treatment and were cooler on the new drug, while neuro-oncologists knew it best. The authors say the variation shows where shared evidence and cross-specialty discussion are most needed.
pmc-13247246:
Labena, Moghazy, and Abdelhamid turned fruit waste into dye-cleaning films in this 2026 Scientific Reports study. Powdered banana and pomegranate waste can absorb synthetic dyes from wastewater, but fine powders are hard to fish back out of treated water. The team ground the wastes and embedded them, at a tenth of the mix, into polyvinyl chloride films that can simply be lifted out afterward.

The composite films came out highly porous, swelling to nearly five times their dry weight in water, with very large internal surface areas, especially the banana version. Tuned through systematic experiments, they removed methylene blue dye efficiently from test water. The authors present the films as a cheap, recoverable, and greener cleanup material for dye-polluted wastewater.
pmc-13247646:
Kim, Han, and Hwang evaluated extra counseling for suicide attempters in financial hardship, in this 2026 Journal of Korean Medical Science study. Drawn from a Korean emergency-room follow-up service, ninety-three people who had attempted suicide entered the program during or after the COVID-19 period, and forty-nine completed it. Tailored support was associated with reduced suicidal ideation, particularly among vulnerable participants during the pandemic period. Hopelessness emerged as the key mechanism to address: those starting more hopeless improved differently than expected, sharpening the target. The authors call for larger randomized trials of context-sensitive, economically aware aftercare.
pmc-13248746:
Blaschke and a large materials team widened the pores of a metal-organic framework, reported in 2026. These crystal sponges, called MOFs, usually have tiny pores that shut out big catalyst molecules. Into those spaces they anchored a bulky rhenium complex used for light-driven chemistry. Nearly perfect crystals refused the guest, while the defect-rich ones took it up evenly and in adjustable amounts. The loaded material turned carbon dioxide mainly into carbon monoxide under light. pmc-13249046:
Huang and a large team used genetics to test whether chronic back pain raises dementia risk, reported in 2026. Ordinary studies cannot easily separate cause from coincidence, so the authors applied Mendelian randomization, which uses inherited gene variants as natural experiments. Data came from two population sources, and they also checked whether brain structure changes carried the effect.

Genetic liability to chronic back pain pointed toward higher Alzheimer's disease risk, roughly doubling the odds in the main estimate. No link appeared for other dementia types, and Alzheimer's genes did not predict back pain back. Nine brain structures shifted with back pain but did not explain the link. The authors urge caution, since the estimate is imprecise.
pmc-13249446:
Essers and a European team measured how daily temperature moves teenagers' activity, in a 2026 study. They combined two cohorts, more than thirteen hundred Dutch adolescents and about five hundred Spanish ones, each wearing wrist accelerometers for up to nine days. Fine-grained weather modeling estimated the temperature at each home address for the same days.

Warmer days brought more light and moderate activity in both countries, on the order of five to sixteen extra minutes at the warm extreme. Vigorous exercise did not budge with temperature. The authors suggest activity programs and school schedules should reckon with weather, a point that grows sharper as summers heat up under climate change.
pmc-13250246:
Ge, Zhao, and Zhang hunt for the molecular switches behind active generalized vitiligo, an autoimmune disease that destroys skin pigment cells. Their 2026 ImmunoTargets and Therapy paper combines protein and whole-transcriptome readings from blood samples. Three patients and three healthy volunteers supplied the discovery samples, with checks in a separate group.

The team found changed levels of many messenger, long non-coding, and circular RNAs, plus a small set of altered proteins. Network analysis highlighted ten hub genes tied to inflammation signals. Validation tests confirmed higher levels of two inflammatory cytokines, IL-8 and TNF-alpha, in patients. The authors propose a competing RNA network that may drive the inflammation and offer future treatment targets.
pmc-13252746:
Xuye Kang, Jianying Li, and Huipan Wu survey teen sleep across China in this 2026 study. Sleep quality is sliding among Chinese adolescents, and the team set out to measure how it splits by sex and by city versus countryside.

Data covered 5,713 students aged 13 to 18, averaging about 15 years old. A standard sleep questionnaire found a third sleeping poorly. Rural teens fared worse than urban ones, at about 36 versus lower urban rates, and girls worse than boys, at about 38 percent. Fitness and mental health protected sleep, while higher body weight, sitting time, and screen time hurt it. Place and sex changed the strength of those links.
pmc-13254046:
Daniela Nürnberg and Mareike Altgassen study future memory in autistic adults in a 2026 paper. Prospective memory means remembering to do a planned action later, like buying bread when passing a bakery. Thirty autistic and 30 non-autistic adults, matched for age, gender, and non-verbal skills, did an event-based memory task and three thinking tasks.

Non-autistic adults did better on the memory task overall. In both groups, stronger executive functions, the mind's planning and control skills, tied to better memory scores, and planning task time predicted performance. The authors suggest supports such as planning training, agendas, and reminder tools.
pmc-13255346:
Amr A. Othman and a large team describe tuberous sclerosis in Egyptian patients in a 2026 case series. Tuberous sclerosis complex is a multi-organ disease caused by faults in the TSC1 or TSC2 genes, and Egyptian genetic data are scarce. The team studied 23 patients from 20 unrelated families at two centers between 2022 and 2025, using exams, imaging, and full gene sequencing.

Pale skin patches appeared in all patients, brain tubers in 96 percent, and seizures in 87 percent. Eighteen distinct gene variants were found, 16 in TSC2 and two in TSC1, and nine were new. Most variants appeared in just one family each.
pmc-13256046:
Wang and a large team picked apart the shared genetics of sleep traits and epilepsy using genome-wide association data from European cohorts. Standard linkage and local correlation scans probed overlap between epilepsy and sleep length or insomnia. Cross-trait meta-analysis and gene-activity scans then hunted for genes shaping both sides of the link.

The analyses found modest but solid global and local genetic links, and flagged shared candidate genes including SPAG7, VRK2, and a long non-coding RNA, all tied to neuroimmune signaling. Mendelian randomization hinted that epilepsy risk nudges people toward shorter sleep, not the reverse, though the effect was small. The authors stress that lab tests must come before any treatment claims.
pmc-13256146:
Shiyu Hu and co-authors wrote a 2026 journal article on the world burden of COPD, a long-term lung disease that limits airflow. They used Global Burden of Disease 2021 data to count deaths and DALYs, meaning years of healthy life lost. Their focus was how much of that burden came from smoking and from secondhand smoke between 2019 and 2021, during COVID-19.

In 2021 there were about 213 million people living with COPD and 3.7 million deaths, both up from 2019. Smoking caused about 1,334,961 of those deaths, and secondhand smoke caused 266,125 more. The authors say COVID-19 did not seem to change the overall trend, but they call for continued monitoring and stronger action on tobacco use.
pmc-13261146:
Ngo Cheung presents a 2026 genetic study of obsessive-compulsive disorder and hoarding. The two often occur together but differ in onset, course, and treatment response. The study set diagnosis-based OCD liability against hoarding-symptom risk, not measured expression in patients.

The team combined large genome-wide data with brain gene-activity panels across six brain regions. OCD liability showed positive enrichment for intrinsic apoptosis, the cell self-destruct pathway, with a Z score of +5.707 in the analysis. It also showed positive complement signal, with a Z score of +4.932 in the analysis, and a negative synapse-pruning profile, with a Z score of −4.802 in the same analysis. Hoarding risk showed a more positive cell-aging profile than OCD. Signals involving NAD and sirtuins skewed toward hoarding but were early findings. The author calls the signatures tentative. They need checking with further genetic and functional studies.
pmc-13262446:
Akram S Al-Mughalles and co-authors review tiny pores in liver blood vessel cells in a 2026 journal article. The cells line the liver's small blood channels and carry openings called fenestrations that let fats and other materials pass. In fatty liver disease linked to metabolism, these pores are lost early, a change called capillarization.

Loss of the pores upsets the balance of signals that keep them open, the review argues, and drives disease toward its inflamed, more severe form. The authors map the signal web that controls the pores and weigh treatments meant to restore them. They propose combined drug approaches and cell-specific markers to guide care that is matched to each patient.
pmc-13262546:
Jia Guo and co-authors rank exercise styles by how well they rescue sleep in sedentary adults with insomnia. Thirty-one randomized trials and over fourteen hundred participants feed their 2026 network meta-analysis. Aerobic work, weights, interval sprints, and mind-body practice all enter the comparison.

Exercise improved sleep scores substantially across the board. The largest gains clustered in adults aged forty-five to fifty-nine and in programs running up to sixteen weeks. Different measures, from falling-asleep time to total sleep, moved unevenly by modality. The authors present the ranking as a menu for prescribing movement instead of pills, matched to patient age and routine.
pmc-13262646:
David Ledingham and colleagues grade how ready digital tremor measures are for real clinical use. Essential tremor is the commonest movement disorder, yet trials still lean on shaky rating scales. Their 2026 scoping review proposes a five-tier readiness ladder, TRACE, and scores one hundred sixty-five studies against it.

Wearable motion sensors dominated the literature, trailed by digitized handwriting and camera methods. Almost every study stalled at the second tier, supervised clinical validity. Only one wrist-worn platform reached trial readiness, and none reached economic readiness. Home testing and patient-anchored change thresholds are the missing rungs, they conclude.
pmc-13263146:
Alexander Landry and colleagues assemble the largest single-cell portrait yet of meningioma, the commonest primary brain tumor. Over seven hundred tumors contributed some layer of data, from single-nucleus sequencing to spatial maps. Their 2026 study asks which cell states steer the tumor's neighborhood and course.

Immune myeloid cells changed character across molecular tumor groups and matured as they crossed from the dura into tumor tissue. Their partnerships with tumor cells matched distinct gene programs. Several non-tumor cell states sharpened outcome forecasts beyond molecular grouping alone. The atlas nominates microenvironment players as future therapeutic levers in a surgically managed disease.
pmc-13263246:
Damilola A Ibirogba and colleagues measure daily movement and heart-metabolic health in Sub-Saharan Africans living in the United Kingdom in a 2026 journal article. Wrist sensors tracked sleep, sitting, light activity, and stronger activity over full days. The cross-sectional study enrolled 75 adults, about half women, with a mean age of 40, between March 2024 and March 2025.

Median daily time was dominated by sitting, followed by sleep, light activity, and stronger activity. Stronger activity was the only movement type linked to fitness, and it tracked with a better cholesterol measure. Longer sleep tracked with lower body mass and waist size. Swapping 30 minutes of sitting for sleep or activity did not significantly change health markers, suggesting longer exposure may be needed.
pmc-13263946:
Sadia Hakeem led a 2026 journal article on seabuckthorn, a fruit shrub rich in vitamin C, iron, and zinc. The team studied plants from the Gilgit area of northern Pakistan, high in the hills. They hoped the fruit could help fight poor diets that lack key nutrients.

The team checked 70 plant samples and found wide ranges for iron, zinc, and vitamin C. Orange and yellow fruit from lower sites held the most iron. They also found 18 HrAKR genes, with 10 confirmed by lab tests and three active in many tissues. Plants from Sost, the highest site, paired high nutrients with strong gene activity, marking them as good breeding stock.
pmc-13264446:
Adeola Bamgboje-Ayodele led a 2026 study on note writing in a virtual hospital, where all care runs through digital tools. Staff must juggle many systems to record care. The team asked what goes wrong and what fixes fit this setting, using a task-technology fit lens.

The group ran focus talks and a design workshop with 28 nurses and doctors. Staff said data were hard to find and using many tools at once slowed them down, causing repeat work and less time with patients. They backed fixes like auto-made handover notes, less free text, and AI scribes. The authors say the virtual setting magnifies known note problems and needs team-based tools and simpler rules.
pmc-13264846:
Jing Guo and a large team present a 2026 protocol for a network meta-analysis of treatments for depression in children and young people. A network method can rank treatments by mixing direct and side-by-side indirect proof.

pmc-13264946:

Clinics increasingly message women through apps and platforms. The team mapped women's perceptions and experiences across the published evidence.

Six studies met the rules, covering WhatsApp, Facebook, Instagram, and WeChat. Problems included generic content, uneven moderator skill and speed, low digital literacy, data costs, privacy worries, and cultural pressures. pmc-13265846:
Yinpeng Hu and a large team wrote a 2026 photonics paper on tiny mechanical light switches built on silicon chips. Such switches steer light in optical networks and AI computing hardware. They say standard chip foundry steps can make it, aiding large photonic circuits.
pmc-13266046:
El Khansa Bourenane and colleagues wrote a 2026 study on lavender essential oil as a selective killer of the green citrus aphid. pmc-13267546:

The authors stress that scans alone cannot identify this cancer; tissue study with protein staining is the key step.
pmc-13269146:
Alison Hayes and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on quality of life among children in Australia from varied cultural and language backgrounds. pmc-13269446:

pmc-13269646:
Aurélie Buffetau and co-authors published a case report in 2026 about a 29-year-old woman admitted after her unborn baby died at 21 weeks of pregnancy. pmc-13269846:
Zishuo Huang and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on older women in China, their ties with adult children, and combined anxiety and depression symptoms. pmc-13270546:

pmc-13271746:

pmc-13272246:

pmc-13272946:

pmc-13273446:

pmc-13273846:

pmc-13275146:

The authors call for continued surveillance and targeted exposure reduction for vulnerable groups.
pmc-13275546:

pmc-13276346:

pmc-13277046:

Uses range from brain and clinical research to traditional Chinese medicine and rehabilitation, including studies of acupuncture. Limits remain, such as shallow reach into the brain. The authors map where the tool is strong today and what must improve for wider medical use.
pmc-13277446:
Jacob Cabrejas and Wesley Eilbert present a 2026 case report of a man with ear pain and blisters on his eardrum. He had no fever, and exam showed blood-filled blisters on his left tympanic membrane, the eardrum.

It mostly affects children and often follows a viral cold. Pain usually settles in one to two days, and hearing loss is temporary. Treatment uses a systemic antibiotic such as amoxicillin or azithromycin, the authors note.
pmc-13278246:

The standard was meant to benchmark image interpretation and reasoning, the authors say, not to re-prove each original diagnosis. They agree tissue testing remains definitive for pathological classification of such lesions.
pmc-13279246:
Aneesh Karir and Sydnee Tuckett write a 2026 commentary on a review of wrist bone breaks in children. The bone is the scaphoid, the most often broken wrist bone in youth. pmc-13280446:

pmc-13280746:

pmc-13281546:

pmc-13281746:

A positive view of birth control raised it more than threefold. Muslim women had lower odds of use than others. The authors urge outreach that teaches methods plainly and fights stigma. Services, they say, must be built so these women can truly reach them.
pmc-13282846:
Wenbiao Hu and Ting Gan wrote a 2026 commentary on how climate change is reshaping the risk of diseases jumping from animals to people. Recent hantavirus events supply their lesson. Hantaviruses, carried by rodents, were linked to cases on South American cruise routes. The World Health Organization rates the current event's public risk as low, but the authors treat it as a warning.

About sixty percent of emerging human infections come from animals, mostly wildlife. Climate shifts, habitat loss, farming expansion, and city growth alter host and vector behaviour, pathogen survival, and human exposure, opening new spillover paths. The cruise-linked event shows how eco-tourism and global travel can carry a local risk worldwide. Preparedness systems, the authors argue, still over-focus on single outbreaks instead of the ecological drivers.
pmc-13282946:
Frances Varty Bayar and Irem Daloglu Cetinkaya present a 2026 study of water transfers that supply Istanbul. The city relies on transfers from other basins as demand rises and climate stress grows. The work asks whether those transfers are efficient and fair for donor regions.

A case study covered transfers from Duzce, Tekirdag, and Kirklareli between 2000 and 2023. Two indexes compared moved water with renewable supply and tracked stress relief for people. Document review added views on governance and trade-offs. Results varied widely across the three systems. The Melen system is discussed in detail. Fair sharing with donor areas is the central concern.
pmc-13283446:
Flares after birth outnumber flares during pregnancy in axial spondyloarthritis, Maria Mouyis's UK survey respondents report in 2026. The condition causes spinal inflammation and stiffness in younger adults. Patient-reported data fill gaps that clinic records often miss for pregnancy care.

A total of 139 pregnancies from 89 women after diagnosis were analyzed. Most pregnancies were planned and conceived without medical aid within a year. Flares arose in a third of pregnancies and in over half after birth. The live birth rate was just over three quarters in the survey. Cesarean birth occurred in over half of pregnancies in the group. Many women said the illness affected early baby care.
pmc-13283946:
Patterning a bendable electronic material without chemical resist is the advance claimed by Kaimin Luo and colleagues in 2026. Their heated probe writes directly on a precursor film that converts into pentacene where touched. Pentacene channels then serve in flexible transistors for wearable devices.

By tuning probe pressure and scan speed, the team formed lines as narrow as 200 nanometers at the measured width. Finished channels were built into working field-effect transistors with clear electrical function. Avoiding resist, developer, and etchant removes common contamination routes in fabrication. The route offers a clean path toward denser organic circuits.
pmc-13284546:
Muhammad Evy Prastiyanto and co-authors report a 2026 study of hard-to-treat germs in newborn patients at a hospital in Semarang. Blood infection in newborns is a grave risk, and germs that resist drugs make care much harder. The team took 223 germ samples from sick newborns from January 2022 to December 2024 and tested which drugs still worked.

About two thirds of cases resisted many drugs in the lab tests reported here. Blood samples showed a very high share, and lung samples were higher still. Two common germs often resisted first-line drugs. The authors urge tighter drug use and stronger steps to stop spread in newborn care units.
pmc-13284746:
European Food Safety Authority authors present an annual assessment, published in 2026, of surveillance for the parasite Echinococcus multilocularis. Finland, Ireland, Northern Ireland, and Norway each run programs to keep dogs free of this infection under European Union rules. This marks the sixteenth yearly check of their sampling, target groups, and detection methods.

All four countries met the legal technical needs across the four review areas, the assessment reports. No positive samples were found in the twelve-month reporting period covered by this review. The finding supports the current control approach, while yearly checks remain in place to catch any change in parasite spread.
pmc-13285646:
Not all helper fungi serve an endangered orchid at every life stage, Shan Du and co-authors show in a 2026 germination study. Paphiopedilum malipoense cannot sprout without fungal partners, which snarls rescue work. Twelve fungal strains from wild roots all proved to be Tulasnella, backing strict partner loyalty.

Three strains carried seeds all the way to seedlings with the best sprouting rates of those on test here. One strain that failed at sprouting later more than doubled seedling bulk. Each strain shone at a different job, from food uptake to leaf green and stress defense. Strain MLP232 starred at both stages. The authors urge mixed fungal teams matched to each growth stage for orchid rescue.
pmc-13285746:
Yiheng Xie and colleagues review glucan-based nanoparticles for cancer immunotherapy in a 2026 survey of design and early results. Glucans are natural sugars that immune cells readily sense, which makes tiny glucan carriers attractive for precise delivery. The review asks how these carriers can wake the immune system against tumors that normally hide from it.

The carriers can haul tumor antigens, immune boosters, and other agents straight to the cells that present targets to the immune system. They also reshape soldier cells inside tumors, curb cells that damp the response, and stir both fast and lasting defenses. Pairings with checkpoint drugs, light-based therapy, and cell therapy show added force in early work. Safety over time, large-scale making, and clear rules still stand between lab promise and clinic use.
pmc-13286546:
Claudia Consentino and colleagues describe a posture study of orchestral musicians in a 2026 protocol article. Years of holding asymmetric instruments in fixed poses saddle players with pain that can end careers, yet hard numbers on orchestra posture remain scarce. The OPErA project will photograph 250 Italian professionals, pianists aside, with skin markers placed to measure tilt, rotation, and asymmetry with and without the instrument in hand.

Pain and disability questionnaires accompany the calibrated photos, covering arm, back, and neck function. Recruitment ran from 2023, and 240 of the target players had enrolled by February 2026. Analysis now under way will link posture faults to pain that limits performance, hunting instrument-specific patterns. The team expects the map to guide ergonomic fixes and prevention programs tuned to each section of the orchestra.
pmc-13287146:
Antonia Kleeberg and co-authors tested a simple blood-based score in 2026 as a predictor of death after a stroke caused by a blocked brain artery. The score, called EASIX, combines creatinine and lactate dehydrogenase values with platelet count and is meant to reflect stressed blood vessel linings.

Registry data came from Heidelberg, with 4,188 patients, and Vienna, with 2,273 patients for checking the result. Higher values tracked with higher mortality over short and long follow-up, even after other risk factors were considered. A threshold of 1.211 separated risk groups in the second cohort. The authors propose the score as an aid to early risk sorting.
pmc-13287546:
Meifang Wang, Ansheng Tan, and Fenglin Zhuo ran a split-face trial in 2026 for rosacea, a long-term facial flushing condition. Thirty-six patients had light pulse treatment on the whole face each month for three sessions. One random half of each face also got a salicylic acid peel at each visit.

Thirty-three patients finished. After three months the peel side showed larger drops in redness scores on two device measures than the light-only side. Doctor and patient ratings improved on both sides without a clear gap. Skin water rose and water loss fell on both sides. Side effects were mild and similar. The authors favour the pairing for stubborn redness.
pmc-13288546:
Ulluwis Hewawansa and colleagues test a sugarcane drink rich in polyphenols against gut damage from hard exercise in heat, in a 2026 double-blind placebo-controlled trial. Fourteen volunteers each ran for two hours at a set effort in 34.4 degree heat twice, drinking either the extract beverage or a matched placebo daily for fourteen days beforehand and taking gels during each run.

Core temperature and strain ran slightly higher on the extract trial, which complicates any simple benefit story. Still, a gut leak marker started lower after the extract fortnight, the rise in the inflammatory signal IL-8 was blunted, and gut symptoms, though common in both trials, averaged milder. The authors read the pattern as modest protection for the gut lining and immune response.
pmc-13289346:
Xuedi Ma and colleagues present a 2026 multilevel study on drug burden, adherence, and quality of life in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in China. This long-term lung disease needs care at many levels of the health system. Taking many drugs can wear people down, yet how burden, adherence, and daily well-being connect was unclear.

Clinics in a national pharmaceutical care network enrolled 2125 patients from September 2023 to September 2024. Burden was counted by drug number and a complexity index, while adherence and quality of life used standard scales. More drugs tied to worse quality of life both directly and through lower adherence in the models. The chain suggests simpler regimens could help people stick with care and feel better.
pmc-13290746:
Automated insulin pumps give preschoolers with type 1 diabetes better blood sugar control in real-world use, Risa Wolf and colleagues report in a 2026 multicenter analysis. Data on the youngest children have lagged behind older groups, so the team drew on the T1D Exchange collaborative across 37 pediatric sites.

The cohort held 3,521 children aged six and under. Just under half, 48%, used automated insulin delivery, and their average HbA1c was 7.9%, against 8.8% for children on multiple daily injections, a significant gap. Only a quarter of all children met the target below 7%, but automated users had nearly double the odds of getting there after adjustment. Wolf and colleagues say the findings support offering these systems to the youngest patients, not only to older children.
pmc-13290846:
Adjuvant capecitabine delays bile duct cancer's return without clearly extending life, Fabian Bartsch and colleagues report in a cohort study from 2026. Since the BILCAP trial, the drug became standard after surgery for intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, though that trial mixed several biliary cancers and left this one's benefit uncertain.

A German center compared resected patients from before and after the practice change, 2008 to 2017 versus 2018 to 2023, then matched 75 patients per era. Median survival was 29.1 months in the later group against 20.5 earlier, a gap that was not statistically significant. Recurrence, though, came significantly later after BILCAP-era care, and recurrence-free survival improved too. Bartsch and colleagues say longer follow-up may yet reveal whether delayed recurrence converts into longer lives.
pmc-13291046:
Alip Ghosh and colleagues profile a new intravenous drug called MP-04 in a 2026 preclinical study aimed at failing energy balance inside cells. MP-04 is a form of dihydronicotinamide riboside meant to restore NAD+, a molecule that drops in severe liver disease, sepsis, and acute kidney injury, where current care mostly supports rather than repairs.

Cell work in liver, T-cell, and kidney lines plus human blood cells showed fast, dose-linked rises in NAD+ after MP-04 exposure. Energy output, immune behavior, and drug handling were tracked in cells, rats, and a mouse model of drug-induced kidney injury, with formal safety studies in rats and dogs. Kidney protection in the injury model anchors the claim that restoring NAD+ could defend organs during severe illness.
pmc-13291146:
Yan Huang leads a 2026 study on judging liver scarring in autoimmune hepatitis. A stiffness scan often helps grade scarring. But active inflammation can stiffen the liver too. That mix-up can mislead doctors who rely on one scan value.

Records came from 86 patients who had both a biopsy and a stiffness scan. Biopsy set the true scarring stage. Patients were split by how strong their inflammation was. The scan worked far better in the mild group than in the severe group. A correction model built from these data improved accuracy. Sorting patients by inflammation first should make scan results safer to trust.
pmc-13291246:
Newborn screening in the Emirates is counted by Khadija Shafique and colleagues in a 2026 review of records. Screening spots hidden gene, hormone, and body chemistry faults early. Early care can cut harm and death in babies. The team asked how common each fault is.

Data came from a national reference lab for 2021 to 2023. Samples spanned 20 hospitals and labs in four emirates. Of 29,290 babies screened, about one in fourteen tested positive. A lack of one enzyme, G6PD, was by far most common. Cystic fibrosis came next in rate. Carriers of blood gene faults formed a large group too.
pmc-13292046:
Yangyang Zhang and co-authors map a 2026 study of an immune checkpoint called TIM3 inside the prostate cancer environment. Prostate tumors answer immunotherapy poorly, so the team mined single-cell data from primary, metastatic hormone-sensitive, and castration-resistant disease. They combined gene expression, regulon analysis, and cell-communication modeling, then tested leads in lab-grown macrophages.

A regulator named PRDM1 emerged as the switch driving that program, confirmed by binding assays and reporter tests. Galectin-9 signaling through TIM3 pushed macrophages toward a suppressive M2-like state, and blocking TIM3 weakened that push. The authors propose myeloid TIM3 as a drug target for reprogramming prostate tumors.
pmc-13292346:
Patrik Ulvdal and colleagues test a 2026 upgrade for forest planning software: adding stochastic programming so long-term plans can reckon with bad or uncertain data. Decision support systems for forestry seldom handle uncertainty head-on. The team plugged a stochastic model into a classic long-term planning problem, compared it with plain deterministic optimization, and workshopped the result with potential users.

The stochastic version lifted total expected net present value by at least 2 percent over the deterministic plan in their comparison. Workshop users liked the decision gains but worried about harder setup and murkier outputs. The authors recommend friendly presentation, with intuitive charts and simple summary statistics, to win adoption. They judge integration feasible on both the numbers and the user side, despite longer computing times.
pmc-13292446:
Zihao Liu and co-authors chase a 2026 target in multiple myeloma, starting from the toad-venom compound bufalin as a molecular fishing hook. Proteomics pulled out MAGEC2 as a direct binding partner. Checking patient cohorts, the team found high MAGEC2 matched poor overall survival in this incurable plasma cell cancer.

Beyond its known habit of boosting E3 ligases, it grabbed the deubiquitinase USP16 and cranked up its activity, which stabilized the growth driver c-Myc by trimming its ubiquitin tags. pmc-13292846:
Chen Sun and Hongye Zhang review 160 young children with flat brown marks on the face in a 2026 hospital study from Nanjing. Most marks appeared in the first year of life, often on the forehead or temples, and parents worried when color deepened as a child cried.

Clinic notes and skin-scope images showed two patterns, one with tiny blood vessels visible and one without. Among 110 children followed over time, nearly all marks faded fully by about age three, based on the share the authors report. The authors class the condition as harmless and short-lived, needing no set treatment, which can reassure families.
pmc-13293746:
Amanda Blanque Becceneri and co-authors test, in a 2026 study, a light-activated ruthenium drug for breast cancer across three-dimensional tumor models of rising realism. Light therapy can kill tumors precisely, yet flat dish tests overstate how well drugs will work in bodies.

Needed doses rose with model realism, from the lowest in loose balls to the highest in organoids, which resisted most. Printed models thus give a sterner, truer test before patient trials, the authors argue.
pmc-13294046:

pmc-13294246:
Yuhan Yao and colleagues test whether the allergy drug desloratadine can ease schizophrenia-like traits in mice for a 2026 study. pmc-13294346:

Reported scores reached 0.97 accuracy, 0.99 F1-score, 0.98 specificity, and 0.97 sensitivity in the authors' metrics. Clear heatmaps aid trust and cut manual reading slips. Fast, explainable sorting could speed heart care where expert readers are scarce.
pmc-13294446:
Olivia F Krol and coauthors forge a consensus syllabus for consumer health informatics in a 2026 eDelphi study. pmc-13295846:

pmc-13295946:

The study extends an existing cohort of 2,436 affected workers with two further survey rounds, plus interviews with sixty workers about care routes and treatment experiences. Thirty workers will also log symptoms and coping day by day, and insurance records add another view. Findings aim to show where care for these workers succeeds or leaves gaps.
pmc-13297446:
Car dampers that adjust themselves could ride better if their controls borrowed tricks from chameleons, proposes a 2026 engineering study led by Niancheng Guo. pmc-13298446:
A vibrating, cooling bee-shaped device may take some sting out of dental injections for children, test Prabhadevi C Maganur and colleagues in a 2026 crossover study. Thirty-eight children aged 6 to 10 needing numbing injections on both sides of the lower jaw received the Buzzy BEE device on one visit and standard care on the other.

However, effects carried over between visits, muddying the subjective results. The authors recommend bigger studies with longer washout periods before firm conclusions.
pmc-13299846:
Fit older folks who take the right mind drugs walk as fast as those who take none. Wrong-picked mind drugs, though, walk with them more slow. pmc-13302346:

Frailty, age, and body shape muddy the conversion further at the prescribing desk.

Their plea is for aligned rules and practical tools, reframing dosing as clinical judgment rather than arithmetic.
pmc-13302846:

One hundred thirty men on androgen receptor targeted therapies, abiraterone or enzalutamide among them, completed quality-of-life and mood questionnaires at one center. Groups were compared and poor quality of life modeled directly.

Unadjusted scores favored some drugs over others, with the abiraterone group lowest overall. Once mood entered the model, treatment type lost its grip: anxiety multiplied the odds of poor quality of life by 6.62 and depression by 3.40. Routine psychological screening belongs in these clinics, the authors argue.
pmc-13304746:

Gene scans showed weaker stress-response and calcium-linked pathways in the mutant. The altered yeast grew, formed filaments, and built biofilms less well under fluconazole. Blocking this stress route may restore drug power against resistant infections.
pmc-13305846:

Tiny rotors about 1.8 mm wide ran stably at high speed, helped by a probe layout that eases angle alignment in tight space. The authors present the design as a route to cheaper, portable high-speed instruments.
pmc-13306446:

One group barely changed with layer order, holding support factors near 2.6 to 2.7 in reported values, while the other varied widely and recovered less. The authors argue that layer sequence matters only for some builds, so single-material tests miss real cushion behaviour.
pmc-13306746:
Aung Min Naing built a low-cost indoor watcher joining air, vibration and network checks in a 2026 study. Small sensor nodes based on ESP32 boards feed a Raspberry Pi gateway that interprets conditions without using cameras.

Carbon dioxide readings separated ventilation states clearly, rising from 395.47 ppm in an open empty baseline to 1083.16 ppm in a closed occupied room in reported trials. Vibration patterns split calm, footstep, play and jump states by signal strength features. Message tests confirmed the linked system can flag both stale air and local disturbance. The set up is low cost and guards privacy since it uses no camera at all.
pmc-13308646:

Scans showed the left liver lobe pushed through a small wall gap, and blood tests flagged liver strain from poor flow. Robot aided surgery freed the starved liver part, which bore a small surface tear, and no cut out was needed at all. She healed with no snags. Small rural teams can thus tackle rare, urgent hernia cases with robot help.
pmc-13308946:

Blood work showed a mild white cell rise, and plain films showed nothing of note for the care team. Contrast scans found a dense line like body that pierced the end of the small bowel wall. Surgeons cut out the hurt span and joined the ends, and he healed with no snags. Herbs join the list of odd causes to weigh.
pmc-13309346:
Waseem Jerjes and Azeem Majeed argue in 2026 that patient centred care, for all its worth, leaves the real power with the clinic. They press for patient shaped care in its place. Fixed slot lengths, split duties, and stiff access routes can crush care for people with many long term states, no matter how kind the doctor is. Shared calls mean little when the paths on offer bend to stock and risk caps, not to patient aims. The pair urge joint rule over access, follow up, and what counts as success.
pmc-13309746:
Nabilah Anzoom and co-authors screen gene changes in the RET gene for harm and drug effects in a 2026 computer study. RET drives several cancers and developmental disorders when altered. Single-letter changes that swap one protein building block for another may break the protein or shift drug response.

Eleven variants looked most likely to cause disease, clustered in the protein active region. Docking tests with eight RET drugs showed binding shifts by variant, with one drug holding strong binding across all. Motion simulations backed the split. The authors offer the ranked list for lab follow-up.
pmc-13309946:

A study by Li and colleagues reported full response in all patients given CAR-T cells afterward, a striking result.

The letter welcomes the finding but probes what response rates hide. Prior antibody exposure may tire T cells, which could weaken the CAR-T product grown from them. Whether longer prior therapy tracked with slower cell growth in the lab went unreported in the study under discussion. The author asks for T-cell fitness data before the sequence becomes standard practice.
pmc-13310646:

Tax rises, a Sunday sales ban, a marketing ban, and Lithuania integrated package were each applied to drinking data for 27 countries, with a ten-year lag to cancer outcomes. An estimated 146,194 cancer cases in 2022, or 16.1 percent across the seven linked sites in the model, were tied to alcohol. Each scenario cut cases by a modeled share. The authors present the numbers for policy debate.
pmc-13310746:
Takuto Nosaka reports a 2026 case of acute fatty liver of pregnancy that a common scan tool failed to show. A woman aged 29 years, pregnant for the first time, grew jaundiced at 33 weeks with liver, blood, and kidney problems. The rare disease can turn fatal fast, so an urgent cesarean birth was done.

Weeks later a stiffness scan tool read the liver fat level as normal. A liver sample told a different story, with tiny fat drops seen under both standard and electron scopes. Stains backed the finding. The case warns that the scan tool can miss this fat pattern and that tissue checks still matter.
pmc-13311146:
Jiacheng Xie and co-authors study an RNA binding protein that shields colon cancer from chemo in a 2026 paper. Colon cancer kills many people yearly, and oxaliplatin based care often fails as resistance grows. Iron driven cell death offers a bypass, yet tumor guards can block that death route.

The protein PUM2 binds and mutes a helper gene message, which lets a guard protein pile up and block iron death. Tumors with high PUM2 thus shrug off oxaliplatin. In mouse models, pairing oxaliplatin with a guard blocker restored strong tumor control. The chain gives clinics a target pair for resistant disease.
pmc-13311246:
Linjia Guo and co-authors share their 2026 case of pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1B with normal blood calcium but low potassium. The disorder makes the body resist parathyroid hormone and stems from faults near the GNAS gene.

The patient, a 32-year-old Han Chinese man, had bouts of numbness and clear low potassium. Hormone levels were high, yet calcium stayed normal and brain scans showed no calcium deposits. A methylation test found the gene imprint pattern typical of type 1B, with no family history. The case warns that odd mineral shifts can appear even when calcium looks fine.
pmc-13311946:

The discussed study by Monari and colleagues interviewed culturally and linguistically diverse immigrants about what helps or blocks self-care. The commentators argue that staff must build culturally responsive habits into routine care, not treat them as extras. Health teaching should mirror patients' values, beliefs, and communication likes in both content and delivery. They call for studies on how such approaches play out over time.
pmc-13312546:
