The 5 millitesla treatment froze fastest, cutting the phase transition time by 40.32 percent against plain immersion freezing in the reported comparison, and it best preserved phenolics, flavonoids, color, and texture. Starch analysis showed the treatment kept granules intact and raised relative crystallinity and short-range order, which limited water movement and rearrangement on thawing. The authors identify the mild field treatment as an effective option for high-moisture starchy foods.
pmc-13312846:
Jae Hyeok Choi and colleagues report a 2026 case of a 69-year-old woman whose dream-acting sleep disorder proved to be the front edge of two overlapping brain diseases. REM sleep behavior disorder, in which the normal paralysis of dreaming sleep fails, is one of the strongest known warnings of Lewy body and related synuclein diseases. Most patients convert over time.

The woman arrived with confusion and behavior changes after starting antiseizure and antipsychotic drugs, showing slowness and rigidity when doctors checked her. Dopamine transporter imaging showed reduced uptake, a sleep study showed lost muscle atonia in REM sleep, and dream enactment seen in the lab completed the picture of dementia with Lewy bodies. Brain scans also showed multiple cortical microbleeds pointing to amyloid in vessel walls, and amyloid imaging showed widespread cortical deposits. The authors stress sorting true signals from drug and seizure confounders in such mixed cases.
pmc-13313246:
Yujing Tan and fellow authors compare a breast cancer drug class across high and low land in China in their 2026 study. CDK4/6 blockers are the standard care for advanced breast cancer that feeds on hormones and lacks HER2, but whether altitude changes their effect was unknown.

The team gathered records on 350 patients from four cancer centers, with 268 patients in the low-altitude group and 82 patients in the high-altitude group. In first-line use, low-altitude patients did better on each measure the authors report: response rate, benefit rate, and time with no growth, stated as 42.1 months versus 15.2 months for that span. Gaps also showed in later lines of care. The study warns that place and height may shape drug results, so care plans may need to adjust by region.
pmc-13314746:
Munkhsuvd Chimed and colleagues report a 2026 case of scarring around blood vessels that spread far beyond its usual range. Perivascular fibrosis wraps the aorta and its branches in thick soft tissue, and it can mimic big-vessel inflammation or lymph tumors on scans.

Their patient was a 55-year-old man with long-standing scarring behind the belly and a blocked lower aorta. The disease also gripped his chest aorta, a coronary artery, and the branches above the aorta, a spread seldom seen. Over 20 years of follow-up, as the report states, a narrowed coronary artery caused a full heart attack that needed a stent and bypass surgery. Tests for the usual IgG4 marker came back negative. The case shows why layered imaging matters to tell this scarring from its many doubles.
pmc-13314946:
Tarek Sallam and Ahmed M. Attiya use a physics-guided neural network to shape antenna beams, in their 2026 paper. Radar and broadcast arrays often need a cosecant-squared beam shape, which lights a zone evenly while keeping stray side lobes low.

Their method tunes only the phase of each array element, which keeps the hardware simple. A deep network trained with a loss that enforces match to the wanted pattern learns the phase set for big flat arrays. Two aims rule the training: crush side lobes and smooth ripples inside the shaped beam. The team set their method against genetic algorithms and particle swarm optimization, the standard search tools named in the report. Number tests gave their approach the edge on pattern quality, by the results reported.
pmc-13316646:
Adilson J M de Oliveira reports a 2026 national cohort of the first 100 brachial plexus operations in Angola. It covers babies hurt at birth and adults with arm nerve injuries, treated from January 2021 to December 2025. One nerve surgeon assessed and operated on every patient.

Sixteen babies were included, most with upper trunk injuries treated by a nerve transfer, and seven reached useful strength grades at follow-up. Among 86 adults, most had complete injuries and nearly all suffered nerve pain, which eased in nine of ten after surgery. Recovery rates stayed low, blamed on long waits averaging 14 months for adults. Lessons stress full care teams, child specialists, and partnerships beyond the surgeon alone.
pmc-13317546:
Xiang Qi and colleagues review, in a 2026 article, how colorectal cancer spreads to bone, a rarer landing site that brings fractures, cord pressure, and calcium crises when it comes. The cancer ranks third worldwide in frequency, and bone spread usually travels with liver or lung disease.

The review walks through the TGF-beta pathway, shape-shifting of tumor cells, the Wnt pathway, chemical beacons, and immune dealings inside the bone niche. It carefully separates proof gathered in this cancer from findings borrowed from others, and grades evidence in a table for clinical use. By naming where knowledge is solid and where it is guesswork, the authors aim to steer drug development toward targets that truly fit this disease.
pmc-13318546:
Elisabetta Cozzi and colleagues present a 2026 screening study hunting for long non-coding RNAs that help drive acute myeloid leukaemia or shape response to the drug venetoclax. Protein-coding genes in this blood cancer are well mapped, but these RNA molecules are not.

Using CRISPR interference in the MOLM-13 cell line, the team dampened 7,996 candidate RNAs and watched growth, maturation, and drug sensitivity. Altogether 58 RNAs affected growth, 4 affected maturation, and 23 changed venetoclax response in the screens reported. Four were followed up in depth, including CATG00000106133.1, tied to immune signalling, and AC009299.3, tied to drug response and poorer patient outcomes, giving new leads for prognosis and treatment.
pmc-13318646:
Günhal Şatırtav leads an international expert group whose 2026 review gives guidance on when injections for wet age-related macular degeneration can safely stop. The Vision Academy panel read the literature and agreed on recommendations plus a step-by-step algorithm.

Stopping can be considered when the eye shows no fluid, no sight loss, and no new bleeding across at least three visits at the longest treatment interval a clinic uses. People whose disease stays active, or who rely on one good eye and have relapsed before, may do better continuing. After stopping, scan and vision checks should continue at an agreed pace set with the patient, since the disease can wake again.
pmc-13318746:
Chengjian Cao and co-authors review, in 2026, natural anti-inflammatory compounds for chronic rhinosinusitis. Current treatments calm downstream inflammation but miss the immune faults driving recurrence. The review centres on a regulatory axis of three players. They are FOXP3, the complement receptor C5aR1, and the factor LIF.

Literature from 2000 to 2026 across three databases was searched. In sinus disease with polyps, protective regulatory T cells are heavily depleted. Complement signalling through C5aR1 blocks new regulatory cells forming. LIF pushes the other way, raising FOXP3 and calming harmful responses. Compounds such as curcumin and rosmarinic acid act on these pathways. Bromelain and cineole already have clinical support in acute sinusitis.
pmc-13319046:
Fengjiao Chen and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of ozone injections into arthritic knees, focused on how long benefits last. Sixteen randomised trials with 1,172 patients were included. Searches ran across five databases to December 3, 2025. Pain, stiffness, and function scores were tracked by follow-up time.

Benefits were clear early on. At one month, total arthritis scores improved with a standardised effect of −0.63 in the pooled result. At two months, pain, function, and pain-scale scores all improved significantly. By three months, no outcome differed significantly from control. The authors conclude the effect is time-limited rather than sustained. They offer the timeline as a guide for phased treatment planning in knee osteoarthritis care.
pmc-13319946:
Lingyun Xiang and co-authors study how reward and punishment reshape learning from surprise in a 2026 brain wave study. People update beliefs when outcomes clash with what they expect, and wins and losses may not weigh those clashes in the same way. A sorting task with shifting odds was paired with scalp brain wave records and a layered math model of belief change.

People did better when learning for reward than when learning to dodge punishment. Yet punishment drove faster belief updates in the model, without turning into better scores. Brain wave marks of surprise grew stronger under punishment at key points. The split shows that fast updating alone does not mean good learning, and motive colors how the brain weighs surprise.
pmc-13320046:
Lindsey West and co-authors dig into why floating wind farms at sea stall in tangled rule systems in a 2026 study of the Celtic Sea in Britain. Floating wind could speed the shift to clean power and lift coastal areas, yet growth unfolds inside split marine rule systems that serve many aims at once. Past work named the blocks but rarely traced their deep roots.

Using ideas from the study of institutions, the team traced blocks to root traits that set who does what, who links to whom, and who holds power. Blocks fed each other as a system rather than acting as lone faults, through habits such as clinging to old paths and piling new rules on old ones. Fixes must reshape the rule system itself, with more room to learn and adapt.
pmc-13320346:
Jeong-Uk Eom and co-authors study how storage before cooking shapes harmful compounds in grilled chicken in a 2026 food safety study. Harsh heat on meat makes compounds tied to cancer risk, yet past work stared at the cooking step and skipped what storage does first. Cold and frozen holds were compared for how they prime the meat chemistry that feeds those compounds.

Two weeks in the fridge drove fat and protein decay and reshaped the pool of free building blocks and sharp carbonyl compounds in the breast meat. That primed pool then fed most of the harmful compounds when the meat was cooked. Frozen storage held decay back and cut total harmful load, bar one compound. Storage checks could flag risky meat before it hits the heat.
pmc-13320446:
Zheyu Fan and co-authors study how a withdrawn gut drug harms nerves by draining a vitamin form in a 2026 study. The drug was pulled after it was tied to a nerve illness wave in Japan in the last century. A link to lack of thiamine, a B vitamin, was long suspected but unproven. Chemical scans of cells flagged the active form of that vitamin as the chief casualty.

The drug was shown to wreck that vitamin form through stress driven chemical change, which starved cell power houses and forced a shift to sugar burning. In a mouse model of Alzheimer disease the same drain and nerve harm showed in the brain. Topping up the vitamin form or a shield compound eased the harm and even boosted plaque clearing by the drug.
pmc-13320546:
Daiji Nagayama and co-authors look back at records in a 2026 Japanese study of the weight and diabetes drug tirzepatide. The drug aids weight loss and blood sugar control, but its effect on stiff arteries was less clear. The team tracked vessel stiffness with a heart to ankle index in adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes.

Weekly treatment in 24 people, over a median of about a year, lowered the stiffness index from 8.5 to 7.8 at the median. Weight, muscle and fat measures, and blood sugar marks also fell, with the sugar mark HbA1c dropping from 6.6 to 5.6 percent at the median. Higher doses gave larger weight loss in this small group.
pmc-13321046:
Fatai Lu and colleagues test a human defence peptide against bone cancer in a 2026 study. Osteosarcoma is an aggressive bone tumour with poor outlook once it spreads or returns. The peptide LL-37, part of innate defence, can fight tumours in some settings, but its role in this cancer was undefined.

In cell tests, LL-37 curbed cancer cell survival while barely harming normal bone marrow stem cells. It cut colony growth, movement, and invasion, stalled the cell cycle, and triggered two forms of cell death. Gene scans showed cholesterol making was turned down, with the key enzyme SQLE sharply reduced. Mouse tumour graft work was used to check the effect in living tissue.
pmc-13321546:
Pooja Yashwant Pawar and colleagues assemble first genomes for four threatened Asian hornbills in a 2026 study. Hornbills are flagship birds of wet tropical forests, hit by hunting and habitat loss, yet whole genomes existed for only two of 32 Asian species. Long and short read sequencing were combined for the new assemblies.

Genomes for Great, Rufous-necked, Malabar Pied, and Wreathed Hornbills ran from 1.1 to 1.3 billion letters, with completeness above 95.9 percent in the report. Over 10,000 gene groups were shared, and keratin related families had expanded. Past population tracking showed falling numbers during the late Pleistocene, which sharpens the case for protection.
pmc-13321746:
Mohsen Kamali and Amirmohammad Atashinsadaf survey nurse leadership and staff satisfaction in Iranian hospitals in a 2026 study. Head nurses shape how ward teams feel and perform, yet styles may work differently in specialist and general wards. The census study covered 1354 nurses in 71 wards across six teaching hospitals tied to Zanjan University of Medical Sciences.

Satisfaction with head nurses averaged 68.94 in specialised wards and 66.11 in general wards on the study scale, fairly high in both. Balanced leadership, mixing task and relationship focus, was most common in specialised wards, while relationship led style led in general wards. Task only leadership was rarest in both settings and scored lower on satisfaction.
pmc-13322946:
Atthaphong Phongphithakchai and colleagues test an international kidney risk tool in Thai patients, in a 2026 validation study. Their cohort held 133 adults with biopsy-proven IgA nephropathy at a tertiary centre, followed for a median of 3.4 years of care.

The tool predicts a halving of filtration rate or progression to end-stage kidney disease, and 45 patients reached that endpoint during follow-up. Both versions of the model, with and without a race term, sorted patients well and split kidney survival clearly across risk groups. Fit to observed outcomes looked broadly sound, though ranges around the estimates were wide. The authors support using the tool for risk talks in Thai practice.
pmc-13323146:
Adwoa Asante-Poku leads a community survey in Ghana on knowledge of tuberculosis and diabetes, published in 2026 after outreach on World Tuberculosis Day in 2022 and 2023. Sessions ran in a hospital outpatient area, schools, a nursing college and a market, with screening offered.

Replies came from 285 adults, mostly women with basic schooling in the reported profile. Among 179 people who knew of tuberculosis, just under half correctly named bacteria or germs as the cause, while a small share held myths such as spiritual causes. People found with either disease were referred to Korle-Bu Teaching Hospital. The authors stress that gaps in knowledge and attitudes can slow care-seeking and weaken control work.
pmc-13323446:
Elif Tunc-Ozcan reviews neurons that release more than one chemical messenger, in a 2026 article on co-transmission. The classic picture of one neuron and one transmitter has given way to evidence that many neurons juggle several, with distinct release arrangements.

Transmitters may share one vesicle, sit in separate vesicle pools at one terminal, or split across different branches of the same cell. Each layout sets its own rules for release timing, target reach and short-term change, letting signals span several timescales and shift with firing pattern. No single method proves the release route, so the field joins molecular profiling, electrical recording, fine anatomy, light-based control and live sensors.
pmc-13324446:
Wei Wang and co-authors survey genetic variants in neuroblastoma, a childhood solid tumor, in a 2026 study. The cancer varies widely between patients, and its mutation patterns in Chinese patients were little known.

Whole-exome sequencing covered tumor, nearby tissue, and blood from nine Chinese patients with confirmed disease. The team found 77 missense variants, with C to T changes the most common type. Variants in MAP1A and RBM33 had not been reported in this cancer before, though each was rare. No MYCN growth or ALK, ATRX, or DAXX changes appeared. High-risk cases showed distinct patterns tied to the tissue matrix, a lead for further study in larger groups.
pmc-13325146:
Tugba Celik Caglar and Birol Kayranli test raw date seeds as a reusable sponge for the dye Rhodamine B in a 2026 water study. Dye waste from industry harms water life, and cheap plant sorbents could cut cleanup costs.

Best removal came at pH 3 with 1.0 g of seeds at 303 K and 30 minutes of contact. Modeling pointed to a varied surface holding several dye layers, with surface binding as the slow step. Charge tests backed charge attraction as a main grip. Among four regeneration routes, alkali washing plus drying at 120 °C kept the surface most intact. That route still removed 88.1 percent of dye in the fourth cycle, down from 96.3 percent at first.
pmc-13325446:
Spoorthy Sandras and co-authors track metabolism inside living neuron-like cells with a fast NMR method in a 2026 study. As neurons mature, their fuel use shifts, but the change unfolds in under a minute at each step.

Cells were grown in alginate beads and matured inside the gel while nuclear magnetic resonance watched labeled pulses pass through. Maturation slowed sugar breakdown through glycolysis and raised TCA cycle activity and glutamate output. Fructose 1,6 bisphosphate marked the young state, while glutathione marked the mature one. The method can now probe how stress or drugs reroute neuron metabolism in near real time.
pmc-13326946:
Roberto Bonanni and co-authors review how exercise may calm epilepsy through neurosteroids in a 2026 narrative review. Brain-made steroids tune GABA signaling, the main braking system whose failure lets seizures fire.

Steroids such as allopregnanolone and pregnenolone rise with moderate to hard exercise in the evidence surveyed. Those same steroids steady inhibitory transmission and may raise the seizure threshold. Clinical views of exercise in epilepsy have flipped from danger to asset, with gains in thinking and life quality reported. Many patients stay drug-resistant, which keeps non-drug routes valuable. The authors call for trials that pin dose and mechanism down.
pmc-13327446:
Viktor Olsson and colleagues tackle a hidden source of MRI error in a 2026 methods study. Extra magnetic fields, called concomitant gradients, distort diffusion scans, and the harm grows at low field strength and with very strong gradients. The team derived a compact formula for these fields and tested fixes in simulation.

They modeled fields from 0.03 to 7 tesla and gradients from 20 to 600 mT/m, splitting the error into lost signal and extra diffusion weighting. Signal loss came mostly from resampling steps that broke the built-in compensation, reaching 100 percent error in bad cases, while a design-stage waveform fix cut bias below 1 percent for most systems. Using the true waveform during analysis handled the weighting error.
pmc-13330446:
Xiaolong Li and co-authors review how neutrophil traps help cancers resist immune therapy in a 2026 article. Traps are webs of DNA and proteins cast out by neutrophils. Inside tumours they can wall off immune cells and wear T cells down, blunting checkpoint drugs that help many patients.

Trap parts in blood, such as DNA complexes and altered histones, may serve as signs of disease course and therapy response. Tumour signals and tiny vesicles steer trap formation. The review sorts resistance into physical blocking and biological dampening, then gathers counter-moves: stop trap making, dissolve formed webs, or block their downstream effects. Such moves could restore anti-tumour immunity, the authors propose.
pmc-13336846:
Simon W J Dietzmann and co-authors question whether some reported carbon pores are real in a 2026 analysis. Pore charts from gas uptake often show narrow micropores in activated carbons and metal-nitrogen-carbon catalysts. The authors argue many are artifacts of the math models used, not true holes.

By building carbons with known surface sites, they showed the phantom pores match gas molecules preferring certain sites. Zinc-nitrogen sites in a framework-derived carbon become nitrogen sites after zinc removal, each with its own gas pull. Comparing nitrogen, carbon dioxide, and argon uptake plus energy calculations pinned the effect down. Reading these artifacts correctly could speed work on batteries, capacitors, and catalysts.
pmc-13341546:
Anticipating movement outcomes is tested in children with cerebellar disorders by S. Gazzellini's team in the 2026 dual-task study. Twenty-four patients and 24 typically developing peers, both about 13 years old, did a hand task. They did it alone and with verbal anticipation, timing, or memory tasks.

Speed and accuracy merged into an inverse efficacy score. The cerebellum acts as a hub of the predictive brain, and the team expected its patients to suffer most when the second task tapped anticipation or timing rather than plain memory work. Comparing these pairings clarifies how prediction failure, not just clumsiness, burdens everyday movement.
pmc-13342046:
Ovarian overstimulation without fertility treatment is reported by M. J. Nuñez Burbano's team in the 2026 pair of case reports. Two women, aged 21 and 23, developed spontaneous ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome in early single-baby pregnancies, both with liver involvement.

The first showed belly swelling, fluid buildup, and raised bilirubin with hugely enlarged ovaries; the second had pain, bilious vomiting, and elevated liver enzymes. Both also had gallstones, and one needed gallbladder surgery, while the syndrome itself was managed with watchful care and close checks. The cases remind doctors to weigh this syndrome even without fertility help.
pmc-13342946:
Xiaojuan Wang and colleagues report a 2026 retrospective cohort study of live births after treatment with vitrified donated eggs in China. The team reviewed 377 women treated at a large fertility center between 2015 and 2024 and asked which factors raise or lower the chance of a baby.

Among 369 women who reached embryo transfer, the first-transfer live birth rate was 51.5 percent, and the cumulative rate reached 58.5 percent. Older recipients and a past history of poor egg or embryo quality lowered success, while more usable day-3 embryos raised cumulative odds. Longer egg storage caused no harm, which supports careful batch planning for donated eggs.
pmc-13343146:
Puduo Zhu and co-authors characterize a new H6N6 bird flu virus tied to breeding failure in ducks, in a 2026 study. Surveillance on affected duck farms isolated a strain whose genome mixes three distinct lineages, a triple reassortant, with two notable changes in its hemagglutinin protein.

Lab challenges showed the virus could infect mice, young Muscovy ducks, and clean laboratory chickens, causing mild illness in each. In breeding ducks, though, infection damaged the reproductive tract and sharply cut egg laying. Even low-harm bird flu, the authors warn, can cross species lines and hurt farm output, which makes steady flock surveillance essential for poultry regions.
pmc-13345646:
Macleod and colleagues studied in 2026 how a virtual kidney care service took root in northern British Columbia, a vast rural and remote region of Canada. Rollout plans usually treat such work as a fixed project focused on what to do, leaving the how poorly understood. The team interviewed eight kidney care providers, two technology staff, and 17 patients about delivering and receiving care at a distance, including changes during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Six shared patterns ran through the accounts: naming core concerns, building new shared understandings, acting together, surfacing tensions, responding to local context, and keeping dialogue going. Rather than a neat, time-bound project, rollout appeared as an ongoing, relational process tied to place and never fully finished. The authors argue that an open, humble stance built on dialogue and relationships is the real engine of lasting change in such settings.
pmc-13345946:
Janaka Senarathna and a large team introduce CloudScope in 2026, a mini microscope that watches animal brains around the clock through the cloud. Existing miniscopes run under two hours and see one signal at a time, far too little for diseases such as seizures and brain tumors that unfold over whole lifetimes.

CloudScope images neuron activity, blood flow, volume, oxygenation, and cell behavior together in freely moving animals, with remote operation from anywhere. Tests predicted behavior from a full day of imaging, charted vessel changes during natural acts and seizures, and profiled tumor surroundings cell by cell. Time-sharing the device across animals could also trim animal use, the team notes.
pmc-13346846:
Dong-Joon Lee, Jang-Hyun Park, and Jaehan Park test a printable soft denture liner. Their study was published in 2026. The liner is a polyurethane-acrylate material. It was made by digital light processing printing. Cell tests came first, using fibroblast cultures. Rat tests came next. Plates sat against the cheek lining for one and three days. Sham controls ran beside them.

Extracts left cell survival above 97 percent. That held at every strength tested. Tissue slices showed no surface break. No inflamed cells rushed in. No damage appeared either. Marker proteins for surface integrity looked alike in both groups. A brief rise in gene signals settled by day three.
pmc-13347246:
Abdullah Hilal Zafar and a large team measure frailty in South Asian dialysis patients. Their cross-sectional study came out in 2026. It also measures quality of life. A total of 448 adults took part. All had been on haemodialysis for three months or more. The Edmonton Frail Scale gave each frailty score. A kidney disease questionnaire gave life scores. Age, sex, and treatment history were compared.

Frailty tracked lower quality of life closely. Women scored frailer than men. Women also scored lower on quality of life. Older age went with more frailty. Older age also went with poorer life scores. Longer dialysis added to the burden. So did more frequent dialysis and more illnesses. Routine frailty checks are urged during dialysis care.
pmc-13347646:
Hsiu-Ming Hsu and colleagues devise a light-based way to find harmful crystal defects in silicon carbide wafers, in a study from 2026. Pure silicon carbide serves high-power devices, yet threading dislocations hide well because free charge is scarce. So the team etched defect pits, read their shapes by laser scattering, and linked each shape to glow from the line below.

Only a small share of pure screw-type defects gave broad deep-level glow, tied to states inside the defect core itself in the joint counts. Such glowing defects could form leak paths in a device through trap-assisted flow, so spotting them without damage matters for wafer screening before costly device builds.
pmc-13350046:
Abedalrahman Shqaidef and co-authors proposed a chairside reasoning framework in 2026 to help dentists spot genetic syndromes early. Mouth and face features appear in more than 900 genetic syndromes, but dentists often see them as isolated quirks and miss the pattern.

The authors define sentinel findings: common features that, past a set threshold or in a telling pattern, raise the chance of an underlying syndrome. Six such findings are detailed with their linked syndromes, what to ask, and what else to check on the face and body. A four-step path separates findings to watch from those needing referral, aiming to catch syndromes while early help still counts.
pmc-13350546:
Meilu Du and co-authors tested a combined inflammation and nutrition score in 2026 for forecasting survival in advanced colorectal cancer on third-line treatment. Records covered 320 patients at a Shanghai hospital for traditional Chinese medicine.

The score blends several blood measures of inflammation, immunity, and nutrition. Patients grouped by score level were compared for time until next treatment and overall survival, using survival curves, adjusted models, and time-varying accuracy checks. By third-line therapy, options narrow and bodies weaken, so a cheap score that separates likely survivors could guide whether further treatment helps or merely burdens.
pmc-13351446:
Ákos Őrsi and co-authors compared gut microbes in two migrating shorebirds in a 2026 field study. The two species forage alike. Yet their gut microbes differed clearly. Small differences in feeding technique and food choice are the likely cause.

Wood sandpipers carried far more Fusobacteria than expected. Migratory birds can shuttle microbes across great distances. These include potential pathogens and drug-resistant bacteria. The birds themselves stay healthy. Cataloguing what they carry shows how diet shapes the load. It also feeds into judging the health hazards bird migration poses. Farms, wildlife, and people along the flyway all share that risk.
pmc-13351746:
Jennifer Owusu Adjei leads a 2026 case report on heterotopic pregnancy, where a pregnancy grows inside the womb and another outside it at the same time. The rare mix can threaten life, and a healthy womb pregnancy on scan does not rule out a second one elsewhere. A 26-year-old woman at about eight weeks arrived unstable with free fluid in her belly.

Scans confirmed a living womb pregnancy and no clear mass beside it, so care began with watchful waiting for a bleeding ovarian cyst. Over forty-eight hours her haemoglobin fell from 105 g/L to 69 g/L and fluid grew. Keyhole surgery found a burst left tube pregnancy, the tube was removed, and the womb pregnancy was saved.
pmc-13351946:
Ali Mehaidli leads a 2026 statewide study of how COVID-19 changed spine surgery results over time. The pandemic forced delays to planned surgery, shifted who was chosen, and stretched hospital resources. Data came from the Michigan Spine Surgery Improvement Collaborative for neck and lower back operations.

Four phases were compared: before COVID-19 from January 2019, onset and active phases, and a later phase ending in December 2022. Patient traits, surgery details, harms at 30 and 90 days, and patient-reported outcomes were set side by side. Earlier work conflicted and often covered one centre or a short span. A statewide view over four years gives a fuller picture of lasting effects.
pmc-13355346:
Bonan Lv and co-authors found in 2026 that a cell protein called ARL8B helps several single-stranded RNA viruses copy themselves. Viruses such as foot-and-mouth disease virus and enterovirus 71 reshape fat stores in host cells, but how they break those stores down was unclear. The team used imaging and lab tests to track fat droplets during infection.

ARL8B drove the breakdown of fat droplets through a selective cleanup path, freeing fatty acids that feed virus copying sites. It also helped new virus particles leave the cell through an unusual exit route. Computer screening found small drugs that block ARL8B, and they protected mice from enterovirus infection, marking a lead for broad antiviral drugs.
pmc-13356046:
Eva-Maria Sunzel and co-authors report two 2026 studies of a once-daily extended-release form of deutetrabenazine, a drug for involuntary movements in tardive dyskinesia and Huntington's disease. Healthy volunteers took single doses in crossover studies: one tested whether blood levels rise in step with dose, and the other whether food changes uptake of a 24-milligram dose.

Blood levels of the drug and its active breakdown products rose in step with dose across the full approved range up to 48 milligrams. Eating did not change uptake, with all key ratios inside the accepted range. The authors conclude the once-daily tablet can be taken with or without meals.
pmc-13358846:
Han-Yu Deng and co-authors set out the plan for a cancer trial in a 2026 protocol paper. Some lung cancers carry a gene fusion called RET, and a targeted drug, pralsetinib, can shrink them. The trial asks whether patients whose tumors start out inoperable can, after months on the drug, become fit for surgery that removes the tumor.

The single-arm phase II study will enroll 25 patients with stage III disease who have not had prior treatment. They will take the drug for up to six months, then have surgery if the tumor can be removed. Publishing the plan in advance lets other teams judge the results fairly when they arrive.
pmc-13359646:
Bianca Santo and co-authors measure a painful side effect of head and neck cancer treatment in a 2026 study. Radiation, with or without chemotherapy, often inflames and ulcerates the mouth lining, a condition called oral mucositis. It makes eating and swallowing hard and can force breaks in treatment. Doctors grade it in clinic, but their grade may miss the patient's own experience.

The team combined clinical grading, direct looks at the mouth damage, and patient-reported outcomes, and tracked weight change as well. Joining the three views gave a fuller picture of the burden. The approach could flag high-risk patients earlier and sharpen supportive care during treatment.
pmc-13361446:
Katarzyna Stępnik reviews curcumin for Alzheimer's disease in a 2026 paper. Curcumin, the yellow compound in turmeric, is one of the most studied plant compounds for this brain disease. Alzheimer's grows from tangled causes: protein clumps, oxidative stress, inflammation, and failing cells. The review weighs lab, animal, and human evidence on how curcumin touches each cause.

Lab studies show curcumin calms inflammatory signals, fights oxidative stress, and slows clumping of the amyloid protein. Proof for effects on the tau protein is thinner. In animals, it improved thinking performance and lowered disease markers. The author then faces the hard part: turning strong lab promise into human benefit, given curcumin's poor absorption. New forms of the compound may help, and the review maps those strategies.
pmc-13361546:
Min-Chang Jang and co-authors studied thigh bone breaks during hip replacement in a 2026 paper. A crack in the femur while the new joint is fitted is a worrying problem that often goes under-counted. The team reviewed 3,137 primary hip replacements in 2,622 patients at one hospital, done from 2011 to 2018 with cementless tapered stems. Thigh shape was graded into three Dorr types.

Stems came in flat, rectangular, and four-sided tapered designs. Breaks were found from surgery notes and follow-up X-rays. Layered analysis then weighed which shapes and stem designs raised the risk. Knowing the risky pairings helps surgeons choose implants and technique for each patient's bone shape. Fewer breaks mean fewer repairs and faster recovery for a very common operation.
pmc-13364346:
Gustavo Chaves leads a large team in a 2026 test of guard compounds on cuttings of gabiroba, a fruit tree of the Brazil savanna. Its seeds store poorly, so growers need cuttings to root. Air damage to cut plant parts can block that rooting, so the team tried three guards at set doses.

Cuttings were grown in a glass house and checked after 60 days for sprouts, life, and root callus. No guard made roots form in any season. Warm seasons did lift sprouts and callus. The clear word is that guards alone will not solve rooting for this tree.
pmc-13364746:

pmc-13407246:

pmc-13408146:

pmc-13408346:

pmc-13408446:

pmc-13410746:

pmc-13410946:

pmc-13411146:

pmc-13411946:

pmc-13412546:

pmc-13412646:

pmc-13413946:

pmc-13414046:

Growth of Staphylococcus aureus fell as the dose rose, clearly held back from five milligrams per millilitre up.
pmc-13415046:

pmc-13415246:

pmc-13415646:

pmc-13415746:

pmc-13415846:

pmc-13416146:

pmc-13416246:

pmc-13417346:

pmc-13417646:

pmc-13418046:

pmc-13418246:

pmc-13418546:

pmc-13418746:

pmc-13421346:

pmc-13422346:

pmc-13422846:

pmc-13422946:

pmc-13423446:

pmc-13423946:

pmc-13424546:

pmc-13425046:

pmc-13425846:

pmc-13426346:

pmc-13426446:

pmc-13427446:

pmc-13427546:

pmc-13427646:

pmc-13427746:

pmc-13428246:

pmc-13429046:

pmc-13429246:

pmc-13431746:

pmc-13431846:

pmc-13433946:

The front crowd sits past the first arch and builds the midface, long cast as outside the band line.

In zebrafish, cuts to the clan flip front bones into mirror twins of arch bones, a swap that marks lost segment name. The team drew the line where front and arch crowds part. pmc-13434646:
Yunhui Ge and colleagues solve the working cycle of Wntless in 2026, the carrier that ferries Wnt signals out of cells. Wnt signals guide body building in the womb and drive disease when misused. Images with and without Wnt aboard show how the carrier grips its cargo.

Three small loops on Wnt plug into the carrier, and all three are needed for exit. Release comes when the carrier twists hard, much like a hormone receptor switching on. One Wnt type pairs up while aboard, which may tune its signal. The cycle view gives drug hunters clear steps to block or boost.
pmc-13435446:

Dish grown gum cells made fewer swelling signals under the drug. Downstream death marks fell in step. Local dosing at the gum may calm disease without body wide effects.
pmc-13435646:
Lalitya M Sudarsono and coauthors fit a hollow fiber rig to study a herpes drug against cytomegalovirus in 2026. The virus preys on weak patients, and best dose targets for ganciclovir were never set. Cheap dialyzer cartridges stand in for costly bespoke rigs here.

pmc-13436646:
Gregory Muller and coauthors track gunshot deaths by transport mode in a national trauma bank from 2007 to 2021 in 2026. The set holds 355,913 patients, with 83.7 percent arriving by ambulance. Private car arrivals form the rest, bound for top trauma centers.

Raw death rates ran far higher for ambulance patients in every period. That gap reflects worse wounds, not worse care, as adjusted math shows. The adjusted odds gap shrank over the years as field care improved. Rates still sat near nineteen percent for ambulance cases in the last period. Fair gauges must adjust for wound severity first.
pmc-13437246:

About seventy-one percent of the acute group responded by day twenty-eight, and the best rate at any point reached about eighty-nine percent. The chronic group answered at similar rates early on, though fewer held their gains or cleared disease fully. The authors present the pairing as a workable path for very sick children.
pmc-13440046:
Zhongcan Xiao, Leyi Zhang, Guannan Zhang, and Xiaoping Wang describe an AI agent that shepherds neutron crystal data from beamline to publishable structure, reporting in 2026. At large scattering facilities, the wait between experiment and finished structure often stretches through many hand-run steps. The authors frame governed automation, not raw speed, as the way to cut instrument-to-publication delay.
pmc-13440446:
Shant Torkom Yeretzian and colleagues map how economic studies count lost productivity for patients and caregivers, reporting a 2026 scoping review. Evaluations that take a societal view should include work losses, yet practice varies widely. The team screened nearly four thousand records from 2019 to 2025 and kept forty studies, plus ten guidance documents from assessment agencies. Instruments for measuring loss and methods for pricing it were catalogued side by side.

Twenty-five instruments turned up, most covering patients rather than caregivers and many covering presenteeism, working while unwell, alone. Only three instruments suited both main pricing approaches. The human capital approach is simple but can overstate losses, while the friction cost approach fits labour markets better and needs hard-to-find vacancy data. Guidance across countries split between the two. The authors urge shared standards for this neglected cost category.
pmc-13442446:
Praveen Krishna Veerasubramanian and colleagues hunt for paired drug blocks that calm T cells in a 2026 study. The TNF family holds 47 proteins that steer immune signals, yet single blocks often fail as bodies route around them. The team scored family genes for links to joint and bowel illness, gene data, drug ease, and path roles.

Ten targets rose to the top and went into a mixed cell test that mimics immune clash. Four pairs cut two T-cell signal goods, IL-2 and IFN-gamma, by a clear margin. Gene reads then showed broad drops in genes for T-cell switch-on, growth, and split. The authors argue that paired blocks can close the detours that beat single drugs. They offer the four pairs as leads for immune illness care, pending tests in living systems.
pmc-13443046:
Anjali Kumari and Mahaboobkhan Rasool review two sibling signal goods, IL-1 beta and IL-18, in osteoarthritis in a 2026 paper. Both come from the IL-1 family and drive joint decay, yet they play distinct parts. The first sparks early cartilage breakdown and cell aging, while the twin fans immune fire through the inflammasome hub.

Shared wiring runs through the MyD88 path, so the pair act as partners rather than spare copies. The review sorts joint harm into three linked phases: cytokine start, growth, and chronic grind, all tied to cell aging. Drugs that hunt the first signal have flopped in trials so far. The authors urge paired hunts and mark-guided care, since twin blocks may beat single blocks for worn joints.
pmc-13443746:
Tao Xie and colleagues report amygdala ablation that eased trauma-linked fear bias in one patient in a 2026 case paper. The man had stubborn epilepsy plus chronic PTSD, and he read vague faces as more fearful than peers did. Depth probes logged his right amygdala, then heat ablation targeted that spot.

Before the burn, his amygdala split fearful from happy faces with a late signal surge that tracked his bias. Right after the burn, his gloomy read of vague faces fell, and his PTSD scores fell with it. Seizure counts held steady through the change. Late signal size shrank in step with his fear drop. The authors flag that signal as a mark that may guide care, while one case sets the limit of the claim.
pmc-13444646:
Limei Hu and colleagues report the case of a 72-year-old man whose gut parasite infection turned severe during steroid treatment for a blood vessel disease, published in 2026. The man had belly pain and a skin rash, and doctors first treated him for IgA vasculitis. Steroids calm that disease, yet they can let a quiet worm infection spread through the body.

When his state failed to improve, tests found the worm Strongyloides stercoralis in his sputum and stool. The two diseases can look alike, since both bring belly pain and skin spots, which helps explain the missed call. The authors stress screening for the worm before steroid treatment starts, above all where the parasite is common.
pmc-13447146:
Saad Aldosari and co-authors review 2026 records on advanced arthritis drugs at a single centre in Dammam, Saudi Arabia. People with rheumatoid arthritis often start a biologic or targeted pill after older drugs fail. How long they stay on a first drug, switch, or stop in routine Saudi care was poorly known.

One hundred seventy-five adults who were new to these drugs were followed from treatment starts between 2013 and 2023. A tumour necrosis factor blocker was the most common first choice. Estimated time on drug at five years looked broadly similar across drug classes, with no clear gap in formal tests. Loss of benefit drove most switches, while pregnancy and missed doses drove many stops, though the small cohort limits firm conclusions.
pmc-13448646:
Lei Zhang and co-authors break high-temperature limits for polymer capacitor films by locking down charge movement in a 2026 materials study. Aromatic polymers resist heat well, yet charges leak along and between their chains under hot, high-field conditions, gutting stored energy and efficiency. Blending and crosslinking fixes are blunted by the polymers' flat, stacking-prone backbones, the authors argue.

Adding a strong Lewis acid compound at four percent by weight reorganised chain packing through coordination bonds, hydrogen bonds and steric twisting. Ordered same-type chain arrangements replaced the leaky mixed stacking pattern. Stored energy at high field reached values the authors report as beyond existing polymer composites, holding above ninety percent efficiency at both moderate and extreme test temperatures. Electric vehicles, aircraft and deep drilling converters are the target settings.
pmc-13448846:
Chang Liu and a large team ask in 2026 whether nerve damage visible in the cornea can flag patients with diabetes whose feet are at greatest risk. They studied 710 participants across diabetic foot risk categories with foot examinations, microscope scans of corneal nerves, eye surface tests, and tear fluid measurements. Nerve fiber length, density, and branching all worsened as foot risk rose.

Even the lowest-risk patients already showed impaired corneal nerves compared with controls, alongside shorter tear stability and altered tear chemistry. High-risk patients showed the strongest nerve changes. A simple model using nerve fiber length, fiber width, and a blood kidney measure identified high-risk feet with an area under the curve of 0.80. Fiber length below 5.7 millimeters per square millimeter came with over fourfold odds of high-risk status, suggesting eye scans could warn earlier.
pmc-13449146:
Adrian Ybañez and co-authors survey in 2026 what high-risk groups in Cebu, Philippines, know and do about toxoplasmosis, a parasite infection spread largely through cats. They questioned 416 people across three groups with heavy cat contact: cat owners, veterinary students, and veterinary personnel. A subset of 250 also gave blood samples for rapid antibody testing against Toxoplasma gondii.

Students showed the strongest knowledge, with 61 percent rated high, against 46 percent of personnel and 24 percent of owners, and attitudes followed the same order. Daily practice reversed the ranking, with personnel highest at 54 percent. Overall, 29.2 percent of those tested carried antibodies, rising to 43.8 percent among veterinary personnel and 39 percent among cat owners. Testing positive tracked with age, education, medical history, and how often a person handled cats.
pmc-13449346:
Xian and colleagues present a 2026 review arguing that cancer's drug resistance is bounded by development. A tumor's cell of origin, the normal cell it came from, sets limits on which states its cells can reach.

The authors sort resistance into three kinds: cells keep their lineage, cells flip back to an earlier state, or cells settle into a new stable state. Gene-wide tools can spot these flexible states, but only lab tests that try to reverse them prove a state is truly changeable. The team proposes a prime-then-kill plan: first push tumor cells into a state where they are exposed, then strike that state.
pmc-13449446:
Layng and colleagues evaluated in 2026 an electronic consult tracking tool in the emergency department of a large academic hospital. Specialist consults often stall emergency care, but measuring their turnaround is hard with ordinary notes. The team embedded a tracker in the record system to stamp each step, then checked it against manual review of over five thousand consults during a three-month validation.

Layng found the tracker logged a shorter median turnaround than any paperwork stand-in, at about 139 minutes against 179 to 273 minutes for the proxy measures. Over the next year it recorded nearly thirty-five thousand consults across 26 services. Use averaged just over half of consults each month. pmc-13450946:
Tang writes this 2026 editorial, titled The Missing Axis, arguing that gestational diabetes research has a blind spot shaped like a kidney. About 14 percent of pregnancies worldwide involve gestational diabetes, and the condition is known to forecast roughly ten-fold higher type 2 diabetes risk and doubled cardiovascular risk for the mother. Kidney outcomes, Tang notes, have been comparatively ignored.

A history of the condition carried a 46 percent higher adjusted risk of later hospitalized chronic kidney disease. It also carried an 18 percent higher risk of acute kidney injury in the analysis. Risk rose with the number of affected pregnancies. Tang urges that postpartum follow-up add kidney surveillance to the usual glucose and heart watch.
pmc-13452046:
Mukhammad Amonov studies in 2026 a urine protein that may flag kidney harm from high blood pressure years before standard tests stir. The protein, nephrin, slips from the kidney's filter cells when they are hurt. His study enrolled 60 adults in Bukhara, Uzbekistan, split evenly across three pressure stages, with other kidney risks kept out.

Urine nephrin already ran high at the first stage, while the usual blood marks sat normal, and it climbed with each stage. Six months of pressure care cut the protein by about a quarter to a third, with a partial return of kidney reserve. The author offers urine nephrin as an early watch tool for clinics.
pmc-13452146:
Tobar Palacios and colleagues ask in 2026 whether adding a second treatment to steroids improves recovery from severe sudden sensorineural hearing loss. That is hearing that vanishes within days and counts as an ear emergency. In the worst grades of loss, steroids alone rarely restore hearing.

Their systematic review and meta-analysis gathered nine studies of combination therapy, including steroid injections through the eardrum paired with other treatments. Combined approaches consistently outperformed steroid treatment alone on standard hearing tests and on speech discrimination, the ability to understand words. Starting treatment early produced the best auditory outcomes. The authors caution that the studies differed widely and carried a moderate risk of bias. So the apparent advantage, while consistent, awaits confirmation in large randomized trials before it can anchor routine practice.
pmc-13452246:
Gong and co-authors map how brain networks differ between new and long-standing tinnitus in people whose hearing tests normal. Their 2026 study records resting brain waves from 45 participants: fifteen with acute tinnitus under six months, fifteen with chronic tinnitus, and fifteen healthy controls. Two analysis styles were combined: one tracking brief recurring brain states, one tracking fluctuating network connections.

Acute tinnitus tilted the brain toward its salience network, the system that flags important stimuli, while the central executive network participated less, and state transitions skewed toward salience processing. Its executive network also ran with unusual high-frequency efficiency. Chronic tinnitus looked different: transitions had normalised, overall network behaviour was more stable, and efficiency gains appeared instead at low frequencies in executive and auditory networks. The authors frame acute tinnitus as a salience-executive imbalance and chronic tinnitus as compensatory rebalancing, suggesting stage-specific biomarkers.
pmc-13453946:

pmc-13454046:
Patrizia Brunner and seven co-authors profile the users of dibi, a German digital companion app for type 2 diabetes. pmc-13454346:

The effect held while power ranged across a hundredfold span. Because the absorber regulates itself, no sensors or controls were needed. pmc-13454446:
Chengxing Lu and nine colleagues report, in 2026, a binder trick that wakes up plain sulfur, selenium, and tellurium electrodes for sodium batteries. pmc-13455346:

pmc-13456646:

pmc-13456746:

pmc-13456946:

pmc-13457046:

pmc-13457646:

pmc-13459246:

pmc-13459946:

Thickening in the wall's tiny feeder vessels ran about double the rate in cyst free patients. After age and sex adjustment, cysts tracked with elastic fibre thinning at two and a half times the odds. pmc-13460746:

pmc-13461446:

The patient was a 62-year-old man whose left lower leg mass, first noticed in 2023, was removed and read as spindle cell disease. It returned quickly, the type was confirmed, and he had three rounds of chemotherapy, but the disease still advanced.

Yu describes how the leg was amputated in late 2024, yet weeks later he arrived with belly fullness, nausea, and vomiting. Scans and emergency surgery showed spread to stomach and small bowel, where a segment had telescoped into itself, causing blockage. Surgeons removed part of the small bowel, and tissue tests confirmed the spread. The authors blame broken care and urge vigilance for gut symptoms in sarcoma patients.
pmc-13461646:
Dinçer and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how extracellular vesicles, tiny parcels shed by cells, may interact with epigenetic aging clocks, DNA-based gauges that estimate biological age from chemical marks. Skin serves as their main example, since it is easy to reach and study. They propose a feedback loop linking vesicle traffic and clock marks as a testable idea, not a proven pathway, and offer skin as a model for probing it.
pmc-13461746:

Two farm species with similar histories but different social lives and foraging styles make a clean comparison for theories linking self control to ecology. In their 2026 experiment, seven sheep and seven goats faced repeated delay of gratification trials. The team recorded waiting times plus the strategies animals used to endure the wait, such as looking away.

Goats waited somewhat longer on average, 62.9 seconds against 54.3 seconds for sheep, with individuals of both species holding out up to eighty seconds. Both species adjusted decisions to the length of the coming delay and the relative value of rewards rather than waiting blindly. Both also deployed distraction behaviors that raised their success. The modest goat advantage may reflect their dispersed browsing ecology, the authors suggest.
pmc-13461846:
Tomoyo Hamana and colleagues warn, in a 2026 commentary, that a wave of failing tissue valves placed by catheter may arrive in decades. Repeat procedures, once rare rescue work, would then become part of lifelong care for valve narrowing.

In one trial, repeat procedures grew more common after catheter treatment than after surgery by six to seven years, though death and disabling stroke rates matched. Another trial found closer results, with valve failure rates alike between groups, though clotting was more common after catheter treatment. Repeat work after surgery meant removing the old valve, a major operation. The authors urge teams to plan the first valve choice with later fixes in mind and track durability longer.
pmc-13462046:
Fan wrote in 2026 a psychoanalytic essay on traffic anxiety, the distress that online content producers feel over their view counts. Working from Lacanian theory, Fan treats traffic as an ever-escaping object of desire, staged before the algorithmic big Other, the platform system that seems to watch and judge every creator. The essay sorts the theory's terms, separating the object-cause of desire from surplus enjoyment, and two forms of enjoyment from each other.

Fan then sets out five mechanisms behind the anxiety. They cover frustration when emotional investment is blocked, panic when a creator's public identity feels threatened, and anxiety shifting into body symptoms or social blame. Repetition within platform time cycles and failing defences that deepen self-exploitation complete the set. Diary material serves as an illustrative case rather than proof, backed by past studies. Fan argues platforms reorganise desire itself, not only work output.
pmc-13462846:
Lan Wu and colleagues review, in a 2026 article, why children with obstructive sleep apnea rarely join trials. The team searched four databases through February 2026. Twenty-eight studies passed their quality checks.

Barriers sorted into fourteen types across three homes: outside factors, care providers, and patients with caregivers. Strict entry rules led the outside factors. Families refusing follow-up visits, disagreement over treatment, and the child's other health problems were reported often. Provider-linked barriers appeared in fewer studies, yet still shaped who gets asked. The authors list underused fixes: unified trial standards, more attention to parents, and trials designed for children from the start. They warn that advice alone will not close the gap, and they call for formal, targeted recruitment strategies.
pmc-13462946:

pmc-13463046: Tariq and colleagues published a correction in 2026 to their earlier systematic review and meta-analysis comparing a radially adjustable stroke device with standard stent-retrievers. On the Council's agenda, Iraq drew Resolution 1546, adopted unanimously on 8 June 2004. The occupation authority was about to hand power to a sovereign interim government. That handover was set for 30 June 2004. Baghdad had asked the multinational force to stay on.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council endorses the interim government and the timetable that follows. Elections to a transitional assembly are due by January 2005. A permanent constitution and an elected government are to follow by the end of 2005. The force may take all necessary measures to keep security, working in partnership with Baghdad. The UN mission will lead on election advice and national dialogue.
un-sc-res-1646:
A new Peacebuilding Commission was taking shape at the end of 2005. Resolution 1645 had created it that same day, 20 December 2005. This companion text settled the Security Council's seats on its steering body. The Council decided that all five permanent members would sit on the Organizational Committee. Two elected Council members would join them each year. The Council would pick those two annually.

The Commission's yearly report would also go to the Council. The Council would hold an annual debate on it. The body was meant to help countries recover after war. Its steering committee mixed Council, Assembly, and other members. This resolution fixed the Council's share of that mix.
un-sc-res-1746: Resolution 1746, adopted in 2007, is a formal Security Council act kept here in its record text via English Wikisource. Fifteen delegations voted the words that follow in the full document; ten rotating members join the five permanent ones. The entry preserves their joint product whole, ready for citation as S/RES/1746 in UN usage.
un-sc-res-1846:
Piracy off Somalia occupied the Council on 2 December 2008, when it adopted Resolution 1846 on Piracy off Somalia. Growing ransom payments were fueling more attacks. Somalia's government could not patrol its own waters or guard the sea lanes. Many states and the European Union had sent warships to escort food aid convoys.

The Council renews the anti-piracy powers for twelve more months. States working with Somalia's government may enter its waters to stop piracy. They may use all necessary means there, as the law of the sea allows on the high seas. Pirate boats and gear may be seized. States should share news of attacks, help coastal states build patrol strength, and work together on trials for captured pirates.
un-sc-res-1946:
Côte d'Ivoire's sanctions were renewed on 15 October 2010, weeks before a long-delayed presidential vote. The voters list had been certified, and the first round was set for 31 October 2010 under the Ouagadougou Political Agreement. The Council noted the expert group's reports on the arms embargo. It also recorded continuing abuses against civilians, including sexual violence, despite a better overall human rights picture.

The Council renewed the arms, finance, and travel measures of resolution 1572 (2004) and the diamond ban of resolution 1643 (2005) to 30 April 2011. It promised a review tied to progress in the elections and the peace process. Ivorian parties and all states had to apply the measures in full and give inspectors free access. The Council underlined that it was ready to impose targeted measures on persons named by its committee. It also flagged media reports inciting violence and a return to civil war.
un-sc-res-246:
South Africa's trial of South West African detainees drew censure from the Security Council on 14 March 1968. Resolution 245 (1968) had ordered Pretoria to stop the illegal trial and free the men. The General Assembly had ended South Africa's mandate over the territory in 1966 and taken direct responsibility for it. South Africa refused to comply and went on with the trial and sentencing.

The Council censured South Africa for flagrant defiance of resolution 245 and of the United Nations itself. It demanded that the South West Africans be released and sent home at once. Member states were called to help the Council give the resolution effect. The Council warned it would meet again to weigh further steps if South Africa still refused. The text treats the trial as an illegal act against people under direct United Nations responsibility.
un-sc-res-346: Resolution 346 stands in the official record of the United Nations Security Council, catalogued here with a 1974 date. Such texts can call for cease-fires, set up missions, impose duties, or settle points of UN procedure and membership. Its value lies in the primary wording: the decision as adopted, kept through the Wikisource transcription of the record. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-446:
Israeli settlements are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 446, adopted on 22 March 1979 by twelve votes to none, with three abstentions. Jordan had brought the matter to the Council. Building had spread across land taken in the 1967 war, including Jerusalem. The Council saw the growth of settlements as a block to peace.

The Council holds that the settlement policy and practice have no legal validity. It says the Fourth Geneva Convention of 1949 covers the occupied Arab lands. Israel must undo past steps and change nothing in the lands' status or makeup. Moving its own civilians into those lands must stop. A three-member panel will study the settlements and report by 1 July 1979.
un-sc-res-46:
Fighting between Arabs and Jews in Palestine brought a truce call from the Security Council on 17 April 1948. Resolution 43 (1948) had opened talks with the Jewish Agency and the Arab Higher Committee. Britain, as the Mandatory Power, still bore responsibility for peace and order. The Council said an immediate halt to the violence was of the utmost urgency.

The Council called on all persons and groups in Palestine to cease military and paramilitary action, violence, terrorism, and sabotage. No armed bands or fighters were to enter Palestine, and no weapons were to be brought in or bought. Both sides had to avoid political acts that might prejudice the other community's claims while the General Assembly weighed Palestine's future government. They were told to cooperate with the Mandatory authorities on law, order, transport, health, and food and water supplies, and to keep the Holy Places safe and open.
un-sc-res-746:
Somalia's famine and fighting drew the Security Council's first steps toward intervention on 17 March 1992. Cease-fire agreements had been signed at Mogadishu on 3 March, with a United Nations monitoring mission in view. The factions had not kept the truce, and aid still could not reach people in need. The Secretary-General had reported on 11 March on the scale of the suffering.

The Council urged the Somali factions to honor the Mogadishu cease-fire at once. All factions were told to work with the Secretary-General and clear the way for aid delivery. He was asked to press his humanitarian effort with every resource he had. Member states and aid groups were appealed to for contributions. The Council backed his decision to send a technical team to Somalia at once. The team would also plan safe aid delivery. All parties had to protect aid staff.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Security Council resolution 1046, adopted on 13 February 1996, adjusts UNPREDEP, the United Nations Preventive Deployment Force in the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia. Its mandate ran to 30 May 1996. The Council authorizes 50 more military personnel, so the force can keep its engineering work going. It backs the creation of a Force Commander position. It asks the Secretary-General for fresh advice on the makeup, strength and mandate by 20 May 1996.

Sierra Leone's fragile ceasefire frames Resolution 1346, adopted on 30 March 2001. Fighting ran along the borders with Guinea and Liberia, and refugees faced grave hardship. The UN Mission in Sierra Leone, UNAMSIL, was growing under a revised plan. The Council deplored abuses by the Revolutionary United Front, including forced recruitment of adults and children, and said the Abuja Ceasefire Agreement was not being kept in full.

The Council extends UNAMSIL for six months and raises its military strength to 17,500, including 260 observers already in place. It demands that the RUF free UN movement across the country, return seized weapons and gear, and rejoin the disarmament program. It urges the government to restore civil services across its land and pushes for quick setup of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission and the Special Court planned under Resolution 1315.

Rough diamonds from Sierra Leone stay banned for six more months under this text of 4 December 2002. Illegal diamond trading had helped fuel the country's civil war. Though the war had ended and security had improved, large volumes of diamonds still moved outside government control.

The measures stay in force from 5 December 2002, with one standing exception. Rough diamonds certified under the government's Certificate of Origin regime remain exempt from the ban. At the end of the period the Council would review the situation, including how far government authority reached over the diamond areas, before deciding whether to extend or change the measures.

Katanga's split from Congo pushed the young UN to a hard call. The rich province had broken away in July 1960. Belgian troops still stood on its soil. UN men had been kept out of Katanga though they stood ready to go in. The chief's new report told the tale. Resolution 146 passed on 9 August 1960 by nine votes to none. France and Italy held back.

Belgium had to pull its troops out of Katanga at once. The chief would set the pace and the way. The UN force's entry to Katanga was ruled a must. One guard rail was set down with care. The force would not take sides in Congo's own fights. It would not tip the scales of any home clash. All states were told to back the Council's word in full.

Resolution 1546 was adopted by the Security Council on 8 June 2004. It endorsed Iraq's return to full sovereignty after the occupation period. It welcomed the new Interim Government of Iraq, which was to take full authority on 30 June 2004. It also backed a set timetable toward elections and a permanent constitution.

The resolution gave the United Nations Assistance Mission for Iraq, known as UNAMI, a leading role in helping Iraq. UNAMI was to help with a national conference, elections, and talks on a constitution. The resolution also kept the multinational force in Iraq, at the new government's request, with power to act for security. It set that mandate to end once the political transition was complete.

A new UN body took shape at the end of 2005. The Peacebuilding Commission would help states heal after wars. It was born the same week as its twin text, Resolution 1645. Resolution 1646, passed on 20 December 2005, set the Council's own stake in the new body.

The five veto powers would sit on the steering group as of right. The Council would also pick two of its rotating members each year. Those picks would join the same group. One more rule was set. The body's yearly report would come to the Council too. Members would debate it once a year. The text is short and dry. It still fixed the Council's seat at the table of the UN's newest organ.

Afghanistan's assistance mission, UNAMA, is extended for a further year on 23 March 2007. The Afghanistan Compact, endorsed in 2006, set the shared plan for the country's security, governance, and development. A Council mission had visited Afghanistan in November 2006, and its report fed into this renewal.

UNAMA's mandate stays as laid out the year before, covering political support, human rights, aid coordination, and counternarcotics. Afghan parties are called on to join an inclusive political process, and the government to press ahead with reform, justice, and the fight against the drug trade. All sides are told to respect humanitarian law and protect aid workers, and donors are urged to deliver on their pledges.

Piracy off Somalia is fought at sea under Resolution 1846, adopted on 2 December 2008. Attacks threatened aid deliveries and shipping lanes. The Monitoring Group found escalating ransom payments were fuelling more piracy. Somalia's Transitional Federal Government asked for the Resolution 1816 (2008) powers to be renewed. The EU was about to launch a 12-month naval operation protecting World Food Programme convoys.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council decides that for 12 months, states and regional organizations cooperating with the Somali government may enter Somalia's territorial waters. They must have its consent, notified in advance. They may use all necessary means there to repress piracy and armed robbery, as international law allows on the high seas. It urges naval deployments, seizure of pirate boats and equipment, shared information, and cooperation on jurisdiction and prosecution. The authorization is limited to Somalia and sets no precedent in customary law.

Resolution 1946, adopted on 15 October 2010, renews the sanctions regime on Côte d'Ivoire on the eve of a long-delayed presidential vote. An arms embargo, a ban on rough diamond exports, and targeted travel and financial measures had been in place since 2004 and 2005. Experts monitoring the regime had reported in 2009 and 2010, and a certified voters list was finally ready.

The Council kept the measures in force and extended the mandate of the experts group, judging that sanctions still supported the peace process as the first-round election approached on 31 October. It pressed Ivorian leaders to hold the vote on schedule, in open and fair conditions. Weeks later the disputed result plunged the country into crisis anyway.

Namibians seized and tried by South Africa are the cause taken up in Resolution 246, passed by a full vote on 14 March 1968. Pretoria had seized men from South West Africa and tried them under its own laws. Yet the Assembly had ended South Africa's mandate in 1966. The UN had taken charge of the land on paper. A vote in January had told South Africa to stop the trial.

South Africa did not stop. The Council voiced its distress at this defiance. It treated the arrests, the trial, and the jail terms as unlawful acts. It pressed for the men to be freed and sent home. The case became proof of the UN claim that Namibia was not South Africa's to rule.

The buffer force between Egypt and Israel was reviewed by the Council in the spring of 1974. The United Nations Emergency Force had been set up after the October war of 1973. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 1 April 1974, held that the force was still required. Resolution 346 was adopted on 8 April 1974.

The Council thanked the states that had sent troops to the force. It also thanked those that had given money and material. The force was praised for its contribution to the search for a just and durable peace. The Council noted a shared view about the recent disengagement of forces. Pulling Egyptian and Israeli troops apart was only a first step toward a settlement. The plan to keep the force's size under review was welcomed, so it could be cut when conditions allowed.

Few Council texts on the Middle East are quoted as often as Resolution 446. It was adopted on 22 March 1979 by twelve votes to none. Norway, Britain, and the United States abstained. Jordan's ambassador had just addressed the members about Israeli settlements in occupied Arab land.

The Council ruled that building those settlements had no legal validity. It called them a serious block to a just and lasting peace. It said the Fourth Geneva Convention covers the territories taken in 1967, including Jerusalem. Israel was told to stop moving its own civilians into them. A three-member commission was created to inspect the settlement situation and report by 1 July 1979.

Resolution 46, adopted on 17 April 1948 by nine votes to none with two abstentions, tries to arrange a truce in Palestine. Britain still held the Mandate and was responsible for order, while fighting between Arab and Jewish forces was growing. The Council had already called for a truce two weeks earlier and now set out concrete measures.

All groups in Palestine were called on to stop military and paramilitary activity, violence, terrorism, and sabotage at once. Armed bands and fighters were not to be brought in from outside. The text pressed both leadership bodies in particular, the Arab side's Higher Committee and the Jewish Agency, to cooperate. The step was meant to guard the country's future while its political fate stayed undecided.

On 17 March 1992 the Council passed Resolution 746 by a full vote. It backs a truce in Somalia that was fraying at the edges. The warring clans had signed a ceasefire pact in Mogadishu on 3 March. It let a UN team watch the truce on the ground. A UN report of 11 March warned that the clans had not kept their word. Aid could not reach the starving in safety.

The Council deplored the broken pledge and the scale of the pain the war caused. It backed the UN chief's plans for help. A small team would go first to work out a watch force. Aid flights and food convoys would grow. In a month the Council set up its first Somalia force.
witches-of-huntingdon-1646:
Justices take down witch tales in The Witches of Huntingdon, a brief tract of 1646. In the shire town and its fields, poor folk were charged with pacts with the Devil, who, the tales say, tempts poor souls with coin, food, and ease. The tract prints the quizzes and words of guilt as the justices of the peace took them in the midst of the great war time hunt in the east.

Names, dates, and small grim facts crowd the pages. No scribe shapes them to a tale. The tract is the hunt's raw paper trail. Its plain, prim tone is its worth.
zoist-vol-04-1846:
The Zoist's fourth volume runs from April 1846 to January 1847. Elliotson's journal of mesmerism and cerebral physiology keeps its presses hot. Painless operations under mesmeric trance still headline the case lists. Ether, newly arrived in surgery, begins to shadow the journal's cause in these years.

Reports of clairvoyant somnambulists mix with sober hospital notes. Elliotson defends his methods against a hostile medical establishment. The movement's record grows volume by volume toward thirteen in all. Volume four catches mesmerism at a turning point in its fortunes. Anaesthesia by gas would soon steal its surgical crown. The pages hold the moment before that fall.
